**Change gate:** This document was produced by the multi-agent pipeline and is subject to the human review gate. It is a research and implementation reference, **not legal advice**. It covers **two regimes in parallel** — the EU GDPR and the UK GDPR — which have **diverged** on subject access since the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18)** commenced its data-protection provisions on **5 February 2026**. Where the UK position now differs (reasonable-and-proportionate searches; "stop-the-clock"; the legal-professional-privilege exemption), the divergence is flagged inline. Confirm the in-force status of any specific UK provision before relying on it [3][4][5][7].

legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (Arts. 12–23); Data Protection Act 2018; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18)

text:
Chapter III of the GDPR (Articles 12–23) confers the **data-subject rights** and sets the **modalities** by which controllers must honour them: transparency (Art. 12), the information duties (Arts. 13–14), the **right of access / DSAR** (Art. 15), rectification (Art. 16), **erasure / the "right to be forgotten"** (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), notification (Art. 19), **portability** (Art. 20), **objection** (Art. 21) and rights around **solely automated decisions and profiling** (Art. 22) [1]. This document details the Chapter III material introduced at foundation level in `gdpr-foundations` and adds a practical DSAR-handling workflow.

The **right of access** dominates operational compliance. On a valid request a controller must confirm whether it processes the individual's data and, if so, provide a **copy** of that data plus prescribed information (purposes, categories, recipients, retention, source, the existence of other rights, and whether solely automated decision-making occurs) — normally **within one month**, extendable by **two further months** for complex or numerous requests, and generally **free of charge** [1][18]. The Court of Justice has read the right broadly: the identity of **specific recipients** must be disclosed on request (C-154/21) [11]; "copy" means a **faithful reproduction** that may require document extracts (C-487/21) [12]; and a first copy of medical records is **free**, the requester's **motive irrelevant** (C-307/22) [13].

The **UK regime has diverged**. The **DUAA 2025** amended UK GDPR Article 15 to confirm controllers need only conduct a **"reasonable and proportionate" search** (new Art. 15(1A), s.78) [5], and amended Article 12 to insert **Article 12A** — a **"stop-the-clock"** rule under which the response period does not run while the controller awaits **identity confirmation, a fee, or reasonably-required clarification** (s.76) [4]. These provisions commenced on **5 February 2026** (SI 2026/82) [7]. The intended audience is DPOs, legal, privacy-engineering and support teams who operate rights processes across the EU and the UK. Three conclusions dominate: rights are **modality-bound** (how you respond is itself an obligation); the right of access is **broad but bounded** by others' rights and by the UK's new proportionality test; and **automated decision-making** (Art. 22) is now the sharpest EU–UK fault line (contrast `duaa-2025-detail`).

text:
- Chapter III rights must be facilitated **transparently and without undue delay**; Art. 12 sets the modalities (concise, intelligible, plain language; normally free; normally one month) that apply to **all** the rights [1][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **right of access (Art. 15)** requires confirmation of processing, a **copy** of the personal data, and eight categories of supplementary information; the copy of the first request is **free** and due **within one month** (extendable by two months) [1][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- A controller may refuse or charge for requests that are **manifestly unfounded or excessive**, and **bears the burden** of demonstrating that character (Art. 12(5)) [1][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The CJEU construes access broadly: **specific recipients** must be named on request (C-154/21) [11]; **"copy"** can require reproductions of documents (C-487/21) [12]; a first medical-records copy is **free** and the **motive is irrelevant** (C-307/22) [13]. *(Case law.)*
- **Erasure (Art. 17)** — the "right to be forgotten" — is **not absolute**; it applies on defined grounds and is subject to exceptions (freedom of expression, legal obligation, public-interest, legal claims). Its origin is **Google Spain (C-131/12)**; de-referencing is generally **EU-wide, not global** (C-507/17) [8][16]. *(Legal obligation / case law.)*
- The **objection right (Art. 21)** to direct marketing is **absolute** — once exercised, the controller must stop; for other processing the controller may continue only on **compelling legitimate grounds** [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect (Art. 22)** are prohibited unless an exception applies, with safeguards; automated **credit scoring** can itself be a "decision" (C-634/21 SCHUFA) [14]. *(Legal obligation / case law.)*
- **UK divergence (DUAA 2025, in force 5 Feb 2026):** searches need only be **reasonable and proportionate** (Art. 15(1A), s.78) [5][7]; the clock **stops** pending identity/fee/clarification (Art. 12A, s.76) [4][7]; and a new **legal-professional-privilege exemption** (s.79) applies [6]. *(Legal obligation — UK; live-verified.)*

text:
This document is the DSAR / data-subject-rights sub-topic deep-dive. It supports:

- **Legal research** — a mapped index of Chapter III rights, anchor CJEU case law, and the corresponding UK modifications.
- **Compliance implementation** — a repeatable DSAR-handling workflow, exemption analysis, and a checklist teams can operate under both regimes.
- **Developer / support enablement** — plain-language framing of what "confirm, copy, inform" means and how identity verification, third-party redaction and the one-month clock work in practice.

It **details** `gdpr-foundations` (which introduces Arts. 12–23 at overview level) and cross-references `duaa-2025-detail` for the full UK reform picture (recognised legitimate interests, Arts. 22A–22D, PECR). It does **not** restate the GDPR's scope, principles or lawful bases (see `gdpr-foundations`), nor the UK's constitutional/adequacy position (see `uk-gdpr-foundations`).

text:
**In scope:** Chapter III of the GDPR — transparency and modalities (Art. 12); the information duties (Arts. 13–14); the right of access / DSAR (Art. 15), including the deadline, the two-month extension, manifestly-unfounded/excessive requests, identity verification, third-party data and exemptions; rectification (Art. 16); erasure (Art. 17); restriction (Art. 18); notification (Art. 19); portability (Art. 20); objection (Art. 21) including direct marketing; automated individual decision-making and profiling (Art. 22); restrictions (Art. 23); the corresponding **UK GDPR / DUAA 2025** modifications; and a practical DSAR workflow and checklist.

**Out of scope (cross-referenced):** The GDPR's principles and lawful bases → `gdpr-foundations`; the full UK reform (recognised legitimate interests, Arts. 22A–22D detail, complaints duty, PECR) → `duaa-2025-detail` and `uk-gdpr-foundations`; international transfers (Chapter V) → `gdpr-transfers` / `uk-transfers`; DPIAs (Art. 35) → `dpia-methodology`. **DPA 2018 exemptions** (Schedules 2–4) are summarised, not exhaustively reproduced. Law-enforcement/intelligence-services access rights (DPA 2018 Parts 3–4) are noted only where the DUAA touched them.

**Assumptions:** The reader has read `gdpr-foundations` and, for UK-specific points, `uk-gdpr-foundations` / `duaa-2025-detail`. Article references are to the consolidated EU GDPR unless the text says "UK GDPR" [1]. UK provisions reflect the position on the `sources_verified` date, after DUAA commencement on 5 February 2026 [7].

*Shared terms (personal data, controller, processor, consent, special-category data) are in `GLOSSARY.md` and carry over. Only terms specific to this document are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Data-subject access request (DSAR / SAR) | A request by which a data subject exercises the Art. 15 right of access to obtain confirmation of processing, a copy of their personal data, and prescribed information. | [1][18] |
| Right to be forgotten | Shorthand for the right to erasure (Art. 17), originating in the CJEU's de-referencing case law (Google Spain). | [1][8] |
| Manifestly unfounded or excessive | The Art. 12(5) threshold at which a controller may charge a reasonable fee or refuse to act; the controller bears the burden of proof. | [1][18] |
| Solely automated decision | A decision based solely on automated processing (no meaningful human involvement) producing legal or similarly significant effects (Art. 22(1)). | [1][14] |
| Reasonable and proportionate search | The **UK-only** standard (UK GDPR Art. 15(1A), inserted by DUAA s.78) confining the access duty to what a proportionate search yields. | [5] |
| Stop-the-clock | The **UK-only** rule (UK GDPR Art. 12A, inserted by DUAA s.76) under which the response period does not run while the controller awaits identity confirmation, a fee, or reasonably-required clarification. | [4] |

text:
Rights of access, rectification and objection existed under **Directive 95/46/EC**, but the GDPR strengthened and expanded them: it added the rights to **erasure** (codifying Google Spain), **restriction**, **portability**, and reinforced rules on **automated decision-making**, while imposing hard **modalities** — deadlines, plain-language transparency, and (as a default) no charge [1]. The animating idea is **control**: individuals should be able to see, correct, move, limit and stop processing of their data, and to understand automated decisions taken about them.

Because much of this built on the Directive, foundational case law (Google Spain; YS and Others; Nowak, C-434/16 — confirming exam scripts and examiner comments are personal data accessible under the right) decided under the old regime remains authoritative for the equivalent GDPR concepts [8][9][10]. Since 2018 the CJEU has issued a steady line of access judgments (C-154/21, C-487/21, C-307/22, C-634/21) that flesh out what "copy", "recipients", "free" and "decision" mean in practice [11][12][13][14].

The **UK** retained Chapter III on withdrawal from the EU (as the "UK GDPR", read with the DPA 2018), then began to edit it. The **DUAA 2025** made the first substantive changes to subject access — codifying the ICO's long-standing "reasonable and proportionate search" position and adding a statutory "stop-the-clock" — most of which commenced on **5 February 2026** [3][5][7]. This is the principal EU–UK divergence for day-to-day rights handling.

text:
Chapter III is structured in five sections: **general modalities** (Art. 12), **information to be provided** (Arts. 13–14), **access, rectification and erasure** (Arts. 15–17 plus restriction 18, notification 19, portability 20), the **right to object and automated decisions** (Arts. 21–22), and **restrictions** (Art. 23) [1]. Two framing points govern the whole chapter. First, Article 12 is the **operating system** for every right: it fixes how requests are received, verified, timed, priced and answered. Second, most rights are **conditional** — they bite only in defined circumstances and yield to defined exceptions; only the objection to **direct marketing** (Art. 21(3)) is effectively absolute [1].

Distinguish throughout: **OBLIGATION** (what the law requires), **REGULATORY INTERPRETATION** (EDPB/ICO reading), **BEST PRACTICE** (standards/consensus), and **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (this pipeline's suggestion).

## Relevant Articles

*"Article" is the EU GDPR article unless marked "UK GDPR". UK modifications made by the DUAA 2025 are listed in the final rows.*

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 12(1)–(2) | Transparency & facilitation — information and communications must be concise, transparent, intelligible, in plain language; controllers must **facilitate** the exercise of rights. | [1] |
| Art. 12(3) | Respond **without undue delay** and **within one month**; extendable by **two further months** for complex/numerous requests (notify within the first month). | [1] |
| Art. 12(4) | If not acting, inform the data subject without delay and at latest within one month, with reasons and the right to complain / seek a remedy. | [1] |
| Art. 12(5) | Requests are normally **free**; where **manifestly unfounded or excessive**, the controller may charge a reasonable fee or refuse — and **bears the burden** of proving that character. | [1] |
| Art. 12(6) | Where there are reasonable doubts about identity, the controller may request additional information to confirm it. | [1] |
| Arts. 13–14 | Information duties — what must be told to data subjects when data is collected from them (13) or obtained otherwise (14), including purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention and rights. | [1] |
| Art. 15(1)–(2) | **Right of access** — confirmation of processing; access to the data; and information on purposes, categories, recipients, retention, rights, source, and automated decision-making (incl. meaningful information about the logic, significance and consequences). | [1] |
| Art. 15(3) | Provide a **copy** of the personal data undergoing processing; further copies may attract a reasonable fee. | [1] |
| Art. 15(4) | The right to obtain a copy must **not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others** (basis for third-party redaction). | [1] |
| Art. 16 | **Rectification** — correct inaccurate data and complete incomplete data without undue delay. | [1] |
| Art. 17 | **Erasure / right to be forgotten** — erase on defined grounds, subject to exceptions; if data was made public, take reasonable steps to inform other controllers. | [1] |
| Art. 18 | **Restriction of processing** — a "freeze" in defined situations (e.g. accuracy contested, processing unlawful, pending an objection). | [1] |
| Art. 19 | **Notification obligation** — communicate rectification/erasure/restriction to each recipient, unless impossible/disproportionate. | [1] |
| Art. 20 | **Data portability** — receive data provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and transmit it, where processing is by consent/contract **and** carried out by automated means. | [1] |
| Art. 21 | **Right to object** — object to processing based on public-task/legitimate-interests (controller must stop unless compelling legitimate grounds); the objection to **direct marketing (21(2)–(3))** is absolute. | [1] |
| Art. 22 | **Automated individual decision-making** — right not to be subject to a **solely** automated decision with legal/similarly significant effects, save exceptions (contract, law, explicit consent) with safeguards; special-category limits. | [1][14] |
| Art. 23 | **Restrictions** — Union/Member State law may restrict these rights for defined objectives (national security, crime prevention, etc.), subject to safeguards. | [1] |
| UK GDPR Art. 12A (DUAA s.76) | **UK — "stop-the-clock":** the "applicable time period" runs from the latest of request receipt, receipt of identity confirmation / requested information, or fee payment; time awaiting **reasonably-required clarification** does not count. | [3][4] |
| UK GDPR Art. 15(1A) (DUAA s.78) | **UK — reasonable-and-proportionate search:** the data subject is entitled only to what the controller can provide **based on a reasonable and proportionate search**. | [3][5] |
| DPA 2018 s.45A (DUAA s.79) | **UK — legal-professional-privilege exemption** from the access right, with a duty (subject to the privilege) to notify the data subject of reliance and their rights. | [3][6] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are interpretive aids, not binding operative provisions [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 59 | Modalities should facilitate the exercise of rights, including means for requests to be made electronically and free of charge. | [1] |
| Recital 63 | The access right lets a data subject be aware of, and verify, the lawfulness of processing; where a controller processes a **large quantity** of information, it may ask the subject to **specify** the request. | [1] |
| Recital 64 | Controllers should use all reasonable measures to **verify identity**, especially for online services. | [1] |
| Recital 65 | Basis of the right to erasure / right to be forgotten, and its limits where processing is necessary (e.g. freedom of expression, legal obligations, public interest). | [1] |
| Recital 66 | In the online environment, a controller that made data public should inform other controllers processing it of an erasure request. | [1] |
| Recital 68 | Basis of the portability right; it should not adversely affect the rights of others. | [1] |
| Recital 69–70 | Basis of the objection right; direct-marketing objection should be brought explicitly to the data subject's attention and offered free of charge. | [1] |
| Recital 71 | Automated decision-making/profiling should carry safeguards — the right to human intervention, to express a view, and to contest the decision. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Google Spain SL v AEPD & Costeja González | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-131/12, ECLI:EU:C:2014:317 | Search-engine indexing is "processing"; individuals may require de-listing of results — the "right to be forgotten". | Origin of Art. 17 erasure/de-referencing [8]. |
| YS and Others | CJEU, C-141/12 & C-372/12, ECLI:EU:C:2014:2081 | The access right covers personal data in a legal analysis but **not the legal analysis itself**. | Bounds the scope of "personal data" disclosable under Art. 15 [10]. |
| Österreichische Post (RW) | CJEU (Third Chamber), C-154/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:3 | Under Art. 15(1)(c) the data subject may require the **actual identity of recipients**, not merely categories, unless identifying them is impossible or the request is manifestly unfounded/excessive. | Sets the default: name recipients on request [11]. |
| Österreichische Datenschutzbehörde & CRIF | CJEU (First Chamber), C-487/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:369 | "Copy" means a **faithful and intelligible reproduction**; providing extracts of documents (or whole documents) is required where indispensable to enable effective exercise of rights. | Defines the "copy" deliverable under Art. 15(3) [12]. |
| FT v DW (medical records) | CJEU (First Chamber), C-307/22, ECLI:EU:C:2023:811 | A patient is entitled to a **first copy of medical records free of charge**; the **motive** for the request is irrelevant. | Confirms "free first copy" and motive-neutrality [13]. |
| SCHUFA Holding (automated credit scoring) | CJEU (First Chamber), C-634/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:957 | Automated establishment of a **credit score** that third parties draw strongly upon is itself a "decision" within Art. 22(1). | Extends Art. 22 to upstream scoring [14]. |
| GC and Others v CNIL | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-136/17, ECLI:EU:C:2019:773 | De-referencing of **special-category** data requires balancing rights; a stricter test applies. | Refines erasure/de-referencing for sensitive data [15]. |
| Google LLC v CNIL | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-507/17, ECLI:EU:C:2019:772 | A de-referencing order generally applies **EU-wide, not globally**. | Territorial limit of the right to be forgotten [16]. |
| TU and RE v Google | CJEU (Fourth Chamber), C-460/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:962 | A search engine must de-reference where the requester shows the indexed content is **manifestly inaccurate**. | Practical trigger for de-listing [17]. |

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).** The authoritative readings are the **EDPB Guidelines 01/2022 on the right of access** (adopted final in 2023) and, in the UK, the **ICO** right-of-access and DUAA guidance; the ICO's **individual-rights hub** gives per-right operational guidance across all of Chapter III [18][19][21][23].

- **Facilitation is the default posture.** The EDPB stresses that controllers should make rights **easy to exercise**, apply a **generous** reading of ambiguous requests, and not use identity checks or clarification as friction; a request need not mention "Article 15" or use any form [18]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **"Manifestly unfounded or excessive" is a high bar.** The EDPB and ICO treat refusal/charging as **exceptional**, assessed case-by-case, with the **controller bearing the burden**; a request is not excessive merely because it is broad or the data voluminous [18][19]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
- **Clarification does not reset the clock (EU).** Under the EU GDPR, seeking clarification does **not** automatically pause the one-month period; the EDPB permits narrowing only where the controller genuinely processes a large quantity of data and asks the subject to specify (Recital 63), and even then time generally continues to run [1][18]. *(Regulatory interpretation — contrast the UK "stop-the-clock" below.)*
- **UK — "reasonable and proportionate" and "stop-the-clock".** The ICO has **updated its right-of-access guidance** to reflect the DUAA: controllers must make a **reasonable and proportionate** search (not an exhaustive one), and may **pause the response period** where they reasonably require identity confirmation, a fee, or clarification of scope — informing the requester promptly [19][21]. GOV.UK frames these as **codifying existing ICO practice** rather than lowering the substance of the right [22]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a UK legal obligation.)*
- **Automated decisions must be explained.** For Art. 22, the EDPB expects **meaningful information about the logic** and real safeguards (human review, the ability to contest); SCHUFA confirms scoring can trigger these duties upstream [14][18]. The **UK diverges** here — DUAA Arts. 22A–22D move to a permission-plus-safeguards model (see `duaa-2025-detail`) [21]. *(Regulatory interpretation; divergence.)*

text:
- **Data discovery / retrieval.** Honouring Art. 15 requires the ability to **locate all personal data** about an individual across production stores, backups, logs, email, ticketing and third-party processors. A **data map / RoPA** and identity-to-record linking are prerequisites; without them, one-month compliance is unrealistic. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Identity verification.** Build proportionate identity checks (Art. 12(6)/Recital 64) — stronger for sensitive datasets, lighter for low-risk — avoiding **over-collection** of new identity data purely to answer a request. In the **UK**, the response clock does not start until identity is confirmed (Art. 12A) [4]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Third-party redaction (Art. 15(4)).** Access must not adversely affect others' rights; implement **redaction/pseudonymisation** of third-party personal data in exported material, with a documented balancing decision rather than blanket withholding [1][18]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **Copy production (C-487/21).** The deliverable is a **faithful, intelligible reproduction** — often structured exports plus, where necessary, extracts or whole documents; plain data dumps that the subject cannot understand may not satisfy the right [12]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Portability tooling (Art. 20).** Provide **structured, machine-readable** exports (e.g. JSON/CSV) for consent-/contract-based, automated processing; where feasible, support **direct controller-to-controller** transmission [1][20]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **Rectification, erasure & restriction propagation (Arts. 16–19).** Changes must **cascade** to backups, replicas, caches, search indexes and downstream processors; implement suppression lists for erasure/objection so data is not re-ingested. Art. 19 notification to recipients should be automatable. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **UK proportionality (Art. 15(1A)).** Record what a **reasonable and proportionate** search covered and why certain systems were out of scope — the burden to justify proportionality still sits with the controller [5][19]. *(Legal obligation — UK.)*

text:
- **Processor assistance (Art. 28(3)(e)).** Hosting providers and SaaS processors must, by contract, **assist** the controller in responding to rights requests. Confirm the DPA obliges the processor to surface, export and delete personal data on instruction, within timeframes that let the controller meet the one-month deadline. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Backups and immutability.** Erasure/rectification interacts awkwardly with immutable/WORM backups and long-retention object storage; document a **backup-cycle erasure policy** (suppress on restore; delete on next cycle) as the ICO/EDPB accept where immediate backup deletion is not feasible. *(Best practice.)*
- **Data location for retrieval.** Multi-region hosting and sharding complicate "find all data about X"; maintain an index of **where** a subject's data resides. Cross-border storage also engages Chapter V (see `gdpr-transfers`). *(Best practice.)*
- **Log and telemetry stores.** Access and erasure requests reach into logs, analytics and security telemetry that often hold identifiers (IP, device, account IDs); scope these into DSAR tooling and retention/erasure workflows. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*

text:
- **Player DSARs at scale.** Games generate high-volume, cross-service player data (accounts, telemetry, chat, purchases, anti-cheat, matchmaking). Build **self-service export/deletion** where possible; the UK **reasonable-and-proportionate** standard helps bound searches across sprawling telemetry, but the search rationale must be documented [5][19]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **Children's requests.** Requests may come from or concern **children**; verify who is entitled to exercise the right (child vs. parent), apply age-appropriate, plain-language communication (Art. 12), and take special care over third-party data in shared social/chat features [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Objection to marketing / profiling.** In-game and cross-game **direct marketing** attracts the absolute objection right (Art. 21(3)); personalisation/ad profiling engages Art. 21(1) and, where consequential, Art. 22 [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Automated bans / moderation.** Solely automated **account bans, restrictions or matchmaking penalties** with significant effect can engage Art. 22 (EU) — provide human review and a contest route; note the **UK's** Arts. 22A–22D shift the analysis (see `duaa-2025-detail`) [14][21]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
- **Access to profiling and ADM logic (Art. 15(1)(h)).** Where AI/ML makes solely automated significant decisions, the access right includes **meaningful information about the logic involved** and the significance/consequences — a live explainability requirement for model-driven decisions [1][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Scoring as a "decision" (SCHUFA, C-634/21).** An AI-generated **score** that others rely on can itself be an Art. 22 "decision", pulling upstream models into the safeguards regime [14]. *(Case law / legal obligation.)*
- **Training data and erasure.** Erasure/objection requests interact with models **trained on** personal data; suppression at the data layer is straightforward, but removing influence from trained weights is not — treat retraining/unlearning as an open risk and minimise personal data in training sets. *(Best practice / editorial recommendation.)*
- **Access requests against AI systems.** DSARs may seek inputs, outputs, inferences and derived data; **inferred data** about an identifiable person is personal data and in scope, subject to third-party-rights and trade-secret balancing [1][12]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **EU–UK ADM divergence.** The EU Art. 22 prohibition-plus-exceptions model contrasts with the UK **Arts. 22A–22D** permission-plus-safeguards model — AI decisions about UK vs. EU subjects may need **different controls** (detailed in `duaa-2025-detail`) [21]. *(Editorial note / divergence.)*

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**. A practical **DSAR workflow** follows.

1. **Recognise and log the request.** Any channel counts (email, phone, in-app, verbally); a request need not cite Article 15. Record receipt date and route it to the rights process. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][18]
2. **Verify identity (proportionately).** Confirm the requester's identity using data you already hold where possible; escalate checks only for sensitive datasets (Art. 12(6)/Recital 64). **UK:** the clock does not start until identity is confirmed (Art. 12A). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][4]
3. **Clarify scope where genuinely needed.** For large data volumes, you may ask the subject to specify (Recital 63). **EU:** time generally keeps running. **UK:** the clock **stops** while awaiting reasonably-required clarification (Art. 12A). *(OBLIGATION / interpretation.)* [1][4][19]
4. **Start (or re-start) the clock.** Respond **without undue delay** and within **one month**; extend by **two months** for complex/numerous requests, notifying within the first month with reasons (Art. 12(3)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **Search — proportionately.** Search the systems where the subject's data is reasonably likely to be. **UK:** the duty is expressly a **reasonable and proportionate** search (Art. 15(1A)); document scope and exclusions. *(OBLIGATION.)* [5][19]
6. **Assess exemptions.** Apply relevant DPA 2018 exemptions (e.g. crime, legal privilege, management forecasting, negotiations); **UK:** the DUAA added a **legal-professional-privilege** exemption (DPA 2018 s.45A, s.79). Record the basis for each withheld item. *(OBLIGATION.)* [2][6]
7. **Redact third-party data (Art. 15(4)).** Balance others' rights; redact or withhold third-party personal data unless they consent or it is reasonable to disclose. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][18]
8. **Produce the copy.** Deliver a **faithful, intelligible** copy plus the Art. 15(1)(a)–(h) information; provide securely and, for the first copy, **free of charge** (C-487/21; C-307/22). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][12][13]
9. **Handle refusal / fee properly.** Only refuse or charge where **manifestly unfounded or excessive**, with reasons and complaint/remedy rights (Art. 12(4)–(5)); keep the evidence. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][18]
10. **Operate the other rights on the same rails.** Rectification (16), erasure (17), restriction (18), portability (20) and objection (21) share the Art. 12 modalities; **stop processing immediately** on a direct-marketing objection (21(3)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
11. **Run distinct EU vs. UK playbooks.** Because the UK has diverged (searches, stop-the-clock, LPP, ADM), maintain **jurisdiction-aware** procedures rather than one global setting. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [4][5][21]

- **Phase 4 — UK divergence & ADM:** Add reasonable-and-proportionate search logging, Art. 12A stop-the-clock, the s.79 LPP exemption, and jurisdiction-aware ADM controls. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 5 — Assurance:** Metrics (timeliness, volumes, refusal rates), periodic audit, staff training, and guidance-watch for ICO/EDPB updates. *Effort:* Ongoing.

2. How do you **verify identity** proportionately, and (UK) how do you record that the clock started only on confirmation? *(Art. 12(6); Art. 12A [1][4].)*
3. When you seek **clarification**, on what basis, and (UK) how do you evidence the stop-the-clock pause? *(Recital 63; Art. 12A [1][4].)*
4. How do you decide what is a **reasonable and proportionate** search (UK) or a complete search (EU), and how is scope documented? *(Art. 15(1A); [5][19].)*
5. How do you disclose **specific recipients** and produce an **intelligible copy**? *(Art. 15(1)(c),(3); C-154/21; C-487/21 [11][12].)*
6. How do you balance and **redact third-party data**? *(Art. 15(4) [1].)*
7. On what evidence do you treat a request as **manifestly unfounded or excessive**? *(Art. 12(5) [1][18].)*
8. How are **erasure/objection** decisions propagated to backups and processors, and how do you honour **direct-marketing objections** immediately? *(Arts. 17–19, 21(3), 28 [1].)*
9. How do you identify **solely automated significant decisions**, and what safeguards (human review, contest) apply — distinguishing EU (Art. 22) from UK (Arts. 22A–22D)? *(Art. 22; C-634/21; [14][21].)*

text:
The General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, "GDPR") is the European Union's primary data-protection instrument. It entered into force on 24 May 2016 and has applied directly across all Member States since **25 May 2018** [1][2]. As a Regulation it is binding in its entirety and directly applicable without national transposition, although it leaves defined margins for Member State law.

This document establishes the *foundations*: the material and territorial scope of the GDPR, its core definitions (personal data, processing, controller, processor), the seven data-protection principles in Article 5, and the six lawful bases for processing in Article 6 [1]. It also situates these within the accountability model that makes controllers responsible for demonstrating — not merely asserting — compliance [1].

The intended audience is compliance, legal, and engineering teams who need a single authoritative reference before engaging with more specialised topics (data-subject requests, international transfers, DPIAs, AI Act overlap). Three conclusions dominate. First, the GDPR is **principle-based**: obligations flow from Article 5, and every downstream control should trace to a principle. Second, **lawfulness is a gate**: no processing is permitted without a valid Article 6 basis, chosen before processing begins. Third, **accountability is operational**: Article 5(2) converts good intentions into an evidentiary burden the controller must be able to discharge on demand [1].

Foundational case law from the Court of Justice of the EU (Google Spain, Breyer, Nowak, Schrems II) confirms the broad construction of "personal data" and the robustness of data-subject rights, and is summarised in the Legal Framework section [3][4][5][6].
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
- The GDPR has applied directly in all EU Member States since **25 May 2018**; it comprises 11 chapters, 99 articles and 173 recitals [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Seven principles** govern all processing: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity & confidentiality, and accountability (Art. 5) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Processing requires at least one of **six lawful bases** (Art. 6(1)(a)–(f)); the basis must be identified before processing and cannot be swapped retrospectively to fix a problem [1]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- "**Personal data**" is construed broadly; a dynamic IP address can be personal data where the controller has legal means to identify the individual (Breyer, C-582/14) [5]. *(Case law.)*
- Even exam scripts and examiner comments can be personal data (Nowak, C-434/16), illustrating the concept's reach [4]. *(Case law.)*
- **Accountability (Art. 5(2))** shifts the burden: controllers must be able to *demonstrate* compliance, not merely comply [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The GDPR distinguishes **controllers** (determine purposes and means) from **processors** (act on the controller's instructions); the distinction drives who bears which obligations [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Non-compliance can attract administrative fines up to **€20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Art. 83(5)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
This document is the entry point to the GDPR topic area. It supports:

- **Legal research** — a mapped index of the principles, lawful bases and anchor case law.
- **Compliance implementation** — a foundation on which DSAR handling, transfers, DPIA and records documents build.
- **Developer guidance** — plain-language framing of obligations that shape system design (privacy by design, minimisation, security).
- **Onboarding** — a single reference before staff engage specialised material.

It deliberately does *not* cover, in depth: data-subject rights procedures, international transfers (Chapter V), Data Protection Impact Assessments (Art. 35), or records of processing (Art. 30). Those are separate documents in the research backlog (see `PROJECT_STATUS.md`).

text:
| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Personal data | Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person ("data subject"); an identifiable person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly (Art. 4(1)). | [1] |
| Processing | Any operation performed on personal data — collection, recording, storage, use, disclosure, erasure, etc. (Art. 4(2)). | [1] |
| Controller | The natural/legal person that, alone or jointly, determines the purposes and means of processing (Art. 4(7)). | [1] |
| Processor | A natural/legal person that processes personal data on behalf of the controller (Art. 4(8)). | [1] |
| Consent | Any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes, by a statement or clear affirmative action (Art. 4(11)). | [1] |
| Special category data | Data revealing racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious/philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership; genetic, biometric, health, sex-life or sexual-orientation data (Art. 9). | [1] |
| Supervisory authority | An independent public authority established by a Member State to monitor GDPR application (Art. 4(21), Art. 51). | [1] |

text:
Before the GDPR, EU data protection rested on **Directive 95/46/EC**, transposed unevenly across Member States, producing fragmentation and legal uncertainty for cross-border processing. The GDPR replaced the Directive with a directly applicable Regulation to harmonise rules, strengthen data-subject rights, and modernise the framework for the digital and cross-border economy [2][9].

Because the transition spanned the Directive-to-Regulation shift, much foundational case law (Google Spain, Breyer, Nowak) was decided under Directive 95/46/EC but remains authoritative for interpreting equivalent GDPR concepts, since the definitions were carried forward substantially unchanged [3][4][5]. The GDPR entered into force on 24 May 2016 (twenty days after OJ publication) and became applicable on 25 May 2018, giving organisations a two-year implementation window [1][2].
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
The GDPR is a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council. It is **binding in its entirety and directly applicable** in all Member States, though it contains "opening clauses" permitting or requiring national law on specific points (e.g., age of consent for information-society services, employment context). It comprises 11 chapters and 99 articles, preceded by 173 recitals that aid interpretation but are not themselves binding operative provisions [1].

The architecture, at a glance:

- **Chapter I** — General provisions (subject-matter, scope, definitions).
- **Chapter II** — Principles (Arts. 5–11), including lawful bases and conditions for consent and special-category data.
- **Chapter III** — Rights of the data subject (Arts. 12–23).
- **Chapter IV** — Controller and processor obligations (Arts. 24–43), including security, DPIA, and DPOs.
- **Chapter V** — Transfers to third countries (Arts. 44–50).
- **Chapters VI–VII** — Supervisory authorities and cooperation/consistency.
- **Chapter VIII** — Remedies, liability and penalties (Arts. 77–84).
- **Chapters IX–XI** — Specific situations, delegated acts, final provisions.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 2 | Material scope — applies to processing of personal data wholly/partly by automated means and to non-automated processing forming part of a filing system. | [1] |
| Art. 3 | Territorial scope — applies to controllers/processors established in the EU, and to those outside the EU offering goods/services to, or monitoring, data subjects in the EU. | [1] |
| Art. 4 | Definitions (personal data, processing, controller, processor, consent, etc.). | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(a) | Lawfulness, fairness and transparency. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(b) | Purpose limitation. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(c) | Data minimisation. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(d) | Accuracy. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(e) | Storage limitation. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(f) | Integrity and confidentiality (security). | [1] |
| Art. 5(2) | Accountability — controller must demonstrate compliance. | [1] |
| Art. 6(1)(a)–(f) | Six lawful bases for processing. | [1] |
| Art. 9 | Prohibition on processing special categories, subject to exceptions. | [1] |
| Art. 24 | Responsibility of the controller — implement appropriate technical and organisational measures. | [1] |
| Art. 25 | Data protection by design and by default. | [1] |
| Art. 28 | Processor obligations and mandatory contract terms. | [1] |
| Art. 32 | Security of processing. | [1] |
| Art. 83 | Administrative fines (up to €20m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover). | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are interpretive aids, not binding operative provisions [1].*

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).** The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issues guidelines, recommendations and best practices that, while not binding law, represent the consensus interpretation of EU supervisory authorities and are highly persuasive [8]. National authorities (e.g., the UK ICO for the UK GDPR, Ireland's DPC, France's CNIL) publish complementary guidance [7].

Key interpretive positions relevant to the foundations:

- **Lawful basis must be determined before processing** and documented; the ICO stresses that controllers cannot switch basis retrospectively to remedy a problem, and that consent is not automatically the "best" basis [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f))** requires a three-part test — purpose (identify the interest), necessity (is processing necessary), and balancing (against the data subject's rights) — reflected in Recital 47 and ICO/EDPB guidance [7][8]. *(Regulatory interpretation / best practice.)*
- **Consent** must meet the Art. 4(11) and Art. 7 conditions; the EDPB Guidelines on consent treat bundled consent and non-genuine choice as invalid [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **accountability principle** is operationalised through records of processing (Art. 30), DPIAs (Art. 35), and demonstrable technical and organisational measures (Arts. 24, 32) [1][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
The principles translate directly into system-design constraints:

- **Data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c))** — collect and retain only what the purpose requires; prefer schemas that avoid optional over-collection; avoid "collect now, decide later." *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e))** — implement retention schedules and automated deletion/anonymisation; time-to-live on records; documented retention rationale.
- **Integrity & confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f), Art. 32)** — encryption in transit and at rest, access control, pseudonymisation, logging, and tested backup/restore. Align with ISO/IEC 27001 controls [10][11].
- **Data protection by design and by default (Art. 25)** — privacy-preserving defaults, minimisation baked into architecture, DPIA triggers in the SDLC.
- **Lawful-basis enforcement** — where consent is the basis, systems must record consent capture, scope and withdrawal, and must honour withdrawal as easily as it was given (Art. 7(3)).
- **Identifiability boundary (Recital 26)** — genuine anonymisation removes data from GDPR scope, but *pseudonymised* data remains personal data; teams frequently conflate the two [1][5].
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
- **Controller/processor allocation** — a hosting provider is typically a **processor**; an Art. 28 data-processing agreement with the mandatory terms is required, including sub-processor controls and assistance obligations. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Location & transfers** — where hosting entails storage or access from outside the EEA, Chapter V transfer mechanisms apply; Schrems II requires assessing third-country government-access risk and supplementary measures [6]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Security (Art. 32)** — infrastructure controls (tenant isolation, key management, patching, monitoring) should map to a recognised framework (ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF) [10][11].
- **Shared responsibility** — cloud shared-responsibility models must be reconciled with the controller/processor split; the customer usually remains controller and cannot outsource accountability. *(Editorial recommendation: document the responsibility matrix explicitly.)*
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
- **Children's data** — games frequently attract minors. Art. 8 sets conditions for consent to information-society services offered to children; the applicable age threshold (13–16) is set by Member State law, so multi-territory games face varying thresholds. Age-assurance and parental-consent flows are needed. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Player identifiers & telemetry** — usernames, device IDs, IP addresses and in-game telemetry are typically personal data (cf. Breyer on IP addresses) [5]; minimisation and retention rules apply to matchmaking, anti-cheat and analytics data.
- **Real-time processing** — voice/chat moderation and anti-cheat may process personal (and sometimes special-category) data; lawful basis and transparency must be established.
- **UGC and third parties** — user-generated content and third-party SDKs (ads, analytics) create controller/processor and joint-controller questions that must be mapped. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
- **Training data** — using personal data to train models is "processing" and needs a lawful basis; purpose limitation (Art. 5(1)(b)) constrains reuse of data collected for another purpose. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Automated decision-making** — Art. 22 gives data subjects rights regarding solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects; foundational to any AI system making consequential decisions. *(Legal obligation; detailed in a dedicated document.)*
- **Data minimisation vs. model appetite** — the tension between minimisation and data-hungry ML is a recurring compliance friction point; techniques include pseudonymisation, synthetic data and federated approaches. *(Best practice.)*
- **AI Act overlap** — the GDPR operates alongside the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689); the two are complementary, and this overlap is addressed in the AI Act and AI Governance documents. *(Cross-reference.)*
title: GDPR: Foundations & Core Principles

text:
The following distinguishes **OBLIGATION** (the law requires), **BEST PRACTICE** (standards/regulator consensus), and **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (this pipeline suggests).

1. **Map your processing** — maintain records of processing activities (Art. 30). *(OBLIGATION for most organisations.)*
2. **Assign each processing activity a lawful basis** before it begins, and document the reasoning; for legitimate interests, complete and retain a Legitimate Interests Assessment. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [7]
3. **Classify data** — flag special-category (Art. 9) and children's data for elevated controls. *(OBLIGATION.)*
4. **Trace every control to a principle** — build a matrix linking technical/organisational measures to Art. 5 principles to evidence accountability. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)*
5. **Operationalise rights** — build repeatable DSAR, erasure and objection workflows (detailed in a dedicated document). *(OBLIGATION.)*
6. **Contract with processors** — ensure Art. 28 terms are in place with every processor and sub-processor. *(OBLIGATION.)*
7. **Assess transfers** — inventory data flows leaving the EEA and apply Chapter V mechanisms with a transfer risk assessment. *(OBLIGATION.)* [6]

title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
Chapter V of the GDPR (Articles 44–50) governs the transfer of personal data to **third countries** (outside the EEA) and to international organisations. Its animating rule is that the level of protection guaranteed by the GDPR must **travel with the data**: a transfer is only lawful if the exporter uses one of the Chapter V mechanisms and the protection afforded to data subjects is not undermined [1]. This document details the Chapter V material introduced at foundation level in `gdpr-foundations` and goes deeper on each mechanism.

The transfer toolbox has a defined hierarchy [1]. First, an **adequacy decision** under **Article 45** — the Commission's finding that a country ensures an "essentially equivalent" level of protection — permits transfers with no further safeguard. Second, where there is no adequacy, **appropriate safeguards** under **Article 46** (chiefly the **2021 Standard Contractual Clauses**, **Binding Corporate Rules** under Art. 47, and approved codes/certifications) may be used, each providing enforceable rights and effective remedies. Third, the **Article 49 derogations** (consent, contract necessity, important public interest, etc.) are narrow, situational exceptions of last resort, not a routine basis for systematic transfers [1][11].

Since **Schrems II** (2020), Article 46 tools cannot be used mechanically: the exporter must run a **transfer impact assessment (TIA)** of the destination country's law and practice and, where protection falls short, add **supplementary measures** (technical, contractual, organisational) — or not transfer [2][11]. The **EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF)**, adopted by adequacy decision on **10 July 2023** [4], is the successor to the invalidated Safe Harbor and Privacy Shield. **As of this document's date it remains in force**: the General Court **dismissed** the first annulment challenge in **Latombe v Commission (3 September 2025)** [6], but that judgment is **under appeal to the Court of Justice (C-703/25 P, lodged 31 October 2025)** [7], and a June 2026 US Supreme Court development on FTC-commissioner removal has renewed doubts about the framework's redress architecture. Treat the DPF as **valid but contingent**. The document closes with the **UK regime** — UK adequacy regulations, the ICO's **International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA)** and the **UK Addendum** to the EU SCCs [14][15].
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
- Chapter V (Arts. 44–50) restricts transfers of personal data outside the EEA; **Article 44** makes clear that all its provisions must be applied so the GDPR-level of protection is **not undermined** [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Adequacy (Art. 45)** is the simplest route: transfers to a country/territory covered by a Commission adequacy decision need **no additional safeguard** [1][9]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Absent adequacy, **appropriate safeguards (Art. 46)** — principally the **2021 SCCs** (Decision (EU) 2021/914), **BCRs (Art. 47)**, and approved codes/certifications — are required, each giving data subjects **enforceable rights and effective legal remedies** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Schrems II** invalidated Privacy Shield and held that SCCs remain valid **only if** the exporter verifies essentially equivalent protection case-by-case and adds **supplementary measures** where needed [2][11]. *(Case law / regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** (adequacy decision of **10 July 2023**) is currently **in force**; it survived **Latombe v Commission** at the General Court (3 Sep 2025) but is **under appeal (C-703/25 P)** — treat its future as uncertain [4][6][7]. *(Legal obligation — live-verify.)*
- **Article 49 derogations** (explicit consent, contract necessity, important public interest, legal claims, vital interests, public register, compelling legitimate interests) are **exceptional and narrowly construed** — not a basis for large-scale, repetitive transfers [1][11]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- A **transfer impact assessment (TIA)** is required before relying on Art. 46 tools; EDPB **Recommendations 01/2020** set out the six-step methodology and a supplementary-measures catalogue [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation / best practice.)*
- The **UK** operates a parallel regime: UK adequacy ("data bridges"), the **IDTA**, and the **UK Addendum** to the EU SCCs; the EU's adequacy decision for the UK was **renewed to 27 December 2031** [13][15][16]. *(Legal obligation.)*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Restricted transfer | A transfer of personal data to a third country or international organisation that triggers Chapter V. | [1] |
| Adequacy decision | A Commission decision under Art. 45 that a third country/territory/sector ensures an essentially equivalent level of protection, permitting transfers without further safeguards. | [1][9] |
| Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) | Commission-approved model clauses providing Art. 46(2)(c) safeguards; the current modular set is Decision (EU) 2021/914. | [5] |
| Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) | Supervisory-authority-approved intra-group data-protection rules enabling transfers within a corporate group (Art. 47). | [1] |
| Transfer impact assessment (TIA) | The Schrems II case-by-case assessment of whether the destination's law/practice ensures essentially equivalent protection, and what supplementary measures are needed. | [2][11] |
| Supplementary measures | Technical, contractual and organisational measures added to an Art. 46 tool to bring protection up to the EU standard. | [2][11] |
| Data bridge | UK government term for a UK adequacy determination permitting transfers without further safeguards (e.g., the UK Extension to the EU-US DPF). | [17] |
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
Under Directive 95/46/EC the EU already restricted transfers to "third countries" without adequate protection. The GDPR carried this forward and strengthened it, reflecting the **Charter of Fundamental Rights** (Arts. 7, 8, 47) and a line of CJEU authority insisting that data subjects retain **essentially equivalent** protection wherever their data goes [1][2].

The transatlantic dimension has been especially turbulent. The Commission's **Safe Harbor** adequacy decision was struck down in **Schrems I** (2015) [3]; its replacement, the **Privacy Shield**, was struck down in **Schrems II** (2020) [2]. Each time the CJEU found that US surveillance law and the absence of effective redress for EU data subjects prevented essential equivalence. In response the US enacted **Executive Order 14086** (2022) and created a two-layer redress mechanism culminating in the **Data Protection Review Court**; on that basis the Commission adopted the **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** adequacy decision on 10 July 2023 [4][10]. Predictably, the DPF was itself challenged — the **Latombe** litigation — making the current-status question a moving target that this document live-verifies [6][7].
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
Chapter V builds a **layered permission system**. Article 44 states the general principle; Articles 45–47 and 49 supply the specific gateways; Article 48 addresses foreign court/authority orders; Article 50 concerns international cooperation. The exporter must identify a valid gateway **before** the transfer and be able to evidence it [1].

The layers, in order of preference:

- **Article 45 — Adequacy.** Transfer to a country/territory/sector covered by a Commission adequacy decision. No further authorisation needed.
- **Article 46 — Appropriate safeguards.** Where there is no adequacy: SCCs, BCRs, approved codes of conduct, approved certification mechanisms, or (with authorisation) ad hoc clauses. Each must provide enforceable rights and effective remedies.
- **Article 47 — BCRs.** A specific Art. 46 route for intra-group transfers, approved by the lead supervisory authority via the consistency mechanism.
- **Article 49 — Derogations.** Exceptional, situation-specific gateways where neither adequacy nor safeguards are available.
- **Article 48.** Judgments/decisions of third-country courts or authorities are only enforceable grounds for transfer if based on an international agreement (e.g., MLAT).

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 44 | General principle — any transfer must comply with Chapter V so that the level of protection is **not undermined**; applies to onward transfers too. | [1] |
| Art. 45 | Transfers on the basis of an **adequacy decision**; sets the criteria the Commission assesses and provides for periodic review and amendment/repeal. | [1] |
| Art. 46 | Transfers subject to **appropriate safeguards** (SCCs, BCRs, codes, certification, ad hoc clauses) providing enforceable rights and effective remedies. | [1] |
| Art. 46(2)(c) | Standard data protection clauses **adopted by the Commission** — the 2021 SCCs (Decision (EU) 2021/914). | [1][5] |
| Art. 47 | **Binding Corporate Rules** — content requirements and the approval route via the consistency mechanism. | [1] |
| Art. 48 | Third-country court/authority orders are enforceable grounds only under an international agreement. | [1] |
| Art. 49 | **Derogations** for specific situations (explicit consent; contract; important public interest; legal claims; vital interests; public register; compelling legitimate interests). | [1] |
| Art. 50 | International cooperation for the protection of personal data. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are interpretive aids, not binding operative provisions [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 101 | Flows of personal data to and from third countries are necessary but must not undermine the level of protection; sets the frame for Chapter V. | [1] |
| Recital 103–104 | Adequacy — the Commission may decide a third country/territory/sector ensures an adequate (essentially equivalent) level of protection. | [1] |
| Recital 108–109 | Appropriate safeguards and the use of standard clauses/BCRs where adequacy is absent. | [1] |
| Recital 111–112 | Derogations must be construed **restrictively** and relate to occasional, non-systematic transfers. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Schrems I (Schrems v DPC) | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-362/14, ECLI:EU:C:2015:650, 6 Oct 2015 | Invalidated the **Safe Harbor** adequacy decision; a supervisory authority must be able to examine transfer complaints even under an adequacy decision. | Establishes that adequacy decisions are reviewable and that surveillance access defeats adequacy [3]. |
| Schrems II (DPC v Facebook Ireland & Schrems) | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-311/18, ECLI:EU:C:2020:559, 16 July 2020 | Invalidated the **Privacy Shield**; upheld the **SCCs** in principle but required exporters to assess destination law and apply **supplementary measures**, suspending transfers where equivalence cannot be ensured. | The foundational transfers judgment; source of the TIA/supplementary-measures duty [2]. |
| Latombe v Commission | General Court (Tenth Chamber, Extended), T-553/23, judgment 3 Sep 2025 | **Dismissed** the action to annul the EU-US DPF adequacy decision; ruled on the substance and upheld the 2023 Decision on the facts/law at adoption. | First judicial test of the DPF; confirms it stands at first instance [6]. |
| Latombe v Commission (appeal) | Court of Justice, **C-703/25 P**, appeal lodged 31 Oct 2025 (**pending**) | No ruling yet; seeks to set aside the General Court's judgment. | The DPF's continued validity is **not finally settled**; a merits reversal would be the third invalidation of a transatlantic framework [7]. |

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **EDPB Recommendations 01/2020** set out the **six-step** transfer roadmap: (1) map transfers; (2) identify the Art. 46 tool; (3) assess whether the tool is effective in light of destination law/practice (the **TIA**); (4) adopt **supplementary measures** if needed; (5) take any procedural steps; (6) re-evaluate periodically [11]. The EDPB stresses that measures must be **effective in practice**, and that where problematic laws apply, only robust **technical** measures (e.g., strong encryption with keys held in the EEA, effective pseudonymisation) may suffice [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Derogations are a last resort.** The EDPB (Guidelines 2/2018) reads Art. 49 restrictively: derogations are for **occasional, non-repetitive** transfers; "necessity" for a contract is interpreted strictly; and consent must be **explicit, specific and informed of the risks** of transferring without adequacy or safeguards [11][12]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **European Commission** maintains and periodically reviews the **adequacy list**; adequacy decisions are living instruments that can be amended, suspended or repealed if protection deteriorates [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **ICO** operates the UK equivalents: it publishes the **IDTA**, the **UK Addendum** to the EU SCCs, and a **transfer risk assessment (TRA)** tool that is methodologically distinct from (though compatible with) the EDPB TIA [14][15][18]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

## Adequacy — the current list (Art. 45)

As of this document's date, the Commission recognises (fully or partially) a set of third countries/territories including **Andorra, Argentina, Canada (commercial organisations), Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Israel, Isle of Man, Japan, Jersey, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, the United States (commercial organisations certified under the DPF), and Uruguay** [9]. The **authoritative, current** list is the Commission's adequacy-decisions page — consult it directly, because entries are added and reviewed over time [9]. With the exception of the UK, these decisions do not cover the law-enforcement sector (Directive (EU) 2016/680) [9].
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
- **Map the flows first** — a transfer occurs whenever personal data is sent to, **or made accessible from**, a third country, including remote support access, global admin consoles, and CDN/edge nodes; "no data at rest abroad" does not by itself avoid Chapter V [1][11]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **Supplementary measures are mostly technical** — where the Art. 46 tool alone is insufficient, the effective options are strong **encryption in transit and at rest with EEA-held keys**, effective **pseudonymisation**, and split/multi-party processing; access-in-the-clear by the importer generally defeats these protections [2][11]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Key management is the crux** — a technical measure is only as good as key custody; keys accessible to the importer (or to the importer's jurisdiction) undermine the measure [11]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Instrument your data map** — maintain transfer records inside the Art. 30 RoPA (destinations, mechanism, TIA reference, supplementary measures) so the mechanism is evidenced on demand [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
- **Cloud = transfers, usually** — most hyperscale and SaaS hosting entails at least remote access from outside the EEA; assess each provider's regions, sub-processors, and support-access model against Chapter V [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Provider transfer paperwork** — providers typically offer the **2021 SCCs** (and, for UK data, the **IDTA/UK Addendum**) in their DPAs; the customer, as exporter, still owns the **TIA** and cannot delegate that judgement [5][11][15]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **DPF-certified importers** — where a US provider is on the **Data Privacy Framework List**, transfers to it can rely on Art. 45 adequacy instead of SCCs — but only while the DPF stands, and only for the certified entity/scope; keep an SCC fallback ready [4][19]. *(Legal obligation / editorial recommendation.)*
- **EEA data residency options** — provider "EU data boundary"/sovereign-cloud offerings reduce but do not always eliminate third-country access (e.g., global support); verify the access model, not just the storage region. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
- **Global player bases mean constant transfers** — matchmaking, telemetry, anti-cheat, voice/chat and crash reporting frequently route player data (usernames, device IDs, IP addresses) to third-country servers or vendors; each is a restricted transfer needing a Chapter V basis [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Third-party SDKs** — ads, analytics and crash SDKs often transfer to the US or elsewhere; inventory them and confirm their transfer mechanism (DPF certification or SCCs + TIA) [4][5][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Children's data raises the bar** — where minors are involved, rely-on-consent derogations are especially fragile and supplementary measures should be stronger; align with the ICO Children's Code where UK children are in scope. *(Best practice.)*
- **Live-ops latency vs. residency** — the pressure to place edge servers close to players must be reconciled with transfer rules; prefer EEA/adequate regions for identifiable player data where feasible. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
- **Training and inference transfers** — sending personal data to a third-country model provider (or a model hosted there) for training or inference is a restricted transfer; a Chapter V basis and TIA are required in addition to a lawful basis under Art. 6 [1][2][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **US model APIs** — many foundation-model APIs are operated by US entities; check for **DPF certification** (Art. 45 route) or fall back to **SCCs + supplementary measures**, noting that clear-text prompt/response access by the importer weakens technical measures [4][11]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **AI Act runs in parallel** — Chapter V does not displace the EU AI Act; where an AI system processes personal data across borders, both regimes apply (cross-ref `ai-act-foundations`). *(Cross-reference.)*
- **Minimise before you transfer** — pseudonymise/aggregate training data before export where possible, reducing both transfer risk and lawful-basis exposure. *(Best practice.)*
title: GDPR: International Data Transfers (Chapter V)

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** (the law requires) / **BEST PRACTICE** (standards/regulator consensus) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (this pipeline suggests).

1. **Inventory all transfers** — build a transfer register (destination, importer, data categories, mechanism, TIA, supplementary measures) within the RoPA. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
2. **Prefer adequacy** — where the destination is covered by an adequacy decision (or DPF certification for the specific US importer), rely on Art. 45 and record the basis. *(OBLIGATION.)* [4][9]
3. **Use the 2021 SCCs correctly** — select the right **module** (C2C, C2P, P2P, P2C), complete the annexes, and integrate them with the Art. 28 DPA where the importer is a processor. *(OBLIGATION.)* [5]
4. **Run a TIA before relying on Art. 46** — follow the EDPB six-step method; document destination-law analysis and the equivalence conclusion. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [11]
5. **Add supplementary measures** where the TIA shows a gap — prioritise strong encryption/pseudonymisation with EEA-held keys; if no measure suffices, **do not transfer**. *(OBLIGATION.)* [2][11]
6. **Treat Art. 49 derogations as exceptional** — do not use consent or contract necessity to justify routine, bulk transfers; document why a derogation genuinely applies. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][11]
7. **For UK data, use UK tools** — the **IDTA**, or the **EU SCCs + UK Addendum**, plus a UK **TRA**; rely on UK data bridges (incl. the UK Extension to the DPF, made by SI 2023/1028) where available. *(OBLIGATION.)* [8][15][16][17]
8. **Keep a fallback and monitor the DPF** — because the DPF is under appeal (C-703/25 P), maintain SCC fallbacks for US flows and track the litigation. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [6][7]

- **Phase 0 — Transfer discovery:** Map every flow leaving the EEA/UK, including remote access and sub-processors. *Depends on:* data map/RoPA. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Mechanism selection:** Assign a Chapter V basis per flow (adequacy/DPF → SCCs/BCRs → derogation); document rationale. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 2 — TIAs & supplementary measures:** Run TIAs for Art. 46 flows; implement technical measures (encryption/pseudonymisation, key custody). *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 3 — UK alignment:** Apply IDTA/UK Addendum and TRAs for UK data; confirm data-bridge reliance where used. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 4 — Contracts & BCRs:** Integrate SCCs with Art. 28 DPAs; for intra-group flows, evaluate BCRs. *Effort:* Medium–High.
- **Phase 5 — Monitor & re-verify:** Track adequacy changes and the DPF appeal; re-evaluate TIAs periodically. *Effort:* Ongoing.

text:
The **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18)** ("DUAA") is the UK's first substantive reform of its post-Brexit data-protection framework. It received **Royal Assent on 19 June 2025** and does **not replace** the UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018) or the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR); it **amends** them through targeted, mostly permission-widening changes [1][10]. This deep-dive details the DUAA material introduced at foundational level in `uk-gdpr-foundations`, going provision-by-provision rather than restating the overview.

The reforms most relevant to controllers are: a new **"recognised legitimate interests"** lawful basis for a closed list of public-interest purposes that carries **no balancing test** [10][13][15]; a rebuilt **automated decision-making** regime (new UK GDPR Articles 22A–22D via s.80) that lifts the general prohibition for non-special-category data but mandates safeguards [2][10]; clarified **scientific-research** provisions (including a workable "broad consent") [10][13]; a statutory **complaints-handling** duty on controllers (electronic route, 30-day acknowledgement) [10][12]; a duty to consider **children's higher protection** in service design [12][13]; a recast **international-transfers** "data protection test" ("not materially lower") [10][13]; **PECR** changes (cookie-consent exemptions, extended soft opt-in, and maximum fines raised from £500,000 to **£17.5m / 4% of turnover**) [10][13][16]; and reconstitution of the ICO as the **Information Commission** [9][11].

Three conclusions dominate. First, **most data-protection provisions are already live** (5 February 2026), so this is operational law, not a future project [3][9][14]. Second, the reforms **increase UK–EU divergence** while the Commission has **renewed UK adequacy to 27 December 2031** having assessed the DUAA [17]. Third, the changes are **enabling, not deregulatory in substance** — the new freedoms are conditional on documented safeguards, and the ICO has signalled a supportive-but-watchful enforcement posture [14].
title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: Detailed Analysis

text:
- The **DUAA (c.18)** received Royal Assent on **19 June 2025** and amends — does not replace — the UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and PECR [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **majority of the data-protection provisions in Part 5 came into force on 5 February 2026** via the **Commencement No. 6 Regulations (SI 2026/82)** [3][9][14]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- The **complaints-handling duty (s.103)** is scheduled to commence **19 June 2026** — organisations must have a compliant process by then [9][10]. *(Legal obligation — pending commencement.)*
- **Recognised legitimate interests** is a new lawful basis for a **closed list of public-interest purposes** (e.g. national/public security, crime detection/prevention, safeguarding, emergencies, democratic engagement) that requires **no legitimate-interests balancing test** — but **cannot** be used for significant automated decisions [10][13][15]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The DUAA replaces UK GDPR **Article 22 with new Articles 22A–22D (s.80)**: the general ban on solely automated significant decisions is lifted for **non-special-category** data, subject to **safeguards** (information, representations, human intervention, contestation); special-category ADM stays tightly restricted [2][10][13]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **PECR** maximum penalties rise from **£500,000 to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover**, cookie **consent exemptions** are added for low-risk purposes (e.g. analytics, security), and **soft opt-in** is extended to charities/non-profits [10][13][16]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- International transfers move to a **"data protection test"** — protection in the destination must be **"not materially lower"** than the UK standard — a lower threshold than the EU's "essentially equivalent" [10][13]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- The ICO is reconstituted as the **Information Commission** (a body corporate with a board and statutory objectives) [9][11][13]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **EU adequacy** for the UK was **renewed to 27 December 2031** after the Commission assessed the DUAA reforms [17]. *(Regulatory / legal.)*

*Shared terms (personal data, controller, processor, consent, special-category data, legitimate interests, ISS, PECR, adequacy) are in `GLOSSARY.md` and carry over. Only DUAA-specific terms are defined here; keep short.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| DUAA / DUAA 2025 | Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18), amending the UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and PECR. | [1] |
| Recognised legitimate interest | A specified public-interest purpose (listed in the new Annex introduced by the DUAA) for which a controller may process personal data **without** performing the legitimate-interests balancing test. | [13][15] |
| Significant decision | A decision producing legal effects concerning, or similarly significantly affecting, a data subject (new UK GDPR Art. 22A). | [2][13] |
| Data protection test | The DUAA test for approving transfers / adequacy: whether the destination's standard of protection is **not materially lower** than under UK law. | [10][13] |
| Information Commission | The body corporate that replaces the Information Commissioner's Office as the UK data-protection regulator under the DUAA. | [9][11] |
| Commencement regulations | Secondary legislation (a series of SIs) that bring individual DUAA provisions into force on staged dates. | [3][4][9] |

text:
UK data-protection reform has a long gestation. Earlier attempts (the Data Protection and Digital Information Bill of 2022–23, reintroduced 2023) fell with the 2024 general election. The DUAA is the successor vehicle: narrower and more targeted than a wholesale rewrite, it keeps the UK GDPR/DPA 2018 architecture and edits it [10]. Its stated aims are to enable safe data use to support growth and public services, reduce compliance friction on lower-risk processing, and modernise the regulator — while preserving the high level of protection on which **EU adequacy** depends [10][17].

The Act reached **Royal Assent on 19 June 2025** [1]. Because it edits three instruments at once and depends on secondary legislation and updated ICO guidance, the Government adopted a **staged commencement plan** run by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) [9]. Some provisions commenced automatically on assent or shortly after; the bulk of the data-protection reforms were switched on by the **Commencement No. 6 Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82)** on **5 February 2026** [3][9]. A small number of provisions — most visibly the complaints-handling duty — commence later [9].
