text:
The DUAA is a large Act; its data-protection substance sits mainly in **Part 5** (data protection and privacy), with the regulator reconstituted elsewhere in the Act [1][10]. The mechanism is amendment-in-place: DUAA sections insert, substitute or repeal text in the UK GDPR (retained/assimilated under EUWA 2018 s.3 [7]), the **DPA 2018 [5]** and PECR. The consolidated effect must therefore be read in the **amended** UK GDPR/DPA 2018/PECR, not in the DUAA alone [1][10].

The principal data-protection reforms, and where they land, are set out below. Distinguish throughout: **OBLIGATION** (what the amended law requires), **REGULATORY INTERPRETATION** (ICO/GOV.UK reading), **BEST PRACTICE**, and **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

## Relevant Articles

*"Article" here means the amended UK GDPR article (or the DUAA / DPA 2018 / PECR provision) as the case may be.*

| Provision | Obligation / effect | Source |
|-----------|---------------------|--------|
| UK GDPR Art. 6 + new Annex (recognised legitimate interests) | New lawful basis for a closed list of public-interest purposes; **no balancing test** for listed purposes. | [10][13][15] |
| UK GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) / recitals (listed legitimate interests) | Certain commercial interests (e.g. direct marketing, intra-group transmission, network/information security) expressly recognised as **capable of being** legitimate interests — balancing test still required. | [13][15] |
| UK GDPR Arts. 22A–22D (DUAA s.80) | Replaces Art. 22: lifts the general prohibition on solely automated significant decisions for **non-special-category** data, subject to safeguards; restricts special-category ADM; empowers the Secretary of State to define thresholds. | [2][10][13] |
| UK GDPR Arts. 4/8a-area + DPA 2018 (scientific research) | Clarified definition of "research and statistical purposes"; workable **broad consent** to areas of scientific research; confirms commercial research can qualify. | [10][13] |
| DPA 2018 (DUAA s.103) (complaints) | Controllers must facilitate complaints (incl. an **electronic route**), **acknowledge within 30 days**, and investigate/respond without undue delay; ICO gains related powers. | [10][12] |
| UK GDPR Art. 25-area (children) | Providers of ISS likely to be accessed by children must consider **"children's higher protection matters"** in data-protection-by-design/default decisions. | [12][13] |
| UK GDPR Ch. V + DPA 2018 (transfers) | New **"data protection test"**: destination protection must be **"not materially lower"** than the UK standard; Secretary of State may approve countries/mechanisms. | [10][13] |
| PECR (SI 2003/2426) as amended | Cookie **consent exemptions** for low-risk purposes; **soft opt-in** extended to non-commercial bodies; maximum fines raised to **£17.5m / 4%** of turnover. | [10][13][16] |

## Relevant Recitals

The UK GDPR retains its recitals as interpretive aids (see `gdpr-foundations`). The DUAA operates by amending the enacting text and, in places, by adding definitional and Annex material rather than new recitals; it is construed against the **Act's own provisions, Explanatory Notes and ICO guidance** rather than EU-style recitals [1][10]. **Not Applicable** as a distinct set — no new UK GDPR recitals are introduced; interpretation of the new lawful basis and ADM regime rests on the statutory text and ICO guidance [13][15].

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** The DUAA is new (Royal Assent June 2025; most data-protection provisions in force February 2026), so there is no judicial interpretation of its provisions yet. Pre-2021 retained/assimilated CJEU case law continues to inform the **unamended** UK GDPR concepts (see `uk-gdpr-foundations`), but the DUAA-specific provisions — recognised legitimate interests, Arts 22A–22D, the transfers test — are as yet untested in the courts [1][8]. Early disputes are more likely to surface first as ICO enforcement and guidance than as litigation.

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).** The authoritative UK readings are DSIT's commencement materials and the ICO's DUAA guidance suite [9][11][12][13].

- **Commencement is staged and mostly complete for data protection.** DSIT's plan sets out phased entry into force; the ICO confirms that the **main UK GDPR and PECR changes took effect on 5 February 2026**, with the complaints duty to follow and some ICO-governance provisions later [9][14]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **"Amend, don't replace."** The ICO frames the DUAA as building on existing compliance — organisations already compliant with the UK GDPR have a foundation, but must adjust for the new provisions as they commence [11][13]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Recognised legitimate interests is narrow and public-interest.** The ICO's final guidance (published 23 March 2026) stresses that a recognised legitimate interest is a **specified public-interest purpose**, is **different from** the ordinary legitimate-interests basis, and — while it removes the balancing test — still requires the processing to be **necessary** for the listed purpose; it **cannot** support significant automated decisions [13][15]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
- **ADM freedom is conditional.** GOV.UK and the ICO present the Art. 22A–22D reform as removing the need for a *qualifying* lawful basis before making a significant automated decision (except for special-category data), **provided** the safeguards are in place; the ICO has consulted on ADM/profiling guidance [10][13]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Enforcement posture.** On commencement the ICO signalled a **supportive but watchful** approach — expecting organisations to work towards compliance and prioritising engagement — while retaining its enforcement powers, now materially larger for PECR [14][16]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

text:
- **Lawful-basis registers** must add **recognised legitimate interests** as a distinct basis (not a variant of Art. 6(1)(f)), recording the specific listed purpose and the necessity assessment; do **not** attach a balancing-test record to it (there is none) but **do** document why the purpose falls within the list [13][15]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **ADM pipelines** relying on Arts 22A–22D need: (i) detection of whether a decision is *solely* automated (no genuine, meaningful human involvement) and *significant*; (ii) a **special-category gate** (Art. 22B) blocking automated significant decisions on special-category data absent explicit consent or legal authorisation; and (iii) implemented **safeguards** (Art. 22C) — proactive information, a channel to make representations, human intervention/review, and a contest route [2][13]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Consent-management platforms (CMPs)** should be reconfigured for the new **cookie exemptions** (e.g. statistical/analytics to improve the service, security, fraud prevention, technical delivery) — but exemptions are purpose-scoped, so mixed-purpose tags still need consent [13][16]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Complaints tooling** (ahead of 19 June 2026): an **electronic complaints form/route**, a workflow enforcing **30-day acknowledgement**, case tracking and outcome communication [10][12]. *(Legal obligation — pending commencement.)*
- **Research data flows** benefit from the clarified definitions and broad consent, but require documented scoping of the research area and recognised ethical/safeguarding standards [10][13]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Jurisdiction-awareness** — because the DUAA widens UK-only freedoms (RLI, ADM, transfers test), systems serving both EU and UK subjects should apply rules per jurisdiction rather than a single global setting [10]. *(Best practice.)*

text:
- **International transfers** now turn on the **"data protection test"** ("not materially lower"): re-paper transfer risk assessments against the UK test rather than the EU "essentially equivalent" standard for **UK-origin** exports, while keeping the EU standard for EU-origin data [10][13]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **EU→UK adequacy** subsists (renewed to **27 December 2031**), so hosting EU personal data in the UK remains lawful without additional safeguards — but this is **conditional on the UK not diverging too far**, making the DUAA's transfer and ADM liberalisations a watch-item [17]. *(Legal / editorial.)*
- **Processor contracts (Art. 28)** are unchanged in structure, but processors offering analytics/telemetry should surface which cookie/PECR exemptions their tooling relies on so controllers can document them [16]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Log retention for ADM** — safeguards (human-review, contestation) imply retaining decision logs and model inputs long enough to service data-subject challenges, balanced against minimisation/retention limits [2][13]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*

- **Children's higher-protection duty** is acute for games: providers of ISS **likely to be accessed by children** must consider "children's higher protection matters" in DPbDD decisions — children merit specific protection, are less aware of risks, and have different needs at different ages [12][13]. This layers on top of the UK **age-13** consent threshold (DPA 2018 s.9) and the ICO Children's Code (see `uk-childrens-code`) [6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Automated moderation / anti-cheat / matchmaking** that makes *significant* decisions about players (e.g. bans, account restrictions) may now fall under Arts 22A–22D — assess whether the decision is solely automated and significant, and implement the safeguards, especially where minors are affected [2][13]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **In-game marketing** benefits from the extended **soft opt-in** only for the narrow conditions (existing supporters/customers, related purposes, opt-out at collection and each message); higher PECR fines (£17.5m/4%) sharpen the cost of unlawful marketing to players [16]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Analytics/telemetry** on player behaviour may use the new cookie exemptions where genuinely for service-improvement statistics or security — but profiling for personalisation/ads still needs consent [16]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
- **ADM liberalisation is the headline AI change.** Arts 22A–22D (s.80) shift the UK from a *prohibition-plus-exceptions* model to a *permission-plus-safeguards* model for solely automated significant decisions on non-special-category data — directly relevant to AI-driven credit, hiring, pricing and fraud systems [2][10][13]. This **diverges** from the stricter EU Art. 22 position and the EU AI Act overlay (see `ai-act-foundations`). *(Legal obligation; divergence risk.)*
- **Special-category ADM remains restricted** (Art. 22B): AI making significant decisions on health, biometric or other special-category data needs **explicit consent or legal authorisation** — a hard constraint on, e.g., health-AI and biometric systems [2][13]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Recognised legitimate interests cannot power significant ADM** — a deliberate carve-out preventing the balancing-test-free basis from being used to automate consequential decisions [13][15]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Scientific-research clarifications** ease lawful reuse of personal data for AI/ML research, including **commercial** research, via clarified definitions and broad consent — but purpose-scoping and safeguards remain [10][13]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **Explainability gap** — commentators note the safeguards (information, human review, contest) do not by themselves guarantee algorithmic *explainability*; controllers should treat transparency as a live design requirement, not a checkbox [13]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
- **UK has no AI Act equivalent** — AI governance stays principles-based; the DUAA's ADM rules are the closest hard-law touchpoint for AI decisions about UK data subjects [10]. *(Editorial note.)*

Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Re-baseline your compliance to the 5 Feb 2026 changes** — treat the amended UK GDPR/PECR as current law, not a future project. *(OBLIGATION.)* [3][9]
2. **Add recognised legitimate interests to the lawful-basis register** where used, recording the specific listed purpose and necessity; do not use it for significant ADM. *(OBLIGATION.)* [13][15]
3. **Re-engineer significant-ADM systems to Arts 22A–22D** — special-category gate, plus information/representations/human-intervention/contest safeguards. *(OBLIGATION.)* [2][13]
4. **Stand up a complaints process before 19 June 2026** — electronic route, 30-day acknowledgement, investigation and outcome communication. *(OBLIGATION — pending commencement.)* [9][10][12]
5. **Reconfigure your CMP** for the new cookie exemptions, keeping consent for non-exempt/profiling purposes. *(OBLIGATION.)* [13][16]
6. **Update marketing rules** for the extended soft opt-in and the £17.5m/4% PECR fine ceiling. *(OBLIGATION.)* [16]
7. **Re-paper UK transfer risk assessments** against the "not materially lower" data-protection test. *(OBLIGATION.)* [10][13]
8. **Embed the children's higher-protection duty** into DPbDD for services likely accessed by children. *(OBLIGATION.)* [12][13]
9. **Maintain a commencement watch-list** for outstanding provisions (complaints, ICO-governance) and track ICO guidance updates. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [9]
10. **Keep an EU/UK divergence register and an adequacy contingency plan** — DUAA freedoms increase divergence even though adequacy runs to 2031. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [17]

- **Phase 0 — Gap assessment (now):** Map current processing to the amended UK GDPR/PECR; identify uses of legitimate interests, ADM, cookies, marketing and transfers affected by the DUAA. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Lawful bases & ADM:** Add recognised legitimate interests where apt; re-engineer significant-ADM systems to Arts 22A–22D with safeguards and the special-category gate. *Effort:* Medium–High.
- **Phase 2 — Complaints readiness (by 19 June 2026):** Build the electronic complaints route, 30-day acknowledgement SLA and outcome workflow. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 3 — PECR & marketing:** Reconfigure the CMP for new cookie exemptions; update soft opt-in rules; brief on the £17.5m/4% ceiling. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 4 — Transfers & children:** Re-paper UK transfer assessments to the "not materially lower" test; embed the children's higher-protection duty in DPbDD. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 5 — Assurance & monitoring:** Update DPIAs, RoPA, policies and training; maintain a commencement watch-list and EU/UK divergence register; monitor adequacy. *Effort:* Ongoing.

2. Where you rely on **recognised legitimate interests**, is the purpose within the statutory list, is necessity documented, and have you ensured it is **not** used for significant ADM? *([13][15].)*

5. Have you reconfigured your **cookie/CMP** setup for the new exemptions without over-claiming them? *([13][16].)*

7. Have you re-papered **UK transfer** risk assessments to the **"not materially lower"** test while preserving the EU standard for EU-origin data? *([10][13].)*
8. How is the **children's higher-protection** duty embedded in your DPbDD for services likely accessed by children? *([12][13].)*

title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)

text:
The **UK Children's Code** — formally the **Age-Appropriate Design Code (AADC)** — is a **statutory code of practice** prepared by the ICO under **section 123 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018)** and laid before Parliament under s.125 [1][2]. It sets **15 standards** that any provider of an "information society service" (ISS) **"likely to be accessed by children"** in the UK must apply when it processes children's personal data [10][11]. The Code came into force on **2 September 2020**, with a 12-month transition period, and has been **fully enforceable since 2 September 2021** [11][14]. It is not a new source of obligation so much as an authoritative interpretation of how the **UK GDPR and DPA 2018** apply to under-18s — the ICO must take it into account when exercising its enforcement powers, and courts and tribunals must take it into account where relevant [1][10].

This document builds on `uk-gdpr-foundations` (the UK consent age of **13** under DPA 2018 s.9) and `duaa-2025-detail`. It goes deep on the statutory basis; the **"likely to be accessed by children"** threshold; each of the **15 standards** (best interests, DPIAs, age-appropriate application, transparency, detrimental use of data, policies, **high-privacy default settings**, data minimisation, data sharing, geolocation, parental controls, **profiling off by default**, **nudge techniques**, connected toys/devices, online tools); **age assurance**; how the **DUAA 2025 children's duty** strengthens the position by putting a children's obligation on the face of UK GDPR Art. 25; and the interplay with the **Online Safety Act 2023** and **Ofcom's Protection of Children Codes** [5][8][11][15].

Three conclusions dominate. First, the Code's reach is **wide**: "likely to be accessed by children" is a lower bar than "aimed at" children, so most consumer-facing services — games especially — are caught [10]. Second, the DUAA has **hardened** the children's position: from 2026 there is an **express statutory duty** in Art. 25 to have regard to "children's higher protection matters", and conforming to the Code is the ICO's expected route to satisfying it [5][12][13]. Third, the Code (data-protection/privacy design) and the **Online Safety Act** (content-safety, Ofcom-regulated) are **distinct but complementary** regimes that both turn on a "likely to be accessed by children" test and both expect proportionate **age assurance** [11][15][16].

text:
- The Children's Code (AADC) is a **statutory code** under **DPA 2018 s.123**, laid before Parliament under s.125; it interprets how the UK GDPR/DPA 2018 apply to children and the ICO must take it into account in enforcement [1][2][10]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- It applies to **relevant ISS "likely to be accessed by children"** (under-18s) in the UK — a **lower threshold** than services "directed at" or "intended for" children [10][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- It sets **15 standards**, anchored on the **best interests of the child** as a primary consideration, and including **high-privacy default settings**, **data minimisation**, **geolocation off by default**, **profiling off by default**, and **no nudge techniques** that push children to weaken privacy [11]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
- The Code came into force **2 September 2020** and has been **enforceable since 2 September 2021** after a 12-month transition [11][14]. *(Fact — live-verified.)*
- The UK **age of consent** for ISS is **13** (DPA 2018 s.9); the Code applies to **all under-18s**, so it reaches children **above** the consent age too [3][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **DUAA 2025 (s.81)** inserts **UK GDPR Art. 25(1A)/(1B)** — an **express duty** on controllers providing an ISS likely to be accessed by children to consider **"children's higher protection matters"** in data-protection-by-design — strengthening and codifying the Code's expectations [5][12][13][17]. *(Legal obligation — DUAA commencement per `duaa-2025-detail`.)*
- **Age assurance** is central: the Code requires a **risk-based** approach — either establish age with a level of certainty appropriate to the data risks, **or** apply the standards to **all** users [11]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
- Enforcement uses the **ICO's ordinary UK GDPR/DPA 2018 powers** (assessment notices, enforcement notices, and fines up to **£17.5m or 4%** of global turnover); non-conformity with the Code is strong evidence of a breach of the underlying law [10][14]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The Code is **distinct from** the **Online Safety Act 2023**: the OSA (Ofcom-regulated) governs **content safety**, and its **Protection of Children Codes came into force 25 July 2025**; the two regimes overlap on "likely to be accessed by children" and age assurance but pursue different aims [8][15][16]. *(Legal fact — live-verified.)*

text:
*Shared terms (personal data, controller, processor, consent, ISS, special-category data, DPbDD, DPIA) are in `GLOSSARY.md` and carry over. Only Code-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Children's Code (AADC) | The ICO statutory code of practice under DPA 2018 s.123 setting 15 standards of age-appropriate design for relevant ISS likely to be accessed by children. Also called the Age-Appropriate Design Code. | [1][10][11] |
| Relevant information society service (ISS) | An ISS as defined for the UK GDPR/DPA, excluding certain preventive/counselling services; the class of service to which the Code and the s.9 consent rule attach. Online games, apps and websites are ISS. | [3][10] |
| Likely to be accessed by children | The Code's scope test: the possibility of the service being accessed by under-18s is **more probable than not**, judged on the nature and appeal of the service and evidence of its actual user base — a lower bar than "directed at" children. | [10][11] |
| Age assurance | The umbrella term for techniques used to establish or estimate a user's age or age range (self-declaration, age estimation, age verification, hard identifiers), applied proportionately to the data risks. | [11] |
| Children's higher protection matters | The matters a controller providing an ISS likely to be accessed by children must consider under UK GDPR Art. 25(1A)/(1B) (inserted by DUAA s.81): how to protect and support children, children's lower awareness of risks, and their differing needs at different ages and stages of development. | [5][17] |
| Best interests of the child | The primary consideration in designing services likely to be accessed by children (Standard 1), drawn from Article 3 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and reflected in the Code. | [11] |

text:
Children's data protection sat uneasily in a framework built for adults. GDPR **Recital 38** recognised that children "merit specific protection" because they may be less aware of the risks, and **Article 8** introduced a child-consent rule for ISS — but neither told designers *how* to build for children [4]. In the UK, DPA 2018 set the ISS consent age at **13** (s.9) and, unusually, **required the regulator to write a design code**: s.123 obliges the Information Commissioner to produce a code of practice on "standards of age-appropriate design" for relevant ISS likely to be accessed by children, and s.125 sets the Parliamentary procedure for laying and issuing it [1][2][3].

The ICO consulted and published the final Code in 2020. It **came into force on 2 September 2020**, the first age-appropriate design code laid under s.123/s.125, with a **12-month transition** so organisations could adapt; it has been fully in effect since **2 September 2021** [11][14]. The Code drew international attention and influenced comparable measures abroad. Since then, two developments have reshaped the landscape: the **Online Safety Act 2023**, which put content-safety duties on user-to-user and search services under Ofcom (its Protection of Children Codes came into force 25 July 2025) [8][15]; and the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025**, which — via s.81 — put an **express children's duty on the face of UK GDPR Art. 25**, aligning the primary law with what the Code already expected [5][12]. The ICO has said it will **revise and re-lay the Code** to reflect the DUAA and its updated children's-data guidance in due course [12][13].

text:
The Children's Code is a **statutory code of practice**, not a statute in itself. Its legal force is indirect but real: it interprets the **UK GDPR** and **DPA 2018** as they apply to children, and DPA 2018 requires the ICO to **take the Code into account** when exercising its functions (and courts/tribunals to take it into account where relevant to a question before them) [1][10]. A controller that does not conform to the Code is not automatically unlawful, but the ICO treats **non-conformity as strong evidence of a breach** of the underlying UK GDPR/DPA obligations it interprets [10][14].

The obligation stack for a service likely to be accessed by children is therefore:

1. **UK GDPR** — principles (Art. 5), lawful basis (Art. 6, incl. child consent under Art. 8 as modified), **data-protection by design and by default (Art. 25)**, and **DPIA (Art. 35)** — as assimilated under EUWA 2018 s.3 [4][9].
2. **DPA 2018** — s.9 (13-year ISS consent age), s.123 (duty to produce the Code), s.125 (procedure), and the ICO's enforcement powers [1][2][3].
3. **DUAA 2025 s.81** — inserts UK GDPR **Art. 25(1A)/(1B)**, an express duty to consider "children's higher protection matters" in DPbDD for ISS likely to be accessed by children, commenced as part of the DUAA Part 5 data-protection provisions (SI 2026/82; dates in `duaa-2025-detail`) [5][7][17].
4. **The Children's Code** — the 15 standards operationalising all of the above [11].

## Relevant Articles

*"Article" spans the UK GDPR, the DPA 2018 sections and the DUAA amendment as relevant.*

| Provision | Obligation (as relevant to the Children's Code) | Source |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------|--------|
| DPA 2018 s.123 | Requires the ICO to prepare an **age-appropriate design code** for relevant ISS likely to be accessed by children — the Code's statutory basis. | [1] |
| DPA 2018 s.125 | Procedure for issuing the Code (laid before Parliament; the ICO and courts must have regard to it). | [2] |
| DPA 2018 s.9 | Sets the UK ISS **child-consent age at 13** (modifying UK GDPR Art. 8(1)). | [3] |
| UK GDPR Art. 8 | Conditions for a child's consent to ISS; controller must make reasonable efforts to verify parental authorisation for younger children. | [4] |
| UK GDPR Art. 25 | **Data-protection by design and by default** — the anchor for high-privacy defaults and minimisation for children. | [4] |
| UK GDPR Art. 25(1A)/(1B) (DUAA s.81) | **Express duty** on controllers of ISS likely to be accessed by children to consider **"children's higher protection matters"** in DPbDD. | [5][17] |
| UK GDPR Art. 35 | **DPIA** required where processing is likely to result in a high risk — the ICO treats services likely to be accessed by children as normally requiring one (Standard 2). | [4][11] |
| UK GDPR Recital 38 | Interpretive anchor: children merit **specific protection** as they may be less aware of risks/consequences. | [4] |
| Online Safety Act 2023 | Separate content-safety regime (Ofcom) for user-to-user/search services likely to be accessed by children — complementary to, not part of, the Code. | [8] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals of the UK GDPR are retained as interpretive aids (see `gdpr-foundations`); they are not binding operative provisions.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| UK GDPR Recital 38 | Children merit **specific protection** with regard to their personal data, especially for marketing, profiling and services offered directly to a child — the core rationale for the Code. | [4] |
| UK GDPR Recital 58 | Information addressed specifically to a child should be in **clear, plain language** the child can easily understand (informs Standard 4, transparency). | [4] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** The Children's Code is a regulator's statutory code rather than a provision generating its own body of judicial interpretation, and there is no reported UK judgment squarely construing the Code's 15 standards. Enforcement to date has run through **ICO regulatory action and audits** rather than litigation, and the DUAA children's duty (Art. 25(1A)/(1B)) is too new to have been tested in court [5][10]. The general UK GDPR concepts the Code interprets (personal data, DPbDD) rest on the retained/assimilated case law noted in `uk-gdpr-foundations`. Early disputes are more likely to surface as ICO enforcement than as case law.
title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
legal_basis: Data Protection Act 2018 (esp. ss.123, 125, 9); UK GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as assimilated), esp. Arts. 8, 25, 35; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18) s.81

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).** The authoritative reading is the **ICO's** Children's-code guidance suite and its DUAA children's-data guidance, supported by DSIT/GOV.UK materials [10][11][12][13][14].

- **Scope is deliberately broad.** The ICO reads **"likely to be accessed by children"** as a lower bar than "aimed at" children: the question is whether the service's nature and appeal, and evidence of its actual users, make access by under-18s **more probable than not**. If children are unlikely to access the service (robustly evidenced, e.g. by effective age assurance), the Code may not bite — but the default assumption for consumer services is that it does [10][11]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **The child is under 18, not 13.** The Code protects **all under-18s**, so it applies to children who are **old enough to consent** (13+) as well as younger ones; the 13 threshold governs *consent* (DPA s.9), while the Code governs *design* for the whole 0–17 population, expecting age-band-appropriate treatment [3][10][11]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Best interests as the lens.** Standard 1 requires the **best interests of the child** to be a **primary consideration** in design — the ICO frames every other standard as an application of this principle, drawing on the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Conform-or-justify defaults.** Several standards (default settings, geolocation, profiling, data sharing) require **high-privacy/off-by-default** settings **"unless you can demonstrate a compelling reason"** taking account of the child's best interests — a documented-justification model rather than an absolute ban [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
- **The DUAA reinforces, it does not replace.** The ICO's position is that organisations **already conforming to the Children's Code should already satisfy** the new Art. 25(1A)/(1B) "children's higher protection matters" duty; the DUAA puts the expectation on the face of the primary law and the ICO updated its children's-data guidance (15 May 2026) to reflect it, with a revised Code to follow and be re-laid before Parliament [12][13]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Distinct from the Online Safety Act.** The ICO (data protection) and **Ofcom** (online safety) regulate different things — privacy-by-design versus content safety — but coordinate; both use a "likely to be accessed by children" test and both expect **proportionate age assurance**. Conforming to one does **not** discharge the other [15][16]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
legal_basis: Data Protection Act 2018 (esp. ss.123, 125, 9); UK GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as assimilated), esp. Arts. 8, 25, 35; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18) s.81

text:
- **Age assurance architecture.** Implement a **risk-based** age-assurance layer: either establish age/age-range with certainty proportionate to the data risks, or apply the Code's protections to **all** users. Options range from self-declaration (low assurance) through **age estimation** to **hard age verification**; escalate assurance with the risk, and **minimise** the identity data the assurance step itself collects (do not turn age-gating into a data-grab) [11]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
- **High-privacy defaults by construction.** Ship child accounts with **high-privacy defaults**, **geolocation off**, **profiling off**, social discovery/visibility off, and behavioural advertising off — changing them should require a deliberate, age-appropriate action, not a pre-ticked box [11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Data minimisation and separated choices.** Collect only what is needed for the element of the service the child is **actively and knowingly** engaged in, and give **separate** toggles for optional elements rather than an all-or-nothing bundle [11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **DPIA-first.** Treat a **DPIA** (see `dpia-methodology`) as the mandatory front door for any service likely to be accessed by children; it must cover differing ages/capacities and bake in Code conformance (Standard 2) [4][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **No dark patterns / nudges.** Do not use **nudge techniques** or deceptive design to push children to provide unnecessary data or lower protections; this overlaps with DSA Art. 25 and consumer law for services in those regimes (see `game-hosting-foundations`) [11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Connected devices.** For **connected toys/devices**, build in the tooling (clear information, controls, secure defaults) needed to conform, including at set-up when an adult may configure on the child's behalf [11]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
legal_basis: Data Protection Act 2018 (esp. ss.123, 125, 9); UK GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as assimilated), esp. Arts. 8, 25, 35; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18) s.81

text:
- **Controller/processor split.** The service provider (studio/app publisher) is typically the **controller** and bears the Code duties; cloud/hosting and age-assurance vendors are usually **processors** needing Art. 28 contracts (see `gdpr-foundations`). Age-assurance providers process potentially sensitive identity/biometric data — scrutinise their minimisation and retention [11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Data residency and transfers.** Children's data is ordinary personal data for transfer purposes; apply the UK transfer mechanisms (adequacy, IDTA/Addendum) — see `uk-transfers`. *(Legal obligation; cross-reference.)*
- **Retention and deletion.** Standard 8 (minimisation) implies **short retention** and prompt deletion/aggregation of children's data; hosting/log pipelines must support age-band-aware retention and honour deletion. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)* [11]
- **Age-assurance data isolation.** Store any hard identifiers collected for age verification **separately** from the service profile, encrypted, with tight access controls and minimal retention — the assurance purpose does not license general profiling [11]. *(Best practice.)*
title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
legal_basis: Data Protection Act 2018 (esp. ss.123, 125, 9); UK GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as assimilated), esp. Arts. 8, 25, 35; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18) s.81

text:
- **Games are the paradigm case.** The Code names **games** among the services it targets, and games are almost always **"likely to be accessed by children"**; treat a game as in-scope unless robust, evidenced age assurance shows otherwise [10][11]. This sits on top of the UK **13** consent age (DPA s.9) [3]. See `game-hosting-foundations` for the full games overlay. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Defaults for players.** Child players should get **high-privacy defaults**: geolocation off, profiling/behavioural-ad features off, friend/visibility discovery off, and voice/chat exposure minimised — with age-appropriate, non-nudging routes to change them [11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Engagement mechanics vs best interests.** Retention loops, streaks, autoplay, loot-box nudges and reward-based prompts to share more data are exactly the **nudge techniques** Standard 13 restricts for children; design against them and document the child's best interests [11]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **Overlap with OSA and DSA.** A game with chat/UGC also faces **Online Safety Act** children's-safety duties (Ofcom) and, in the EU, DSA Art. 28 minors' protections — reconcile age assurance and children's-risk assessments across all three (see `game-hosting-foundations`) [8][15]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Parental controls.** Where parental controls exist, give the child **age-appropriate information** that they are in place (Standard 11) — do not use them as covert monitoring [11]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
legal_basis: Data Protection Act 2018 (esp. ss.123, 125, 9); UK GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as assimilated), esp. Arts. 8, 25, 35; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18) s.81

text:
- **Profiling and recommender systems.** AI-driven **personalisation/recommendation** that profiles children is restricted: Standard 12 requires profiling to be **off by default** for children unless a compelling, best-interests-justified reason exists; content-recommender models trained on children's behaviour must respect this [11]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
- **Automated decisions about children.** Where AI makes **solely automated** decisions with significant effect about children, the UK GDPR Art. 22 regime (as recast by DUAA Arts. 22A–22D — see `duaa-2025-detail`) applies with heightened caution; the Code's best-interests lens and the new Art. 25 children's duty reinforce the need for human oversight and contestability for minors [5][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Age-estimation AI.** AI-based **age estimation** (e.g. facial age estimation) is itself high-risk processing: it may involve **biometric/special-category** data, needs a DPIA and a lawful basis, and must be minimised and accurate across ages and demographics to avoid discriminatory mis-gating [4][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Nudge/engagement AI.** Optimisation models that maximise engagement can amount to prohibited **nudge techniques** when they push children to over-share or weaken privacy; align model objectives with the child's best interests [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **AI Act overlap (EU-facing services).** UK-only services are outside the EU AI Act, but multi-territory services should note its Art. 5 protections against exploiting children's vulnerabilities and Art. 50 transparency (see `ai-act-foundations`, `game-hosting-foundations`). *(Editorial note.)*
title: UK Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code)
legal_basis: Data Protection Act 2018 (esp. ss.123, 125, 9); UK GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as assimilated), esp. Arts. 8, 25, 35; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18) s.81

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**. The 15 standards are the operational core; each is stated with its expectation.

**The 15 standards of the Children's Code** [11]:

1. **Best interests of the child** — make it a **primary consideration** in design and development. *(OBLIGATION as interpreted.)*
2. **Data protection impact assessments** — complete a **DPIA** covering differing ages/capacities and building in Code conformance. *(OBLIGATION — Art. 35.)*
3. **Age-appropriate application** — take a **risk-based** approach to recognising users' ages; establish age with proportionate certainty **or** apply the standards to all users. *(OBLIGATION.)*
4. **Transparency** — give **clear, child-friendly** privacy information at the point of use, in language a child can understand. *(OBLIGATION — Arts. 12–13.)*
5. **Detrimental use of data** — do **not** use children's data in ways shown to be **detrimental** to their wellbeing or that go against industry codes/regulatory provisions. *(OBLIGATION.)*
6. **Policies and community standards** — **uphold your own published** terms, policies and community standards for children's data. *(OBLIGATION.)*
7. **Default settings** — settings must be **"high privacy" by default** unless a compelling best-interests reason justifies otherwise. *(OBLIGATION.)*
8. **Data minimisation** — collect and retain only the **minimum** needed for the element the child is actively engaged in; offer **separate** choices. *(OBLIGATION — Art. 5(1)(c).)*
9. **Data sharing** — do **not** disclose children's data without a **compelling reason** in the child's best interests. *(OBLIGATION.)*
10. **Geolocation** — **off by default**; show an obvious sign when tracking is active; visibility-to-others defaults back to off each session. *(OBLIGATION.)*
11. **Parental controls** — if provided, give the child **age-appropriate information** about them. *(OBLIGATION as interpreted.)*
12. **Profiling** — **off by default** unless a compelling best-interests reason justifies otherwise. *(OBLIGATION.)*
13. **Nudge techniques** — do **not** nudge children to provide unnecessary data or weaken privacy protections. *(OBLIGATION.)*
14. **Connected toys and devices** — include tools to enable **conformance** with the Code. *(OBLIGATION.)*
15. **Online tools** — provide **prominent, accessible tools** for children to exercise their data-protection rights and report concerns. *(OBLIGATION.)*

**Cross-cutting actions:**

1. **Run a "likely to be accessed by children" assessment** for each service and record the conclusion and evidence. *(OBLIGATION.)* [10][11]
2. **Satisfy the DUAA Art. 25 children's duty** — document how "children's higher protection matters" are considered in DPbDD; conforming to the Code is the ICO's expected route. *(OBLIGATION.)* [5][12][13]
3. **Coordinate with Online Safety Act obligations** where the service has UGC/chat — align age assurance and children's-risk assessments, but treat the regimes separately. *(OBLIGATION.)* [15][16]
4. **Keep a children's-compliance watch-list** for the revised Code, updated ICO guidance and DUAA commencement. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [12]

text:
The **UK GDPR** is the United Kingdom's post-Brexit version of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. It was created by retaining the EU GDPR in domestic law under **section 3 of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018** and amending it (via the "DPPEC" EU-Exit Regulations 2019) so it operates in a UK-only context from 1 January 2021 [1][6]. It works **alongside the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018)**, which supplements it with exemptions, special-category conditions, law-enforcement and intelligence-services regimes, and the powers of the regulator [2][6].

This document assumes familiarity with `gdpr-foundations`; rather than restate the principles and lawful bases, it focuses on **what is different in the UK**: the constitutional basis, the UK GDPR/DPA 2018 division of labour, the key substantive divergences (notably the age of consent for online services, set at **13** by DPA 2018 s.9), the reforms introduced by the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA, c.18)**, and the **EU adequacy** position that permits EEA→UK data flows [3][4][9].

Three conclusions dominate. First, the UK framework is *substantially aligned* with the EU GDPR but is now **actively diverging** through the DUAA, which amends — but does not replace — the UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and PECR [7][8]. Second, **adequacy is secured**: the European Commission renewed its UK adequacy decisions on 19 December 2025, valid until 27 December 2031, having assessed the DUAA reforms [9]. Third, organisations operating in both the EU and UK must now track **two diverging rulebooks** rather than one.
title: UK GDPR: Foundations & Divergence from the EU GDPR

text:
- The UK GDPR is retained/assimilated EU law under **EUWA 2018 s.3**, operable domestically from 1 January 2021, and sits alongside the **DPA 2018** [1][2][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **DPA 2018 supplements** the UK GDPR (exemptions, Art. 9 conditions, law-enforcement and intelligence regimes, ICO powers) — the two must be read together [2][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **age at which a child can consent** to an information-society service is **13** in the UK (DPA 2018 s.9 modifying Art. 8(1)), versus the EU default of 16 [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18)** received Royal Assent on **19 June 2025** and is being **phased in between June 2025 and June 2026**; it amends the UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and PECR [4][7][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The DUAA introduces a new **"recognised legitimate interests"** lawful basis for specified public-interest purposes, liberalises **automated decision-making**, clarifies **scientific research**, adds duties on **children's online services** and **complaints handling**, and reconstitutes the regulator as the **Information Commission** with a new strategic framework [7][8]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **EU adequacy** for the UK, first granted on **28 June 2021** [10], was **renewed on 19 December 2025 to run to 27 December 2031**, following a technical extension in June 2025 — this keeps EEA→UK transfers free of additional safeguards [9][11]. *(Regulatory / legal.)*
- The **ICO** (transitioning to the Information Commission) is the UK supervisory authority; UK-based controllers deal with the ICO, not EU authorities [6][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Organisations subject to **both** regimes must manage **divergence**: the cores align, but consent age, ADM, recognised legitimate interests and future reforms differ. *(Editorial recommendation.)*

text:
When the UK left the EU, the EU GDPR ceased to apply directly. To avoid a legal vacuum, the **European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018** retained the GDPR in UK law [1]. The **Data Protection, Privacy and Electronic Communications (Amendments etc.) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019** ("DPPEC Regulations") then amended the retained text and the DPA 2018 so the framework functions domestically — for example, replacing EU institutions and cross-border mechanisms with UK equivalents [6]. From **1 January 2021** the UK operated the "UK GDPR" plus the DPA 2018 [6]. Following the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023, "retained EU law" was renamed **"assimilated law"** from 1 January 2024; the UK GDPR is assimilated direct legislation [1].

The UK has since pursued its own reform agenda. After earlier proposals lapsed, the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025** reached Royal Assent on 19 June 2025 and is being commenced in stages to June 2026 [4][8].

text:
The UK data-protection framework has three principal statutory pillars, read together:

1. **UK GDPR** — the retained/assimilated Regulation, carrying the principles (Art. 5), lawful bases (Art. 6), data-subject rights, controller/processor obligations and transfer rules, adapted for the UK [1][6].
2. **DPA 2018** — supplements the UK GDPR (Part 2), and separately governs law-enforcement processing (Part 3) and the intelligence services (Part 4); it also constitutes the regulator and its enforcement powers [2].
3. **DUAA 2025** — amends the above (and PECR), introducing targeted reforms rather than a new regime [4][7][8].

Because the UK GDPR's article numbering mirrors the EU GDPR, the `gdpr-foundations` article map applies in the UK **except** where the DPA 2018 or DUAA modifies it. The principal foundational modifications are set out below.

## Relevant Articles

| Provision | Effect in the UK | Source |
|-----------|------------------|--------|
| UK GDPR Art. 5–6 | Principles and lawful bases carry over from the EU GDPR (see `gdpr-foundations`). | [1] |
| UK GDPR Art. 8(1) (as modified) | Age of consent for information-society services reduced from 16 to **13**. | [3] |
| DPA 2018 s.9 | Modifies Art. 8(1) to set the 13-year threshold; disapplies for online preventive/counselling services. | [3] |
| DPA 2018 Sch. 1–4 | Conditions for special-category/criminal-offence data and exemptions. | [2] |
| DPA 2018 Part 3 | Law-enforcement processing regime (separate from UK GDPR). | [2] |
| UK GDPR Art. 6 (new basis) | DUAA adds a **"recognised legitimate interests"** basis for listed public-interest purposes (no balancing test for those purposes). | [4][7][8] |
| UK GDPR Art. 22 (as amended) | DUAA provides a more permissive framework for solely automated decisions with legal/similar effect, subject to safeguards. | [7][8] |

## Relevant Recitals

*The UK GDPR retains recitals as interpretive aids; see `gdpr-foundations` for the core recitals (26, 32, 39, 47). No UK-specific recitals are added, but DUAA provisions are construed against the Act's own provisions and explanatory materials rather than EU recitals.* Not Applicable (no distinct UK recitals). [1]

## Relevant Case Law

*EU case law decided before 31 December 2020 (e.g., Google Spain, Breyer, Nowak) is "retained/assimilated case law" and remains persuasive/binding on lower UK courts, subject to UK courts' power to depart. Post-2020 CJEU decisions are not binding in the UK.* [1]

**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).** The **ICO** publishes the authoritative UK guidance (Guide to the UK GDPR, plus DUAA-specific guidance and consultations) [6][7]. Key foundational positions:

- The UK GDPR and DPA 2018 **must be read together**; the ICO frames the DPA 2018 as supplementing the UK GDPR (e.g., exemptions, Art. 9 conditions) [6]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The DUAA **amends, and does not replace**, existing law; organisations already compliant with the UK GDPR have a foundation to build on, but must adjust for the new provisions as they commence [7][8]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The DUAA adds duties to **help complainants** (e.g., an electronic complaints route; acknowledge within 30 days; respond without undue delay) and to consider **children's needs** when designing online services likely to be used by children [7][8]. *(Legal obligation, per ICO summary.)*
- The regulator is being reconstituted as the **Information Commission** with a new strategic framework (a principal objective plus regard to innovation, competition and children's protection) [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

- **Dual-regime configuration** — systems serving both EU and UK users should be able to apply the correct rules per data subject's jurisdiction (e.g., 13 vs 16 consent age; ADM safeguards; recognised legitimate interests). *(Best practice.)*
- **Consent-age gating** — UK information-society services relying on a child's consent must gate at 13 and verify parental responsibility for under-13s (DPA 2018 s.9) [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **ADM safeguards** — where relying on the DUAA's more permissive automated-decision framework, implement the required safeguards (information, human intervention, contestation) [7][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Records & lawful-basis mapping** — add "recognised legitimate interests" as a distinct basis in the processing register where used, and document the qualifying purpose [7][8]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- Core security and privacy-by-design expectations mirror the EU GDPR (Arts. 25, 32) — see `gdpr-foundations` and `privacy-engineering-foundations`.

text:
This document details how the **UK GDPR** restricts transfers of personal data outside the United Kingdom, and the mechanisms available to make such transfers lawful. It is the UK counterpart to `gdpr-transfers` (which covers EU GDPR Chapter V): the architecture is deliberately parallel, but the UK operates its **own adequacy list**, its **own model contracts**, and — since **5 February 2026** — its **own statutory transfer test** [1][5][7].

The UK regime rests on the same three-tier logic as the EU's. A transfer is permitted if (a) the destination is covered by **UK adequacy regulations** — informally "**data bridges**" — made by the Secretary of State [15]; or (b) the exporter puts in place **appropriate safeguards**, principally the ICO's **International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA)** or the **UK Addendum** to the EU Standard Contractual Clauses [16]; or (c) a narrow **Article 49 derogation** applies [1]. Where a safeguard is used, the exporter must also carry out a risk assessment — the ICO's **Transfer Risk Assessment (TRA)**, now referred to in UK legislation as the **"data protection test"** [18].

Three UK-specific points dominate. First, the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA)** rebuilt the statutory basis for transfers: it **repealed** the old DPA 2018 transfer sections, inserted a new **Article 44A** approval framework, and set a single **"data protection test"** — protection in the destination must be **"not materially lower"** than under UK law — for both adequacy regulations and exporter assessments [5][6][18]. This wording replaces the EU's Schrems II standard of **"essentially equivalent"** and the ICO's former term "sufficiently similar" [11][15]. Second, the current **data bridges** include the EEA, the countries the UK carried over from the EU adequacy list, Gibraltar, the Republic of Korea, and — for the US — the **UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework** (live since 12 October 2023) [15][17][19]. Third, in the reverse direction, **EU→UK adequacy** was **renewed to 27 December 2031**, having been assessed against the DUAA reforms [21].
title: UK GDPR: International Data Transfers
legal_basis: UK GDPR (Chapter V, Arts. 44–50, as amended); Data Protection Act 2018; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c.18)

text:
- The **UK GDPR restricts transfers** of personal data to third countries and international organisations; the general principle (Art. 44) requires that the level of protection is **not undermined**, and applies to onward transfers [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **DUAA 2025 rebuilt the transfer regime**: it **repealed** DPA 2018 ss.17A–18, inserted a new **Article 44A** ("transfers approved by regulations"), and its transfer provisions (**s.85, Schedules 7–9**) came into force on **5 February 2026** via **SI 2026/82** [4][5][6][7]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- The DUAA sets a single statutory **"data protection test"**: the destination's standard of protection must be **"not materially lower"** than under UK law — replacing the EU/Schrems II threshold of **"essentially equivalent"** and the ICO's former "sufficiently similar" [5][6][15][18]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **UK adequacy regulations ("data bridges")** currently cover the EEA, the EU-legacy adequate countries (e.g. Andorra, Argentina, Canada (PIPEDA, commercial), Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Isle of Man, Israel, Japan (APPI, PIHBOs), Jersey, New Zealand, Switzerland, Uruguay), **Gibraltar**, the **Republic of Korea**, and the **US (UK Extension to the EU-US DPF)** [15][17]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Absent adequacy, the UK **appropriate safeguards** are principally the ICO **IDTA** (a standalone UK contract) or the **UK Addendum** to the EU SCCs, both issued under **s.119A DPA 2018** and laid before Parliament on **2 February 2022** [13][16]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Before relying on a safeguard, exporters must complete a **Transfer Risk Assessment (TRA)** — now the statutory **"data protection test"** — for which the **ICO's own risk-based TRA tool** is an alternative to (not a copy of) the EDPB's **Schrems II** transfer-impact methodology [18][23]. *(Regulatory interpretation / obligation.)*
- The **UK-US data bridge** (UK Extension to the EU-US DPF) lets UK exporters transfer to US importers **certified and listed** on the DPF List, under **Art. 45 UK GDPR**, without further safeguards — but only for FTC/DoT-eligible organisations and with special handling for sensitive/criminal-offence data [17][19][22]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The UK-US bridge is an **extension of the EU-US DPF** and therefore **contingent on that framework's continued validity**, which is under appeal (**Latombe**, C-703/25 P); keep an IDTA/Addendum fallback [9][12][17]. *(Legal obligation — live-verify.)*
- In the reverse direction, **EU→UK adequacy was renewed to 27 December 2031** after the Commission assessed the DUAA — but this is conditional and reviewable, making UK divergence a watch-item [21]. *(Regulatory / legal.)*

**In scope:** The UK GDPR restricted-transfer rules (Arts. 44–50 as assimilated and amended); the DUAA 2025 transfer reforms (new Art. 44A, the "data protection test", the repeal of DPA 2018 ss.17A–18); UK adequacy regulations / data bridges and the current list; the IDTA and the UK Addendum to the EU SCCs; the ICO Transfer Risk Assessment (TRA) and how it differs from the EU TIA; the UK-US data bridge and its dependence on the EU-US DPF; and EU→UK adequacy.

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Data bridge | UK government's informal term for a **UK adequacy regulation** — a Secretary of State determination that a country/territory/sector or international organisation provides protection **not materially lower** than UK law, permitting transfers without further safeguards. | [15][20] |
| Data protection test | The DUAA-introduced statutory standard for transfers: whether the destination's protection is **"not materially lower"** than under UK law. It governs both **adequacy regulations** (the Secretary of State's assessment) and the **exporter's own assessment** (the TRA) when relying on Art. 46 safeguards. | [5][6][18] |
| International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA) | The ICO's **standalone** UK Article 46 model contract, issued under s.119A DPA 2018; an alternative to the EU SCCs + UK Addendum. | [13][16] |
| UK Addendum | The ICO's **addendum** that bolts onto the EU SCCs (Decision (EU) 2021/914) so they can be relied on for UK restricted transfers. | [10][16] |
| Transfer Risk Assessment (TRA) | The UK exporter's assessment of whether the appropriate-safeguard mechanism will be effective given the destination's law and practice; since the DUAA it is referred to in legislation as the **"data protection test"**. | [18] |
| UK Extension to the EU-US DPF | The US-facing data bridge: an Art. 45 route allowing transfers to US organisations **certified to the UK Extension** and on the **DPF List**. | [17][19] |

text:
Before Brexit, UK transfers were governed by EU GDPR Chapter V and the Commission's adequacy decisions and SCCs. On assimilation, the UK "onshored" both the Chapter V text and the **then-existing EU adequacy decisions**, so day-one UK adequacy covered the same countries the EU recognised, plus the EEA [2][15]. Because the EU SCCs (2010/2021) were EU instruments, the UK needed its own model contracts: the ICO issued the **IDTA** and the **UK Addendum** under s.119A DPA 2018, laying them before Parliament on **2 February 2022** [13][16].

The transatlantic route followed the EU's. After Schrems II invalidated Privacy Shield, the US built a new redress architecture (Executive Order 14086, the Data Protection Review Court) that underpinned the Commission's **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** adequacy decision of 10 July 2023 [9][11]. The UK then negotiated a **UK Extension** to that framework; the Secretary of State made **SI 2023/1028**, and from **12 October 2023** UK organisations could transfer to UK-Extension-certified US importers under Art. 45 UK GDPR [8][17][19].

The most significant UK-only development is the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025**. Rather than tinker at the edges, its transfer provisions **replaced the statutory scaffolding**: DPA 2018 ss.17A–18 (adequacy regulations, standard clauses, safeguards) were repealed, a new **Article 44A** ("transfers approved by regulations") was inserted into the UK GDPR, and a single **"data protection test"** was adopted [4][5][6]. These provisions were commenced on **5 February 2026** by **SI 2026/82** [7]. The Commission had already assessed the DUAA when it **renewed EU→UK adequacy to 27 December 2031** in December 2025 [21].

text:
The UK transfer regime is a **layered permission system**, mirroring EU Chapter V but sitting in assimilated UK GDPR text as amended by the DUAA. The exporter must identify a valid gateway **before** transferring and be able to evidence it [1].

The layers, in order of preference:

- **Adequacy — UK adequacy regulations ("data bridges") (Art. 45, and new Art. 44A).** Transfer to a country/territory/sector or international organisation covered by regulations the Secretary of State has made applying the **data protection test**; no further authorisation needed [5][6][15].
- **Appropriate safeguards (Art. 46).** Where there is no data bridge: the **IDTA**, the **EU SCCs + UK Addendum**, UK Binding Corporate Rules (Art. 47), or approved codes/certifications — each providing enforceable rights and effective remedies, and each requiring a **TRA / data protection test** [6][16][18].
- **Derogations (Art. 49).** Exceptional, situation-specific gateways (explicit consent, contract necessity, important public interest, legal claims, vital interests, public register, compelling legitimate interests) — narrowly construed, not for routine bulk transfers [1][17].

The DUAA's mechanism is **amendment-in-place**: **Schedule 7** rewrites the general-processing transfer rules (inserting Art. 44A and recasting Art. 46), **Schedule 8** does the same for law-enforcement processing (DPA 2018 Part 3), and **Schedule 9** makes consequential amendments and — critically — **repeals DPA 2018 ss.17A, 17B, 17C and 18** and adjusts s.119A [5][6][13]. The consolidated effect must therefore be read in the **amended** UK GDPR and DPA 2018, not in the DUAA alone.

## Relevant Articles

*"Article" means the UK GDPR article (as assimilated and amended); DPA/DUAA provisions are named where relevant.*

| Provision | Obligation / effect | Source |
|-----------|---------------------|--------|
| UK GDPR Art. 44 | General principle — every transfer must comply with Chapter V so the level of protection is **not undermined**; applies to onward transfers. | [1] |
| UK GDPR Art. 45 | Transfers on the basis of **adequacy regulations** (data bridges) — no further safeguard needed. | [1][15] |
| UK GDPR **Art. 44A** (inserted by DUAA Sch. 7) | New framework for **transfers approved by regulations**: the Secretary of State may make adequacy regulations applying the **data protection test**; provides for monitoring/review. | [5][6] |
| UK GDPR Art. 46 (as amended) | Transfers subject to **appropriate safeguards** (IDTA; EU SCCs + UK Addendum; BCRs; codes; certification), each requiring the exporter to be satisfied the **data protection test** is met. | [1][6][16] |
| UK GDPR Art. 47 | **UK Binding Corporate Rules** — intra-group safeguard, approved by the ICO. | [1] |
| UK GDPR Art. 49 | **Derogations** for specific situations; exceptional and narrowly construed. | [1] |
| DPA 2018 **s.119A** | Power of the Commissioner to issue **standard data protection clauses** — the legal basis for the IDTA and the UK Addendum. | [13][16] |
| DPA 2018 ss.17A–18 (**repealed** by DUAA Sch. 9) | Former statutory basis for adequacy regulations, standard clauses and safeguards — now removed and re-based in the amended UK GDPR. | [5][6] |
| DUAA **s.85 + Schedules 7–9** | The operative transfer reforms; **in force 5 February 2026** (SI 2026/82). | [5][6][7] |

## Relevant Recitals

*The UK GDPR retains the EU GDPR's recitals as interpretive aids (Recitals 101–116 frame Chapter V — see `gdpr-transfers`) [1]. The DUAA does not add UK-specific recitals; its transfer provisions are construed against the **Act's own text, Schedules and Explanatory Notes** and ICO guidance rather than new recitals.* **Not Applicable** as a distinct UK set — interpretation of the "data protection test" rests on the statutory wording and ICO guidance [6][18].

## Relevant Case Law

*Pre-2021 CJEU transfer authority (notably **Schrems II**) is assimilated case law: it remains persuasive for the assimilated Chapter V concepts, subject to UK courts' power to depart, but the DUAA's "not materially lower" test is a **statutory** standard that displaces the EU "essentially equivalent" formula for UK purposes going forward [1][11]. Post-2020 CJEU decisions (including the **Latombe** litigation) are **not binding** in the UK but are **materially relevant** because the UK-US data bridge is built on the EU-US DPF [11][12].*

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Schrems II (DPC v Facebook Ireland & Schrems) | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-311/18, ECLI:EU:C:2020:559, 16 July 2020 | Invalidated Privacy Shield; upheld SCCs in principle but required a case-by-case assessment of destination law and **supplementary measures**. | Assimilated authority behind the UK TRA duty; the DUAA now expresses the assessment as the statutory **"data protection test"** [1][11]. |
| Latombe v Commission (appeal) | Court of Justice, **C-703/25 P**, appeal lodged 31 Oct 2025 (**pending**) | No ruling yet; seeks to set aside the General Court's dismissal of the challenge to the EU-US DPF adequacy decision. | If the EU-US DPF falls, the **UK-US data bridge** (an extension of it) is undermined — a live contingency for UK exporters [9][12]. |
| *(UK-domestic transfer case law)* | — | None yet on the DUAA transfer provisions (in force Feb 2026). | Not Applicable — early disputes likely surface first as ICO guidance/enforcement [6]. |

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).** The authoritative UK readings are the **ICO** international-transfers guidance suite (re-issued in January 2026 to reflect the DUAA) and **DSIT/GOV.UK** materials [14][15][16][17][18][20].

- **The "data protection test" is the new UK standard.** The ICO states that the UK assesses whether a destination has "a level of data protection that is **'not materially lower'** than provided for by UK law", and that "**prior to the Data (Use and Access) Act (DUAA), we referred to this standard as 'sufficiently similar'**" [15]. The ICO also confirms that a **Transfer Risk Assessment (TRA) "is now referred to in UK legislation as a 'data protection test'"** [18]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal standard.)*
- **Two applications, one test.** The same "not materially lower" threshold is applied by the **Secretary of State** when making adequacy regulations (Art. 44A) and by the **exporter** when relying on Art. 46 safeguards (the TRA) — a deliberately unified UK standard [5][6][18]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **The ICO TRA tool is an alternative approach, not the EDPB method.** The ICO offers its **own risk-based TRA tool** as an alternative route to the EDPB's Schrems II transfer-impact methodology; an exporter may use either, but the ICO tool is designed to be more proportionate and focuses on whether the transfer poses a real risk of harm to people, rather than on abstract legal equivalence [18][23]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Data bridges are living instruments.** The ICO frames adequacy regulations as reviewable; the US bridge in particular is **partial** (only the UK Extension to the DPF) and carries **special handling** for sensitive and criminal-offence data because the DPF "Choice" principle does not map exactly onto UK Art. 9 special categories [17][19]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **EU→UK adequacy is conditional.** The Commission renewed UK adequacy to **27 December 2031** having assessed the DUAA, but adequacy is periodically monitored and can be suspended if UK protection deteriorates — so DUAA divergence (including the softer-sounding transfer test) is a standing watch-item [21]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

## Adequacy — the current UK data-bridge list (Art. 45 / Art. 44A)

As of this document's date, UK adequacy regulations ("data bridges") cover, per the ICO's adequacy-regulations guidance [15]:

- **The EEA** — all EU member states plus **Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein** (full adequacy), and EU/EEA institutions, bodies, offices and agencies.
- **Full adequacy:** **Andorra, Argentina, Faroe Islands, Gibraltar, Guernsey, Isle of Man, Israel, Jersey, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea (South Korea), Switzerland, and Uruguay**.
- **Sector/partial adequacy:** **Canada** (only where PIPEDA applies — private-sector commercial activities) and **Japan** (only transfers to PIHBOs within the APPI).
- **Partial adequacy — United States:** only personal data transferred under the **UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework** (the "UK-US data bridge"), to importers certified and on the DPF List [17][19].

The **authoritative, current** list is the ICO adequacy-regulations page and the underlying regulations — consult them directly, because entries are added and reviewed over time [15]. The UK list **largely tracks, but is distinct from, the EU adequacy list**: the UK has since added its own determinations (e.g. the Republic of Korea and the US bridge) and could add or remove entries independently of the Commission's list [24].

- **Map UK flows first.** A restricted transfer occurs whenever UK personal data is sent to, **or made accessible from**, outside the UK — including remote admin/support access, global consoles, and CDN/edge nodes; "stored only in the UK" does not by itself avoid Chapter V [1][14]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **Record the mechanism in the RoPA.** Maintain per-flow records (destination, importer, data categories, mechanism — data bridge / IDTA / Addendum / derogation, TRA reference) so the basis is evidenced on demand (Art. 30) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Supplementary measures remain relevant under the TRA.** Where a TRA/"data protection test" identifies a gap, the exporter should add technical measures — strong **encryption in transit and at rest with UK/EEA-held keys**, effective **pseudonymisation**, split processing — mirroring the Schrems II logic even though the UK test is framed around risk of harm rather than abstract equivalence [11][18][23]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Jurisdiction-tag the data.** Because the UK test ("not materially lower") and the EU test ("essentially equivalent") differ, systems handling both UK- and EU-origin data should assess UK-origin exports against the UK test and EU-origin exports against the EU test, not a single global rule [5][18]. *(Best practice.)*

text:
- **Cloud usually means transfers.** Most hyperscale/SaaS hosting entails at least remote access from outside the UK; assess each provider's regions, sub-processors and support-access model against the UK regime [1][14]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Use UK paperwork for UK data.** Provider DPAs commonly offer the **EU SCCs + UK Addendum**; some offer the standalone **IDTA**. Either is valid, but the EU SCCs **alone are not** valid for UK restricted transfers — they need the Addendum [16]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **DPF-certified US importers.** Where a US provider is certified to the **UK Extension** and on the **DPF List**, transfers to it can rely on the **UK-US data bridge** (Art. 45) instead of an IDTA/Addendum — but verify the specific entity/scope and keep a fallback because the bridge is contingent on the EU-US DPF [17][19][22]. *(Legal obligation / editorial recommendation.)*
- **The exporter owns the TRA.** A provider can supply the contract, but the **customer, as exporter, owns the TRA / "data protection test"** and cannot delegate that judgement [16][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **EU→UK residency is lawful.** Hosting EU personal data in the UK remains lawful under EU→UK adequacy (to 27 December 2031) without additional safeguards, subject to that decision's continued validity [21]. *(Legal.)*

text:
- **Global player bases mean constant UK-out transfers.** Matchmaking, telemetry, anti-cheat, voice/chat and crash reporting frequently route UK player data (usernames, device IDs, IP addresses) to third-country servers or vendors; each needs a UK Chapter V basis — a data bridge, IDTA/Addendum + TRA, or a derogation [1][16][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Third-party SDKs.** Ads, analytics and crash SDKs often transfer to the US or elsewhere; inventory them and confirm the mechanism (UK-US bridge for a UK-Extension-certified US importer, otherwise IDTA/Addendum + TRA) [17][19]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Children's data raises the bar.** Where UK children are in scope, consent-based derogations are fragile and TRAs should weigh the heightened risk of harm; align with the ICO Children's Code and the DUAA children's higher-protection duty (see `duaa-2025-detail`, `uk-childrens-code`) [18]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Latency vs. residency.** Pressure to place edge servers near players must be reconciled with the transfer rules; prefer UK/adequate regions for identifiable player data where feasible. *(Editorial recommendation.)*

- **Training/inference transfers.** Sending UK personal data to a third-country model provider (or a model hosted abroad) for training or inference is a restricted transfer; a UK Chapter V basis **and** a TRA/"data protection test" are required in addition to a lawful basis [1][18]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **US model APIs.** Many foundation-model APIs are operated by US entities; check for **UK-Extension DPF certification** (Art. 45 route via the data bridge) or fall back to **IDTA/Addendum + TRA**, noting that clear-text prompt/response access by the importer weakens technical measures [17][19][23]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **The UK test may ease some AI transfers relative to the EU.** The "not materially lower" / risk-based TRA is intended to be more proportionate than the EU's "essentially equivalent" analysis, but the outcome is not automatically more permissive and remains untested — document the assessment either way [5][18][23]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
- **Minimise before transfer.** Pseudonymise/aggregate training data before export where possible, reducing both transfer risk and lawful-basis exposure [18]. *(Best practice.)*

Labels: **OBLIGATION** (the law requires) / **BEST PRACTICE** (standards/regulator consensus) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (this pipeline suggests).

1. **Inventory UK-out transfers** — build a transfer register within the RoPA (destination, importer, data categories, mechanism, TRA). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
2. **Prefer a data bridge** — where the destination is covered by UK adequacy regulations (or the US importer is UK-Extension-certified on the DPF List), rely on Art. 45 and record the basis. *(OBLIGATION.)* [15][17][19]
3. **Use UK safeguards for UK data** — the **IDTA**, or **EU SCCs + UK Addendum**; never rely on bare EU SCCs for UK restricted transfers. *(OBLIGATION.)* [16]
4. **Complete a TRA / "data protection test"** before relying on an Art. 46 safeguard — use the ICO's risk-based TRA tool **or** the EDPB method, and document the "not materially lower" conclusion. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [18][23]
5. **Add technical measures** where the TRA shows a gap (encryption with UK/EEA-held keys, pseudonymisation); if no measure suffices, do not transfer. *(OBLIGATION.)* [11][18]
6. **Treat Art. 49 derogations as exceptional** — do not use consent or contract necessity to justify routine, bulk transfers; document why a derogation genuinely applies. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
7. **Manage US flows actively** — verify UK-Extension certification and scope on the DPF List, handle sensitive/criminal-offence data per the factsheet, and keep an IDTA/Addendum fallback against the Latombe appeal. *(OBLIGATION + EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [12][17][19][22]
8. **Re-base to the DUAA regime** — confirm your transfer paperwork and TRAs reflect the amended UK GDPR (in force 5 Feb 2026), and separate UK-origin (UK test) from EU-origin (EU test) assessments. *(OBLIGATION.)* [5][7][18]
9. **Monitor EU→UK adequacy** — renewed to 2031 but reviewable; hold a contingency plan should divergence threaten it. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [21]

- **Phase 0 — Transfer discovery:** Map every UK-out flow, including remote access and sub-processors. *Depends on:* RoPA/data map. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Mechanism selection:** Assign a UK Chapter V basis per flow (data bridge → IDTA/Addendum → derogation); record rationale. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 2 — TRAs / data protection tests:** Run a TRA for each Art. 46 flow (ICO tool or EDPB method); implement technical measures where needed. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 3 — US flows:** Verify UK-Extension certification/scope on the DPF List; implement sensitive-data handling; prepare IDTA/Addendum fallback. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 4 — DUAA re-basing:** Confirm paperwork/TRAs reflect the amended UK GDPR (5 Feb 2026); split UK-origin vs EU-origin assessments. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 5 — Monitor & re-verify:** Track the Latombe appeal, EU→UK adequacy reviews, and new/updated data bridges; re-evaluate TRAs periodically. *Effort:* Ongoing.

1. Can you produce a register mapping each UK-out flow to a UK Chapter V mechanism? *(Arts. 44–46 [1].)*
2. For UK data under safeguards, do you use the **IDTA** or **EU SCCs + UK Addendum** (never bare SCCs)? *(s.119A [13][16].)*
3. Where a safeguard is used, where is the **TRA / "data protection test"**, and does it document the "not materially lower" conclusion? *(Art. 46 as amended; TRA [6][18].)*
4. For US flows, is the importer **UK-Extension-certified and on the DPF List**, and how is sensitive/criminal-offence data handled? *([17][19][22].)*
5. Do your transfer records reflect the **DUAA regime in force since 5 February 2026** (amended UK GDPR / new Art. 44A)? *([5][7].)*
6. How do you separate **UK-origin** (UK test) from **EU-origin** (EU "essentially equivalent") transfer assessments? *([5][11].)*
7. How do you monitor the **Latombe appeal** and the continued validity of the UK-US bridge? *([9][12].)*
8. How are **onward transfers** by importers controlled? *(Art. 44 [1].)*

text:
This document is the practical implementation companion to `eprivacy-foundations`. It translates the **Article 5(3) ePrivacy cookie rule** [1] and the GDPR conditions of consent [2] into concrete design requirements for **cookie banners, consent-management platforms (CMPs), tag governance and consent records**.

The controlling standard is settled. Storing or accessing information on a user's terminal equipment (cookies, and — per **EDPB Guidelines 2/2023** — pixels, URL/link decoration tracking, local storage, IP-only tracking and device fingerprinting) requires **consent** unless *strictly necessary* for a service the user requested [1][7]. That consent must meet the GDPR's **Art. 4(11)/Art. 7** conditions — freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, by clear affirmative action — as confirmed for cookies by **Planet49 (C-673/17)**: a **pre-ticked box is never valid consent**, whether or not the data is personal [2][3]. Regulators (EDPB, ICO) require **reject to be as easy as accept**, **granular** per-purpose control, **no consent before the choice is made**, and consent that can be **withdrawn as easily as given** [6][8][10].

Three live, contested frontiers dominate 2024–2026 practice. First, **"consent or pay" / "pay-or-okay"**: in **EDPB Opinion 08/2024** the Board held that large online platforms generally **cannot** obtain valid consent by offering only a binary "consent to tracking or pay" choice, and should offer a genuine, usually free, equivalent alternative [6]. Second, the **IAB Europe Transparency & Consent Framework (TCF)**: in **C-604/22** the CJEU ruled that a **TC String is personal data** and that IAB Europe is a (limited) **joint controller** for it — a finding the Brussels Market Court largely upheld on 14 May 2025 [4][11]. Third, **dark-pattern avoidance**, where data-protection, DSA and consumer law converge [9]. The document closes with an **implementation checklist** and a **CMP requirements specification**.
