text:
- **Consent before set:** no non-essential cookie/SDK/tracker may fire before the user gives valid consent; only *strictly necessary* technologies are exempt from Art. 5(3) [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Planet49 standard:** a pre-ticked checkbox, "continue browsing" or inactivity is **not** consent; consent must be active and unambiguous, personal data or not [3]. *(Case law.)*
- **GDPR conditions govern the quality of consent:** freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give (Arts. 4(11), 7) [2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Reject-as-easy-as-accept + granularity:** a "reject all" must be as prominent and low-friction as "accept all", with independent per-purpose toggles and no pre-selected non-essential options [6][8][10]. *(Regulatory interpretation grounded in obligation.)*
- **Art. 5(3) is technology-neutral:** EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 confirm it captures pixels, link decoration/URL tracking, local storage, unique identifiers, IP-only tracking and fingerprinting — not just HTTP cookies [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **"Consent or pay":** per EDPB Opinion 08/2024, large online platforms generally cannot rely on a binary consent-or-pay wall; a real (usually free) equivalent alternative is expected [6]. *(Regulatory interpretation — contested; under legal challenge.)*
- **TCF / TC String:** the CJEU held in C-604/22 that a TC String is **personal data** and IAB Europe a **joint controller** for creating/encoding it (not for downstream ad processing); upheld by the Brussels Market Court on 14 May 2025 [4][11]. *(Case law.)*
- **"Strictly necessary" is narrow:** it means necessary to deliver the service the *user* requested (e.g. session, load-balancing, security, consent-state) — **not** analytics or advertising [1][7][10]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Dark patterns are unlawful across regimes:** deceptive consent UX breaches GDPR fairness (EDPB Guidelines 03/2022) and overlaps with the DSA and consumer law [9]; empirical study shows "reject all" is rarely as easy as "accept all" and that design nudges consent [13]. *(Regulatory interpretation / academic.)*
- **Reform watch:** the Digital Omnibus (Nov 2025) proposes moving cookie rules into the GDPR with machine-readable/browser consent signals — a **proposal only**; the Directive and PECR remain in force [12]. *(Regulatory — proposal.)*

text:
*Shared terms (consent, controller, personal data, dark pattern) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only terms specific to cookie-consent implementation are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Consent-management platform (CMP) | A tool that presents consent choices to users, records the decision, and signals it to tags/vendors so that non-essential technologies fire only with consent. | [7][10] |
| Strictly necessary | An Art. 5(3) exemption: storage/access essential to provide the information-society service *explicitly requested by the user* (e.g. session state, security, load-balancing, consent-preference storage). Analytics and advertising are **not** strictly necessary. | [1][10] |
| Cookie wall / "take-it-or-leave-it" | Blocking access to a site/service unless the user consents to non-essential cookies, leaving no genuine choice; treated as invalidating "freely given" consent. | [6][8] |
| Consent or pay ("pay-or-okay") | A model offering users a binary choice: consent to tracking-based advertising, or pay a fee for a tracking-free version. | [6] |
| Transparency & Consent Framework (TCF) | IAB Europe's industry standard for capturing and transmitting users' consent/objection signals across the online-advertising (RTB) supply chain. | [4][11] |
| TC String (Transparency & Consent String) | The encoded character string produced under the TCF recording a user's consent/objection preferences; held to be **personal data** in C-604/22. | [4] |
| Link decoration / URL tracking | Appending identifiers to URLs to track users across pages/domains; within Art. 5(3) per EDPB Guidelines 2/2023. | [7] |
| Global Privacy Control (GPC) / browser signal | A machine-readable, automated signal by which a user expresses a consent/objection preference at browser or device level. | [12] |

text:
The 2009 amendment (Directive 2009/136/EC) reshaped Art. 5(3) from a notice-and-opt-out rule into a **consent** rule for storing or accessing information on terminal equipment [1]. When the GDPR replaced Directive 95/46/EC in 2018, the ePrivacy consent standard was read as **GDPR-standard consent** (Art. 4(11)) [1][2]. The **Planet49** judgment (2019) then removed any doubt that a **pre-ticked box** is invalid and that this holds regardless of whether the stored/accessed data is personal [3].

Two forces have shaped the implementation landscape since. First, the ad-tech industry converged on the **IAB Europe TCF** to manage consent signalling for real-time-bidding advertising; the Belgian DPA's 2022 decision, the CJEU's 2024 ruling in **C-604/22** and the Brussels Market Court's **14 May 2025** judgment together clarified that the **TC String is personal data** and that the framework operator bears controller responsibility for it [4][11]. Second, platforms responded to tighter enforcement by deploying **"consent or pay"** walls, prompting the **EDPB's Opinion 08/2024** and a wave of national scrutiny and litigation [6].

Meanwhile the regulatory reading of *what counts as a tracker* broadened: **EDPB Guidelines 2/2023** (adopted October 2024) confirmed Art. 5(3) reaches well beyond cookies to pixels, URL/link tracking, local processing, unique identifiers and IP-only tracking [7]. Enforcement has been substantial — national authorities (notably France's CNIL) issued nine-figure cookie-related fines through 2025 — reinforcing that consent UX is a front-line compliance risk.

text:
The obligation is **statutory**: Art. 5(3) of Directive 2002/58/EC (as amended) prohibits storing or gaining access to information on a user's terminal equipment **unless** the user "has given his or her consent, having been provided with clear and comprehensive information", subject to a narrow exemption where storage/access is "strictly necessary" for a service the user "explicitly requested" [1]. Because ePrivacy is a **Directive**, the operative duty arises under national transposition — in the UK, **PECR 2003 reg. 6** [5].

The **meaning and conditions of consent** are supplied by the GDPR: Art. 4(11) (definition) and Art. 7 (conditions — demonstrability, no detriment to withdrawal, withdrawal as easy as giving, freely given assessed with regard to conditionality) [2]. Recital 32 GDPR states expressly that silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity do **not** constitute consent [2].

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| ePrivacy Art. 5(3) | Consent (with prior clear information) required before storing/accessing information on terminal equipment; exemption only where strictly necessary for a service the user explicitly requested. | [1] |
| GDPR Art. 4(11) | Consent means a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication by a statement or clear affirmative action. | [2] |
| GDPR Art. 7(1) | The controller must be able to **demonstrate** that consent was given (consent records). | [2] |
| GDPR Art. 7(3) | The right to **withdraw** consent at any time; withdrawal must be **as easy as** giving consent. | [2] |
| GDPR Art. 7(4) | "Freely given" — account is taken of whether service provision is conditioned on consent not necessary for that service (conditionality/bundling). | [2] |
| PECR 2003 reg. 6 | UK transposition of Art. 5(3): consent + information before storing/accessing information on terminal equipment; strictly-necessary exemption. | [5] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals aid interpretation but are not binding operative provisions.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| ePrivacy Recital 25 | Cookies can be legitimate (e.g. analysing service effectiveness) but users must receive clear information and the opportunity to refuse. | [1] |
| ePrivacy Recital 66 (2009/136/EC) | Reinforces that storing/accessing information requires consent, the user having been given clear and comprehensive information. | [1] |
| GDPR Recital 32 | Consent by clear affirmative act; pre-ticked boxes, silence or inactivity do not amount to consent; granularity for distinct purposes. | [2] |
| GDPR Recital 43 | Consent is not freely given where there is a clear imbalance, or where separate consents cannot be given for separate processing operations (bundling). | [2] |

## Relevant Case Law

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Planet49 | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-673/17, 1 Oct 2019, ECLI:EU:C:2019:801 | A **pre-ticked checkbox** is not valid consent for storing/accessing cookies; the standard applies whether or not the information is personal data; users must receive information including cookie duration and third-party access. | Sets the consent standard for cookies and CMP design [3]. |
| IAB Europe | CJEU (Fourth Chamber), C-604/22, 7 Mar 2024, ECLI:EU:C:2024:214 | A **TC String is personal data** where it can be combined (e.g. with an IP address) to identify a user; IAB Europe is a **joint controller** for recording consent preferences in the TC String (but not for members' subsequent ad processing). | Governs TCF/CMP deployments and RTB consent signalling [4]. |
| IAB Europe (national follow-on) | Brussels Market Court (Cour d'appel de Bruxelles), 14 May 2025, case 2022/AR/292 | Largely **upheld** the Belgian DPA: TC Strings are personal data; IAB Europe is joint controller for creating/encoding TC Strings only; €250,000 fine and GDPR infringements confirmed. | Applies C-604/22 domestically; confirms TCF compliance obligations [11]. |

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 (technical scope of Art. 5(3)):** Art. 5(3) is technology-neutral and captures pixels, tracking links/URL decoration, local storage, cached identifiers, IP-only tracking and device fingerprinting — three cumulative elements ("information", "terminal equipment", "gaining access/storage") determine applicability [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 (consent):** consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; **cookie walls** that condition access on consent are, as a rule, not "freely given"; consent bundled across purposes is invalid; the controller must keep records and enable easy withdrawal [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **EDPB Opinion 08/2024 (consent or pay):** for **large online platforms**, a binary "consent to behavioural advertising or pay" model will in most cases **not** yield valid consent; controllers should offer an **equivalent alternative** that does not entail a fee (e.g. advertising with less or no personal-data processing). Personal data is not a tradeable commodity; fees must not make users feel *compelled* to consent. Free choice is assessed against **conditionality, detriment, imbalance of power and granularity** [6]. *(Regulatory interpretation — contested; see Concerns.)*
- **EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 (deceptive design patterns):** consent interfaces that nudge, obstruct, or mislead ("dark patterns") breach the GDPR **fairness** principle (Art. 5(1)(a)); examples include asymmetric accept/reject buttons, hidden reject options and repeated re-prompting [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ICO (UK):** cookie consent requires **GDPR-standard consent**; "strictly necessary" is read **narrowly** and does not cover analytics or advertising; **"reject all" must be as easy as "accept all"**; the ICO enforces PECR alongside the UK GDPR [10]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Reform status:** the **Digital Omnibus** proposal (Nov 2025) would move cookie rules into the GDPR (new Arts. 88a/88b), add machine-readable/browser-level consent signalling, a single-click refusal and a bar on re-prompting for the same purpose within six months — but it is a **proposal**; the Directive and PECR remain in force [12]. *(Regulatory interpretation — proposal only.)*

text:
- **Prior blocking (consent-before-set):** the CMP must **block** non-essential tags, scripts, SDKs, pixels and storage writes until a valid consent signal exists; "block-then-unblock on consent" — never "load-then-delete" [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Server- and client-side scope:** Art. 5(3) applies to *any* read/write of terminal-equipment information, including **server-side tagging**, SDK reads, `localStorage`/`IndexedDB`, cache-based identifiers and fingerprinting; gating must cover these, not only document.cookie [7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Granular architecture:** implement independent purpose categories (e.g. strictly necessary [always on, no toggle], functional/preferences, analytics/measurement, advertising/targeting) with per-category (and where feasible per-vendor) toggles, all defaulting **off** for non-essential [2][8]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Symmetric controls:** first-layer **"Accept all"** and **"Reject all"** buttons of equal prominence, styling and click-cost; do not hide "reject" behind a second layer or greyed styling [6][10]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Consent record schema:** capture and retain, per decision — a consent ID, timestamp, the specific purposes/vendors consented to or refused, the consent-string/version, the UI/text version presented, and the collection mechanism — to satisfy Art. 7(1) demonstrability [2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Withdrawal parity:** provide a persistent, easily reachable control (e.g. a footer link or floating icon) to re-open preferences and **withdraw** as easily as consent was given; on withdrawal, stop the processing and delete/expire the affected cookies [2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **TCF specifics:** if deploying the IAB TCF, treat the **TC String as personal data** and IAB Europe as a **joint controller** for its creation — meaning joint-controller arrangements, transparency and a valid legal basis for the string itself, distinct from downstream processing [4][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Browser signals (forward-looking):** design CMPs to be capable of reading/honouring automated signals (e.g. GPC), anticipating the Digital Omnibus Art. 88b direction — but do not treat unadopted rules as binding [12]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: Cookie Consent: Implementation & Consent Management
legal_basis: Directive 2002/58/EC Art. 5(3) (as amended by 2009/136/EC); Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Arts. 4(11), 7; PECR 2003 reg. 6

text:
- **CDN and edge features:** CDNs and edge platforms may set device storage (e.g. load-balancing, bot-management, A/B or analytics cookies). Classify each: load-balancing/security are typically strictly necessary; analytics/experimentation are not and must be gated [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Server-side / first-party tagging:** relocating tags to a first-party server endpoint does **not** exempt them from Art. 5(3) where they still read/write terminal-equipment information or set identifiers; gate them on consent [7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Consent-record storage:** consent logs are themselves personal data (they link an identifier to choices) and must be stored securely with a defined retention period and access controls; host them so they are producible on regulator or data-subject request [2]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **Controller responsibility for third-party tags:** the site operator remains responsible for third-party tags it deploys; use tag-manager governance, allow-lists and contractual controls over vendors [4][10]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: Cookie Consent: Implementation & Consent Management
legal_basis: Directive 2002/58/EC Art. 5(3) (as amended by 2009/136/EC); Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Arts. 4(11), 7; PECR 2003 reg. 6

text:
- **Analytics/ads/attribution SDKs:** mobile and console games routinely embed analytics, advertising and attribution SDKs (e.g. IDFA/GAID reads, install attribution) that store/read device information and fall within Art. 5(3); they must not initialise before consent [1][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Consent in constrained UIs:** in-game and TV/console interfaces still require a genuine, granular, symmetric consent flow; a "press A to continue" that bundles tracking consent is invalid on Planet49/EDPB reasoning [3][8]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Children:** games likely accessed by children face heightened scrutiny (see `gdpr-foundations`, `uk-gdpr-foundations`, Children's Code); default tracking off and avoid nudging minors toward consent [9]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **Cross-ref:** in-game/telemetry SDK gating is also covered at foundational level in `eprivacy-foundations` (Game Hosting Considerations). *(Cross-reference.)*

text:
- **Consent is the collection gate for AI personalisation:** where behavioural data captured via cookies/SDKs feeds recommendation, ad-targeting or other ML models, a valid **Art. 5(3) consent** is required for the *collection layer*, in addition to a GDPR lawful basis for downstream training/inference [1][2]. Consent is frequently the **binding constraint**. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **"Consent or pay" and profiling:** EDPB Opinion 08/2024 targets exactly the behavioural-advertising/profiling use case that powers ad-tech ML; a binary pay-wall generally cannot validly consent users into large-scale profiling [6]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **RTB and TC Strings as AI inputs:** TC Strings and bid-stream data flowing into ad-tech models are personal data; C-604/22 confirms controller responsibility attaches to the consent-signal layer [4]. *(Case law.)*
- **AI-generated consent UX:** using AI to optimise banner design toward higher acceptance risks producing **dark patterns** breaching the fairness principle; optimise for comprehension and genuine choice, not consent rate [9]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: Cookie Consent: Implementation & Consent Management

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Inventory every read/write of terminal-equipment information** — cookies, local/session storage, pixels, SDKs, fingerprinting, tracking URLs — and classify each as *strictly necessary* or *consent-required*. Document the necessity rationale for each "strictly necessary" call. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][7]
2. **Enforce consent-before-set** — block all non-essential technologies until a valid consent signal exists; verify with network inspection that nothing non-essential fires on first load. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][10]
3. **Design a symmetric, granular first layer** — equal-prominence "Accept all" / "Reject all"; per-purpose toggles defaulting off; no pre-ticked non-essential boxes; clear, plain-language purpose descriptions. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [2][8][10]
4. **Do not deploy cookie walls** (and, for large platforms, avoid binary consent-or-pay without a genuine equivalent alternative). *(OBLIGATION per EDPB.)* [6][8]
5. **Record consent to Art. 7(1) standard** and provide **withdrawal parity** via a persistent control. *(OBLIGATION.)* [2]
6. **Govern the TCF deployment** — if using IAB TCF, put joint-controller terms in place, treat the TC String as personal data, and confirm CMP certification/version. *(OBLIGATION.)* [4][11]
7. **Audit for dark patterns** — remove asymmetric buttons, confirmshaming, obstruction and nudging; align with EDPB Guidelines 03/2022 and DSA/consumer expectations. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [9]
8. **Interpret "strictly necessary" narrowly** — never classify analytics or advertising as strictly necessary. *(OBLIGATION per ICO.)* [10]
9. **Track reform** — monitor the Digital Omnibus (Arts. 88a/88b, browser signals) without pre-implementing unadopted rules. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [12]

- [ ] Consent-before-set enforced; verified by network inspection that nothing non-essential fires on first load.
- [ ] First layer offers **equal-prominence** "Accept all" and "Reject all" (no buried/greyed reject).
- [ ] Granular per-purpose (and where feasible per-vendor) toggles, all non-essential **off by default**; no pre-ticked boxes.
- [ ] No cookie wall; any consent-or-pay reviewed against EDPB Opinion 08/2024 (equivalent, usually free, alternative).
- [ ] Plain-language, layered information (purposes, vendors, durations, third-party access) before consent.
- [ ] Consent records captured (ID, timestamp, purposes/vendors, string/version, UI version) and retained securely.
- [ ] Persistent withdrawal control; withdrawal stops processing and expires/deletes affected cookies.
- [ ] TCF (if used): joint-controller arrangement, TC-String legal basis, certified CMP/version.
- [ ] Dark-pattern audit passed (symmetry, no confirmshaming/obstruction/nudging/re-prompting).
- [ ] "Strictly necessary" classifications documented and defensible (analytics/ads excluded).
- [ ] Reform watch-list: Digital Omnibus Arts. 88a/88b and browser-signal readiness.

**CMP requirements specification (hand to vendor/build team):** (a) prior blocking of all non-essential technologies incl. server-side/SDK; (b) configurable granular purpose taxonomy, off-by-default; (c) symmetric accept/reject at first layer; (d) tamper-evident consent-record store meeting Art. 7(1) with export; (e) persistent withdrawal/re-consent control with parity; (f) IAB TCF certification and current framework/GVL version if TCF is used; (g) capability to read/honour automated browser signals (e.g. GPC); (h) audit/reporting for consent rates and tag-gating compliance; (i) versioning of banner text/UI for evidential purposes.

legal_basis: COM(2025) 836 (Digital Omnibus on AI, adopted) and COM(2025) 837 (Digital Omnibus Regulation, proposed); amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Directive 2002/58/EC, Regulation (EU) 2023/2854

text:
The **"Digital Omnibus"** is the European Commission's late-2025 digital-simplification package, tabled on **19 November 2025** as part of its 2025 work-programme simplification agenda [6][9][10]. It is not a single instrument but a **package of two separate legislative proposals**, and the single most important compliance point is that **they now have different legal status** [9][10].

The first strand — the **Digital Omnibus on AI** (COM(2025) 836; procedure 2025/0359(COD)) — amends the **AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)** and has been **formally ADOPTED**: the European Parliament approved it in plenary on **16 June 2026** (423–57–174) and the Council gave final green light on **29 June 2026**; it enters into force on the **third day after Official Journal publication** [7][8][9]. It postpones the high-risk obligations (to **2 December 2027** for stand-alone Annex III systems and **2 August 2028** for AI embedded in regulated products), postpones AI-content marking/transparency to **2 December 2026** for systems already on the market, and adds a new **Article 5 prohibition on "nudifier"/non-consensual intimate-image and CSAM generators** [7][9]. These AI-specific effects are detailed in `ai-act-foundations` and `ai-act-high-risk`; this document cross-references them and does not restate the high-risk mechanics.

The second strand — the **Digital Omnibus Regulation** (COM(2025) 837; procedure 2025/0360(COD)) — is the **data-law** simplification proposal and remains **a PROPOSAL, not law** [10]. It would, among other things, **move the cookie-consent rules out of the ePrivacy Directive and into the GDPR**, expand the list of consent-exempt processing, introduce one-click / browser-level consent valid for six months, add a GDPR "legitimate interest" basis for AI training, consolidate the **Data Act** (absorbing the Data Governance Act, Open Data Directive and Free Flow of Non-Personal Data Regulation), and streamline DPIAs and breach reporting [10]. Because this strand is unadopted, **the ePrivacy Directive and national laws such as PECR remain fully in force** and organisations must **not** pre-implement the proposed cookie regime [3][10]. This document is the deep-dive deferred from `eprivacy-foundations` on the cookie-rule migration.

text:
- The **Digital Omnibus** (tabled 19 Nov 2025) is a **package of two proposals**, not one law: a **Digital Omnibus on AI** (COM(2025) 836) and a broader **Digital Omnibus Regulation** on data (COM(2025) 837) [6][9][10]. *(Regulatory fact.)*
- **ADOPTED — LAW:** the **Digital Omnibus on AI** was approved by the **European Parliament on 16 June 2026** and the **Council on 29 June 2026**; it enters into force on **OJ publication + 3 days** [7][8][9]. *(Legal fact — adopted.)*
- The AI strand **postpones high-risk application** to **2 December 2027** (stand-alone Annex III) and **2 August 2028** (AI embedded in regulated products), and postpones **AI-content marking** to **2 December 2026** for systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 [7][9]. *(Legal obligation — adopted; detailed in `ai-act-high-risk`.)*
- The AI strand adds a **new Article 5 AI Act prohibition** on AI generating **non-consensual intimate/sexual imagery ("nudifiers") and child sexual abuse material** [7][9]. *(Legal obligation — adopted.)*
- **PROPOSED — NOT LAW:** the **Digital Omnibus Regulation** would **move cookie-consent rules from the ePrivacy Directive into the GDPR**, expand consent exemptions, and allow **one-click / browser-level consent valid for six months** — but it is **still in the ordinary legislative procedure** [10]. *(Proposal only.)*
- The data strand would also add a GDPR **"legitimate interest" basis for AI training/operation** (subject to conditions) and **streamline DPIAs and breach reporting** — again, **proposal only** [10]. *(Proposal only.)*
- The data strand would **consolidate the Data Act**, merging the **Data Governance Act, Open Data Directive and Free Flow of Non-Personal Data Regulation** into a restructured Data Act, with cloud-switching exemptions for small businesses — **proposal only** [4][5][10]. *(Proposal only.)*
- **Do not pre-implement the data strand.** Until it is adopted, the **ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC) and PECR remain in force**; consent-before-set for non-essential cookies still applies [3][10]. *(Editorial recommendation grounded in current law.)*

text:
During 2025 the Commission launched a **digital-simplification agenda** in its work programme, aimed at reducing administrative burden and improving coherence across the EU's digital rulebook (GDPR, ePrivacy, the AI Act, the Data Act and the cybersecurity acquis) [6][9][10]. To prepare, it ran a **call for evidence from 16 September to 14 October 2025**, seeking views on the data acquis, **cookies and other tracking technologies**, cybersecurity incident reporting, smooth application of the AI Act, and electronic identification/trust services [10].

On **19 November 2025** the Commission tabled the package as **two distinct legislative proposals** [9][10]:

- the **Digital Omnibus on AI** — **COM(2025) 836**, procedure **2025/0359(COD)** — amending the AI Act and the civil-aviation Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 [6][9]; and
- the **Digital Omnibus Regulation** — **COM(2025) 837**, procedure **2025/0360(COD)** — restructuring and simplifying the **data** acquis [10].

The two strands then **diverged procedurally**. The AI strand moved quickly: Council general approach 13 March 2026, trilogue agreement 7 May 2026, Coreper 13 May 2026, IMCO/LIBE committees 2 June 2026, **Parliament plenary 16 June 2026**, and **Council final adoption 29 June 2026** [7][8][9][11]. The data strand advanced only through advisory stages by this document's date — the **European Economic and Social Committee opinion (18 March 2026)** and the **Committee of the Regions opinion (7 May 2026)** — and had **not** been adopted by the co-legislators [10].

The cookie-migration idea did not arise in a vacuum. The 2017 **ePrivacy Regulation** proposal, intended to replace the Directive, stalled for years and was ultimately **withdrawn** in 2025 [12][14]; the Digital Omnibus is the Commission's alternative route — folding cookie rules into the GDPR rather than enacting a standalone ePrivacy Regulation (see `eprivacy-foundations`) [10][14].
title: The EU Digital Omnibus: Simplification Package (2025–2026)
legal_basis: COM(2025) 836 (Digital Omnibus on AI, adopted) and COM(2025) 837 (Digital Omnibus Regulation, proposed); amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Directive 2002/58/EC, Regulation (EU) 2023/2854

text:
The Digital Omnibus operates by **amendment**: neither strand is a free-standing new regime; each edits existing instruments. Their legal status must therefore be read against the instruments they modify.

**Strand 1 — Digital Omnibus on AI (ADOPTED / LAW).** COM(2025) 836 amends **Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)** [1] and **Regulation (EU) 2018/1139**. Having been approved by the **European Parliament (16 June 2026)** and the **Council (29 June 2026)**, it is an **adopted** amending Regulation that enters into force on the **third day after Official Journal publication** [7][8][9]. Its principal legal effects (LAW, subject to OJ publication):

- **Postponed high-risk application** — stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems to **2 December 2027**; AI embedded as safety components in Annex I regulated products to **2 August 2028** [7][9]. *(Detailed in `ai-act-high-risk`.)*
- **Postponed AI-content marking (Art. 50)** — to **2 December 2026** for systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 [9].
- **New Art. 5 prohibition** — AI practices generating **non-consensual intimate/sexual content ("nudifiers") and child sexual abuse material** [7][9].
- **Targeted simplifications** — a simplified, proportionate **registration** obligation for non-high-risk systems; reinstated **strict-necessity** standard for processing special-category data for bias correction; extended simplified **documentation** for medium-sized companies; reinforced **AI Office** powers; and removal of AI-enabled **machinery** products from direct high-risk applicability (handled instead via the Machinery Regulation) [9].

**Strand 2 — Digital Omnibus Regulation (PROPOSED / NOT LAW).** COM(2025) 837 is a **proposal** amending the **GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)** [2], the **ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC)** [3], the **Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854)** [4] and related data instruments including the **Data Governance Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/868)** [5]. As a proposal in the ordinary legislative procedure (2025/0360(COD)), it creates **no obligations and changes no existing rule** until adopted [10]. Its principal **proposed** changes:

- **Cookie-consent migration** — move the Art. 5(3) consent rule from the **ePrivacy Directive into the GDPR**, and **expand the list of processing activities exempt from consent**; consent nonetheless remains the **primary criterion** for accessing information on a user's device [3][10].
- **One-click / browser-level consent** — enable users to give **one-click consent valid for six months** or to set **browser/system-level saved preferences** [10].
- **GDPR "legitimate interest" for AI** — allow reliance on the GDPR **legitimate-interest** basis to use personal data for **training or operating AI systems/models**, subject to conditions [2][10].
- **Streamlined DPIAs and breach reporting** — reduce data-protection-impact-assessment and personal-data-breach-notification burden [2][10].
- **Data Act consolidation** — merge the **Data Governance Act, Open Data Directive and Free Flow of Non-Personal Data Regulation** into a single restructured **Data Act**; introduce cloud-switching exemptions for small businesses and model/standard contractual clauses [4][5][10].

## Relevant Articles

*This table maps the package to the provisions it amends. "Status" states whether the change is adopted law or a proposal.*

| Article / Instrument | Change and status | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| AI Act Art. 113 (application dates) | Postponed high-risk dates (2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028). **ADOPTED.** | [7][9] |
| AI Act Art. 50 (transparency/marking) | AI-content marking postponed to 2 Dec 2026 for pre-existing systems. **ADOPTED.** | [9] |
| AI Act Art. 5 (prohibited practices) | New prohibition on nudifier/CSAM generators. **ADOPTED.** | [7][9] |
| AI Act Arts. 10, 49 and registration/documentation provisions | Bias-data strict-necessity reinstated; simplified registration for non-high-risk; simplified SME/mid-cap documentation. **ADOPTED.** | [9] |
| ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3) (cookie rule) | **Proposed** move of the consent rule into the GDPR; expanded exemptions. **PROPOSED — NOT LAW.** | [3][10] |
| GDPR (consent / lawful basis) | **Proposed** one-click/6-month consent; legitimate-interest basis for AI training. **PROPOSED — NOT LAW.** | [2][10] |
| GDPR Arts. 33–35 (breach notification, DPIA) | **Proposed** streamlining of breach reporting and DPIAs. **PROPOSED — NOT LAW.** | [2][10] |
| Data Act / DGA / Open Data / Free-Flow Regulation | **Proposed** consolidation into one restructured Data Act; SME cloud-switching exemptions. **PROPOSED — NOT LAW.** | [4][5][10] |

## Relevant Recitals

Not Applicable — as amending instruments (one adopted, one proposed), the Digital Omnibus texts do not yet have a stable, citable set of operative recitals suitable for interpretive reliance at this document's date; the authoritative recitals remain those of the **amended** instruments (AI Act, GDPR, ePrivacy Directive, Data Act), which are covered in their own documents [1][2][3][4]. Revisit on OJ publication of the AI strand and on any adoption of the data strand.

## Relevant Case Law

Not Applicable — the Digital Omnibus is a 2025–2026 legislative measure (one strand only just adopted, one still proposed); no court has interpreted it. The relevant interpretive case law is that of the **underlying** instruments — e.g. **Planet49** on cookie consent (see `eprivacy-foundations`) — which the package does not overrule [3].

**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames the Digital Omnibus as a **simplification** and burden-reduction exercise across the digital acquis, prepared through a 2025 call for evidence covering the data acquis, cookies, cybersecurity reporting, the AI Act and eID/trust services [6][10]. The Commission has also signalled a follow-on **"digital fitness check"** stage after the Omnibus adjustments [6]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **European Parliament (Legislative Train):** records the **AI strand** as having completed the legislative procedure (plenary 16 June 2026) with the co-legislators setting the **fixed** postponed dates and the new nudifier/CSAM prohibition, and reinstating the strict-necessity standard for bias-data processing [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation of the adopted text.)*
- **European Parliament (Legislative Train):** records the **data strand** (Digital Omnibus Regulation) as a **tabled proposal** that consolidates the data acquis, adds a GDPR legitimate-interest basis for AI, and **modernises the cookie policy** by moving consent into the GDPR with one-click/6-month or browser-level consent — advanced only through EESC (18 Mar 2026) and CoR (7 May 2026) opinions, i.e. **not adopted** [10]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a proposal.)*
- **Council of the EU:** corroborates the **AI strand's** final adoption on **29 June 2026** (final green light to simplify and streamline the AI rules) [8]. *(Regulatory corroboration; the Council site bot-blocks automated link checks — verify in browser.)*
- **Interpretation caution:** because the two strands share the "Digital Omnibus" name, there is a real risk of conflating an **adopted** AI-timeline change with a **proposed** cookie/GDPR change. Regulators and commentators consistently keep them separate; organisations should too [9][10]. *(Editorial note on interpretation.)*

text:
- **AI strand — re-baseline timelines, keep building.** Engineering teams preparing high-risk AI systems should re-plan to **2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028** and the **2 Dec 2026** content-marking date, but **not** treat obligations as removed — only deferred (see `ai-act-high-risk` for the control build) [7][9]. *(Legal obligation — adopted, subject to OJ publication.)*
- **AI strand — content-provenance work continues.** Watermarking/marking of AI-generated content (Art. 50) is postponed, not cancelled; retain provenance/marking on the roadmap [9]. *(Best practice grounded in adopted obligation.)*
- **Data strand — do NOT re-architect consent yet.** The proposed one-click/6-month consent and browser-level preferences are **not law**; consent-management platforms must continue to enforce **consent-before-set** for non-essential cookies under the current ePrivacy Directive/PECR [3][10]. *(Editorial recommendation grounded in current law.)*
- **Data strand — design for optionality.** Where feasible, build consent tooling that **could** later honour browser/system-level signals (e.g. a Global-Privacy-Control-style mechanism) without hard-coding the unadopted six-month rule — an architecture hedge, not a compliance step [10]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
- **AI-training data basis.** The proposed GDPR legitimate-interest basis for AI training is **not** yet available; current AI training on personal data still needs a valid existing GDPR basis and, where device-level tracking is involved, ePrivacy consent (see `eprivacy-foundations`) [2][3][10]. *(Legal obligation — current law.)*

- **Cookie/tag infrastructure unchanged for now.** Hosting, CDN and tag-management configurations must still gate non-essential cookies/SDKs on consent under the current ePrivacy regime; the proposed exemption expansion is not in force [3][10]. *(Legal obligation — current law.)*
- **Data Act consolidation is a watch item for cloud providers.** The proposed merger of the DGA/Open Data/Free-Flow instruments into the Data Act, plus SME cloud-switching exemptions and standard cloud contractual clauses, could change cloud-switching and data-portability obligations — but only if adopted; the current **Data Act** regime and its cloud-switching duties continue to apply meanwhile [4][5][10][13]. *(Proposal only; track.)*
- **Log/breach tooling.** The proposed streamlining of breach reporting may later reduce notification workload, but current GDPR Art. 33 timelines and NIS2/DORA reporting duties remain unchanged; do not de-scope incident tooling [2][10]. *(Legal obligation — current law.)*

text:
- **In-game tracking SDKs.** Analytics/ads/telemetry SDKs that read or write device information remain subject to Art. 5(3) consent under current law; the proposed cookie reform does not change this today, and heightened scrutiny applies where children are likely users (see `eprivacy-foundations`) [3][10]. *(Legal obligation — current law.)*
- **Generative and image tools in games.** The **adopted** AI-strand prohibition on **nudifier/CSAM generators** is directly relevant to user-generated-content and AI image features; games offering such tooling must ensure they cannot produce prohibited content [7][9]. *(Legal obligation — adopted; see `ai-act-high-risk`.)*
- **AI companions/chatbots.** Art. 50 transparency still applies; only its **marking** timing for pre-existing systems shifts (to 2 Dec 2026) under the AI strand [9]. *(Legal obligation — adopted.)*

text:
- **This document is the ePrivacy-topic view of a package with a large AI component.** The AI-Act-specific effects (high-risk dates, Art. 50 marking, new Art. 5 prohibition, bias-data and registration simplifications) are authoritatively covered in **`ai-act-foundations`** (overview) and **`ai-act-high-risk`** (mechanics); this document records them as **adopted** and cross-refers rather than duplicating [1][7][9]. *(Cross-reference.)*
- **Legitimate interest for AI training (proposed).** The data strand's proposed GDPR change would ease reliance on legitimate interest for training/operating AI — a significant potential shift for AI/ML data pipelines, but **not law**; continue to document a current lawful basis and run DPIAs [2][10]. *(Proposal only.)*
- **Bias-data processing (adopted).** The AI strand **reinstated the strict-necessity standard** for processing special-category data for bias detection/correction under AI Act Art. 10 — relevant to fairness engineering for high-risk systems [9]. *(Legal obligation — adopted; detail in `ai-act-high-risk`.)*
- **Consent remains the AI-tracking gate.** Because much AI personalisation depends on device-level tracking, the **current** ePrivacy consent rule (not the proposed reform) is the binding constraint for such data collection today [3][10]. *(Legal obligation — current law.)*

Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Separate the two strands in every internal briefing.** Treat the **AI strand as adopted law** and the **data strand as a proposal**; never let the shared name blur the status. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [9][10]
2. **Act on the adopted AI dates.** Re-plan high-risk readiness to **2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028** and content-marking to **2 Dec 2026**, confirm the OJ citation, and keep building controls — obligations are deferred, not removed. *(OBLIGATION once in force; EDITORIAL on planning.)* [7][9]
3. **Confirm no prohibited AI generation.** Ensure image/UGC/AI features cannot generate non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM (new Art. 5 prohibition). *(OBLIGATION — adopted.)* [7][9]
4. **Keep current cookie compliance unchanged.** Maintain consent-before-set for non-essential cookies/SDKs, reject-as-easy-as-accept, and consent records under the current ePrivacy Directive/PECR. *(OBLIGATION — current law.)* [3]
5. **Do NOT pre-implement the proposed cookie regime.** No six-month one-click consent, no reliance on expanded exemptions, no browser-level-only consent, until (and unless) adopted. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION grounded in current law.)* [10]
6. **Do NOT rely on a legitimate-interest-for-AI basis yet.** Keep a documented current GDPR basis and DPIAs for AI training on personal data. *(OBLIGATION — current law.)* [2][10]
7. **Maintain a regulatory-change watch.** Track the OJ publication of the AI strand and the Council/Parliament progress of the data strand; assign an owner and review at least quarterly. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [8][9][10]

text:
The **ePrivacy Directive (Directive 2002/58/EC**, as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC) governs privacy in the **electronic-communications** sector. It is the **lex specialis** to the GDPR: where it applies, its specific rules take precedence over the GDPR's general rules, while the GDPR fills gaps (for example, on the meaning and conditions of consent) [1][3]. Its best-known requirement is the **"cookie rule"** in Article 5(3): storing or accessing information on a user's device requires the user's **consent**, unless strictly necessary to provide a service the user requested [1].

This document establishes the foundations: confidentiality of communications (Art. 5), the cookie/consent rule (Art. 5(3)), traffic and location data, and unsolicited **direct marketing** (Art. 13). Because ePrivacy is a **Directive**, it is transposed into national law — in the UK by the **Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003 ("PECR")** [7]. Foundational CJEU authority (**Planet49**, C-673/17) confirms that consent for cookies must be a genuine, active choice — a **pre-ticked box is not valid consent**, regardless of whether the stored data is personal [2].

Two forward-looking points are essential. First, the long-proposed **ePrivacy Regulation** (2017) that would have replaced the Directive was **formally withdrawn** by the European Commission (approved 16 July 2025; announced in the Official Journal 6 October 2025) as "outdated in light of recent legislation" [5]. Second, the Commission's **Digital Omnibus** package (late 2025) proposes to **move cookie-consent rules from the ePrivacy Directive into the GDPR** — but this is a *proposal*, not yet law [6]. Until any such reform is adopted, the Directive (and national laws such as PECR) remain in force.
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
- The **ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC**, amended by 2009/136/EC) is the **lex specialis** to the GDPR for electronic communications; where both could apply, the specific ePrivacy rule prevails and the GDPR supplements it [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 5(3)** — storing or accessing information on a user's terminal (e.g., **cookies**) requires **consent**, unless strictly necessary for a service the user requested [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Consent** takes its meaning from the GDPR (Art. 4(11)): freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, by clear affirmative action [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Planet49 (C-673/17)** — a **pre-ticked checkbox is not valid consent** for cookies, and this holds whether or not the stored/accessed data is personal data [2]. *(Case law.)*
- **Article 13** restricts **unsolicited direct marketing** by electronic means; unsolicited marketing generally requires prior consent, subject to the limited "soft opt-in" for existing customers [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- ePrivacy is a **Directive**, so obligations arise via national transposition — in the UK, **PECR 2003** [7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **2017 ePrivacy Regulation proposal was withdrawn** (Commission approved 16 July 2025; OJ 6 October 2025) [5]. *(Legal/regulatory fact.)*
- The **Digital Omnibus** proposal (late 2025) proposes moving cookie rules into the GDPR, but is **not yet adopted** — the Directive/PECR remain in force [6]. *(Regulatory — proposal only.)*

text:
The 2002 ePrivacy Directive "particularised and complemented" the earlier Data Protection Directive 95/46/EC for the electronic-communications sector, addressing risks specific to networks and services (confidentiality, cookies, unsolicited communications) [1]. The **2009 amendment (2009/136/EC)** strengthened the cookie rule, shifting it decisively towards a **consent** model [1]. When the GDPR replaced Directive 95/46/EC in 2018, the ePrivacy Directive's references to consent were read as references to **GDPR-standard consent**, tightening what "consent" requires for cookies and marketing [3].

The EU intended to modernise the regime with an **ePrivacy Regulation** (proposed 2017) that would apply directly and align enforcement with the GDPR [9]. That proposal stalled for years in inter-institutional negotiation and was ultimately **withdrawn** in 2025 [5]. Attention has shifted to folding ePrivacy's cookie rules into the GDPR through the **Digital Omnibus** simplification package [6].
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
The ePrivacy Directive applies to the processing of personal data in connection with the provision of **publicly available electronic-communications services** over public networks, and — importantly for the cookie rule — to the storing of / access to information on users' **terminal equipment** regardless of whether that information is personal data [1][2]. Because it is a Directive, the operative obligations for organisations arise under **national transposing law** (e.g., PECR in the UK) [7].

Relationship to the GDPR: the ePrivacy Directive is **lex specialis**. Where a matter is specifically governed by ePrivacy (e.g., cookie consent, confidentiality of communications, electronic marketing), the ePrivacy rule prevails; the GDPR continues to apply to questions ePrivacy does not specifically address, and supplies the **definition and conditions of consent** [1][3]. The EDPB has issued an opinion on this interplay [4].

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 5(1) | Confidentiality of communications and related traffic data; prohibition on interception/surveillance without consent or legal authority. | [1] |
| Art. 5(3) | Consent required for storing/accessing information on terminal equipment (cookies and similar), unless strictly necessary for a requested service. | [1] |
| Art. 6 | Traffic data must be erased or anonymised when no longer needed for transmission, subject to billing/consent exceptions. | [1] |
| Art. 9 | Location data (other than traffic data) may be processed only when anonymised or with consent. | [1] |
| Art. 13 | Restrictions on unsolicited communications for direct marketing; prior consent generally required, with the Art. 13(2) "soft opt-in". | [1] |
| Art. 15 | Member States may restrict certain rights for national-security/law-enforcement purposes (basis for data-retention debates). | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*The Directive's recitals aid interpretation but are not binding operative provisions.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 24 | Terminal equipment and any information stored on it are part of the private sphere requiring protection ("spyware/cookies"). | [1] |
| Recital 25 | Cookies can be legitimate (e.g., analysing site effectiveness) but users must be informed and able to refuse. | [1] |
| Recital 66 (2009/136/EC) | Reinforced that storing/accessing information requires the user's consent, having been given clear information. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Planet49 (Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband v Planet49) | CJEU (Grand Chamber), C-673/17, 1 Oct 2019, ECLI:EU:C:2019:801 | A **pre-ticked checkbox** does not constitute valid consent for cookies under Art. 5(3); this is independent of whether the stored/accessed data is personal data. | Sets the consent standard for cookies; aligns ePrivacy consent with GDPR-standard consent [2]. |
| *(Data-retention line)* | Digital Rights Ireland; Tele2/Watson; La Quadrature du Net | General/indiscriminate retention of communications data is generally incompatible with EU law (Art. 15 ePrivacy read with the Charter). | Foundational for Art. 15 / national retention laws — deferred to `data-retention-caselaw` (backlog). |

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **EDPB** has clarified the **ePrivacy/GDPR interplay**: where processing triggers a specific ePrivacy rule, that rule applies, and supervisory competence/coordination follows accordingly [4]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **ICO** (UK) enforces **PECR** alongside the UK GDPR, and treats cookie consent as requiring GDPR-standard consent; "strictly necessary" is interpreted narrowly (it does not cover analytics or advertising cookies) [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- Consent must be **active**: reliance on pre-ticked boxes, "continue to browse" implied consent, or cookie walls that leave no genuine choice are treated as non-compliant, consistent with **Planet49** [2][8]. *(Regulatory interpretation / case law.)*
- **Reform status:** the Commission has **withdrawn** the ePrivacy Regulation proposal and is pursuing the **Digital Omnibus** route (moving cookie rules into the GDPR). Organisations should track this but must comply with the **current** Directive/PECR regime meanwhile [5][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation — proposal.)*
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
- **Consent-before-set** — non-essential cookies/SDKs must not fire until the user has given consent; "strictly necessary" cookies (e.g., session, load-balancing, security) are exempt [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Granularity & symmetry** — provide granular purpose controls and make **rejecting** as easy as accepting; record consent (what, when, scope) and support withdrawal [2][8]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Device access beyond cookies** — Art. 5(3) is technology-neutral: local storage, fingerprinting, pixel tags and SDK reads are in scope [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Traffic/location data** — minimise, anonymise or erase when no longer needed; gate value-added uses on consent (Arts. 6, 9) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Marketing suppression** — maintain consent/opt-out and suppression lists to honour Art. 13; separate the "soft opt-in" path for existing customers [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
- **Analytics & CDN cookies** — first-/third-party analytics and some CDN features set device storage and typically require consent unless strictly necessary; configure hosting/CDN so non-essential cookies are gated [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Log/traffic data** — server and network logs may constitute traffic data; apply retention and minimisation, and be aware of Art. 15/retention-law constraints [1]. *(Legal obligation; see `data-retention-caselaw`.)*
- **Controller responsibility** — the site/service operator (controller) remains responsible for third-party tags it deploys; contractual and technical controls over tag vendors are needed. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
- **Analytics, ads and telemetry SDKs** in games routinely store/read device information and fall under Art. 5(3); consent must be obtained before non-essential SDKs initialise [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Children** — combined with the low consent age and children's-code expectations (see `uk-gdpr-foundations`, `gdpr-foundations`), advertising/tracking SDKs in games likely to be used by children face heightened scrutiny. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **In-game messaging & marketing** — push notifications and promotional emails are electronic marketing subject to Art. 13 consent/soft-opt-in rules [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
- **Tracking data for personalisation/AI** — behavioural data gathered via cookies/SDKs to train recommendation or ad-targeting models requires a valid Art. 5(3) consent for the collection layer, in addition to a GDPR basis for subsequent processing [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Consent as the gate** — because much AI personalisation depends on device-level tracking, ePrivacy consent is often the **binding constraint**, not the GDPR basis. *(Editorial note.)*
- No ePrivacy-specific AI regime exists; AI-specific obligations are covered in `ai-act-foundations` / `ai-governance-foundations` (backlog). *(Cross-reference.)*
title: ePrivacy: Foundations, Cookies & Electronic Communications

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Audit all device storage/access** (cookies, local storage, SDKs, pixels, fingerprinting) and classify each as strictly necessary or consent-required. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
2. **Deploy a compliant consent mechanism** — no non-essential storage before consent; reject as easy as accept; record and allow withdrawal. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [2][8]
3. **Interpret "strictly necessary" narrowly** — analytics and advertising are not strictly necessary. *(OBLIGATION per ICO.)* [8]
4. **Govern marketing** — apply Art. 13: consent by default, soft opt-in only where its conditions are met; honour opt-outs and suppression. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **Manage third-party tags** — inventory vendors, gate their loading on consent, and contract for compliance. *(BEST PRACTICE.)*
6. **Track reform** — monitor the Digital Omnibus proposal and any migration of cookie rules into the GDPR; do not pre-implement unadopted rules. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [5][6]

title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
A **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)** is the GDPR's principal instrument for assessing, in advance, the risks that a processing operation poses to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, and for demonstrating that those risks have been managed. Its legal anchor is **Article 35 GDPR**, reinforced by **Article 36 (prior consultation)** [1]. This document is the methodology layer beneath `privacy-engineering-foundations`, which introduces the Article 35 trigger at a foundational level; here we set out **when a DPIA is mandatory, how to screen for it, how to run one step by step, and how to sustain it as an operational capability**.

A DPIA is **mandatory** where processing is "likely to result in a high risk" (Art. 35(1)); Article 35(3) lists three cases that always qualify, and each supervisory authority must publish its own **Article 35(4) list** of operations requiring a DPIA [1][7]. The Article 29 Working Party guidelines **WP248 rev.01** — formally endorsed by the EDPB — supply a **nine-criteria test**: as a rule of thumb, processing meeting **two or more** criteria is likely high risk and needs a DPIA [4][5][7]. The **minimum statutory content** of a DPIA is fixed by Article 35(7): a systematic description of the processing, an assessment of **necessity and proportionality**, an assessment of the **risks**, and the **measures** to mitigate them [1].

Three conclusions dominate. First, the DPIA is an **accountability obligation, not a form-filling exercise** — it must be done *before* processing and *reviewed* when risk changes (Art. 35(1), 35(11)) [1]. Second, if residual risk remains high after mitigation, the controller **must consult the supervisory authority** before proceeding (Art. 36) [1][8]. Third, the DPIA is becoming the **hub of a family of assessments** — it dovetails with the AI Act **Article 27 Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)** and with the **Article 30 records of processing** [1][2].
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
- A DPIA is **legally required before** processing "likely to result in a high risk" to rights and freedoms (Art. 35(1)); it must be done at the design stage, not retrospectively [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 35(3)** names three cases that always require a DPIA: systematic and extensive **automated evaluation/profiling** with significant effects; **large-scale** processing of special-category or criminal-offence data; and **systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area** on a large scale [1][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Each supervisory authority must publish an **Article 35(4) "blacklist"**; the ICO's list adds **ten** operation types (e.g., innovative technology, denial of service, large-scale profiling, biometrics, genetic data, data matching, invisible processing, tracking, targeting of children, risk of physical harm) [1][7]. *(Legal obligation, as specified by the SA.)*
- **WP248 rev.01** (endorsed by the EDPB) gives **nine risk criteria**; meeting **two or more** ordinarily indicates a DPIA is needed, though a single criterion can suffice [4][5][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Article 35(7)** fixes the minimum content: systematic **description**, **necessity & proportionality** assessment, **risk** assessment, and **mitigation** measures [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **DPO must be consulted** (Art. 35(2)); where appropriate, so must **data subjects** (Art. 35(9)); the DPO also **monitors** DPIA performance (Art. 39(1)(c)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- If residual risk stays high, **prior consultation with the supervisory authority is mandatory** (Art. 36); the authority responds within **8 weeks, extendable by 6** [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- A DPIA must be **reviewed** when the risk represented by processing changes (Art. 35(11)); it is a living document, not a one-off [1][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The DPIA **interlocks** with the AI Act **Art. 27 FRIA** and the **Art. 30 RoPA**; the standards **ISO/IEC 29134** (PIA) and **ISO/IEC 42005** (AI system impact assessment) provide auditable process structure [1][2][10][11]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text: This document gives privacy, engineering, product and legal teams an **evidence-based, repeatable methodology** for deciding whether a DPIA is required, conducting it to the Article 35(7) standard, escalating to prior consultation where necessary, and operating DPIAs at scale across a portfolio of processing. It operationalises the Article 35 trigger described in `privacy-engineering-foundations` and supports DPIA integration into the SDLC, the AI Act conformity workstream, and the accountability evidence base.
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
**In scope:** The Article 35 DPIA obligation and screening/threshold assessment; the Article 35(3) mandatory cases and Article 35(4)/(5) national lists; the WP248 rev.01 nine-criteria "likely high risk" test; the end-to-end DPIA process (describe → necessity & proportionality → risk assessment → mitigation → sign-off → review); Article 36 prior consultation; the DPO and data-subject roles; links to the AI Act Art. 27 FRIA and the Art. 30 records; ICO guidance and template; a practical methodology and maturity view.

**Out of scope (covered elsewhere or in the backlog):** The DPbDD and Art. 32 security controls a DPIA relies on → `privacy-engineering-foundations`; privacy threat-modelling techniques (LINDDUN) that feed the risk step → `privacy-threat-modelling` (planned); anonymisation/re-identification analysis → `anonymisation-techniques` (planned); the full AI Act high-risk regime and FRIA mechanics → `ai-act-high-risk`; running the wider accountability programme → `compliance-operations-foundations`.

**Assumptions:** The reader has read `gdpr-foundations` (principles, accountability, high-risk concept) and `privacy-engineering-foundations` (DPbDD, TOMs). "Controller", "processor", "special category data" and "RoPA" carry their `GLOSSARY.md` meanings.

text:
*Shared terms (controller, processor, personal data, special category data, RoPA, accountability, FRIA) are defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only DPIA-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) | An assessment of the impact of envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data, required where a type of processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons (Art. 35(1)). | [1] |
| Screening / threshold assessment | The preliminary step of determining whether the mandatory Art. 35(3) cases, an SA Art. 35(4) list entry, or the WP248 criteria are met, such that a DPIA is required. | [1][7] |
| "Likely to result in a high risk" | The threshold triggering a DPIA; assessed against the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, aided by the WP248 nine criteria. | [1][4][7] |
| Article 35(4) list ("blacklist") | The list, published by each supervisory authority, of processing operations that require a DPIA. | [1][7] |
| Article 35(5) list ("whitelist") | An optional SA list of processing operations that do **not** require a DPIA. | [1] |
| Prior consultation | The Art. 36 duty to consult the supervisory authority before processing where a DPIA indicates a high residual risk that the controller cannot mitigate. | [1][8] |
| Residual risk | The level of risk remaining after planned mitigation measures are applied; determines whether Art. 36 consultation is triggered. | [1][8] |
| Necessity and proportionality | The Art. 35(7)(b) assessment of whether the processing is necessary for, and proportionate to, its purpose(s) — a lawfulness test distinct from the security-risk assessment. | [1] |
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
Before the GDPR, EU data protection relied on a **prior-notification** model: controllers notified processing to the regulator. The GDPR abolished general notification and replaced it with a **risk-based accountability** model in which the controller itself must identify and manage high-risk processing (Recital 89) [1]. The **DPIA** is the centrepiece of that shift — a structured, documented, forward-looking risk assessment that the controller performs, retains and can produce on demand (Recital 84) [1].

The concept did not appear from nowhere. **Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs)** had been practised for years in Canada, Australia, the UK (the ICO ran a PIA code from 2007) and elsewhere, and were codified internationally in **ISO/IEC 29134** [10]. The GDPR "hardened" the PIA into a **statutory** instrument with mandatory triggers, minimum content and an escalation route to the regulator. The Article 29 Working Party issued **WP248** in 2017, revised as **WP248 rev.01**, to explain when processing is "likely to result in a high risk"; the EDPB **endorsed** these guidelines on becoming operational in 2018, so they remain the authoritative interpretive source [4][5]. The instrument continues to spread: the **AI Act** (2024) introduced a parallel **Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment** for certain high-risk AI deployers, expressly designed to sit alongside the DPIA [2].
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
The DPIA regime lives in **Chapter IV, Section 3 of the GDPR (Articles 35–36)**, supported by Articles 30 (records) and 39 (DPO tasks) and by Recitals 84 and 89–96 [1]. The obligation rests on the **controller**.

- **Article 35(1)** — where a type of processing, in particular **using new technologies**, is **likely to result in a high risk** to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, taking account of the nature, scope, context and purposes, the controller **shall, prior to the processing, carry out a DPIA** [1].
- **Article 35(2)** — the controller **shall seek the advice of the DPO**, where designated [1].
- **Article 35(3)** — a DPIA is **required in particular** in three cases: (a) systematic and extensive **evaluation** based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions producing **legal or similarly significant effects** are based; (b) processing **on a large scale** of **special categories** (Art. 9(1)) or **criminal-offence** data (Art. 10); (c) **systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area** on a large scale [1].
- **Article 35(4)–(6)** — each supervisory authority **shall publish a list** of operations requiring a DPIA (the "blacklist"), **may publish** a list of operations not requiring one, and must run cross-border lists through the **consistency mechanism** [1].
- **Article 35(7)** — the DPIA **shall contain at least**: (a) a systematic **description** of the processing and its purposes; (b) an assessment of the **necessity and proportionality**; (c) an assessment of the **risks** to rights and freedoms; and (d) the **measures** envisaged to address the risks (safeguards, security, mechanisms to demonstrate compliance) [1].
- **Article 35(9)** — where appropriate, the controller **shall seek the views of data subjects** or their representatives [1].
- **Article 35(10)–(11)** — a limited exemption applies where a DPIA-equivalent assessment was already made at the **legislative** stage; and the controller **shall review** whether processing is performed in line with the DPIA, at least when the **risk changes** [1].
- **Article 36** — where a DPIA indicates a **high residual risk** absent mitigation, the controller **shall consult** the supervisory authority **before** processing; the authority responds within **8 weeks (extendable by 6)** [1].

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |

| Art. 24 | Controller's general duty to implement, review and update appropriate measures (context for DPIA). | [1] |
| Art. 25 | Data protection by design and by default — DPIA outputs feed DPbDD (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`). | [1] |
| Art. 30 | Records of processing activities (RoPA) — the inventory from which DPIA candidates are screened. | [1] |
| Art. 35(1) | Obligation to carry out a DPIA prior to high-risk processing. | [1] |
| Art. 35(2) | Seek the DPO's advice. | [1] |
| Art. 35(3) | The three mandatory-DPIA cases. | [1] |
| Art. 35(4)–(6) | SA lists (blacklist/whitelist) and consistency mechanism. | [1] |
| Art. 35(7) | Minimum content of a DPIA. | [1] |
| Art. 35(9) | Seek data subjects' views where appropriate. | [1] |
| Art. 35(10)–(11) | Legislative-basis exemption; obligation to review. | [1] |
| Art. 36 | Prior consultation with the supervisory authority on high residual risk. | [1] |
| Art. 39(1)(c) | DPO to advise on and monitor DPIA performance. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the articles above.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 84 | A DPIA should be carried out to enhance compliance where processing is likely to result in a high risk. | [1] |
| Recital 89 | General notification abolished; replaced by focused obligations (incl. DPIAs) for genuinely high-risk processing. | [1] |
| Recital 90 | The DPIA should describe processing, assess necessity/proportionality and risks, and determine mitigating measures. | [1] |
| Recital 91 | "Large scale" and the mandatory cases; individual physicians/lawyers processing patient/client data are not "large scale". | [1] |
| Recital 92 | A single DPIA may address a set of similar operations with similar high risks. | [1] |
| Recital 94–95 | Prior consultation where risk cannot be mitigated; processor to assist the controller. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

Not Applicable at the methodology level. The Article 35–36 DPIA obligation is elaborated principally through **regulatory guidance** (WP248 rev.01; national SA lists; ICO guidance) rather than a distinct line of CJEU authority; enforcement decisions turning on a missing or inadequate DPIA are taken by national supervisory authorities and are better treated as sector examples in `compliance-operations-foundations`. General GDPR case law on high risk and profiling (see `gdpr-foundations`) informs the threshold. [1][4][7]
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **WP248 rev.01** (Article 29 Working Party, **endorsed by the EDPB**) is the authoritative reading of "likely to result in a high risk". It offers **nine criteria**: (1) evaluation or scoring; (2) automated decision-making with legal or similar significant effect; (3) systematic monitoring; (4) sensitive data or data of a highly personal nature; (5) large-scale processing; (6) matching or combining datasets; (7) data on vulnerable subjects; (8) innovative use of new technology/organisational solutions; (9) processing that prevents subjects from exercising a right or using a service/contract [4][5][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **"two or more" rule of thumb**: WP248 and the ICO agree that processing meeting **two or more** criteria will in most cases require a DPIA, though a **single** criterion may suffice, and a controller may justify *not* doing a DPIA only if it documents why the processing is nonetheless unlikely to be high risk [4][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **ICO** frames the trigger as three layers: the **Art. 35(3)** cases, its own **Art. 35(4) list of ten** operation types, and the **European (WP29) criteria**; where processing fits none but is arguably high risk, the controller must still decide, and "if in doubt, do a DPIA" [6][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- On **process**, the ICO sets out a staged method — identify the need; describe the processing; consult where appropriate; assess necessity, proportionality and compliance; identify and assess risks; identify measures; sign off and record; integrate outcomes and keep under review [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- On **consultation**, both the statute and the ICO confirm the controller **cannot begin** high-residual-risk processing until it has consulted the authority, which generally responds within **8 weeks** [1][8]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
A DPIA is only as good as the system description and risk model beneath it. Engineering practices that make DPIAs reliable:

- **Derive DPIA scope from the RoPA and data-flow diagrams** — the Art. 30 record and current data-flow/DFD artefacts give the "systematic description" required by Art. 35(7)(a); keep them versioned so the DPIA can be re-run on change [1]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Feed the risk step from threat modelling** — privacy threat-modelling (e.g., LINDDUN) and security threat modelling produce the harm scenarios the Art. 35(7)(c) risk assessment scores; align the DPIA risk register with the security risk register (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`). *(Best practice.)*
- **Bind mitigations to controls** — each Art. 35(7)(d) measure should map to a concrete technical/organisational control (encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, minimisation, retention automation) with an owner and a verification method [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Instrument the trigger in the SDLC** — a lightweight screening questionnaire at design-gate/change-control automatically flags Art. 35(3)/35(4)/WP248 hits, so DPIAs are raised before build, not after launch [7]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
- **Adopt a process standard** — **ISO/IEC 29134** structures the PIA lifecycle and report; **ISO/IEC 27701** provides the management-system wrapper that keeps DPIAs auditable and repeatable [10][12]. *(Best practice.)*
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
- **Processor assistance is contractual and legal** — under Art. 28(3)(f) and Recital 95 the processor (including a hosting/cloud provider) must **assist** the controller with DPIAs; the DPIA should reflect real infrastructure facts (regions, sub-processors, encryption, key custody) [1]. *(Legal obligation — reflected in the DPA/contract.)*
- **The controller owns the DPIA** — hosting a workload does not transfer the Art. 35 duty; the controller must obtain the technical evidence it needs from the provider to complete the description and risk steps [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Transfers feed the risk assessment** — where hosting entails a restricted transfer, the Chapter V analysis and any transfer risk assessment are inputs to (not substitutes for) the DPIA (see `gdpr-transfers`). *(Best practice.)*
- **UK context** — for UK controllers the obligation is the assimilated **UK GDPR** Art. 35/36 read with the **DPA 2018**; the ICO's list and template apply [3][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
- **Children trigger DPIAs readily** — services likely to be accessed by children engage the WP248 "vulnerable subjects" criterion and the ICO "targeting of children" list item; a DPIA is effectively expected, and the ICO Children's Code treats it as integral (see `game-hosting-foundations`, `uk-gdpr-foundations`) [7]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory expectation.)*
- **Profiling and matchmaking** — behavioural profiling, engagement optimisation and ad targeting can meet the "evaluation/scoring" and "automated decision-making" criteria, raising a DPIA even before scale is considered [1][7]. *(Legal obligation once high risk.)*
- **Biometrics and voice** — anti-cheat, age-assurance or voice-moderation features processing biometric data hit both Art. 35(3)(b) (if large scale/special category) and the ICO biometrics list item [1][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Innovative technology** — novel AI-driven features (generative NPCs, AI companions) engage the "innovative use" criterion and should be DPIA-screened at design [7]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
- **DPIA vs FRIA — related but distinct** — the **AI Act Art. 27** requires certain **deployers** of Annex III high-risk AI systems to run a **Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment**; Art. 27 expressly provides that where obligations are already met through a **DPIA**, the FRIA **complements** it rather than duplicating it [2]. *(Legal obligation under a separate regime.)*
- **Run them together** — for AI that processes personal data, the DPIA (GDPR) and FRIA (AI Act) share inputs (system description, affected persons, risk scenarios, mitigations); a combined assessment template avoids divergence and evidences both [1][2]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Automated decision-making** — solely automated decisions with legal/significant effect engage Art. 35(3)(a) **and** GDPR Art. 22; the DPIA must document the logic, safeguards and human-oversight measures [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **AI-specific impact standard** — **ISO/IEC 42005** gives a process for **AI system impact assessment** that can structure the AI-risk portions of a combined DPIA/FRIA [11]. *(Best practice.)*
- **New technology is an explicit trigger** — Art. 35(1) singles out "new technologies", so novel AI/ML pipelines should be screened for a DPIA by default [1][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: Data Protection Impact Assessments: Methodology

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** (must, per statute) / **BEST PRACTICE** (should, per standards/regulators) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (we suggest).

**A. Screen every new or changed processing operation.**

1. Run a **threshold/screening assessment** against Art. 35(3), the SA's Art. 35(4) list, and the WP248 nine criteria; treat **two or more** criteria (or a single strong one) as a trigger. *(OBLIGATION to assess; BEST PRACTICE for the questionnaire form.)* [1][7]
2. **Document a negative screen** — if you decide no DPIA is needed, record why (the processing is unlikely to be high risk). *(OBLIGATION.)* [7]

**B. Conduct the DPIA to the Art. 35(7) standard.**
3. **Describe** the processing systematically — nature, scope, context, purposes, data categories, recipients, retention, transfers; reuse the RoPA and data-flow diagrams. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Assess necessity and proportionality** — lawful basis, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, retention, transparency, data-subject rights. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **Assess the risks** to rights and freedoms — identify harm scenarios, estimate likelihood and severity, and record the risk rating. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Identify measures** to eliminate or reduce each risk, with owners and residual-risk ratings. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
7. **Consult the DPO** (Art. 35(2)) and, **where appropriate, data subjects** (Art. 35(9)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]

**C. Escalate, sign off and sustain.**
8. **Prior consultation** — if residual risk remains high, **consult the supervisory authority before processing** (Art. 36) and do not start until you have. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][8]
9. **Sign off and record** — obtain documented approval; retain the DPIA as accountability evidence and link it to the RoPA entry. *(OBLIGATION for accountability; BEST PRACTICE for the register.)* [1]
10. **Review on change** — re-assess at least when the risk changes and on a periodic cadence (Art. 35(11)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
11. **Use a recognised template** — the **ICO DPIA template** and **ISO/IEC 29134** report structure are known-good starting points; adapt, don't reinvent. *(BEST PRACTICE / EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [9][10]
