text:
- **Phase 0 — Inventory & screening baseline:** Reconcile the RoPA; build a screening questionnaire mapped to Art. 35(3), the SA list and WP248; triage the existing portfolio. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Method & template:** Adopt a DPIA template covering all Art. 35(7) elements (ICO template / ISO 29134 structure); define risk-scoring and sign-off. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 2 — SDLC integration:** Wire screening into design-gates/change-control; define residual-risk escalation to Art. 36. *Effort:* Medium–High.
- **Phase 3 — Backlog remediation:** Run DPIAs for high-risk processing already live; consult the SA where required. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 4 — AI & assessment convergence:** Merge DPIA with the AI Act FRIA and (where used) ISO/IEC 42005 for AI systems. *Effort:* Medium–High.
- **Phase 5 — Assurance & metrics:** DPIA coverage KPIs, review cadence, internal audit, and continuous improvement. *Effort:* Ongoing.

text:
1. How do you **screen** new/changed processing for a DPIA, and how is the decision recorded? *(Art. 35(1), 35(3)–(4) [1][7].)*
2. Show a DPIA that addresses **all four Art. 35(7) elements** — description, necessity/proportionality, risk, measures. *(Art. 35(7) [1].)*
3. How do you evidence that DPIAs are done **before** processing begins? *(Art. 35(1) [1].)*
4. Where a DPIA identified **high residual risk**, how did you handle **prior consultation**? *(Art. 36 [1][8].)*
5. How is the **DPO** involved, and when are **data subjects'** views sought? *(Art. 35(2), 35(9), 39(1)(c) [1].)*
6. How and when are DPIAs **reviewed** after changes? *(Art. 35(11) [1].)*
7. For AI systems, how do the **DPIA and Art. 27 FRIA** relate and avoid duplication? *(AI Act Art. 27 [2].)*
8. How do **processors** provide the assistance and evidence your DPIAs need? *(Art. 28(3)(f); Recital 95 [1].)*

title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
**Privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs)** are technical measures that minimise the personal data processed, or protect it while it is processed, so that data-protection principles can be met without abandoning the analytical or operational value of the data [1][2]. This document is the technique-by-technique catalogue promised by the parent reference `privacy-engineering-foundations`, which introduces PETs (pseudonymisation, encryption, differential privacy, aggregation) only at a foundational level [7]. Here each technology is examined on four axes: **what it is**, its **formal guarantee and its limits**, its **GDPR relevance** (data minimisation under Article 25, security under Article 32, and — critically — whether it produces *anonymous* or merely *pseudonymised* data), and its **engineering maturity**.

The catalogue covers **pseudonymisation and tokenisation**; the syntactic anonymisation models **k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness**; **differential privacy** (global vs local, and the meaning of the ε privacy budget); **synthetic data**; **secure multi-party computation (SMPC)**; **homomorphic encryption**; **trusted execution environments (TEEs)**; **federated learning**; **zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs)**; and **encryption in transit, at rest and in use**. It draws the primary techniques from the peer-reviewed literature that defined them [13][14][15][16][17][18][19][20][21], and grounds the legal and selection guidance in ENISA and ICO output [2][3][4][5][6] and in ISO/IEC and NIST standards [9][10][11][12].

Three conclusions dominate. First, **most PETs do not, by themselves, anonymise** — pseudonymisation, encryption, SMPC, TEEs and federated learning all leave the data in scope of the GDPR, and only techniques that provide a demonstrable, quantified identifiability guarantee (well-parameterised differential privacy; robustly generated synthetic data; strong k-anonymity/aggregation) can approach the Recital 26 anonymisation threshold [1][2][6]. Second, **PETs are controls, not compliance** — they reduce risk and evidence Article 25/32, but do not discharge the accountability obligation or replace a DPIA [1][2][7]. Third, **maturity varies enormously**: pseudonymisation and encryption are production-grade, while homomorphic encryption and general-purpose SMPC remain computationally expensive and use-case specific — so PET selection must be risk-driven, not fashion-driven [2][3].
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
- A **PET** minimises or protects personal data; PETs help meet **Article 25 (data protection by design and by default)** and **Article 32 (security)** but do not, on their own, discharge accountability [1][2][7]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- The **anonymisation/pseudonymisation line (Recital 26; Art. 4(5))** is decisive: *pseudonymised* data remains personal data and in scope; only *anonymous* data — no longer attributable by means reasonably likely to be used — falls outside the GDPR [1][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pseudonymisation and tokenisation** are expressly named risk-reduction measures (Arts. 25(1), 32(1)(a)), but keep the data in scope because a re-identification key exists [1][4][5]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness** are *syntactic* models that bound re-identification by generalisation/suppression; each fixes a weakness in the prior model but none gives a formal, composable guarantee against a strong adversary [13][14][15]. *(Best practice / academic.)*
- **Differential privacy (DP)** gives a formal, quantified, composable guarantee governed by a **privacy budget ε** (smaller ε = stronger privacy, more noise); it exists in a **global/central** model (trusted curator) and a **local** model (noise added at source) [16][17][9]. *(Best practice / academic.)*
- **SMPC, homomorphic encryption, TEEs and federated learning** enable computation on data without centralising the raw records, supporting minimisation — but the **inputs/outputs and models can still be personal data**, so they are not automatic anonymisation [2][3][18][19][21]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Encryption** (in transit, at rest, and increasingly *in use*) is the baseline confidentiality control named in Article 32(1)(a); encrypted personal data held by a party with the key remains personal data [1][12]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **PET maturity is uneven**: pseudonymisation, tokenisation and encryption are established; DP, synthetic data, TEEs and federated learning are maturing; general SMPC and homomorphic encryption remain performance-constrained — regulators warn PETs are **not a silver bullet** [2][3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Selection is risk-driven**: choose the PET by the risk it must address (identifiability, confidentiality, or collaborative computation), assess residual risk in a **DPIA**, and combine PETs where a single technique is insufficient [2][3][4]. *(Best practice.)*

text: This document gives privacy, engineering, data-science and compliance teams an **evidence-based catalogue** to select, justify and correctly characterise privacy-enhancing technologies. It supports three decisions: (a) *which* PET (or combination) addresses a given privacy risk; (b) *whether* a chosen PET renders data anonymous or leaves it pseudonymised and in scope; and (c) *how mature* and operationally realistic each option is. It operationalises the PETs overview in `privacy-engineering-foundations` and feeds the necessity, risk and mitigation steps of a DPIA (`dpia-methodology`).

text:
*Shared terms (personal data, pseudonymisation, anonymous data, PET, differential privacy, TOMs) are defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only technique-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Tokenisation | A form of pseudonymisation that substitutes a data element (e.g. a card number) with a non-sensitive surrogate ("token"), with the mapping held in a secured token vault. | [4][5] |
| k-anonymity | A dataset property: every record is indistinguishable from at least *k−1* others on its quasi-identifiers, so no individual can be singled out below a group of size *k*. | [13] |
| l-diversity | A strengthening of k-anonymity requiring each equivalence class to contain at least *l* "well-represented" values of each sensitive attribute, resisting attribute disclosure. | [14] |
| t-closeness | A further strengthening requiring the distribution of a sensitive attribute in each class to be within distance *t* of its distribution in the whole table. | [15] |
| Differential privacy (ε-DP) | A formal guarantee that the presence or absence of any one individual changes the probability of any output by at most a factor of e^ε; ε is the "privacy budget". | [16][17][9] |
| Global (central) DP | The trusted-curator model: a trusted party holds the raw data and adds calibrated noise to query results/aggregates. | [9][17] |
| Local DP | Each individual perturbs their own data *before* it leaves their device, so the collector never sees raw values (e.g. randomised response). | [9][17] |
| Synthetic data | Artificial data generated from a model of a real dataset's statistical properties, intended to preserve utility while (ideally) not corresponding to real individuals. | [2][3] |
| Secure multi-party computation (SMPC) | Cryptographic protocols letting several parties jointly compute a function over their inputs while keeping each input private from the others. | [3][18] |
| Homomorphic encryption (HE) | Encryption allowing computation directly on ciphertext, producing an encrypted result that decrypts to the correct plaintext output. | [3][19] |
| Trusted execution environment (TEE) | A hardware-isolated, attestable enclave in which code and data are protected from the rest of the host, enabling "confidential computing". | [2][3] |
| Federated learning (FL) | A distributed machine-learning approach that trains a shared model by exchanging model updates, not raw data, which stays on local devices/silos. | [21][22] |
| Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) | A protocol by which a prover convinces a verifier that a statement is true while revealing nothing beyond the truth of the statement. | [20] |
| Encryption in use | Protection of data while it is being processed in memory (e.g. via TEEs or HE), complementing encryption in transit and at rest. | [2][3] |
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
The idea that technology can protect privacy rather than only threaten it dates to the 1990s coinage of "privacy-enhancing technologies", but the field matured as two research strands converged: **statistical disclosure control** (how to release useful data without re-identifying individuals) and **cryptography** (how to compute without disclosing inputs). The statistical strand produced **k-anonymity** (Sweeney, 2002) and its successors **l-diversity** (Machanavajjhala et al., 2007) and **t-closeness** (Li et al., 2007), each answering an attack the previous model left open [13][14][15]. A more ambitious answer came from **differential privacy** (Dwork, 2006), which replaced dataset-shape heuristics with a provable, quantified guarantee and became the dominant formal notion of privacy in analytics [16][17].

The cryptographic strand is older still: **secure computation** was framed by Yao in 1982 [18]; **zero-knowledge proofs** by Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff in 1985 [20]; and **fully homomorphic encryption** — long a "holy grail" — was first realised by Gentry in 2009 [19]. **Federated learning** (McMahan et al., 2017) then applied the "move computation, not data" principle to machine learning at scale [21]. The GDPR gave this technical field a legal centre of gravity by naming **pseudonymisation** and **encryption** in Articles 25 and 32 and by making genuine **anonymisation** the boundary of its own application (Recital 26) [1]. Regulators and standards bodies followed with practitioner guidance: ENISA on pseudonymisation and data-protection engineering [3][4][5], the ICO with dedicated **PETs guidance** [2], NIST with evaluation criteria for differential privacy [9], and ISO/IEC with a de-identification taxonomy [10].
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
PETs have no single "PET article"; they are the technical means by which several GDPR obligations are met [1]. The load-bearing provisions are:

- **Article 5(1)(c) — data minimisation:** personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. PETs that reduce what is collected, centralised or exposed (federated learning, local DP, aggregation) implement this principle directly [1].
- **Article 5(1)(f) & Article 32 — integrity, confidentiality and security:** appropriate technical measures for a level of security appropriate to the risk, **expressly naming pseudonymisation and encryption** (Art. 32(1)(a)), plus confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience [1].
- **Article 25 — data protection by design and by default:** controllers must implement appropriate measures — **pseudonymisation is given as the example** — to embed the principles effectively (Art. 25(1)), and to ensure only necessary data is processed by default (Art. 25(2)) [1].
- **Article 4(5) — definition of pseudonymisation:** processing such that data can no longer be attributed to a subject **without additional information kept separately and secured** — the legal reason pseudonymised data stays personal [1].
- **Recital 26 — the identifiability test:** the principles do not apply to anonymous information; identifiability is judged by "all the means reasonably likely to be used"; **pseudonymised data that could be attributed using additional information is data on an identifiable person** [1].
- **Article 89(1) — safeguards for research/statistics:** requires appropriate safeguards, **naming pseudonymisation**, and the data-minimisation principle, for archiving, research and statistical processing — a common home for PETs [1].

DPbDD and Article 32 operationalise the **accountability** (Art. 5(2)) and **security** (Art. 5(1)(f)) principles established in `gdpr-foundations`; the anonymisation boundary is elaborated in `gdpr-foundations` and `privacy-engineering-foundations`.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 4(5) | Definition of pseudonymisation (additional information kept separately). | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(c) | Data minimisation — PETs reduce data collected/exposed. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(f) | Integrity and confidentiality (security) principle. | [1] |
| Art. 5(2) | Accountability — PETs evidence but do not replace it. | [1] |
| Art. 25(1) | Data protection by design — pseudonymisation named as the example measure. | [1] |
| Art. 25(2) | Data protection by default — minimise amount, extent, retention, accessibility. | [1] |
| Art. 32(1)(a) | Security of processing — pseudonymisation and encryption named expressly. | [1] |
| Art. 89(1) | Safeguards for research/statistics — pseudonymisation and minimisation. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the articles above.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 26 | Identifiability judged by means reasonably likely to be used; anonymous data is out of scope; pseudonymised data remains personal data. | [1] |
| Recital 28 | Pseudonymisation can reduce risks to data subjects and help controllers meet their obligations, but does not by itself take data out of scope. | [1] |
| Recital 29 | Pseudonymisation measures should be possible within the same controller when the additional information is kept separately. | [1] |
| Recital 78 | DPbDD examples — minimising processing, pseudonymising as soon as possible, transparency, enabling monitoring. | [1] |
| Recital 83 | Security — risk-based measures against accidental/unlawful destruction, loss, alteration or disclosure. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

Not Applicable. The choice and characterisation of PETs is a technical and interpretive matter driven by the GDPR text, regulator guidance and standards, not by a distinct line of judgments. The **relative/contextual identifiability** test that determines whether a PET output is anonymous or pseudonymised is, however, informed by CJEU authority on the meaning of personal data (*Breyer*, C-582/14; *Nowak*, C-434/16), which is treated in `gdpr-foundations`. [1]

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **ICO's dedicated PETs guidance** frames PETs as technologies that "can help you demonstrate a data protection by design and by default approach", grouping them by function — reducing identifiability (e.g. differential privacy, synthetic data), hiding/protecting data during processing (e.g. homomorphic encryption, SMPC, TEEs, federated learning), and splitting or minimising data — while warning that PETs are **not a silver bullet**, that their **maturity and effectiveness vary**, and that a PET must be assessed for residual re-identification and security risk before reliance [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The ICO advises using PETs **as part of**, not instead of, a DPIA and broader accountability measures, and cautions that some PETs are **computationally costly or immature** and can introduce their own risks (e.g. poor DP parameter choices, weak synthetic-data generation) [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ENISA** treats pseudonymisation as a spectrum of techniques with differing re-identification resistance (counter, RNG, hash, HMAC, encryption-based) and stresses that the **choice of technique and secret must match the adversary model**; it also positions PETs within "data protection engineering" as design building blocks, not compliance guarantees [3][4][5]. *(Regulatory / technical guidance.)*
- Both regulators, and **ENISA's design-by-default work**, agree that pseudonymisation and encryption **reduce but do not remove** GDPR scope, and that anonymisation is a **high, context-dependent bar** requiring the residual re-identification risk to be remote given all means reasonably likely to be used [1][6][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal test.)*
- **NIST** provides an evaluation framework for **differential privacy guarantees**, cautioning that a DP claim is meaningful only with a stated ε, a defined "privacy unit", correct composition accounting, and validated implementation — an unqualified "differentially private" label is not evidence [9]. *(Standards interpretation.)*
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
This section is the catalogue. Each technique is assessed on **what it is**, **guarantee and limits**, **GDPR relevance**, and **maturity**. A consolidated view is in the Compliance Maturity Model.

## The anonymisation vs pseudonymisation line (read first)

Every entry below turns on one distinction. Under **Recital 26** and **Article 4(5)**, data is **anonymous** — and outside the GDPR — only if a subject can no longer be identified by "all the means reasonably likely to be used" by the controller or another person; otherwise it is **pseudonymised** and remains **personal data**, fully in scope [1][6]. The test is **relative and contextual**: the same output can be anonymous in one party's hands and personal in another's if that party holds the additional information (cf. `gdpr-foundations` on *Breyer*) [1]. Consequences for PET selection: (a) techniques that retain a reversible mapping or key (pseudonymisation, tokenisation, encryption, TEEs) **cannot** produce anonymous data for the party holding the key; (b) techniques that *transform* the data to bound identifiability (strong k-anonymity/aggregation, well-parameterised differential privacy, robust synthetic data) **may** reach anonymisation, but only after a documented residual-risk assessment [2][6]. *(Legal obligation as interpreted.)*

## Pseudonymisation and tokenisation

- **What it is.** Replacing identifying fields with pseudonyms (via counters, random tokens, keyed hashes/HMAC, or encryption), keeping the re-identification mapping separate and secured (Art. 4(5)). **Tokenisation** is the vault-based variant common in payments [4][5].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Reduces linkability and the impact of a breach, but is **reversible by design** by whoever holds the mapping/key; naive hashing of low-entropy identifiers is vulnerable to dictionary/brute-force attacks, so ENISA recommends keyed constructions (HMAC) or encryption with proper secret management [4][5].
- **GDPR relevance.** The archetypal Article 25(1)/32(1)(a) measure and named in Article 89(1); **pseudonymised data remains personal data** (Recital 26/28) [1]. A recurring compliance error is treating it as anonymisation.
- **Maturity. Established** — production-grade and ubiquitous; the main risk is weak technique or key handling, not immaturity [4][5]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*

## k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness

- **What it is.** *Syntactic* de-identification of tabular data. **k-anonymity** generalises/suppresses quasi-identifiers so each record shares its quasi-identifier values with at least *k−1* others [13]. **l-diversity** additionally requires each such group to hold ≥ *l* well-represented sensitive values [14]. **t-closeness** requires each group's sensitive-value distribution to stay within *t* of the overall distribution [15].
- **Guarantee and limits.** They bound **singling-out** (k) and **attribute disclosure** (l, t), but give **no formal guarantee against an adversary with background knowledge or auxiliary datasets**, and do not **compose** safely across multiple releases; k-anonymity is vulnerable to homogeneity and background-knowledge attacks (the very attacks l-diversity and t-closeness were designed to blunt), and high k/strict t can destroy utility [13][14][15]. ISO/IEC 20889 catalogues these as de-identification models with explicitly bounded assurance [10].
- **GDPR relevance.** A well-parameterised, context-assessed k-anonymised (ideally l-diverse/t-close) release **can** support an anonymisation argument under Recital 26, but only after residual-risk analysis; weak parameters leave the data personal [1][6][10].
- **Maturity. Established** as a method, with mature tooling; but treated by regulators as necessary-not-sufficient and increasingly complemented by differential privacy [2][10]. *(Best practice / academic.)*

## Differential privacy (global vs local, ε)

- **What it is.** A **formal, mathematical** definition of privacy: a randomised mechanism is **ε-differentially private** if adding or removing any single individual's record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor of e^ε [16][17]. Noise (e.g. Laplace/Gaussian) is calibrated to the query's sensitivity. In the **global/central** model a trusted curator adds noise to results; in the **local** model each person perturbs their own data before sending it, so no raw data is centralised [9][17].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Unlike syntactic models, DP's guarantee holds **regardless of the adversary's background knowledge** and **composes** (repeated queries consume a cumulative **privacy budget**). The budget is **ε**: **smaller ε ⇒ stronger privacy, more noise, less utility**; large ε renders the guarantee near-meaningless. Local DP needs far more data/noise than global DP for the same utility. NIST warns a DP claim is only as good as its stated ε, defined privacy unit, correct composition accounting, and validated implementation [9][16][17].
- **GDPR relevance.** DP directly serves **data minimisation** and can support an **anonymisation** argument for *outputs* when ε and the privacy unit are conservative and documented — but the underlying dataset remains personal data, and a poorly chosen ε does not anonymise [1][2][9].
- **Maturity. Maturing** — deployed at scale by large data holders and national statistical offices (which document DP use for official-statistics releases), with growing tooling, but requires scarce expertise to parameterise correctly [2][8][9]. *(Best practice / academic.)*

## Synthetic data

- **What it is.** Artificial records generated from a model (statistical or, increasingly, generative-AI) fitted to a real dataset, intended to preserve aggregate utility while not mapping to real individuals [2][3].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Offers **no inherent formal guarantee**: a model that overfits can memorise and leak real records, and synthetic data can still enable membership-inference or attribute-disclosure attacks. Assurance depends on the generation method and evaluation; combining generation with **differential privacy** ("DP-synthetic data") provides a quantifiable bound [2][3][9]. Utility and privacy trade off.
- **GDPR relevance.** Robustly generated, evaluated synthetic data **may** be anonymous and out of scope; but the **training process uses personal data** and the output must be tested for leakage before that claim is made [2][6].
- **Maturity. Maturing** — active adoption for testing, ML and data sharing, but privacy assurance methods are still consolidating; the ICO cautions against assuming synthetic ⇒ anonymous [2][3]. *(Best practice.)*

## Secure multi-party computation (SMPC)

- **What it is.** Cryptographic protocols (secret sharing, garbled circuits) that let multiple parties jointly compute a function over their combined inputs while each input stays private from the others [3][18].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Provides strong **input privacy** against defined adversary models (semi-honest or malicious), but the **agreed output can still reveal or be personal data**, protocols add communication/computation overhead, and correctness depends on non-collusion assumptions and careful implementation [3][18].
- **GDPR relevance.** Enables collaborative analytics/linkage with **minimised data exposure** (Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25) and reduces the need to pool raw data with third parties; the **inputs and outputs remain personal data** in the hands that can attribute them [1][2].
- **Maturity. Emerging-to-maturing** — real deployments exist (e.g. cross-organisation statistics), but general-purpose SMPC is performance-limited and specialist [2][3]. *(Best practice.)*

## Homomorphic encryption (HE)

- **What it is.** Encryption schemes allowing computation **directly on ciphertext**; the decrypted result equals the result of the same computation on the plaintext. **Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)**, first realised by Gentry (2009), supports arbitrary computation [3][19].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Strong confidentiality: the compute party never sees plaintext. But FHE carries **very high computational and storage overhead**, "partially" homomorphic variants support only limited operations, and key management is critical; the **result and the input are personal data** to the key holder [3][19].
- **GDPR relevance.** Supports **encryption in use** and outsourced/third-party processing with minimal exposure (Art. 32); it does **not anonymise** — it protects confidentiality [1][2].
- **Maturity. Emerging** — practical for narrow, well-bounded computations; general FHE remains too costly for most production workloads [2][3]. *(Best practice.)*

## Trusted execution environments (TEEs)

- **What it is.** Hardware-isolated, **attestable** enclaves that protect code and data in use from the rest of the host, underpinning "confidential computing" [2][3].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Provide **confidentiality and integrity in use** with far lower overhead than HE/SMPC, but rely on **trust in the hardware vendor** and are exposed to side-channel and micro-architectural attacks; data inside the enclave is plaintext to the enclave, so this is a **security**, not an anonymisation, control [2][3].
- **GDPR relevance.** A strong **Article 32** measure for processing sensitive data on untrusted infrastructure and a route to **encryption in use**; the data **remains personal data** [1][2].
- **Maturity. Maturing** — broadly available from major cloud and CPU vendors, though attestation and side-channel hardening require care [2][3]. *(Best practice.)*

## Federated learning (FL)

- **What it is.** Distributed machine learning that trains a shared model by exchanging **model updates** (gradients/weights) computed locally, so raw training data stays on devices or in institutional silos [21][22].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Reduces raw-data centralisation, but **model updates can leak** training data (gradient-inversion, membership-inference), so FL is typically combined with **differential privacy** and/or **SMPC/secure aggregation** for a meaningful guarantee; it adds systems complexity and can be attacked via poisoning [21][22].
- **GDPR relevance.** Advances **data minimisation** and can keep data local (helpful for special-category or cross-border data), but the **updates and the trained model may be personal data**, so FL alone is not anonymisation [1][2][22].
- **Maturity. Maturing** — production use in mobile/keyboard and healthcare settings, with active research on its privacy hardening [2][22]. *(Best practice.)*

## Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs)

- **What it is.** Protocols letting a prover convince a verifier that a statement is true (e.g. "this user is over 18", "this credential is valid") **without revealing any underlying data** beyond the statement's truth [20].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Provide **completeness, soundness and zero-knowledge** under cryptographic assumptions; enable powerful **data minimisation** (attribute proofs, age assurance, selective disclosure). Limits are implementation complexity, proving cost for some schemes, and the fact that the **claim being proven** may still be personal data in context [20].
- **GDPR relevance.** A direct **minimisation/DPbDD** enabler — proving eligibility without disclosing identity or the raw attribute (Arts. 5(1)(c), 25) — increasingly relevant to age assurance and verifiable credentials [1][2].
- **Maturity. Emerging-to-maturing** — mature in specific domains (e.g. some digital-identity and blockchain systems), still specialist for general use [2]. *(Best practice.)*

## Encryption in transit, at rest, and in use

- **What it is.** The baseline confidentiality control: TLS and equivalents protect data **in transit**; disk/database/field encryption protects data **at rest**; TEEs and HE protect data **in use** [1][2][12].
- **Guarantee and limits.** Protects confidentiality (and, with authenticated encryption, integrity) against parties without the key; strength depends on **algorithm choice, key management and rotation** (ISO/IEC 27002 cryptographic controls). Encrypted personal data held by a party **with** the key remains personal data; loss of key control is the dominant risk [1][12].
- **GDPR relevance.** **Named expressly in Article 32(1)(a)**; encryption at rest/in transit is a de facto expectation, and encryption in use extends protection to processing [1][12].
- **Maturity. Established** for transit/at rest (universal); **emerging/maturing** for in use (via TEEs/HE) [2][3][12]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*

## ENISA/ICO selection guide — which PET for which risk

Match the **risk** to the PET's **function**, then validate residual risk in a DPIA [2][3][4]:

| Primary risk to address | Candidate PETs | GDPR function |
|-------------------------|----------------|---------------|
| Records can be linked/attributed by the holder | Pseudonymisation, tokenisation, encryption at rest | Security & risk reduction (Art. 32); *stays personal data* |
| Re-identification in a data **release/publication** | k-anonymity (+ l-diversity/t-closeness), differential privacy, DP-synthetic data | Reduce identifiability toward anonymisation (Recital 26) |
| Repeated **queries/analytics** over sensitive data | Global or local differential privacy | Quantified, composable minimisation |
| **Collaboration/linkage** across organisations without pooling raw data | SMPC, federated learning (+ secure aggregation/DP) | Data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)) |
| **Processing on untrusted infrastructure** | TEEs, homomorphic encryption | Encryption/confidentiality in use (Art. 32) |
| **Proving an attribute** (age, eligibility) without disclosure | Zero-knowledge proofs | Minimisation / DPbDD (Art. 25) |
| Data **in transit / at rest** confidentiality | TLS, disk/field encryption | Security baseline (Art. 32(1)(a)) |

This function-first mapping mirrors the goal-oriented *privacy design strategies* (notably *minimise*, *hide* and *aggregate*), which classify PETs by the data-protection outcome they serve [23]. Editorial guidance: **combine** PETs (e.g. federated learning + secure aggregation + differential privacy) where one technique leaves residual risk; never present a PET as anonymisation without a documented Recital 26 assessment [2][6]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*

text:
- **Confidential computing in the cloud** — TEEs and, for narrow workloads, homomorphic encryption let controllers process sensitive personal data on shared/untrusted infrastructure while limiting the provider's access; assess attestation, side-channel exposure and the **shared-responsibility** split (see `cloud-hosting-foundations`) [2][3]. *(Best practice grounded in Art. 32.)*
- **Key custody is the control that matters** — for pseudonymisation, tokenisation and encryption, hosting must keep the re-identification key/mapping or KMS **separate from the protected data** and under controlled access; co-locating key and ciphertext defeats the measure [1][4][5]. *(Legal obligation — Art. 32.)*
- **Data locality via minimisation PETs** — federated learning, local DP and SMPC can keep raw data in-region, easing transfer and localisation constraints (see `gdpr-transfers`), though model updates/outputs may still constitute a transfer of personal data [1][22]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Provider-managed PET services** — where a host offers managed DP, confidential-computing or tokenisation services, the controller must still evidence correct parameters and residual risk; a managed PET does not transfer accountability [2]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
- **Pseudonymise player analytics** — separate durable account identifiers from behavioural/telemetry payloads via pseudonymisation or tokenisation, holding the mapping separately; high-volume game telemetry is a strong minimisation target [1][4]. *(Best practice grounded in Art. 25(2).)*
- **Aggregate and add DP to published metrics** — leaderboards, heatmaps and "players like you" analytics released externally should use aggregation/k-anonymity or differential privacy to prevent singling-out of individual players, especially minors [2][13][16]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Zero-knowledge age assurance** — ZKP-based age/eligibility proofs can satisfy child-protection expectations (see `game-hosting-foundations`, `uk-gdpr-foundations`) while minimising the identity data collected from players [1][2][20]. *(Best practice grounded in Art. 25.)*
- **Confidential processing of moderation/anti-cheat data** — often sensitive; TEEs and strong encryption (in transit/at rest/in use) plus strict retention apply the *hide* strategy [1][2][3]. *(Best practice.)*
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
- **PETs address the minimisation-vs-model-appetite tension** — the central AI privacy conflict (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`) is mitigated by **differential privacy** (DP-SGD training), **federated learning**, **synthetic data** and **SMPC/HE** for privacy-preserving training and inference [2][3][9][21]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Model updates and models can be personal data** — federated learning and DP reduce, but do not automatically remove, the risk that gradients or a trained model leak training data (membership-inference, gradient inversion); combine FL with DP/secure aggregation for a real guarantee [21][22]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Differential privacy for training/analytics** — provides a bounded, documentable guarantee on the influence of any single training record; state ε, the privacy unit and composition accounting (NIST criteria) so the claim is auditable [9][16][17]. *(Best practice.)*
- **AI Act data-governance overlap** — high-risk AI **data-governance** duties (representative, relevant, error-checked data) and the GDPR's minimisation are complementary; PETs are a shared implementation layer (see `ai-act-foundations` / `ai-act-high-risk`) [1]. *(Cross-reference.)*
- **Synthetic training data ≠ automatic anonymisation** — synthetic data used to train or test AI must be leakage-tested (ideally DP-generated) before any out-of-scope claim [2][3]. *(Best practice.)*
title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: A Catalogue

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** (must, per statute) / **BEST PRACTICE** (should, per standards/regulators) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (we suggest).

1. **Start from the risk, not the technology** — identify whether the risk is identifiability, confidentiality, or collaborative computation, then select the PET(s) by function using the selection guide. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [2][3]
2. **Never assume a PET anonymises** — for any claim that data is out of scope, run and document a **Recital 26** residual-identifiability assessment against means reasonably likely to be used. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][6]
3. **Keep keys and mappings separate** — pseudonymisation/tokenisation/encryption only reduce risk if the re-identification material is segregated and access-controlled (Art. 32). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][4]
4. **Parameterise DP explicitly** — record ε, the privacy unit, composition/budget accounting and the noise mechanism; treat an unqualified "differentially private" label as unproven. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [9][16]
5. **Test synthetic data and model updates for leakage** — membership-inference/attribute-disclosure testing before relying on synthetic-data or FL privacy claims. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [2][3][21]
6. **Combine PETs where one is insufficient** — e.g. FL + secure aggregation + DP; SMPC + DP on outputs. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [2][22]
7. **Right-size to maturity and cost** — prefer established PETs (pseudonymisation, encryption, aggregation) for baseline needs; reserve HE/SMPC for cases that justify their overhead. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [2][3]
8. **Record PET decisions in the DPIA** — capture the PET, its guarantee, residual risk and why it is adequate, as accountability evidence (see `dpia-methodology`). *(OBLIGATION for accountability; BEST PRACTICE for the register.)* [1][2]

text:
- **Phase 0 — Baseline PETs:** Apply pseudonymisation/tokenisation and encryption (transit/at rest) with segregated key management across in-scope processing. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Minimisation by design:** Introduce aggregation and, for external releases, k-anonymity/l-diversity/t-closeness with residual-risk assessment. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 2 — Quantified privacy:** Adopt differential privacy (global first; local where data stays on-device) for analytics/ML, with documented ε and composition accounting. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 3 — Collaborative & in-use protection:** Pilot federated learning + secure aggregation, SMPC, TEEs (and HE for narrow workloads) where raw-data pooling or untrusted infrastructure is unavoidable. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 4 — Advanced minimisation:** Deploy ZKP-based attribute proofs (e.g. age assurance) and DP-synthetic data for sharing/testing. *Effort:* Medium–High.
- **Phase 5 — Assurance:** Leakage testing, PET effectiveness metrics, DPIA integration and periodic re-assessment of parameters and maturity. *Effort:* Ongoing.

| Level | Name | Description | Indicators |
|-------|------|-------------|-----------|
| 1 | Initial | PETs ad hoc or absent; pseudonymisation/anonymisation conflated; encryption patchy. | No PET inventory; "anonymous" claims unassessed. |
| 2 | Managed | Baseline PETs (pseudonymisation, encryption) in place but keys/mappings poorly segregated. | Encryption present; weak key custody; no DP. |
| 3 | Defined | PETs selected by risk/function; Recital 26 assessments documented; aggregation/k-anonymity for releases. | Selection guide used; DPIA records PETs. |
| 4 | Quantitatively Managed | Differential privacy with governed ε/budget; leakage testing for synthetic data/FL; metrics on PET effectiveness. | ε accounting; membership-inference tests; KPIs. |
| 5 | Optimising | PETs combined and automated; confidential computing/SMPC/ZKP where justified; continuous parameter and maturity review. | Layered PETs; secure aggregation + DP; audit. |

**PET selection matrix (function × maturity):** pseudonymisation, tokenisation, encryption in transit/at rest — *security/risk reduction*, **Established** [1][4][12]; k-anonymity/l-diversity/t-closeness — *identifiability reduction*, **Established** [10][13][14][15]; differential privacy, synthetic data, TEEs, federated learning — *minimisation/identifiability/in-use*, **Maturing** [2][3][9][21]; SMPC, homomorphic encryption, ZKPs, encryption in use — *collaborative/in-use/minimisation*, **Emerging** [2][3][18][19][20]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*

title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
**Privacy engineering** is the discipline of translating data-protection obligations into concrete system design, architecture and operational controls. Its legal anchor in the EU/UK is **GDPR Article 25 — data protection by design and by default (DPbDD)** — reinforced by **Article 32 (security of processing)** [1]. Article 25 requires controllers to embed the data-protection principles (Article 5) into processing **from the design stage and throughout the lifecycle**, and to ensure that, **by default**, only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed [1][2].

This document is the implementation layer for the Tier 1 foundations (`gdpr-foundations`, `uk-gdpr-foundations`, `eprivacy-foundations`). It sets out the DPbDD obligation and the EDPB's interpretation [2], the security-of-processing requirements of Article 32 [1], the recognised **frameworks and standards** (ISO/IEC 27701, 27001, 29100; the NIST Privacy Framework) [5][6][7][8], the foundational **privacy design strategies** (Hoepman's eight: minimise, hide, separate, aggregate, inform, control, enforce, demonstrate) [9], and the main **privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs)** — pseudonymisation, anonymisation, encryption and differential privacy [1][4].

Three conclusions dominate. First, **DPbDD is a legal obligation, not best practice** — it binds all controllers regardless of size [2]. Second, **default settings carry legal weight**: the least-privacy-intrusive configuration must be the default. Third, **standards operationalise the law**: ISO/IEC 27701 and the NIST Privacy Framework give controllers a structured, auditable way to demonstrate Article 25/32 compliance and accountability [5][6]. (Note: the **NIST Privacy Framework** current published version is **1.0 (2020)**; version **1.1** is in draft, realigned with CSF 2.0, expected 2026 [5].)
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
- **Article 25 (DPbDD)** is a binding obligation on all controllers: embed data protection by design from the outset, and process only necessary data by default [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 32** requires appropriate technical and organisational measures for security, expressly naming **pseudonymisation and encryption**, and confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **EDPB Guidelines 4/2019** interpret Article 25: measures must be effective, implemented before and during processing, and reviewed continually [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Pseudonymised data is still personal data**; only genuine **anonymisation** removes data from GDPR scope — a distinction engineers routinely get wrong (see `gdpr-foundations`) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Hoepman's eight privacy design strategies** (minimise, hide, separate, aggregate, inform, control, enforce, demonstrate) map obligations to architecture [9]. *(Best practice / academic.)*
- **Standards operationalise compliance:** ISO/IEC 27701 (privacy information management), ISO/IEC 27001 (security management), ISO/IEC 29100 (privacy framework) and the **NIST Privacy Framework** provide auditable structures [5][6][7][8]. *(Best practice.)*
- **PETs** — pseudonymisation, encryption, differential privacy, aggregation — reduce risk but do not by themselves discharge the accountability obligation [1][4]. *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)*
- **Default settings are a compliance surface:** shipping a product with maximal data collection "on" by default breaches Article 25(2) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text: This document gives engineering, product and compliance teams a foundational, evidence-based account of **how** to implement the data-protection obligations established in the Tier 1 legal documents. It supports secure-by-design development, DPIA scoping, standards adoption, and the accountability evidence base. It is the bridge between "what the law requires" (`gdpr-foundations`) and "how systems must be built".

text:
*Shared terms (personal data, pseudonymisation, anonymous data, controller, accountability) are defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only privacy-engineering-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Data protection by design (DPbD) | Implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures to embed the data-protection principles into processing, from the design stage onward (Art. 25(1)). | [1][2] |
| Data protection by default (DPbDefault) | Ensuring that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed — in amount, extent of processing, retention and accessibility (Art. 25(2)). | [1][2] |
| Technical and organisational measures (TOMs) | The combined technical (e.g., encryption, access control) and organisational (e.g., policies, training) controls used to meet Arts. 25 and 32. | [1] |
| Privacy-enhancing technology (PET) | A technology that minimises personal-data processing or protects it (e.g., pseudonymisation, encryption, differential privacy, aggregation). | [1][4] |
| Privacy design strategy | A high-level approach linking data-protection goals to system architecture (Hoepman's eight strategies). | [9] |
| Differential privacy | A formal, mathematical guarantee that the inclusion or exclusion of any single individual's data does not significantly change an analysis's output. | [4][9] |
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text: The idea that privacy should be built into systems — **"Privacy by Design"** — long predates the GDPR, but the GDPR made it a **statutory obligation** in Article 25 [1]. Privacy engineering emerged as the technical discipline that operationalises this obligation, drawing on security engineering, systems architecture and formal methods. Academic work — notably Hoepman's **privacy design strategies** — provided a bridge between legal principles and engineering practice by classifying design patterns and PETs under eight goal-oriented strategies [9]. Standards bodies followed: ISO/IEC published a **privacy framework** (29100) and a **privacy information management** extension to the ISMS standards (27701), while NIST released its **Privacy Framework** to manage privacy risk analogously to its Cybersecurity Framework [5][6][7][8].
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
The primary legal anchors are **Articles 25 and 32** of the GDPR (and their UK GDPR equivalents) [1]:

- **Article 25(1) — data protection by design:** taking account of the state of the art, cost, and the nature/scope/context/purposes of processing, as well as the risks, the controller shall implement appropriate TOMs (e.g., **pseudonymisation**) designed to implement the data-protection principles effectively and integrate necessary safeguards [1].
- **Article 25(2) — data protection by default:** the controller shall implement measures ensuring that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed — covering the amount collected, extent of processing, retention and accessibility [1].
- **Article 32 — security of processing:** appropriate TOMs to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, expressly including pseudonymisation and encryption; confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience; restoration after incidents; and a process for regularly testing effectiveness [1].

DPbDD and Article 32 operationalise the **accountability principle** (Art. 5(2)) and the security principle (Art. 5(1)(f)) established in `gdpr-foundations`.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 5(1)(f) | Integrity and confidentiality (security) principle. | [1] |
| Art. 5(2) | Accountability — demonstrate compliance (DPbDD is a key means). | [1] |
| Art. 24 | Controller responsibility to implement appropriate TOMs, reviewed and updated. | [1] |
| Art. 25(1) | Data protection by design. | [1] |
| Art. 25(2) | Data protection by default. | [1] |
| Art. 32 | Security of processing (pseudonymisation, encryption, CIA + resilience, testing). | [1] |
| Art. 35 | Data protection impact assessment (where high risk) — key privacy-engineering trigger. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |

| Recital 78 | DPbDD elaborated — minimisation, pseudonymisation, transparency, and enabling monitoring; producers of products/services encouraged to consider DPbDD. | [1] |
| Recital 26 | Identifiability test; anonymous data falls outside the GDPR (basis for the anonymisation/pseudonymisation distinction). | [1] |
| Recital 83 | Security — risk-based measures against accidental/unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, disclosure. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

Not Applicable at the foundational level — Article 25/32 obligations are elaborated primarily through **regulatory guidance** (EDPB, ICO) rather than a distinct line of foundational case law. Enforcement decisions turning on inadequate TOMs (e.g., national DPA fines for security failures) will be treated in `privacy-controls-mapping` (backlog). [2][3]

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **EDPB Guidelines 4/2019** confirm DPbDD is an obligation for **all controllers**, irrespective of size; measures must be **effective** in achieving the intended data-protection outcome, implemented **before** processing begins and reviewed **continually** [2]. Cost is a permitted factor, but "state of the art" and effectiveness cannot be traded away for convenience [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **ICO** frames DPbDD as considering data protection "at the start of everything you do" and integral to **accountability**; it must be embedded throughout the processing lifecycle, not bolted on [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- Both regulators treat **default settings** as substantive: the most privacy-protective option must be the default, and users should not have to act to protect themselves [2][3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ENISA** provides technical guidance mapping design strategies and PETs to the DPbDD obligation, aimed at engineers [4]. *(Regulatory / technical guidance.)*
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
Privacy engineering translates the above into architecture. **Hoepman's eight strategies** [9] give a practical taxonomy:

- **Minimise** — collect/retain the least data (Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25(2)); select-before-collect, delete early.
- **Hide** — restrict visibility: encryption at rest/in transit, pseudonymisation, access control (Art. 32).
- **Separate** — distribute/partition data to prevent correlation (e.g., separate identifiers from payloads).
- **Aggregate** — process at the coarsest granularity sufficient (aggregation, k-anonymity, differential privacy) [4].
- **Inform** — transparency to data subjects (Arts. 12–14).
- **Control** — give data subjects agency (consent, preferences, rights tooling).
- **Enforce** — bind processing to a policy and enforce it technically (access policy, retention automation).
- **Demonstrate** — logging, records and evidence to prove compliance (Art. 5(2)) [9].

Core engineering practices:

- **Encryption & key management** (Art. 32) — appropriate algorithms, segregated key custody, rotation.
- **Pseudonymisation** — separate the re-identification key; treat pseudonymised data as personal data still in scope [1].
- **Retention automation** — enforce storage limitation by design (TTLs, scheduled deletion/anonymisation).
- **DPIA triggers in the SDLC** — Article 35 assessments embedded at design gates.
- **Testing** — regular testing of the effectiveness of measures is an explicit Article 32 requirement [1].
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
- **Encryption & tenancy** — encryption at rest/in transit, strong tenant isolation, and customer-controlled keys where feasible support Art. 32 [1].
- **Standards alignment** — hosting/cloud environments should map controls to **ISO/IEC 27001** (ISMS) and evidence privacy controls via **ISO/IEC 27701** (PIMS); cloud-specific PII control sets (e.g., the ISO/IEC 27018 code of practice) extend this where applicable [6][7]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Shared responsibility** — the controller retains DPbDD accountability even when infrastructure is a processor's responsibility; document the control split (see `gdpr-foundations` Hosting Considerations). *(Editorial recommendation.)*
- **Data locality & minimisation** — architect so that only necessary data is replicated across regions; over-replication undermines Art. 25(2). *(Best practice.)*
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
- **Telemetry minimisation** — games generate high-volume telemetry; apply the *minimise* and *aggregate* strategies (sample, aggregate, pseudonymise player analytics) [9]. *(Best practice grounded in Art. 25(2).)*
- **Default privacy for players** — matchmaking, profile visibility and social features should default to the least-exposing setting, especially for likely-child users (Art. 25(2); children's codes — see `uk-gdpr-foundations`) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pseudonymised player IDs** — separate durable account identifiers from behavioural payloads; retain re-identification keys separately [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Anti-cheat & moderation data** — often sensitive; apply *hide* (encryption, access control) and strict retention. *(Best practice.)*
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

text:
- **Minimisation vs. model appetite** — the central privacy-engineering tension for AI; mitigate with **aggregation, pseudonymisation, synthetic data, differential privacy and federated learning** [4][9]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Differential privacy** — provides a formal privacy guarantee for model training/analytics, bounding the influence of any single record [4]. *(Best practice; detailed in `pets-catalogue`.)*
- **DPbDD for AI pipelines** — apply Article 25 across the ML lifecycle (data collection, training, inference, logging); default to not retaining raw training inputs longer than necessary [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Overlap with the AI Act** — technical risk-management and data-governance duties under the AI Act complement Article 25; covered in `ai-act-foundations` / `ai-governance-foundations` (backlog). *(Cross-reference.)*
title: Privacy Engineering: Foundations, Data Protection by Design & Default

Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Embed DPbDD in the SDLC** — design gates, DPIA triggers, privacy requirements in tickets. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2]
2. **Default to least data** — ship the most privacy-protective configuration by default. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2]
3. **Apply Article 32 controls** — encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, resilience, and **regular effectiveness testing**. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Adopt a framework** — implement ISO/IEC 27701 and/or the NIST Privacy Framework to structure and evidence controls. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [5][6]
5. **Use privacy design strategies** — apply the eight strategies as a design checklist. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [9]
6. **Distinguish anonymisation from pseudonymisation** — do not treat pseudonymised data as out of scope. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
7. **Evidence everything** — the *demonstrate* strategy: logs, records, DPIAs, control mappings for accountability. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [9]

text:
The **EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689**, "AI Act") is the world's first comprehensive horizontal law on artificial intelligence. It **entered into force on 1 August 2024** and applies through a **phased timeline** [1][3]. It takes a **risk-based** approach, sorting AI systems into four tiers: **unacceptable risk** (prohibited), **high-risk** (strict obligations), **limited/transparency risk** (disclosure duties), and **minimal risk** (largely unregulated) [3]. It also imposes a separate regime on **general-purpose AI (GPAI) models**, with heightened duties for models posing **systemic risk** [3].

This document establishes the foundations: the risk tiers and what each requires, the GPAI regime, the governance architecture (the **European AI Office**, AI Board, Scientific Panel), the **penalty** structure, the **phased application timeline**, and the AI Act's **relationship with the GDPR**. As of this document's date, the following are already in force: **prohibited practices and AI literacy (from 2 February 2025)** and **GPAI and governance obligations (from 2 August 2025)** [3].

The most important point concerns **high-risk timing**. Under the original text, most high-risk and transparency rules would apply from **2 August 2026**. However, the **"AI Omnibus"** simplification package (Commission proposal of 19 November 2025) was, after a provisional agreement on 7 May 2026, **formally adopted** — European Parliament plenary on **16 June 2026** and Council final approval on **29 June 2026** — postponing high-risk obligations to **2 December 2027** (stand-alone Annex III use cases) and **2 August 2028** (AI as safety components in regulated products), and shifting AI-content transparency/watermarking to 2 December 2026 [4][5][6][7]. It **enters into force on the third day after Official Journal publication**; confirm the OJ citation before relying on the exact dates [7].
title: EU AI Act: Foundations, Risk Tiers & Timeline

text:
- The **AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)** entered into force **1 August 2024** and applies in phases; it is the first comprehensive horizontal AI law [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- It is **risk-based**: **unacceptable** (prohibited), **high-risk**, **limited/transparency**, and **minimal** risk [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Prohibited practices** (e.g., social scoring, certain manipulative AI, untargeted facial-image scraping, some biometric/emotion-recognition uses) and **AI literacy** duties apply from **2 February 2025** [3]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- **GPAI model** obligations (transparency, copyright, technical documentation) and the **governance** framework apply from **2 August 2025**; GPAI models with **systemic risk** face additional risk-assessment and mitigation duties [3]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- **High-risk** systems face the heaviest duties (risk management, data governance, logging, documentation, human oversight, robustness/cybersecurity, conformity assessment) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Timeline updated:** the **AI Omnibus** was **adopted** (EP 16 Jun 2026; Council 29 Jun 2026), postponing high-risk application to **2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028**; it binds on OJ publication (+3 days) [6][7]. *(Adopted; in force on OJ publication.)*
- **Penalties** are severe: up to **€35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover** for prohibited-practice breaches (Art. 99) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The AI Act **operates alongside the GDPR**; where AI processes personal data, both apply, and DPbDD (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`) remains required [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text: AI systems increasingly make or inform consequential decisions, creating risks to safety and fundamental rights that existing law addressed only partially. The EU responded with a **horizontal, risk-based** Regulation rather than sector-by-sector rules, aiming to protect health, safety and fundamental rights while supporting innovation and a single market for trustworthy AI [3]. The AI Act was adopted in 2024 with a deliberately **staggered application** to give providers, deployers and standards bodies time to prepare [1][3]. During 2025 the Commission launched a broader **simplification agenda** ("Digital Omnibus"), part of which — the **AI Omnibus** — adjusts the AI Act's timeline and reduces administrative burden; it was **adopted** by the European Parliament (16 June 2026) and the Council (29 June 2026) [6][7].
title: EU AI Act: Foundations, Risk Tiers & Timeline

text:
The AI Act regulates AI along the value chain, placing most obligations on **providers**, with defined duties for **deployers**, importers and distributors [1]. Its structure:

- **Chapter I** — subject matter, scope, definitions (incl. the Art. 3(1) definition of "AI system").
- **Chapter II (Art. 5)** — **prohibited** AI practices.
- **Chapter III** — **high-risk** AI systems: classification (Art. 6, Annexes I & III) and obligations (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, conformity assessment, registration).
- **Chapter IV (Art. 50)** — **transparency** obligations for certain systems (e.g., chatbots, deepfakes, synthetic content).
- **Chapter V** — **general-purpose AI models**, including systemic-risk models (Arts. 51–56).
- **Chapters VI–VII** — governance (AI Office, AI Board, Scientific Panel, Advisory Forum), national authorities, database.
- **Chapter XII (Arts. 99–101)** — **penalties**.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 3 | Definitions (AI system, provider, deployer, GPAI model, systemic risk). | [1] |
| Art. 5 | Prohibited AI practices (unacceptable risk). | [1] |
| Art. 6 + Annexes I, III | Classification rules for high-risk AI systems. | [1] |
| Arts. 8–15 | Core high-risk requirements (risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, robustness/cybersecurity). | [1] |
| Art. 16 et seq. | Provider obligations for high-risk systems (incl. conformity assessment, registration). | [1] |
| Art. 50 | Transparency obligations (AI interaction disclosure; marking synthetic content/deepfakes). | [1] |
| Arts. 51–56 | GPAI models and systemic-risk obligations. | [1] |
| Art. 99 | Penalties — up to €35m or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for Art. 5 breaches; lower tiers for other breaches. | [1] |
| Art. 113 | Entry into force and staggered application dates. | [1] |

| Recital 26–27 | Risk-based approach and proportionality across tiers. | [1] |
| Recital 60 area | Human oversight rationale for high-risk systems. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

Not Applicable at the foundational level — the AI Act is recent and its high-risk provisions are not yet fully applicable, so there is no established CJEU case law interpreting it. Interpretive weight currently rests on the Regulation's text, Commission guidance and (for personal data) GDPR case law (see `gdpr-foundations`). [1][3]

**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames the AI Act around four risk tiers and stresses that the **majority of AI systems are minimal risk** and unregulated; obligations concentrate on high-risk and prohibited categories [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Transparency (Art. 50):** users must be told when they interact with AI (e.g., chatbots), and providers of generative AI must ensure AI-generated content is **identifiable** (labelling of deepfakes/synthetic content) [3]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
- **GPAI:** providers must meet transparency and copyright duties; **systemic-risk** models require risk assessment and mitigation, supported by guidelines and a **Code of Practice** [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Governance:** the **AI Office** (within the Commission), an **AI Board**, a **Scientific Panel** and an **Advisory Forum** oversee implementation and enforcement [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Reform (AI Omnibus):** after a provisional agreement (7 May 2026), the package was **formally adopted** — EP plenary 16 June 2026 and Council 29 June 2026 — postponing high-risk application (to 2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028) and adjusting content-transparency timing; it binds on OJ publication [6][7]. *(Adopted; confirm the OJ citation. Detailed in `ai-act-high-risk`.)*

It is a Tier 2 **deep-dive** that details the general-purpose AI (GPAI) and systemic-risk material introduced at overview level in `ai-act-foundations`; it does not repeat that overview. **Status note:** unlike the high-risk timeline, the GPAI regime is **already in force** — GPAI provider obligations apply from **2 August 2025** — and the **AI Omnibus** simplification package (adopted by the European Parliament on 16 June 2026 and the Council on 29 June 2026) **did not postpone** the GPAI obligations; it reinforced the AI Office's supervisory role over GPAI [1][3][9].
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
Chapter V of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) creates a **model-level** regime that sits apart from the risk-tier classification applied to AI *systems*. It regulates **general-purpose AI (GPAI) models** — the foundation models (large language, multimodal and generative models) that display significant generality and can be integrated into countless downstream systems [1]. These obligations **entered into application on 2 August 2025** and are enforced centrally by the **European AI Office**, not by national market-surveillance authorities [1][3][7].

Every GPAI-model provider owes four baseline duties under **Article 53**: maintain **technical documentation** (Annex XI); give **information and documentation to downstream providers** who integrate the model (Annex XII); put in place a **policy to comply with EU copyright law** (including the Directive (EU) 2019/790 text-and-data-mining reservation); and publish a **sufficiently detailed summary of training content** using the AI Office template [1][3]. Free and open-source models are relieved of the documentation duties — **but not** of the copyright and training-summary duties, and **not at all** where the model has systemic risk [1][5].

A subset of models is designated **GPAI with systemic risk**. Under **Article 51**, a model is presumed to carry systemic risk when the cumulative training compute exceeds **10²⁵ floating-point operations (FLOP)** — a rebuttable presumption — or where the Commission so decides on Annex XIII criteria [1][3][5]. Such providers must additionally, under **Article 55**, perform **model evaluation including adversarial testing (red-teaming)**, **assess and mitigate systemic risks** at Union level, **track and report serious incidents** to the AI Office, and ensure **adequate cybersecurity** for the model and its physical infrastructure [1][3]. The **General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** — published **10 July 2025** and structured in three chapters (Transparency, Copyright, Safety and Security) — is the primary **voluntary** route to demonstrate compliance pending harmonised standards; major providers (Amazon, Anthropic, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI and others) are signatories [4][6][10].
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
- **GPAI is a model-level regime (Chapter V, Arts. 51–56)**, distinct from the system-level risk tiers; a single GPAI model may be integrated into thousands of systems across the value chain [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **In force since 2 August 2025.** GPAI provider obligations apply now; the **AI Omnibus did not delay them** (contrast the postponed high-risk dates) [1][3][9]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- **A GPAI model (Art. 3(63))** is one trained on large data at scale, displaying **significant generality** and capable of a **wide range of distinct tasks**, regardless of how it is placed on the market; the Commission's guidelines treat **~10²³ FLOP** training compute plus broad generative capability as an indicative threshold for "significant generality" [1][6]. *(Legal obligation, as interpreted.)*
- **Article 53 baseline (all GPAI providers):** technical documentation (Annex XI), downstream information (Annex XII), an EU **copyright policy**, and a public **training-content summary** on the AI Office template [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Open-source relief is partial.** Free/open-source GPAI models are exempt from the Art. 53 documentation duties, but **remain bound** by the copyright and training-summary duties, and the relief **does not apply** to systemic-risk models [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Systemic-risk presumption = 10²⁵ FLOP (Art. 51(2)).** It is **rebuttable**; the Commission may also designate a model on **Annex XIII** criteria, and providers must **notify** the Commission within **two weeks** of meeting (or foreseeing) the threshold (Art. 52) [1][3][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 55 (systemic-risk models):** state-of-the-art **model evaluation / adversarial testing**, **systemic-risk assessment and mitigation** at Union level, **serious-incident tracking and reporting** to the AI Office, and **cybersecurity** of the model and infrastructure [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The GPAI Code of Practice (published 10 July 2025)** and the Commission's **Guidelines (18 July 2025)** are the practical compliance route; the Code is **voluntary** and signing it is **not** a legal safe harbour, but adherence is treated as evidence of compliance pending harmonised standards [4][6][10]. *(Regulatory interpretation + best practice.)*
- **Central enforcement by the AI Office** with GPAI-specific powers (information requests, evaluations, measures) and fines up to **€15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover** (Art. 101); AI Office enforcement powers apply from **2 August 2026** [1][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Value-chain hinge:** GPAI providers feed the **downstream** providers who build high-risk systems; the Annex XII information duty is what lets those integrators meet their own Chapter III obligations — see `ai-act-high-risk` [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*

It is written for legal, compliance, ML-engineering and safety readers at model developers and at organisations integrating third-party foundation models. It presupposes `ai-act-foundations` for the risk-tier overview and cross-refers `ai-act-high-risk` for the downstream system obligations and `ai-governance-foundations` for the operational management-system detail.

text:
**In scope:** the definition of a GPAI model (Art. 3(63)) and of systemic risk (Arts. 3(65)–(66)); the Article 53 provider obligations (technical documentation, downstream information, copyright policy, training-content summary) and the open-source relief; the authorised-representative duty (Art. 54); the systemic-risk classification route (Art. 51, the 10²⁵ FLOP presumption, Annex XIII) and the notification procedure (Art. 52); the Article 55 systemic-risk obligations; the Code of Practice and harmonised standards (Art. 56); the AI Office's role and GPAI enforcement/penalties (Arts. 88–94, 101); the application date (2 August 2025) and the transition for models already on the market; and the value-chain interaction with high-risk systems.

**Out of scope (covered elsewhere):** the four-tier system-level overview and penalty structure at large → `ai-act-foundations`; high-risk classification, the Art. 8–15 requirements and conformity assessment → `ai-act-high-risk`; Art. 50 transparency for AI-generated content (deepfake/synthetic-content marking is a **deployer/system** duty, distinct from the GPAI **model** regime) → `ai-act-foundations`; the AI Omnibus package as a whole → `digital-omnibus` (planned); operational AI management systems (ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF) → `ai-governance-foundations`; and GDPR duties where a GPAI model processes personal data → `gdpr-foundations`, `privacy-engineering-foundations`.

**Assumptions:** the reader has read `ai-act-foundations`. "Provider" throughout means the provider of the **GPAI model** (Art. 3(3)), which may differ from the provider of a downstream **system**. Where training or inference involves personal data, the GDPR applies in parallel and is not restated here.

*Shared terms (AI system, GPAI model, provider, deployer, high-risk AI system) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only GPAI-specific terms are defined here, per sub-topic policy.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| General-purpose AI model | An AI model, including one trained with a large amount of data using self-supervision at scale, that displays **significant generality** and is capable of competently performing a **wide range of distinct tasks**, and that can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems — excluding models used for research/development/prototyping before release (Art. 3(63)). | [1] |
| General-purpose AI system | An AI system based on a GPAI model, which has the capability to serve a variety of purposes, both for direct use and integration in other systems (Art. 3(66)). | [1] |
| Systemic risk | A risk specific to the **high-impact capabilities** of GPAI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to reach, or actual/reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, security, fundamental rights or society, that can propagate at scale (Art. 3(65)). | [1] |
| High-impact capabilities | Capabilities that match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced GPAI models (Art. 3(64)); presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOP (Art. 51(2)). | [1] |
| Downstream provider | A provider of an AI system (including a general-purpose AI system) which integrates a GPAI model, whether the model is its own or sourced from another provider (Art. 3(68)). | [1] |
| Training-content summary | The "sufficiently detailed summary" of the content used to train a GPAI model that the provider must draw up and make publicly available, following the template provided by the AI Office (Art. 53(1)(d)). | [1][3] |

text:
The AI Act was negotiated as a system-level, risk-based product-safety law. Between the Commission's 2021 proposal and the 2023–2024 trilogues, the rapid rise of **foundation models** — trained once, then adapted into innumerable downstream applications — exposed a gap: the risk of such a model cannot be assessed only where it is *deployed*, because the same model underlies many deployments and its capabilities (and failure modes) are set upstream at training time. The co-legislators responded by adding **Chapter V**, a **model-level** regime addressed to the entities that actually build the models, layered on top of the system-level tiers that the Commission presents as the AI Act's core structure [1][2].

The regime has two rings. The **outer ring** (Art. 53) applies to *every* GPAI model and is essentially about **transparency and lawful sourcing** — documentation up and down the value chain, a copyright policy, and a public training-content summary. The **inner ring** (Arts. 51, 55) applies only to the handful of models with **systemic risk** — the frontier models whose scale means a defect or misuse could cascade across the Union — and imposes **safety-engineering** duties: evaluation, red-teaming, risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity [1]. Because harmonised technical standards for these duties do not yet exist, the AI Office facilitated a co-regulatory **Code of Practice**, finalised on **10 July 2025**, three weeks before the obligations applied on **2 August 2025** [4][6]. The 2025–2026 **AI Omnibus** simplification package, which postponed the *high-risk* application dates, deliberately **left the GPAI timeline untouched** [3][9].
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
The GPAI regime is **Chapter V** of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, comprising: **classification** (Arts. 51–52), **obligations of GPAI-model providers** (Arts. 53–54), **obligations of systemic-risk providers** (Art. 55), and the **codes of practice** mechanism (Art. 56). Definitions sit in Chapter I (Art. 3(63)–(66), (68)); governance and enforcement in Chapters VII and IX (the **AI Office**, and Arts. 88–94 on GPAI supervision); penalties in Chapter XII (Art. 101). The substantive detail is filled out by **Annex XI** (technical documentation for the AI Office), **Annex XII** (information for downstream providers), and **Annex XIII** (criteria for designating systemic risk) [1].

The regime is enforced **centrally**: Article 88 confers on the Commission (acting through the **AI Office**) **exclusive competence** to supervise and enforce Chapter V, displacing national market-surveillance authorities for GPAI models [1][7]. This is a structural difference from the high-risk regime, which is enforced by Member State authorities.

**OBLIGATION vs INTERPRETATION note.** The Regulation's text (Arts. 51–56, Annexes XI–XIII) is the **binding obligation**. The Commission's **Guidelines** on the scope of GPAI obligations (18 July 2025) and the **Code of Practice** (10 July 2025) are **not** binding law: the Guidelines express the Commission's interpretation, and the Code is a **voluntary** instrument that adherents may use to *demonstrate* compliance (Art. 56(5)) [4][6]. They are treated below as **regulatory interpretation** / **best practice**, never as the source of the obligation itself.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 3(63) | Definition of "general-purpose AI model" (significant generality; wide range of distinct tasks). | [1] |
| Art. 3(64)–(66) | Definitions of high-impact capabilities, systemic risk, and general-purpose AI system. | [1] |
| Art. 3(68) | Definition of "downstream provider". | [1] |
| Art. 51 + Annex XIII | Classification of a GPAI model as one **with systemic risk**: high-impact capabilities (evaluated by tools/benchmarks) or Commission decision; **presumption at >10²⁵ FLOP** cumulative training compute (rebuttable). | [1] |
| Art. 52 | Procedure: provider must **notify the Commission within two weeks** of meeting/foreseeing the threshold; may argue the presumption does not apply; Commission maintains a public list. | [1] |
| Art. 53(1)(a) + Annex XI | **Technical documentation** of the model (kept up to date; provided to the AI Office / national authorities on request). | [1] |
| Art. 53(1)(b) + Annex XII | **Information and documentation to downstream providers** integrating the model (to enable their compliance) while protecting IP/trade secrets. | [1] |
| Art. 53(1)(c) | **Policy to comply with Union copyright law**, in particular the text-and-data-mining rights reservation under Art. 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. | [1] |
| Art. 53(1)(d) | **Publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary** of training content, per the AI Office template. | [1][3] |
