**Not Applicable — no case law yet.** The GPAI regime is recent (in force from 2 August 2025) and enforced administratively by the AI Office; no CJEU or national judgment has yet interpreted Arts. 51–56. Interpretive weight currently rests on the Regulation's text, the Commission's Guidelines (18 July 2025), the Code of Practice, and — for copyright — the Directive (EU) 2019/790 framework and any future litigation on the text-and-data-mining reservation. text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **What counts as a GPAI model (Commission Guidelines, 18 July 2025).** The Commission reads "significant generality" as an indicative test: a model trained with **more than ~10²³ FLOP** of compute **and** able to generate language (text/audio), text-to-image or text-to-video is a strong candidate for GPAI status; the guidance also clarifies the **lifecycle** (when a model is "placed on the market"), how **fine-tuning / modification** by a downstream actor can make that actor a GPAI provider, and the **notification** duties [6]. Providers should treat these as the Commission's operational reading, not as the legal test (which is Art. 3(63)) [1][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Systemic-risk classification (Commission Q&A and Guidelines).** The **10²⁵ FLOP** presumption is a **rebuttable** trigger; providers reaching or reasonably foreseeing it must **notify the Commission within two weeks**, and may argue that, exceptionally, their model does not present systemic risk despite the compute. The Commission may also designate a model **without** the compute threshold, on the Annex XIII criteria, including via alerts from the **Scientific Panel** [1][3][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **The Code of Practice as the compliance bridge.** The AI Office presents adherence to the **General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** (10 July 2025) as the primary way to **demonstrate** compliance with Arts. 53 and 55 until harmonised standards exist; non-signatories must demonstrate compliance by other, potentially more burdensome, means. Signing is **voluntary** and is **not** a legal safe harbour — the AI Office still assesses actual compliance [4][6][10]. *(Regulatory interpretation + best practice.)*
- **Training-content summary template.** The AI Office published a mandatory **template** for the Art. 53(1)(d) public summary, calibrated to be "sufficiently detailed" (a general description of data sources, types and provenance) while protecting trade secrets — narrower than a dataset-by-dataset disclosure [3][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **AI Omnibus did not touch GPAI.** The Commission's simplification package (adopted June 2026) postponed **high-risk** dates and eased documentation for SMEs, but the co-legislators **kept the GPAI obligations in force from 2 August 2025** and reinforced the AI Office's central role over GPAI [3][9]. *(Regulatory interpretation — confirmed.)*
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
- **Decide GPAI status first, systemic risk second.** Run two gates. Gate 1 (Art. 3(63)): does the model display **significant generality** and perform a **wide range of distinct tasks** (indicatively >~10²³ FLOP + broad generative capability [6])? Gate 2 (Art. 51): does cumulative training compute exceed **10²⁵ FLOP**, or do capabilities otherwise match the most advanced models? If Gate 2 is met, the systemic-risk duties attach and the open-source relief falls away [1][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Instrument training compute now.** Because both gates and the notification duty (Art. 52) turn on **cumulative training FLOP**, providers must **measure and log** training compute as a first-class metric, including for foreseeability ("reasonably foreseen" to reach 10²⁵) — not reconstruct it after the fact [1][3]. *(Best practice supporting obligation.)*
- **Build the Annex XI / Annex XII documentation as pipeline outputs.** Annex XI (for the AI Office) and Annex XII (for downstream integrators) demand model architecture, training process, evaluation results, capabilities and limitations, and integration guidance; generate these from the MLOps pipeline (model cards, eval harness outputs, data statements) rather than retrofitting [1]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **Evaluation and adversarial testing as a standing capability (Art. 55(1)(a)).** Stand up **red-teaming / adversarial evaluation** against the systemic-risk taxonomy (CBRN uplift, offensive cyber, loss of control, harmful manipulation, large-scale disinformation); the Code of Practice's Safety and Security chapter provides the operational model, including a **Safety and Security Framework** and **model reports** [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Serious-incident tracking (Art. 55(1)(c)) is a distinct pipeline.** It reports **model-level systemic-risk events** to the **AI Office** — separate from the Art. 73 serious-incident duty on high-risk **system** providers (which reports to market-surveillance authorities). Use the AI Office's **serious-incident reporting template** for GPAI systemic-risk models and wire in monitoring, triage and "without undue delay" escalation [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Cybersecurity of weights and infrastructure (Art. 55(1)(d)).** Protect **model weights** against exfiltration and the training/inference infrastructure against compromise; treat weight theft as a systemic-risk event. Map to the security baselines in `privacy-engineering-foundations` and the Code's security measures [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Copyright compliance is an engineering problem too (Art. 53(1)(c)).** Operationalise the Directive (EU) 2019/790 Art. 4(3) **TDM opt-out** — honour machine-readable reservations (e.g., robots.txt / TDM Reservation Protocol) at crawl time and record provenance so the copyright policy is auditable [1]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
- **Hosting a model rarely makes you its provider — but modifying it can.** Serving or fine-tuning a third-party GPAI model may be a downstream activity; however, a **substantial modification** or fine-tuning that itself meets the GPAI threshold can make the modifier a **GPAI provider** for the changes (per the Commission Guidelines), with the corresponding Art. 53/55 duties for the modification [1][6]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Infrastructure operators may hold Art. 55(1)(d) obligations by proxy.** Where a systemic-risk model runs on a provider's own or contracted infrastructure, the **cybersecurity** duty covers the **physical infrastructure**; hosting arrangements should allocate weight-protection, access-control and incident-response responsibilities in contract [1][10]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **Documentation access without IP leakage.** Hosting/serving pipelines must be able to surface the **Annex XI** documentation to the AI Office on request and the **Annex XII** package to downstream integrators, while protecting trade secrets and model weights (Art. 53(7)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
- **Integrating a foundation model into a game makes you a downstream provider, not a GPAI provider.** A studio embedding a third-party LLM (NPC dialogue, companion chatbots, content generation) is typically a **downstream provider** relying on the model provider's **Annex XII** information; it does **not** inherit Art. 53/55 model-level duties, but must meet any **system-level** duties (e.g., Art. 50 transparency for AI interaction and synthetic content — see `ai-act-foundations`) [1]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Self-hosted or heavily fine-tuned models can flip the role.** A studio that trains or substantially fine-tunes its own general-purpose model could itself become a **GPAI provider**; most game-specific fine-tunes will not display "significant generality" or approach the 10²⁵ FLOP systemic threshold, but the assessment should be documented [1][6]. *(Legal obligation once triggered.)*
- **Value-chain information hygiene.** Studios should **retain the Annex XII documentation** they receive from model providers — it is the evidence base for their own transparency and (where relevant) high-risk obligations, and for incident triage if the upstream model misbehaves [1]. *(Best practice.)*
title: EU AI Act: General-Purpose AI Models & Systemic Risk

text:
*This document is itself an AI-regulation deep-dive; the "AI Considerations" here concern interaction with adjacent regimes and the operational stack.*

- **Operationalise Art. 55 via management systems.** The systemic-risk duties (evaluation, risk assessment, incident handling, cybersecurity) map onto **ISO/IEC 42001** (AI management system) and the **NIST AI RMF** Generative AI Profile; use them to make the Code of Practice's commitments auditable — detailed in `ai-governance-foundations`, not duplicated here [11]. *(Best practice.)*
- **GDPR runs in parallel over training and inference.** Where a GPAI model is trained on or processes **personal data**, GDPR lawful basis, purpose limitation, data-subject rights, DPbDD (Art. 25) and security (Art. 32) apply alongside Chapter V; the AI Act's training-content summary is **not** a GDPR record and does not discharge GDPR transparency (see `gdpr-foundations`, `privacy-engineering-foundations`) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The GPAI regime is the upstream half of the high-risk value chain.** A high-risk system built on a GPAI model depends on the **Annex XII** information to meet its Art. 8–15 obligations; conversely, Art. 25(4) requires GPAI providers and downstream providers to cooperate. Read this document with `ai-act-high-risk` [1]. *(Cross-reference.)*
- **Copyright and content-provenance overlap.** The Art. 53(1)(c) copyright policy and the Code's Copyright chapter intersect with output-side provenance/watermarking obligations (Art. 50) and with the Directive (EU) 2019/790 regime; treat input lawfulness (TDM opt-out) and output labelling as separate but related workstreams [1][10]. *(Best practice.)*

2. **Measure and log cumulative training compute** as a governed metric, with a foreseeability trigger for the 10²⁵ FLOP notification. *(OBLIGATION-supporting; BEST PRACTICE.)* [1][3]

5. **Publish the training-content summary** using the AI Office template. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][3]
6. **Appoint an EU authorised representative** if established outside the Union (Art. 54). *(OBLIGATION where applicable.)* [1]
7. **If systemic risk: notify the Commission within two weeks** (Art. 52) and stand up **model evaluation / adversarial testing** (Art. 55(1)(a)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
8. **Assess and mitigate Union-level systemic risks** across the taxonomy (CBRN, cyber, loss of control, manipulation, disinformation) (Art. 55(1)(b)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][10]

text:
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) reserves its heaviest obligations for **high-risk AI systems** — the systems most capable of harming health, safety or fundamental rights. This document details, at article level, **how a system becomes high-risk**, **what it must satisfy**, and **who must do what** to place it lawfully on the EU market [1].

Classification runs on two routes. The **product-safety route (Art. 6(1), Annex I)** captures AI that is, or is a safety component of, a product already regulated under Union harmonisation legislation (machinery, medical devices, toys, vehicles, etc.) and subject to third-party conformity assessment. The **use-case route (Art. 6(2), Annex III)** lists eight sensitive domains — biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential public/private services (incl. credit scoring and insurance), law enforcement, migration/border control, and justice/democracy. A **filter (Art. 6(3))** can pull an Annex III system back out of scope where it performs only a narrow, preparatory or human-confirming task and does **not** profile natural persons [1][9].

High-risk providers must build a **risk-management system (Art. 9)**, meet **data-governance (Art. 10)**, **technical-documentation (Art. 11)**, **logging (Art. 12)**, **transparency-to-deployer (Art. 13)**, **human-oversight (Art. 14)** and **accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Art. 15)** requirements; operate a **quality management system (Art. 17)**; complete **conformity assessment (Art. 43)**; draw up an **EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47)**; affix **CE marking (Art. 48)**; and **register in the EU database (Art. 49/71)** [1]. Deployers carry their own duties (Art. 26), and some must run a **fundamental-rights impact assessment (Art. 27)** [1]. Compliance is presumed where **harmonised standards** (Art. 40) are met [1][8]. The single most important planning input is the **amended, now-adopted timeline**: standalone Annex III duties apply from **2 December 2027** and product-embedded (Annex I) duties from **2 August 2028**, subject to Official Journal publication [3][4][5][6].

text:
- **Two classification routes.** A system is high-risk if it is (or is a safety component of) an **Annex I product** subject to third-party conformity assessment (Art. 6(1)), **or** it falls within an **Annex III use case** (Art. 6(2)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The Art. 6(3) filter is narrow.** An Annex III system escapes high-risk status only if it poses no significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights (narrow procedural / preparatory / human-confirming tasks) — but it is **always high-risk if it profiles** natural persons, and the provider must **document** the exemption assessment [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Seven core requirements (Arts. 8–15)** apply to every high-risk system: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping/logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Providers carry the market-access chain:** quality management system (Art. 17), conformity assessment (Art. 43), EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), CE marking (Art. 48) and registration in the EU database (Arts. 49, 71) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Most Annex III systems self-assess** via internal control (Annex VI); **third-party notified-body assessment (Annex VII)** is required for certain biometric systems and via sectoral law on the product route (Art. 43) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Deployers are not passive:** Art. 26 imposes use-per-instructions, human oversight, input-data control, monitoring and log-keeping; **Art. 27** adds a **fundamental-rights impact assessment (FRIA)** for public bodies, public-service providers and certain credit/insurance deployers [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Harmonised standards give a presumption of conformity (Art. 40);** where they are absent the Commission may adopt **common specifications (Art. 41)**. CEN-CENELEC is drafting the standards under a Commission request [1][8]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **Timeline — now adopted, not merely proposed:** the AI Omnibus moves standalone Annex III duties to **2 Dec 2027** and product-embedded duties to **2 Aug 2028**; it was adopted by Parliament (16 Jun 2026) and Council (29 Jun 2026) and awaited OJ publication at this document's date [3][4][5][6]. *(Legal obligation — pending OJ publication.)*

text:
*Shared terms (AI system, provider, deployer, high-risk AI system, human oversight) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only high-risk-specific terms are defined here; keep this table short per sub-topic policy.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Safety component | A component of a product or system which fulfils a safety function for that product/system, or whose failure or malfunction endangers the health and safety of persons or property (Art. 3(14)); central to the Art. 6(1) product-safety route. | [1] |
| Conformity assessment | The process of demonstrating whether the requirements of Arts. 8–15 have been fulfilled (Art. 3(20)); performed by internal control (Annex VI) or a notified body (Annex VII). | [1] |
| Notified body | A conformity assessment body notified under the AI Act to carry out third-party conformity assessment (Arts. 3(22), 28–39). | [1] |
| Harmonised standard | A European standard adopted on the basis of a Commission request under Regulation (EU) 1025/2012; conformity with it confers a presumption of conformity with the corresponding requirement (Art. 40). | [1][8] |
| Common specification | A set of technical specifications adopted by Commission implementing act providing an alternative route to compliance where harmonised standards are absent or insufficient (Art. 41). | [1] |
| Substantial modification | A change to a high-risk AI system after placing on the market/putting into service which affects compliance with Chapter III or changes the intended purpose (Art. 3(23)); can turn a deployer/distributor into a provider (Art. 25). | [1] |
| Fundamental-rights impact assessment (FRIA) | The Art. 27 assessment certain deployers must perform before deploying an Annex III high-risk system, describing use, affected persons, risks of harm, human-oversight and governance measures. | [1] |

text:
The AI Act's high-risk chapter is not built from scratch: it deliberately borrows the EU's **New Legislative Framework (NLF)** for product safety — essential requirements, harmonised standards conferring presumption of conformity, conformity assessment (self-assessment or notified body), the **EU declaration of conformity** and **CE marking**, and market surveillance [1][9]. The AI Act layers onto that machinery a **fundamental-rights** dimension absent from classic product law: a use-case list (Annex III) untethered from any single product, a **deployer-side** duty set, and the **FRIA**. Academic analysis has noted both the strength of reusing a mature compliance architecture and the friction of grafting fundamental-rights protection onto a product-safety chassis that traditionally addresses physical safety, not societal harm [9].

The timeline has been the most contested element. The Regulation's original Art. 113 phased high-risk duties in from **2 August 2026** (Annex III standalone) and **2 August 2027** (Annex I product route). During 2025 the Commission's **Digital Omnibus / AI Omnibus** simplification agenda proposed to postpone these and reduce documentation burden. Crucially for this deep-dive, that package has now **completed the legislative procedure**: the European Parliament adopted it in plenary on **16 June 2026** and the Council gave final approval on **29 June 2026**, with Official Journal publication the remaining step at this document's date [3][4][5][6].

text:
High-risk AI is governed by **Chapter III** of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, supported by definitions in Chapter I and governance/market-surveillance provisions in Chapters VII–IX. Chapter III has four sections: **classification (Arts. 6–7)**, **requirements (Arts. 8–15)**, **obligations of providers, deployers and other operators (Arts. 16–27)**, and **notified bodies / conformity assessment / registration (Arts. 28–49)** [1].

**Classification (Section 1).** Art. 6(1) sets the **product-safety route**: an AI system is high-risk if (a) it is intended to be used as a **safety component** of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in **Annex I**, **and** (b) that product must undergo **third-party conformity assessment** under that legislation. Art. 6(2) sets the **use-case route**: systems in **Annex III** are high-risk. Art. 6(3) is the **filter** (see below); Art. 6(4) requires a provider claiming the filter to **document** its assessment and still **register**. Art. 7 empowers the Commission to amend Annex III.

**Requirements (Section 2, Arts. 8–15).** These are the substantive engineering obligations, met "taking into account the intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art" (Art. 8) [1].

**Obligations (Section 3, Arts. 16–27).** Provider obligations (Art. 16 as the index, elaborated in Arts. 17–22, 25), operator/value-chain rules (Arts. 23–25), **deployer** obligations (Art. 26) and the **FRIA** (Art. 27) [1].

**Conformity, standards and registration (Section 4 + Chapter III standards provisions).** Harmonised standards (Art. 40), common specifications (Art. 41), conformity assessment procedures (Art. 43, Annexes VI/VII), certificates (Art. 44), EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), CE marking (Art. 48), and registration in the EU database (Arts. 49, 71) [1].

## Relevant Articles

| Art. 6(3) | Derogation/filter: Annex III system not high-risk where no significant risk (narrow, preparatory or human-confirming tasks); never applies where the system profiles natural persons. | [1] |
| Art. 6(4) | Provider relying on Art. 6(3) must document the assessment; registration still required. | [1] |

| Art. 13 | Transparency and provision of information (instructions for use) to deployers. | [1] |
| Art. 14 | Human oversight — understand, monitor, intervene, override; two-person rule for certain remote biometric ID. | [1] |
| Art. 15 | Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (incl. resilience to data/model poisoning and adversarial inputs). | [1] |

| Art. 48 | CE marking of conformity. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid construction (Art. 296 TFEU practice); this is stated expressly.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 46–47 | Rationale for the product-safety classification route and its link to existing Union harmonisation legislation. | [1] |
| Recital 52–53 | Rationale for the Annex III use-case list and the fundamental-rights focus of high-risk classification. | [1] |
| Recital 53 area | Basis of the Art. 6(3) filter — systems that do not materially influence decision outcomes should not be high-risk, but profiling always is. | [1] |
| Recital 66 area | Human-oversight rationale — enabling natural persons to prevent or minimise risks. | [1] |
| Recital 74 area | Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity expectations for high-risk systems. | [1] |
| Recital 96 area | Purpose of the fundamental-rights impact assessment for deployers. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable — no CJEU case law yet.** The AI Act is recent and its high-risk provisions are not yet applicable (application dates fall in 2027–2028 as amended), so no court has interpreted Arts. 6–27. Interpretive weight currently rests on the Regulation's text, forthcoming Commission guidelines (Art. 6(5)), harmonised standards, and — for personal-data aspects — GDPR case law (see `gdpr-foundations`) [1]. This section should be revisited once the provisions apply and litigation emerges.

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **European Commission (framework page):** presents high-risk as the tier carrying "strict obligations" — risk assessment/mitigation, high-quality datasets, logging, detailed documentation, clear user information, human oversight, and robustness/accuracy/cybersecurity — and confirms conformity assessment before market placement [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Art. 6(3) guidelines:** the Commission is mandated (Art. 6(5)) to issue guidelines specifying the practical implementation of the classification rules, including the filter; providers should treat the exemption conservatively pending those guidelines and the profiling carve-out [1][2]. *(Regulatory interpretation — track guidance.)*
- **Standardisation:** the Commission has issued a standardisation request to **CEN-CENELEC** (Joint Technical Committee 21) to develop harmonised standards operationalising Arts. 9–15; meeting them will confer the Art. 40 presumption of conformity. Until they are cited in the Official Journal, providers rely on the Regulation directly or on common specifications (Art. 41) [1][8]. *(Regulatory interpretation + best practice.)*
- **AI Omnibus (now adopted):** the co-legislators postponed high-risk application (standalone Annex III to 2 Dec 2027; product-embedded to 2 Aug 2028), introduced new Art. 5 prohibitions (non-consensual intimate imagery / CSAM generators, from 2 Dec 2026), and eased documentation for SMEs and small mid-caps. Unlike the parent foundation document — which recorded only a *provisional* agreement — the measure was **adopted by Parliament (16 Jun 2026) and Council (29 Jun 2026)** and takes effect on OJ publication (+3 days) [3][4][5][6]. *(Legal obligation — pending OJ publication; verify the OJ citation.)*

text:
- **Classify first, and re-classify on change.** Run the Art. 6 decision: (1) is it, or a safety component of, an Annex I product needing third-party assessment? → high-risk (product route). (2) Else, does it match an Annex III entry? → high-risk (use-case route) unless (3) the Art. 6(3) filter applies **and** it does not profile. Record the reasoning (Art. 6(4)) [1][9]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Risk-management as a living loop (Art. 9).** Implement a continuous, iterative process spanning the lifecycle: identify known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; adopt targeted mitigations; test against pre-defined metrics; and give specific consideration to impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Data governance (Art. 10).** Training, validation and testing datasets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and — to the best extent possible — free of errors and complete for the intended purpose; examine for **biases** likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights. Art. 10 permits processing of **special-category data** strictly for bias detection and correction subject to safeguards (a point the AI Omnibus clarified) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Documentation and logging by construction (Arts. 11–12).** Generate **Annex IV** technical documentation and **automatic logs** as pipeline outputs, not retrofits; logs must enable traceability of events, functioning and risk situations across the system's lifetime [1]. See `ai-governance-foundations` for the auto-documentation pattern. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Human oversight designed in (Art. 14).** Build measures enabling overseers to understand capacities and limits, stay alert to **automation bias**, interpret output correctly, and **decide not to use / override / stop** the system; certain remote biometric identification requires separate **two-person verification** before action [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity (Art. 15).** Declare accuracy metrics in the instructions; build resilience to errors, faults and inconsistencies and to feedback loops; and harden against AI-specific attacks — **data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, and model evasion** [1]. Coordinate with `privacy-engineering-foundations` and security baselines. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
- **Role determines obligation set.** Hosting a high-risk system usually makes an organisation a **deployer** (Art. 26 duties). But branding it under one's own name/trademark, or making a **substantial modification** or repurposing it to a new intended purpose, makes the host a **provider** with the full Arts. 8–15 and conformity chain (Art. 25) [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess role explicitly.)*
- **Log retention.** Providers retain automatically generated **logs** (Art. 19) and documentation for **10 years** (Art. 18); deployers keep logs under their control (Art. 26(6)). Hosting must retain these while honouring GDPR storage-limitation and security (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Environment for oversight and robustness.** Hosting must support the Art. 14 oversight controls (e.g., stop/override interfaces, monitoring telemetry) and the Art. 15 resilience/cybersecurity posture (segregation, integrity protection, adversarial-input monitoring) [1]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **EU database registration is not the host's escape hatch.** Registration (Arts. 49, 71) is a provider/deployer duty tied to role, not to who owns the infrastructure [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
- **Most game AI stays minimal-risk and outside Chapter III.** NPC behaviour, matchmaking and procedural generation are not Annex III use cases, so the high-risk requirements do not attach [1][2]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Watch the Annex III edges.** Features doing **biometric categorisation** or **emotion recognition** (Annex III(1)), or AI affecting **access to essential services** (e.g., age-gating tied to services, or credit-like in-game financial features), can cross into high-risk; assess carefully, especially where **minors** are involved [1]. *(Legal obligation once triggered.)*
- **Transparency vs. high-risk are different regimes.** AI chatbots/companions and generative content trigger **Art. 50** transparency (deep-dive in `ai-act-foundations`), not necessarily the high-risk chapter — but the AI Omnibus's new prohibitions on non-consensual intimate-image generators (from 2 Dec 2026) are directly relevant to user-generated-content and image tools in games [3][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
*This document is itself an AI-regulation deep-dive; the "AI Considerations" here concern interaction with adjacent regimes and the operational stack.*

- **Operationalising Arts. 9–17 via management systems.** ISO/IEC 42001 (AIMS) maps closely to the **Art. 17 quality management system** and to the risk-management, data-governance, documentation and oversight duties; the NIST AI RMF supplies the Map/Measure/Manage loop. These are the practical route to conformity and are detailed in `ai-governance-foundations` — do not duplicate here [7]. *(Best practice.)*
- **GDPR runs in parallel.** Where a high-risk system processes personal data, GDPR **lawful basis, DPbDD (Art. 25), security (Art. 32), DPIA (Art. 35)** and **automated-decision (Art. 22)** rules apply alongside Chapter III; the **FRIA (Art. 27)** and a **DPIA** should be run together and cross-referenced, not conflated [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Harmonised standards will define "state of the art."** As CEN-CENELEC standards are cited, they will concretise Art. 8's "state of the art" benchmark; providers should design to draft standards now and adopt final versions on citation to secure the Art. 40 presumption [1][8]. *(Best practice.)*
- **GPAI upstream.** High-risk systems built on general-purpose models inherit documentation and information dependencies from the GPAI provider (see `ai-act-gpai`, planned); value-chain information duties (Art. 25) matter for conformity [1]. *(Cross-reference.)*

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Classify and document every candidate system** against Art. 6(1)/Annex I and Art. 6(2)/Annex III; where relying on the Art. 6(3) filter, record the assessment (Art. 6(4)) and confirm the system does **not profile**. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
2. **Stand up the Art. 9 risk-management system** as a continuous lifecycle process with tested mitigations and explicit vulnerable-group consideration. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
3. **Engineer Art. 10 data governance** — representativeness, error/completeness checks, bias examination, and controlled special-category-data use for bias correction. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Produce Annex IV technical documentation and Art. 12 logs automatically.** *(OBLIGATION; BEST PRACTICE to auto-generate.)* [1]
5. **Write Art. 13 instructions for use** giving deployers the characteristics, limits, performance and oversight measures they need. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Design Art. 14 human oversight** (understand/monitor/intervene/override; two-person rule for relevant biometric ID). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
7. **Meet Art. 15 accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity,** including AI-specific threat hardening; declare accuracy metrics. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
8. **Operate the Art. 17 quality management system;** map it to ISO/IEC 42001 for auditability. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [1][7]
9. **Select the correct conformity route (Art. 43):** internal control (Annex VI) for most Annex III; **notified body (Annex VII)** for the relevant biometric systems and via sectoral law on the product route. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
10. **Draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), affix CE marking (Art. 48), and register (Arts. 49, 71)** before placing on the market. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
11. **Deployers: implement Art. 26** (use per instructions, oversight, input control, monitoring, logs, worker/affected-person information) and, where applicable, **complete the Art. 27 FRIA** and notify the market-surveillance authority. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
12. **Plan to the adopted 2027/2028 dates but confirm OJ publication;** do not treat obligations as removed, only deferred — and prepare now. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [3][5][6]

- **Phase 4 — Deployer duties & FRIA (Arts. 26–27):** Deployer controls, monitoring and logs; FRIA where applicable, integrated with DPIA; authority notification. *Effort:* Medium.

title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
Article 5 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the Regulation's **red line**: it defines the AI practices whose risk to health, safety and fundamental rights is deemed **unacceptable**, and therefore **prohibits** them outright rather than permitting them subject to controls [1]. Unlike the high-risk regime, there is **no conformity-assessment route** back into legality — a prohibited practice may not be placed on the market, put into service or used at all [1][2]. The prohibitions, together with the AI-literacy duty (Art. 4), have applied since **2 February 2025**, ahead of most of the Regulation [1][4].

This document details each of the eight prohibitions in Article 5(1): (a) harmful **subliminal, manipulative or deceptive** techniques; (b) **exploitation of vulnerabilities** of age, disability or socio-economic situation; (c) **social scoring** leading to unjustified or decontextualised detrimental treatment; (d) **predictive policing of individuals based solely on profiling** or personality assessment; (e) **untargeted scraping** of facial images to build or expand facial-recognition databases; (f) **emotion recognition** in the **workplace and education**; (g) **biometric categorisation** inferring sensitive attributes; and (h) **real-time remote biometric identification** in publicly accessible spaces **for law enforcement**, permitted only under narrow, judicially-authorised exceptions [1][3]. It explains the **Commission's interpretive guidelines** [3], the **penalty ceiling** for breach — up to **€35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover** (Art. 99(3)) [1] — and the **new NCII/CSAM ("nudifier") prohibition** added by the adopted AI Omnibus, applicable from **2 December 2026** [6][7][8]. Throughout, it distinguishes **prohibition** (banned) from **high-risk** (permitted with obligations), because several biometric and profiling uses sit just across that line [1][2].
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
- **Article 5 is an outright ban, not a graded obligation.** A practice within Art. 5 cannot be legitimised by documentation, oversight or conformity assessment — it must not be placed on the market, put into service or used [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **In force since 2 February 2025.** Chapters I–II (including Art. 5) and the Art. 4 AI-literacy duty applied first; the penalty and governance machinery followed on 2 August 2025 (Art. 113) [1][4]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- **Eight prohibitions in Art. 5(1)(a)–(h):** harmful manipulation; exploitation of vulnerabilities; social scoring; solely-profiling-based predictive policing; untargeted facial-image scraping; workplace/education emotion recognition; sensitive-attribute biometric categorisation; and real-time remote biometric identification (RBI) in public for law enforcement [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The prohibitions carry tightly-drafted carve-outs**, not loopholes: e.g. the predictive-policing ban spares assessments grounded in objective, verifiable facts; emotion recognition is allowed for medical or safety reasons; and real-time RBI is permitted only for enumerated serious purposes with **prior judicial/independent authorisation** and a fundamental-rights impact assessment (Art. 5(2)–(7)) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The Commission's Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (C(2025) 884, 4 Feb 2025) are the primary interpretive aid** — over 130 pages of scope, examples and exclusions — but they are **non-binding**; only the CJEU can give an authoritative reading [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Breach is the most severely penalised conduct under the Act:** up to **€35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Art. 99(3)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **New "nudifier" prohibition added by the adopted AI Omnibus:** AI systems that generate or manipulate **non-consensual intimate imagery** or **CSAM** become a further Art. 5 prohibited practice, applicable from **2 December 2026**, with a **safe harbour** where the system has adequate technical safeguards; adopted by Parliament (16 Jun 2026) and Council (29 Jun 2026), pending OJ publication [6][7][8]. *(Legal obligation — pending OJ publication.)*
- **Prohibition ≠ high-risk.** Many neighbouring uses (post/non-real-time RBI, emotion recognition outside work/education, non-sensitive biometric categorisation) are **not** banned but fall into the **high-risk** regime detailed in `ai-act-high-risk` [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*

It is written for legal, compliance, product and trust-and-safety readers. It presupposes `ai-act-foundations` for the risk-tier overview and cross-refers `ai-act-high-risk` for the adjacent high-risk regime and `digital-omnibus` for the simplification package as a whole.

**In scope:** The eight prohibitions in Article 5(1)(a)–(h) and their statutory exceptions; the procedural safeguards for real-time remote biometric identification (Art. 5(2)–(7)); the 2 February 2025 applicability date (Art. 113); the Commission's Guidelines on prohibited AI practices; the Art. 99(3) penalty for breach; the AI-Omnibus-added NCII/CSAM prohibition; and the demarcation between prohibited and high-risk practices.

**Out of scope (covered elsewhere):** The four-tier risk framework, GPAI regime and general penalty structure → `ai-act-foundations`; the high-risk classification and obligations that govern the *permitted* biometric/profiling uses → `ai-act-high-risk`; the GPAI/systemic-risk regime → `ai-act-gpai`; the AI Omnibus package in full (timeline postponements, SME relief) → `digital-omnibus`; Art. 50 transparency duties (deepfake/synthetic-content marking) → `ai-act-foundations`. Where a prohibited practice also processes personal data, the GDPR applies in parallel (see `gdpr-foundations`); this document does not restate GDPR duties.

**Assumptions:** The reader has read `ai-act-foundations`. "Placing on the market", "putting into service", "provider" and "deployer" bear their Art. 3 meanings. Dates for the AI Omnibus additions are the adopted-text dates and become binding only on Official Journal publication.

text:
*Shared terms (AI system, provider, deployer, special category data, high-risk AI system) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only Article-5-specific terms are defined here, per sub-topic policy.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Prohibited AI practice | An AI practice listed in Art. 5 whose risk is deemed unacceptable; it may not be placed on the market, put into service or used — no conformity route exists. | [1] |
| Subliminal technique | A technique operating beyond a person's consciousness, or a purposefully manipulative or deceptive technique, that materially distorts behaviour by impairing informed decision-making (Art. 5(1)(a)). | [1][3] |
| Social scoring | Evaluation or classification of persons over time based on social behaviour or personal/personality characteristics, producing detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or that is unjustified/disproportionate (Art. 5(1)(c)). | [1] |
| Emotion recognition system | An AI system for identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data (Art. 3(39)); prohibited in workplace/education subject to medical/safety exceptions (Art. 5(1)(f)). | [1] |
| Biometric categorisation system | An AI system assigning natural persons to categories on the basis of biometric data (Art. 3(40)); prohibited where it infers sensitive attributes (Art. 5(1)(g)). | [1] |
| Remote biometric identification (RBI) | An AI system identifying persons, typically at a distance, by comparing biometric data against a reference database, without active involvement; "real-time" where capture, comparison and identification occur without significant delay (Art. 3(41)–(42)). | [1] |
| Non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) | Images, video or audio depicting an identifiable person's intimate parts or sexually explicit activity produced or manipulated without that person's consent; generation/manipulation by AI is a prohibited practice under the AI-Omnibus addition to Art. 5. | [7][8] |
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
The AI Act's architecture is **risk-based**: the greater the threat an AI practice poses to health, safety or fundamental rights, the heavier the legal response, escalating from no obligation (minimal risk) through transparency and high-risk duties to **outright prohibition** at the apex [1][2]. Article 5 is that apex. It reflects a political judgement — taken during the 2021–2024 negotiation and expanded late in the process to cover more biometric uses — that certain applications are so incompatible with Union values and the Charter of Fundamental Rights that no safeguard can render them acceptable [1]. Academic commentary on the draft Act noted that this list of "unacceptable" practices, and especially its manipulation and biometric limbs, would be among the most contested and hardest-to-interpret provisions, precisely because the prohibitions turn on open-textured concepts such as "material distortion" of behaviour and "significant harm" [10].

The prohibitions were **front-loaded** in the application timeline. Whereas most of the Act phases in across 2025–2028, Chapters I and II — which include Article 5 — and the Article 4 AI-literacy obligation became applicable on **2 February 2025**, six months after entry into force (Art. 113) [1][4]. To support consistent enforcement ahead of the penalty machinery (applicable 2 August 2025), the Commission published extensive **Guidelines on prohibited AI practices** on **4 February 2025** [3][4]. Most recently, the **AI Omnibus** simplification package (Commission proposal of 19 November 2025) — while chiefly *postponing* high-risk obligations — moved in the opposite direction on one point, **adding** a prohibition targeting AI "nudifier" tools that generate non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM [5]. It completed the legislative procedure through trilogue and co-legislator adoption in June 2026 [6][7][8][9].
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
**OBLIGATION.** Prohibited practices are governed by **Article 5** (Chapter II) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, read with the definitions in Chapter I (Art. 3), the penalty rule in **Article 99(3)**, and the application-date rule in **Article 113** [1]. Article 5(1) enumerates the prohibited practices; Article 5(2)–(7) sets out the procedural conditions and safeguards that frame the single most qualified prohibition, real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement [1].

The prohibition operates on the three "market" verbs used throughout the Act: a prohibited AI system may not be **placed on the market**, **put into service**, or **used** (Art. 5(1)) [1]. This is materially wider than the high-risk regime, which principally binds *providers* at market placement and *deployers* in use: Article 5 reaches **every operator** and every stage, and it has **no conformity assessment, no CE marking and no registration** — because these practices are not permitted at all [1][2]. Where an AI system's design straddles a prohibition and a lawful use, the Commission's Guidelines direct that the specific facts (purpose, context, effects) determine whether the prohibition bites [3].

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 5(1)(a) | Ban on AI using subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause (or are likely to cause) significant harm. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(b) | Ban on AI exploiting vulnerabilities of age, disability or a specific social/economic situation to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(c) | Ban on social scoring — evaluating/classifying persons over time by social behaviour or personal characteristics, leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or that is unjustified/disproportionate. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(d) | Ban on assessing/predicting the risk of a person committing a criminal offence based **solely** on profiling or personality-trait assessment; exception where it supports a human assessment based on objective, verifiable facts directly linked to criminal activity. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(e) | Ban on creating or expanding facial-recognition databases through **untargeted scraping** of facial images from the internet or CCTV. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(f) | Ban on inferring emotions of natural persons in the **workplace** and **education** institutions; exception for medical or safety reasons. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(g) | Ban on **biometric categorisation** deducing/inferring race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious/philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation; narrow exception for lawful labelling/filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets and law-enforcement categorisation. | [1] |
| Art. 5(1)(h) | Ban on **real-time remote biometric identification** in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes, save three enumerated exceptions. | [1] |
| Art. 5(2)–(7) | Conditions/safeguards for the Art. 5(1)(h) exceptions: seriousness/necessity/proportionality test, Annex II serious-offence list, prior authorisation by a judicial or independent administrative authority, fundamental-rights impact assessment, registration and notification; Member-State enabling law. | [1] |
| Art. 5 (AI Omnibus addition) | New ban on AI systems that generate or manipulate non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM ("nudifier" tools), subject to a safe harbour for adequate technical safeguards; applicable 2 Dec 2026. | [6][7][8] |
| Art. 4 | AI-literacy duty (applied 2 Feb 2025 alongside Art. 5). | [1][4] |
| Art. 99(3) | Penalty for breach of Art. 5 — up to €35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. | [1] |
| Art. 113 | Application dates — Chapters I–II (incl. Art. 5) apply from 2 Feb 2025. | [1][4] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid construction (Art. 296 TFEU practice); this is stated expressly.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 28 area | Rationale for prohibiting AI practices contrary to Union values and fundamental rights; the outright-ban tier. | [1] |
| Recital 29 area | Meaning of subliminal/manipulative/deceptive techniques and "material distortion" of behaviour (Art. 5(1)(a)–(b)); lawful persuasion and medical uses excluded. | [1] |
| Recital 31 area | Why social scoring is banned — decontextualised, unjustified or disproportionate detrimental treatment; contrast with lawful, context-bound evaluation. | [1] |
| Recital 42 area | Basis of the predictive-policing ban — presumption of innocence; persons should be judged on actual conduct, not profiling. | [1] |
| Recital 43 area | Untargeted facial-image scraping adds to mass-surveillance and fundamental-rights harm. | [1] |
| Recital 44 area | Concerns over emotion recognition's scientific reliability, especially in work/education power imbalances. | [1] |
| Recital 30 area | Biometric categorisation on sensitive grounds; scope of the labelling/filtering exception. | [1] |
| Recital 32–33 area | Necessity/proportionality and safeguards for real-time RBI; serious-harm justification and prior authorisation. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable — no CJEU case law yet.** Article 5 has applied only since 2 February 2025 and no judgment has yet interpreted it; the Commission expressly reserves authoritative interpretation to the CJEU [3]. Interpretive weight currently rests on the Regulation's text and recitals, the Commission's Guidelines on prohibited AI practices [3], and — for the personal-data and biometric dimensions — GDPR/law-enforcement-directive case law (see `gdpr-foundations`). This section should be revisited once enforcement actions and references for preliminary rulings emerge. [1][3]
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **Commission framework page:** presents the top tier as AI posing a "clear threat to the safety, livelihoods and rights of people", which is **banned**, and lists examples — social scoring, certain manipulative or exploitative systems, and certain biometric uses [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (C(2025) 884 final, 4 Feb 2025):** the principal interpretive instrument. Adopted the day AFTER Art. 5 became applicable, they give — across more than 130 pages — the Commission's reading of each prohibition, worked examples, and the boundary with lawful and high-risk uses; the Commission stresses they are **non-binding** and that only the CJEU can interpret the Act authoritatively [3]. Providers and deployers should treat them as the best available guide but not as a safe harbour. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **"First rules now applicable" (2 Feb 2025):** the Commission confirmed that the prohibitions and the AI-literacy obligation were the first parts of the Act to bite, six months after entry into force [4]. *(Regulatory interpretation — in force.)*
- **Narrow construction of exceptions:** the Guidelines read the Art. 5 carve-outs (e.g. medical/safety emotion recognition; objective-fact-based criminal-risk assessment; real-time RBI exceptions) **restrictively**, consistent with their character as derogations from a fundamental-rights protection [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **AI Omnibus (adopted):** the co-legislators added an Art. 5 prohibition on AI tools generating/manipulating NCII or CSAM, with a **safe harbour** where the system carries adequate technical safeguards, applicable from 2 Dec 2026; adopted by Parliament (16 Jun 2026) and Council (29 Jun 2026), pending OJ publication [6][7][8]. This is the one point on which the Omnibus **tightens** rather than eases the Act. *(Legal obligation — pending OJ publication; verify OJ citation. Detailed in `digital-omnibus`.)*
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
Each prohibition raises distinct engineering and product screening questions. The following details Art. 5(1)(a)–(h) and the Omnibus addition, with the discriminating test in each case.

- **(a) Harmful manipulation (subliminal/deceptive).** The ban targets AI deploying techniques beyond conscious perception, or purposefully manipulative/deceptive, that **materially distort** behaviour so a person takes a decision they would not otherwise take, causing or likely to cause **significant harm** [1]. The Guidelines distinguish this from lawful persuasion, personalisation and ordinary advertising; the discriminators are covertness/deception, material distortion, and significant (including psychological or financial) harm [3]. *(Legal obligation.)* **BEST PRACTICE:** review recommender, dark-pattern and "engagement-optimising" designs against these three elements.
- **(b) Exploitation of vulnerabilities.** Prohibits AI exploiting vulnerabilities due to **age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation** to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm [1]. It overlaps with (a) but does not require covert technique — targeting the vulnerability suffices. *(Legal obligation.)* **BEST PRACTICE:** treat products aimed at children, older adults, disabled users or people in financial distress as high-sensitivity for this screen.
- **(c) Social scoring.** Prohibits evaluating/classifying persons **over time** by social behaviour or inferred personal characteristics where the resulting score causes **detrimental or unfavourable treatment in unrelated contexts**, or treatment that is **unjustified or disproportionate** [1]. It is not confined to public authorities — private social scoring is caught. The discriminator from lawful scoring (e.g. regulated credit assessment) is context-decoupling and disproportionality [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **(d) Predictive policing of individuals.** Prohibits assessing or predicting the risk of a natural person committing a **criminal offence** based **solely** on **profiling** or on assessing personality traits [1]. The **exception**: systems that **support** a human assessment already grounded in **objective and verifiable facts directly linked to criminal activity** are not caught [1][3]. It does not cover place-based (geospatial) crime forecasting. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **(e) Untargeted facial-image scraping.** Prohibits creating or expanding **facial-recognition databases** through **untargeted scraping** of facial images from the **internet or CCTV** footage [1]. The discriminator is *untargeted*, mass collection to build a recognition database; targeted, lawful biometric processing is elsewhere regulated. *(Legal obligation.)* This limb directly addresses Clearview-style database building.
- **(f) Emotion recognition in workplace/education.** Prohibits AI to **infer emotions** of persons in **workplaces** and **education institutions**, except where deployed for **medical or safety** reasons (e.g. fatigue monitoring for safety) [1]. Emotion recognition **outside** these two settings is not banned but is **high-risk** (Annex III) and transparency-regulated (Art. 50) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **(g) Biometric categorisation on sensitive grounds.** Prohibits biometric categorisation that **deduces or infers** race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious/philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation [1]. **Exception:** labelling/filtering of **lawfully acquired** biometric datasets (e.g. sorting images) and categorisation in the law-enforcement context, within limits [1]. Categorisation on **non-sensitive** attributes is not banned but may be high-risk/transparency-regulated. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **(h) Real-time remote biometric identification (RBI) in public for law enforcement.** Prohibits **real-time** RBI in **publicly accessible spaces** for **law-enforcement** purposes, save three exceptions: (i) targeted search for specific victims (abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation) and missing persons; (ii) prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or a genuine and present/foreseeable **terrorist** threat; and (iii) localising/identifying a suspect of an offence in the Annex II list punishable by a custodial maximum of at least four years [1]. Even then, Art. 5(2)–(7) require **necessity/proportionality**, a **fundamental-rights impact assessment**, **prior authorisation** by a judicial or independent administrative authority (with a narrow urgency exception), registration and notification, and enabling **national law** [1][3]. **Post** (non-real-time) RBI is not prohibited but is **high-risk** [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **(Omnibus addition) NCII/CSAM generators.** The adopted AI Omnibus adds a prohibition on AI systems that **generate or manipulate** non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material — "nudifier" tools — applicable from **2 December 2026** [6][7][8]. The prohibition bites where such output is a reasonably foreseeable, reproducible outcome and the system **lacks adequate technical safeguards** (data cleaning, refusal training, output filtering, prompt guardrails, abuse detection) — the **safe harbour** [7][8]. *(Legal obligation — pending OJ publication.)*
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
- **Hosts and infrastructure operators can be caught.** Because Art. 5 reaches "use" and "putting into service" by **any** operator — not only providers — an organisation that hosts, offers or operates a prohibited system on behalf of others may itself breach Art. 5 [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess the whole stack, not just first-party features.)*
- **No log-retention or conformity duty attaches to a prohibited practice** — unlike high-risk hosting there is no Art. 12 logging or registration obligation, because the practice is not permitted; the only compliant posture is **not to host it** [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Marketplace / app-store and API operators** should screen third-party AI offerings (especially image-generation and biometric tools) against Art. 5, with particular attention to the incoming NCII/CSAM prohibition and its safe-harbour condition [7][8]. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)*
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
- **Most game AI is untouched by Art. 5.** NPC behaviour, matchmaking and procedural generation are neither manipulative-to-the-legal-threshold nor biometric, so they fall outside the prohibitions [1][2]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Watch three edges.** (i) **Manipulation/exploitation (Art. 5(1)(a)–(b))** — monetisation or engagement mechanics that covertly and materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm, especially to **minors** or users in financial distress, risk the ban rather than merely the consumer-law/high-risk regimes; (ii) **emotion recognition** used on players in an **education/serious-games** setting engages Art. 5(1)(f); (iii) **biometric categorisation** inferring sensitive traits from face/voice engages Art. 5(1)(g) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation once triggered.)*
- **User-generated-content and image tools:** in-game or platform image/video generators must be screened against the incoming **NCII/CSAM prohibition** and must carry the safe-harbour safeguards [7][8]. *(Legal obligation from 2 Dec 2026.)*
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
*This document is itself an AI-regulation deep-dive; the "AI Considerations" here concern interaction with adjacent regimes and the model/product stack.*

- **GDPR runs in parallel and independently.** A practice can be lawful-to-attempt under the GDPR yet still **prohibited** under Art. 5, and vice versa; the biometric limbs (e) and (g) and RBI (h) will almost always also engage GDPR Art. 9 (special-category data) and, for law enforcement, the Law Enforcement Directive [1]. Art. 5 is an **additional, absolute** bar, not a substitute for a lawful basis. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **GPAI and general-purpose image models.** The NCII/CSAM prohibition presses directly on **general-purpose generative models**: providers are expected to build guardrails (refusal training, content filtering, abuse detection) so that producing prohibited content is not a reasonably foreseeable, unguarded outcome — the safe harbour [7][8]. This dovetails with the GPAI regime in `ai-act-gpai`. *(Legal obligation — pending OJ publication.)*
- **Transparency regime is separate.** Art. 50 deepfake/synthetic-content **labelling** is a transparency duty, not an Art. 5 prohibition; NCII/CSAM generation is banned outright regardless of any labelling [1][7]. Do not conflate marking with permission. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The prohibited/high-risk boundary is a design decision.** Emotion recognition, biometric categorisation and RBI can often be **re-scoped** to fall on the high-risk (permitted-with-obligations) side of the line — e.g. post rather than real-time RBI, non-sensitive rather than sensitive categorisation — but this must be a documented, deliberate design choice, not an afterthought [1][2][3]. *(Best practice.)*
title: EU AI Act: Prohibited Practices (Article 5)

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Run an Article 5 prohibited-practice screen** over every AI system and use case, mapping each against (a)–(h) and the Omnibus addition, and record the conclusion. *(OBLIGATION — the prohibitions are in force.)* [1][4]
2. **Test each candidate against the discriminators, not the label** — for (a)/(b): covertness/vulnerability + material distortion + significant harm; for (c): context-decoupling/disproportionality; for (d): "solely profiling" vs. objective-fact-supported; for (f)/(g): setting and sensitive-attribute inference; for (h): real-time + public + law-enforcement. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][3]
3. **Consult the Commission Guidelines (C(2025) 884)** for worked examples and boundary cases, but treat conclusions as provisional pending CJEU interpretation. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [3]
4. **Construe exceptions narrowly and document their basis** — medical/safety emotion recognition, objective-fact criminal-risk assessment, lawful-dataset biometric labelling, and each RBI exception with its Art. 5(2)–(7) safeguards. *(OBLIGATION where relied upon.)* [1][3]
5. **For any real-time RBI use, build the full safeguard chain** — necessity/proportionality assessment, FRIA, prior judicial/independent authorisation, registration, notification, and confirm enabling national law exists. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Screen image/video/audio generation tools against the NCII/CSAM prohibition now** and implement safe-harbour safeguards (data cleaning, refusal training, output filtering, prompt guardrails, abuse detection) ahead of 2 Dec 2026. *(OBLIGATION from 2 Dec 2026; BEST PRACTICE to act now.)* [7][8]
7. **Where a use is high-risk rather than prohibited, route it into the high-risk programme** (`ai-act-high-risk`) — do not treat "not prohibited" as "unregulated". *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2]
8. **Escalate any suspected prohibited practice to legal review before launch** — the €35m/7% ceiling makes this the highest-consequence AI compliance decision. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [1]

title: AI Governance: Foundations, ISO/IEC 42001 & Operational Assurance
legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (operationalised via ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, OECD AI Principles)

text:
**AI governance** is the set of policies, roles, processes and controls through which an organisation directs and assures its development and use of AI — the operational counterpart to the EU AI Act's legal obligations [1][7]. Where `ai-act-foundations` states *what the law requires*, this document describes *how organisations meet it in practice*, using management systems and internationally recognised frameworks [3][7].

Three instruments dominate. **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** is the world's first certifiable **AI management system (AIMS)** standard, applying the familiar Plan-Do-Check-Act structure to AI so that governance is systematic, auditable and continually improved [7]. The **NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0**, January 2023) is a voluntary, outcomes-based framework organised around four functions — **Govern, Map, Measure, Manage** — and now extended by a **Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1**, 26 July 2024) that names twelve GenAI-specific risk categories [11][12][13]. The **OECD AI Principles** (adopted 2019, **updated 3 May 2024**) supply the values baseline — human-centred, transparent, robust, accountable AI — that underpins both the AI Act and national policy [15][16].

The core message: governance frameworks are **voluntary but load-bearing**. They are not legally binding in themselves, yet adopting ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF is the most direct route to demonstrating AI Act conformity, GDPR accountability and trustworthy-AI due diligence [1][2][7]. The most important operational disciplines are **risk management across the model lifecycle**, **clear accountability**, **documentation and audit trails**, and **effective human oversight** [7][12].
title: AI Governance: Foundations, ISO/IEC 42001 & Operational Assurance

text:
- **AI governance operationalises the law.** It translates AI Act obligations (risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight) into management-system controls [1][7]. *(Best practice.)*
- **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** is the first **certifiable** AI management system standard; it uses the ISO harmonised (Annex SL) management-system structure and is auditable by accredited certification bodies [7]. *(Best practice.)*
- **NIST AI RMF 1.0** (Jan 2023) is voluntary and organised around **Govern, Map, Measure, Manage**; its **Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1**, 26 July 2024) adds twelve GenAI risk categories and 200+ suggested actions [11][12][13]. *(Best practice.)*
- **OECD AI Principles** (2019, **updated May 2024**) are the first intergovernmental AI standard — five values-based principles plus five policy recommendations — and were revised to address generative and general-purpose AI [15][16]. *(Best practice / soft law.)*
- **Governance frameworks are not law** but are the primary means of **demonstrating** AI Act and GDPR **accountability**; certification is evidence, not a legal safe harbour [1][2][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Model lifecycle governance** — problem framing, data, training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, retirement — is the spine of operational assurance and maps to the AI RMF functions [12]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Human oversight** is both an AI Act obligation (Art. 14) for high-risk systems and a governance control that frameworks help design and evidence [1][7]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- The **UK** has no horizontal AI statute; it applies a **principles-based, regulator-led** approach, making voluntary frameworks and existing law (data protection, equality) the practical governance baseline [4][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

**In scope:** What AI governance is and why it exists; ISO/IEC 42001 (AIMS) structure and use; the NIST AI RMF 1.0 and its Generative AI Profile; the OECD AI Principles; AI risk management; model lifecycle governance; roles and accountability; documentation and audit; human oversight; the relationship of governance to the AI Act and GDPR; UK and global framing.

**Out of scope (spun off to the research backlog):** Detailed **model risk management** methodology (validation, back-testing, challenger models) → `ai-model-risk-management`; **AI audit and assurance** methodology in depth → `ai-audit-methodology`; **sector-specific** AI governance (financial services, healthcare, public sector) → respective sector documents; the **AI Act's** article-by-article obligations → `ai-act-foundations`, `ai-act-high-risk`, `ai-act-gpai`; GPAI Code of Practice detail → `ai-act-gpai`.

**Assumptions:** The reader has read `ai-act-foundations` and `gdpr-foundations`. "Governance" here means organisational management and assurance, not the AI Act's institutional "governance" bodies (AI Office etc.), which are covered in `ai-act-foundations`.

text:
*Shared terms (AI system, GPAI model, high-risk AI system, accountability) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Governance-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| AI governance | The organisational structures, policies, roles and processes that direct, resource and assure the responsible development, deployment and use of AI systems. | [7][16] |
| AI management system (AIMS) | A set of interrelated elements an organisation uses to establish policies and objectives, and processes to achieve them, in respect of the responsible development and use of AI systems (ISO/IEC 42001). | [7] |
| Trustworthy AI | AI that is lawful, robust and ethical — characterised (per NIST) as valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed. | [12] |
| AI RMF function | One of the four core functions of the NIST AI RMF — **Govern, Map, Measure, Manage** — under which outcomes and actions are organised. | [12] |
| AI system impact assessment | A structured, documented assessment of how an AI system may affect individuals, groups and society across its lifecycle (ISO/IEC 42005:2025). | [10] |
| Model lifecycle | The stages an AI/ML model passes through — problem definition, data acquisition, development/training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and retirement (ISO/IEC 22989 lifecycle concepts). | [9] |
| Human oversight | Measures enabling natural persons to understand, monitor, intervene in, or override an AI system's operation (AI Act Art. 14; a designed governance control). | [1] |

text:
For most of the last decade AI risk was managed, if at all, through general IT, data-protection and model-risk controls not designed for machine learning. Three pressures changed this. First, **general-purpose and generative AI** created capabilities — and failure modes such as hallucination, data leakage and mass content generation — that generic controls did not anticipate [13]. Second, **regulation arrived**: the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) made risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight and robustness legal obligations for high-risk systems [1][3]. Third, a **standards ecosystem** matured to give organisations a repeatable way to meet those expectations [7][12].

The result is a layered landscape. At the top sit **values and soft law**: the **OECD AI Principles** (2019, updated 2024), the first intergovernmental AI standard, adopted by 47 adherents including the EU, which shaped the AI Act's own "trustworthy, human-centric" framing [15][16]. Beneath them sit **frameworks and management standards** that make the values operational: the **NIST AI RMF** (voluntary, outcomes-based) and **ISO/IEC 42001** (certifiable management system) [7][12]. In the EU these are the practical means of demonstrating AI Act conformity; in the UK — which has **no horizontal AI law** and instead relies on a **principles-based, regulator-led approach** [4][5] — they are, for now, the main governance yardstick. This document sits at that operational layer.

text:
AI governance is not itself a legal instrument; it is how organisations **discharge and evidence** obligations that arise elsewhere. Two bodies of law drive it, and a set of voluntary standards operationalise it.

- **EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)** — imposes, for high-risk systems, a **risk-management system (Art. 9)**, **data governance (Art. 10)**, **technical documentation (Art. 11)**, **record-keeping/logging (Art. 12)**, **transparency (Art. 13)**, **human oversight (Art. 14)** and **accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Art. 15)** [1]. These are governance requirements in legal form. Providers must also operate a **quality management system (Art. 17)** — the AI Act's own management-system hook, to which ISO/IEC 42001 maps closely [1][7].
- **GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)** — where AI processes personal data, **accountability (Art. 5(2))**, **data protection by design and by default (Art. 25)**, **security (Art. 32)**, **DPIAs (Art. 35)** and rules on **automated decision-making (Art. 22)** apply in parallel; AI governance must therefore integrate with the data-protection programme [2].
- **Voluntary frameworks** — **ISO/IEC 42001**, the **NIST AI RMF** and the **OECD AI Principles** are not binding, but are the recognised means of meeting the above in a systematic, auditable way [7][12][15].

## Relevant Articles

*The AI Act articles are stated fully in `ai-act-foundations`; listed here only as the obligations that governance operationalises.*

| Article | Obligation (governance operationalises) | Source |
|---------|------------------------------------------|--------|
| AI Act Art. 9 | Risk-management system across the high-risk AI lifecycle. | [1] |
| AI Act Art. 10 | Data and data-governance practices (quality, relevance, bias examination). | [1] |
| AI Act Art. 11 + Annex IV | Technical documentation. | [1] |
| AI Act Art. 12 | Automatic record-keeping (logging) and traceability. | [1] |
| AI Act Art. 14 | Human oversight (understand, monitor, intervene, override). | [1] |
| AI Act Art. 17 | Quality management system for high-risk providers. | [1] |
| GDPR Art. 5(2) / Art. 25 | Accountability; data protection by design and by default. | [2] |
| GDPR Art. 35 | Data protection impact assessment. | [2] |

## Relevant Recitals

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| AI Act Recital 1 | Purpose — promote trustworthy, human-centric AI while protecting health, safety and fundamental rights (the values governance serves). | [1] |
| AI Act Recital 27 | References the trustworthy-AI principles (human agency/oversight, technical robustness, privacy/data governance, transparency, diversity/non-discrimination, societal well-being, accountability) that governance frameworks implement. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** AI governance frameworks (ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, OECD Principles) are voluntary standards and soft law, not statutes interpreted by courts; there is no case law construing them. Litigation touching AI to date turns on the GDPR, equality or consumer law (see `gdpr-foundations`), not on these frameworks. [7][12]

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **European Commission:** presents AI Act compliance as a systematic, lifecycle undertaking and points providers toward harmonised standards and management systems (including a quality management system under Art. 17) as the route to conformity; the **AI Office** coordinates implementation and the GPAI Code of Practice [3][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ICO (UK):** its **AI and data protection** guidance treats governance and accountability as central — organisations must document AI processing, assess risks (including bias and explainability), and embed data protection by design; the ICO frames this as existing-law obligations, not new AI-specific ones [4]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **UK Government:** the **"pro-innovation approach to AI regulation"** declines a horizontal statute in favour of **five cross-sector principles** (safety/security/robustness; transparency/explainability; fairness; accountability/governance; contestability/redress) applied by existing regulators — making voluntary frameworks the practical governance baseline in the UK [5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Interpretive caution:** certification to ISO/IEC 42001 or alignment to the NIST AI RMF is **evidence of diligence, not a legal safe harbour**; regulators assess actual compliance with the AI Act and GDPR, for which a certificate is supporting — not conclusive — proof [1][2][7]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

text:
- **Adopt a management-system spine.** ISO/IEC 42001 follows the ISO harmonised structure (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement) plus AI-specific controls in **Annex A** (e.g., AI policy, roles, impact assessment, data management, lifecycle controls) with implementation guidance in **Annex B** [7]. Build governance on this spine so it is auditable. *(Best practice.)*
- **Use the AI RMF functions as the operating loop.** **Govern** (culture, roles, policy) is cross-cutting; **Map** (context and risk framing), **Measure** (assessment, metrics, testing) and **Manage** (prioritise, respond, monitor) run iteratively across the lifecycle [12]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Instrument the model lifecycle.** Attach controls at each stage — data provenance and quality (AI Act Art. 10), evaluation and red-teaming (especially for GenAI), deployment gates, and post-deployment **monitoring** for drift and incidents [1][12][13]. *(Legal obligation for high-risk + best practice.)*
- **Impact assessment.** Use **ISO/IEC 42005:2025** to conduct AI system impact assessments, and align them with GDPR **DPIAs** where personal data is involved so a single assessment serves both regimes [2][10]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Documentation and logging by design.** Technical documentation (AI Act Art. 11), model/system cards, decision logs and automatic record-keeping (Art. 12) should be generated as a by-product of the pipeline, not retrofitted [1]. *(Legal obligation for high-risk + best practice.)*
- **GenAI-specific controls.** The NIST GenAI Profile flags risks such as confabulation/hallucination, data leakage, harmful bias, CBRN/cyber uplift, and content-integrity harms — address them with input/output filtering, provenance/watermarking, and human review [13]. *(Best practice.)*

legal_basis: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (operationalised via ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, OECD AI Principles)

text:
- **Infrastructure operators are usually deployers or processors, not framework owners.** Hosting an AI system does not by itself require an AIMS, but where the host brands, materially modifies, or takes provider-level responsibility, ISO/IEC 42001 scope and AI Act provider duties may attach [1][7]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Logging and retention.** High-risk logging (AI Act Art. 12) must be retained in the hosting environment while honouring GDPR storage-limitation and security duties (Arts. 5, 32) — coordinate with `privacy-engineering-foundations` [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Shared-responsibility clarity.** Cloud providers increasingly hold ISO/IEC 42001 certification for named AI services; deployers should map which AIMS controls the provider covers and which remain the deployer's own [7]. *(Best practice.)*

text:
- **Most game AI is minimal risk**, so a full AIMS is rarely mandatory; nonetheless a **lightweight governance baseline** (inventory, transparency for AI chatbots/companions, content monitoring for generative features) is advisable, especially where minors are involved [1][3]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Generative content governance.** Player-facing GenAI (NPC dialogue, user-generated content tools) should adopt the GenAI Profile's controls — output filtering, provenance marking, abuse monitoring — to manage toxicity, IP and safety risks [13]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Escalation triggers.** Biometric, emotion-inference or matchmaking features affecting access to services can cross into higher-risk tiers, at which point AI Act governance obligations and a formal AIMS become material [1]. *(Legal obligation once triggered.)*
