text:
*This document is itself about AI operations; the "AI Considerations" here concern how governance interlocks with the AI-regulation and data-protection stack.*

- **Operationalises the AI Act.** ISO/IEC 42001's management system and the NIST AI RMF functions are the practical vehicle for AI Act Arts. 9–17 duties; harmonised European standards (under development via CEN/CENELEC) will formalise this mapping, but 42001 and the AI RMF are the interim best practice [1][7][12]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Integrates with GDPR.** AI governance must not run separately from the data-protection programme: AI impact assessments should dovetail with DPIAs, and lifecycle data controls with DPbDD and Art. 32 security [2][10]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **Values traceability.** The OECD Principles' five values (inclusive growth/well-being; human rights and democratic values; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability) trace directly into both the AI Act's trustworthy-AI recitals and the NIST trustworthiness characteristics — use them as the north star when frameworks are silent [12][15][16]. *(Best practice / soft law.)*
- **GenAI and GPAI.** For organisations building on foundation models, governance must extend up the supply chain — evaluating model providers, documenting model choices, and applying the GenAI Profile — complementing the GPAI obligations covered in `ai-act-foundations`/`ai-act-gpai` [13]. *(Best practice.)*

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Stand up an AI governance function** — assign accountable ownership (e.g., an AI governance board and a named senior owner), an AI policy, and defined roles across the lifecycle. *(BEST PRACTICE; OBLIGATION-adjacent via AI Act Art. 17 QMS and GDPR Art. 5(2).)* [1][2][7]
2. **Maintain an AI system inventory** with tier, role (provider/deployer) and risk rating; this is the precondition for every other control. *(BEST PRACTICE; supports OBLIGATION.)* [1][7]
3. **Adopt a recognised framework and map it to the law** — implement ISO/IEC 42001 and/or the NIST AI RMF and cross-map controls to AI Act Arts. 9–17 and GDPR. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [7][12]
4. **Run risk management continuously** — use ISO/IEC 23894 (AI risk management) and the AI RMF Map/Measure/Manage loop; re-assess on material change. *(OBLIGATION for high-risk via Art. 9; BEST PRACTICE otherwise.)* [1][8][12]
5. **Conduct AI system impact assessments** (ISO/IEC 42005) and align them with GDPR DPIAs. *(OBLIGATION where DPIA triggered; BEST PRACTICE otherwise.)* [2][10]
6. **Design human oversight in, not on** — define who can monitor, intervene and override, with the authority and training to do so. *(OBLIGATION for high-risk via Art. 14; BEST PRACTICE otherwise.)* [1]
7. **Generate documentation and logs automatically** — technical documentation, model/system cards, evaluation records and decision logs as pipeline outputs. *(OBLIGATION for high-risk via Arts. 11–12; BEST PRACTICE otherwise.)* [1]
8. **Apply GenAI-specific controls** using the NIST GenAI Profile and its suggested actions. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [13][14]
9. **Prepare for external assurance** — internal audit against ISO/IEC 42001, then accredited certification where it adds market or regulatory value. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [7]
10. **Use the NIST AI RMF Playbook** for concrete, function-by-function suggested actions when translating outcomes into tasks. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [14]

- **Phase 0 — Foundations:** Establish AI governance ownership, AI policy, and an AI system inventory (tier + role). *Effort:* Medium. *Depends on:* `ai-act-foundations` triage.
- **Phase 1 — Framework adoption:** Select ISO/IEC 42001 and/or NIST AI RMF; map controls to AI Act Arts. 9–17 and GDPR. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 2 — Lifecycle controls:** Implement risk management (ISO/IEC 23894 + AI RMF), impact assessments (ISO/IEC 42005), data governance, documentation and logging. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 3 — Human oversight & GenAI controls:** Design oversight roles; apply the GenAI Profile to generative systems. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 4 — Assurance:** Internal audit; align DPIAs and AI impact assessments; pursue accredited ISO/IEC 42001 certification where valuable. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 5 — Continual improvement:** Monitor performance, incidents and drift; track harmonised standards and framework updates; re-certify. *Effort:* Ongoing.

text:
The **EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854)** is the horizontal EU rulebook on **fair access to and use of data**. Adopted on **13 December 2023**, it **entered into force on 11 January 2024** and its main provisions **became applicable on 12 September 2025** [1][3]. It complements the GDPR: where the Data Act touches **personal** data, the **GDPR (and ePrivacy) continue to govern**, and prevail in the event of conflict (Art. 1(5)) [1][2].

The Act pursues a single objective — unlock the economic and social value of data while keeping its allocation fair — through several distinct regimes: (i) **user access to data from connected products** (IoT) and related services; (ii) **B2B data-sharing** on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms where a data holder is obliged to share; (iii) **business-to-government (B2G)** access in situations of **exceptional need**; (iv) protection against **unfair contractual terms** unilaterally imposed on SMEs; (v) rules to make **switching between cloud/data-processing services** easier and eventually free; (vi) **interoperability** requirements; and (vii) **safeguards against unlawful third-country governmental access** to non-personal data held in the EU [1][3][4].

This document establishes the foundations: purpose and scope, the chapter-by-chapter structure, the **phased application timeline**, the core obligations at a foundational level, and the **relationship with the GDPR**. Deeper mechanics — cloud switching, IoT data-sharing mechanics and B2G access — are deferred to dedicated sub-topic documents (see Scope). The single most important operational fact is that the **headline obligations are already in force (from 12 September 2025)**, with the connected-product **design** duty biting for products placed on the market **after 12 September 2026** [1][2].
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
- The **Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854)** entered into force **11 January 2024** and applies from **12 September 2025** (Art. 50) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- Its purpose is **fair access to and use of data**; it is horizontal (cross-sectoral) and covers **non-personal and personal data**, complementing rather than replacing the GDPR [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Users of connected products (IoT)** and related services gain rights to **access the data they generate** and to have it shared with third parties (Chapter II, Arts. 3–7) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **Article 3(1) "data access by design and by default"** duty applies to connected products and related services **placed on the market after 12 September 2026** [1][3]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- Where a data holder **must** make data available, it must do so on **fair, reasonable, non-discriminatory (FRAND)** terms and may not impose **unfair contractual terms** on SMEs (Chapters III–IV, Arts. 8–13) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **B2G access**: public bodies may obtain data in cases of **exceptional need** (e.g., public emergencies) under strict conditions (Chapter V, Arts. 14–22) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Cloud/data-processing switching**: providers must remove obstacles to switching; **switching charges are gradually withdrawn and prohibited from 12 January 2027** (Chapter VI, Arts. 23–31) [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- **International transfers of non-personal data**: providers must take measures against **unlawful third-country governmental access/transfer** of non-personal data held in the EU (Art. 32) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **GDPR prevails on personal data**: in any conflict, Union/national data-protection and privacy law prevails (Art. 1(5)) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*

*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Data-Act-specific terms are defined here; see the Regulation's Art. 2 for the full list.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Connected product | An item that obtains, generates or collects data about its use or environment and can communicate product data via an electronic communications service, physical connection or on-device access (Art. 2(5)). | [1] |
| Related service | Digital service, other than an electronic communications service, connected with a product at purchase/rental/lease such that its absence would prevent the product performing a function (Art. 2(6)). | [1] |
| Data holder | A legal or natural person that has the right or obligation to use and make available data, including product/related-service data it has the ability to make available (Art. 2(13)). | [1] |
| User | A person who owns, rents or leases a connected product, or receives a related service (Art. 2(12)). | [1] |
| Data processing service | A digital service enabling on-demand, broad remote network access to a shared pool of configurable, scalable computing resources (i.e., cloud/edge services) (Art. 2(8)). | [1] |
| Non-personal data | Data other than personal data as defined in GDPR Art. 4(1) (personal data remains governed by the GDPR). | [1][2] |
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
The EU's data economy strategy identified that a large share of industrial and machine-generated data went unused, and that value was concentrated with a small number of actors who controlled the devices and platforms generating the data. Existing law (GDPR for personal data; the Database Directive; competition law) addressed only parts of the problem, leaving **connected-product data**, **B2B bargaining imbalances**, **cloud vendor lock-in** and **public-sector access in emergencies** without a horizontal framework [3][4].

The Data Act is the second pillar (with the 2022 **Data Governance Act**, Reg (EU) 2022/868) of the European Strategy for Data. Where the Data Governance Act creates structures and trust mechanisms for voluntary data sharing, the **Data Act allocates rights and obligations** over who can access and use data and on what terms [3][4]. It was adopted on 13 December 2023 with a deliberately **staggered application** to give manufacturers, cloud providers and data holders time to redesign products, contracts and systems [1][3].
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
The Data Act is a **Regulation** — directly applicable across the EU without national transposition. It states obligations plainly; interpretation is aided by its recitals and by Commission guidance. Its structure (chapters):

- **Chapter I (Arts. 1–2)** — subject matter, scope, definitions; and the **relationship-with-other-law** clause (incl. Art. 1(5) on GDPR primacy for personal data).
- **Chapter II (Arts. 3–7)** — **data sharing from connected products/IoT**: user access to product and related-service data, and sharing with third parties.
- **Chapter III (Arts. 8–12)** — obligations for data holders **legally obliged to make data available**: **FRAND** terms, non-discrimination, reasonable compensation.
- **Chapter IV (Art. 13)** — protection against **unfair contractual terms** unilaterally imposed (SME protection).
- **Chapter V (Arts. 14–22)** — **business-to-government (B2G)** data sharing on the basis of **exceptional need**.
- **Chapter VI (Arts. 23–31)** — **switching between data-processing (cloud/edge) services**, removal of obstacles and switching charges.
- **Chapter VII (Art. 32)** — safeguards against **unlawful third-country governmental access and transfer** of non-personal data.
- **Chapter VIII (Arts. 33–36)** — **interoperability** of data, data-sharing mechanisms and data-processing services.
- **Chapter IX (Arts. 37–42)** — implementation and **enforcement** by competent authorities; penalties set by Member States.
- **Chapters X–XI (Arts. 43–50)** — sui generis database-right clarification; final provisions incl. **Art. 50 application dates** [1].

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 1(5) | Relationship with data-protection/privacy law — GDPR, Reg (EU) 2018/1725 and ePrivacy apply to personal data and **prevail in case of conflict**. | [1][2] |
| Art. 2 | Definitions (connected product, related service, data holder, user, data processing service, etc.). | [1] |
| Arts. 3–4 | Connected-product/related-service data must be accessible to the user; **Art. 3(1)** = access by design and by default; access "without undue delay, easily, securely". | [1] |
| Art. 5 | User's right to have data shared with a **third party** on request. | [1] |
| Arts. 8–9 | Data holder obligated to share must use **FRAND**, non-discriminatory terms; **reasonable compensation**. | [1] |
| Art. 13 | **Unfair contractual terms** unilaterally imposed on an enterprise are not binding. | [1] |
| Arts. 14–22 | **B2G** data sharing on the basis of exceptional need; conditions and safeguards. | [1] |
| Arts. 23–31 | **Switching** between data-processing services: removal of obstacles; **Art. 29** gradual withdrawal of switching charges. | [1][5] |
| Art. 32 | Measures against **unlawful international access/transfer** of non-personal data by third-country authorities. | [1] |
| Arts. 33–36 | **Interoperability** requirements (data, data spaces, smart contracts, data-processing services). | [1] |
| Art. 50 | **Entry into force and application** — applies from 12 September 2025, with phased dates. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 1 | Data as a key resource; objective of fair access to and use of data across the internal market. | [1] |
| Recital 7 | Horizontal, cross-sectoral framework complementing sectoral and data-protection law. | [1] |
| Recital 34 area | **FRAND** and non-discrimination rationale for mandated B2B data sharing. | [1] |

*Recitals are not binding but aid construction of the operative articles; they are cited here as interpretive aids only.*

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** The Data Act's main provisions applied only from 12 September 2025; there is no CJEU or national case law interpreting it at this document's date. Interpretive weight rests on the Regulation's text, its recitals and Commission guidance [1][3][4].

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames the Data Act as making "more data available for use" while ensuring **fairness** in how value from data is allocated, and stresses it is **horizontal** (applying across sectors and to all connected products placed on the EU market, irrespective of manufacturer establishment) [3][4]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **IoT / connected products:** the Commission explains users should be able to access data generated by their use of connected products and share it with third parties (e.g., independent repairers), improving competition in aftermarket services [3][4]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Cloud switching:** the Commission presents the switching rules as targeting **vendor lock-in**, requiring providers to remove commercial, technical and contractual obstacles and to withdraw switching charges over a transition period [3][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **International transfers / non-personal data:** Art. 32 is presented as protecting EU-held non-personal data against **unlawful** third-country governmental access, mirroring GDPR-style safeguards for the non-personal sphere [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **GDPR interplay:** the Commission and commentators emphasise the Data Act **does not create a new legal basis** for processing personal data; controllers must still identify a GDPR lawful basis, and the GDPR prevails on conflict (Art. 1(5)) [1][2][4]. *(Regulatory interpretation / legal obligation.)*
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
- **Data access by design (Art. 3(1))** — connected products and related services placed on the market **after 12 September 2026** must be engineered so product/related-service data is, by default, **easily, securely and (where feasible) directly accessible** to the user, in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format [1][3]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- **Interfaces and formats** — data holders must provide access "without undue delay, of the same quality as available to the data holder, and, where applicable, continuously and in real-time" (Art. 4); expose stable APIs and machine-readable formats [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Trade secrets and security** — sharing obligations must be reconciled with trade-secret protection and product security/safety; technical measures (e.g., need-to-know disclosure, protective agreements) are contemplated [1]. *(Legal obligation — detail deferred to `data-act-iot-sharing`.)*
- **Switching engineering (Chapter VI)** — providers must support **functional equivalence** (where feasible), open interfaces and export of exportable data/digital assets to enable switching; this is an architectural, not merely contractual, requirement [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — detail deferred to `data-act-cloud-switching`.)*
- **Interoperability (Arts. 33–36)** — align data, metadata and interfaces with essential interoperability requirements and, where adopted, common specifications/standards for data spaces and data-processing services [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
- **Cloud/edge providers are directly in scope** — "data processing services" (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS-type on-demand compute) must meet Chapter VI switching obligations: remove obstacles, provide pre-contractual switching information, support export, and **stop charging switching fees from 12 January 2027** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- **Contractual overhaul** — hosting contracts must include mandated switching clauses (maximum notice/transition periods, assistance obligations); unfair-term protections (Art. 13) also constrain terms imposed on SME customers [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Non-personal-data transfer safeguards (Art. 32)** — providers holding EU non-personal data must implement technical, organisational and legal measures to resist **unlawful** third-country governmental access/transfer; assess jurisdictional exposure and government-access request handling [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Interoperability posture** — position for functional equivalence and open export formats now, ahead of enforcement maturity. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
- **Connected-product angle is usually narrow** — pure online game services are generally not "connected products", but **IoT peripherals, VR/AR headsets, wearables and connected controllers** that collect usage/environment data can fall within Chapter II, triggering user data-access duties for their manufacturers [1][3]. *(Interpretation — assess per device.)*
- **Cloud switching applies to game backends** — studios hosting on cloud/edge "data processing services" benefit from the switching rules as **customers**, and (if they resell managed hosting) may owe them as **providers** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Personal data still governed by GDPR** — player telemetry that is personal data remains under the GDPR; the Data Act adds access/portability expectations but does not displace consent/lawful-basis analysis, especially for minors [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
- **Data Act feeds AI data pipelines** — connected-product and B2B data made available under the Data Act may become **training or operational input** for AI systems; the acquiring party must still hold a GDPR lawful basis for any personal data and honour Art. 1(5) primacy [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Overlap with the AI Act** — high-risk AI **data-governance** duties (AI Act Arts. 10) and the Data Act's data-access/quality provisions are complementary; see `ai-act-foundations`. Sourcing data via Data Act rights does not exempt an AI provider from AI Act obligations. *(Cross-reference / best practice.)*
- **Interoperability and data spaces** — the Data Act's interoperability rules underpin **common European data spaces** that AI developers may draw on; align data formats accordingly. *(Best practice.)*
title: EU Data Act: Foundations, Data Access & Sharing

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Map your role(s)** — determine whether you are a connected-product manufacturer, data holder, user, third-party recipient, or data-processing-service provider; roles drive every obligation. *(OBLIGATION — foundational.)* [1]
2. **Inventory connected products and data** — catalogue products/related services placed (or to be placed) on the EU market and the data they generate. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][3]
3. **Build data-access-by-design** — for products launching **after 12 September 2026**, engineer Art. 3(1) default, secure, machine-readable access. *(OBLIGATION — phased.)* [1]
4. **Regularise B2B sharing terms** — where obliged to share, apply **FRAND**, non-discriminatory terms and reasonable compensation; remove **unfair terms** (Art. 13) from SME contracts. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **Prepare a B2G response process** — define how you assess and answer public-body exceptional-need requests (Arts. 14–22). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Cloud providers: implement switching** — update contracts, expose export/interoperability, and remove switching charges by **12 January 2027**. *(OBLIGATION — phased.)* [1][5]
7. **Address non-personal-data transfer risk** — implement Art. 32 safeguards against unlawful third-country government access. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
8. **Run Data Act and GDPR together** — never treat a Data Act right as a GDPR lawful basis; keep DPIAs/DPbDD in play (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`). *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [1][2]

text:
The **EU Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065**, "DSA") is the EU's horizontal rulebook for **intermediary services** — the ISPs, hosting providers, marketplaces, social networks and search engines that carry, store or index third-party content. Its purpose is a **safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment** in which fundamental rights are protected and illegal content and goods are handled through accountable, transparent processes, under **fully harmonised** EU-wide rules [1][3]. It **entered into force on 16 November 2022** and became **fully applicable to all in-scope entities on 17 February 2024** (Art. 93), with the heaviest tier already binding on designated platforms from mid-2023 [1][3].

The DSA imposes **cumulative, tiered obligations**: rules that apply to **all intermediary services** (points of contact, transparent terms, transparency reporting) are supplemented by additional duties for **hosting services** (notice-and-action, statements of reasons), then for **online platforms** (complaint handling, trusted flaggers, ad and recommender-system transparency, dark-pattern and minor-protection rules), and finally by the strictest regime for **Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs)** and **Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs)** — those with **45 million+ average monthly EU users** — including annual **systemic-risk assessments**, risk mitigation, **independent audits**, a researcher-data-access duty and a compliance function [1][3][4].

Enforcement is split: national **Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs)** supervise most providers under a **country-of-origin** principle, while the **European Commission** has exclusive powers over VLOP/VLOSE systemic obligations. Penalties reach **up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover** [1][3]. This is not theoretical: on **5 December 2025 the Commission issued its first DSA non-compliance fine — €120 million against X** — and in **October 2025 it issued preliminary findings against TikTok and Meta** for transparency and user-protection breaches [6][7].
title: EU Digital Services Act: Foundations & Platform Obligations

text:
- The **DSA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065)** entered into force **16 November 2022** and became **fully applicable on 17 February 2024** (Art. 93) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- Obligations are **tiered and cumulative** by service type: intermediary → hosting → online platform → VLOP/VLOSE; each tier inherits the ones below it [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The DSA **preserves the conditional liability exemptions** (mere conduit, caching, hosting) inherited from the e-Commerce Directive and **bans general monitoring obligations** (Arts. 4–8) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Hosting providers** must operate **notice-and-action** mechanisms (Art. 16) and give **statements of reasons** for content restrictions (Art. 17) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Online platforms** must provide internal complaint handling, out-of-court dispute settlement, **trusted-flagger** priority (Art. 22), **advertising transparency** (Art. 26), **recommender-system transparency** (Art. 27), and must not use **dark patterns** (Art. 25) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **VLOPs/VLOSEs** (45m+ EU users, Art. 33) face **systemic-risk assessment** (Art. 34), **risk mitigation** (Art. 35), **independent annual audits** (Art. 37) and **vetted-researcher data access** (Art. 40) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Enforcement follows a **country-of-origin / Digital Services Coordinator** model, with the **Commission** exclusively supervising VLOP/VLOSE systemic duties; **fines reach up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover** (Arts. 52, 74) [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Enforcement is **live-verified**: the Commission's list (last updated **10 July 2026**) shows **20+ designated VLOPs and two VLOSEs**; the **first fine (€120m against X)** issued **5 Dec 2025**, with **preliminary findings against TikTok and Meta** in October 2025 [4][6][7]. *(Confirmed, not asserted.)*

| Hosting service | An intermediary service that stores information provided by, and at the request of, a recipient (Art. 3(g)(iii)). | [1] |
| Online platform | A hosting service that, at a recipient's request, **stores and disseminates information to the public**, unless that is a minor/ancillary feature of another service (Art. 3(i)). | [1] |

| Notice-and-action | The Art. 16 mechanism by which any person can notify a hosting provider of allegedly illegal content, triggering a duty to act in a timely, diligent, non-arbitrary manner. | [1] |

text: The DSA modernises the **e-Commerce Directive (2000/31/EC)**, whose intermediary-liability "safe harbours" had governed online services since 2000 but predated social media, algorithmic feeds and large marketplaces. Divergent national content laws had fragmented the single market and left illegal content, counterfeit goods and systemic online harms inconsistently addressed. The EU's response, part of the **Digital Services Act package** alongside the Digital Market Act (DMA), keeps the liability exemptions but layers on **binding due-diligence obligations** scaled to a service's type and reach, under **fully harmonised** rules directly applicable across all Member States [1][3]. The DSA entered into force on **16 November 2022**; designation-related provisions applied from that date, the first VLOPs/VLOSEs were designated on **25 April 2023** (with their obligations following ~4 months later), and the regime became **fully applicable to all intermediaries on 17 February 2024** [1][3][5].
title: EU Digital Services Act: Foundations & Platform Obligations

text:
The DSA regulates providers of **intermediary services** offered to recipients established or located in the EU, **regardless of the provider's place of establishment** (Art. 2). Its architecture is **cumulative** — each tier adds to, rather than replaces, the tier beneath it [1]:

- **Chapter I** — subject matter, scope, definitions (Arts. 1–3).
- **Chapter II (Arts. 4–10)** — **liability** of intermediary providers: **mere conduit** (Art. 4), **caching** (Art. 5), **hosting** (Art. 6), the voluntary-investigation "Good Samaritan" clause (Art. 7), **no general monitoring obligation** (Art. 8), and **orders** to act against illegal content / to provide information (Arts. 9–10).
- **Chapter III** — **due-diligence** obligations, structured as nested sections:
  - **Section 1 — all intermediary services (Arts. 11–15):** points of contact (11–12), legal representatives (13), **terms and conditions** transparency (14), **transparency reporting** (15).
  - **Section 2 — hosting services (Arts. 16–18):** **notice-and-action** (16), **statement of reasons** (17), notification of suspected criminal offences (18).
  - **Section 3 — online platforms (Arts. 19–28):** micro/small exemption (19), internal complaint handling (20), out-of-court dispute settlement (21), **trusted flaggers** (22), measures against misuse (23), platform transparency reporting (24), **prohibition of dark patterns** (25), **advertising transparency** (26), **recommender-system transparency** (27), **protection of minors** (28).
  - **Section 4 — marketplaces (Arts. 29–32):** trader traceability / **know-your-business-customer** (30), compliance by design (31), right to information (32).
  - **Section 5 — VLOPs / VLOSEs (Arts. 33–43):** designation (33), **systemic-risk assessment** (34), **risk mitigation** (35), crisis response (36), **independent audit** (37), non-profiling recommender option (38), **enhanced ad repository** (39), **vetted-researcher data access** (40), compliance function (41), enhanced transparency reporting (42), supervisory fee (43).
- **Chapter IV (Arts. 49–88)** — **enforcement**: Digital Services Coordinators and the **country-of-origin** principle (Arts. 49, 56), penalties (52), enhanced Commission supervision of VLOPs/VLOSEs, and **Commission fines** up to 6% of worldwide turnover (74) and periodic penalty payments (76).

**Not Applicable at the foundational level.** The DSA is recent and there is no settled CJEU case law interpreting its substantive due-diligence obligations. Interpretive weight currently rests on the Regulation's text, Commission decisions and guidance. Challenges to VLOP/VLOSE **designation** have been brought before the General Court and enforcement decisions (e.g., the X fine) may be appealed; these are **emerging** and are tracked in the enforcement backlog rather than asserted here. text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** presents the DSA as delivering *"what is illegal offline should be illegal online,"* built on notice-and-action, transparency and accountability, under fully harmonised rules [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Designation is dynamic:** the Commission designates VLOPs/VLOSEs as they cross the 45m threshold and can end designation when they fall below it. Its published list — **last updated 10 July 2026** — shows **20+ VLOPs** (including Amazon Store, Apple App Store, Booking.com, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Google Play/Maps/Shopping, YouTube, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Snapchat, TikTok, X, AliExpress, Temu, Shein, Wikipedia and several adult-content sites) and **two VLOSEs** (Google Search, Bing) [4]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verify the live list.)*
- **Notice-and-action and researcher access are enforcement priorities:** the Commission's **preliminary findings against TikTok and Meta (October 2025)** centred on inadequate **Art. 40 researcher data access**, and (for Meta) deficient illegal-content **notice mechanisms** and appeal processes said to involve dark patterns [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation — preliminary, not final.)*
- **First fine sets the tone:** on **5 December 2025** the Commission fined **X €120 million** — its first DSA non-compliance decision — for the deceptive design of the paid "blue checkmark", a non-compliant advertising repository, and barriers to researcher data access [6]. *(Legal fact — confirmed.)*
- **Country-of-origin with central VLOP oversight:** most providers answer to the **DSC of their Member State of establishment**, but the Commission holds **exclusive** enforcement over the VLOP/VLOSE **Section 5** systemic obligations [1][3]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: EU Digital Services Act: Foundations & Platform Obligations

text:
- **Tier triage first** — determine whether a service is a mere-conduit/caching/hosting intermediary, an online platform (stores **and disseminates to the public**), a marketplace, and whether it approaches the 45m VLOP threshold; the tier drives every downstream obligation [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Notice-and-action pipeline** — hosting services must expose an accessible, electronic **Art. 16** notice mechanism, generate machine-readable **Art. 17 statements of reasons** for every restriction, and (for platforms) submit these to the **DSA Transparency Database** [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Advertising and recommender transparency** — platforms must label ads with who paid and why the user is targeted (Art. 26), disclose the **main parameters** of recommender systems and offer options (Art. 27); VLOPs must maintain a searchable **ad repository** (Art. 39) and a **non-profiling** recommender option (Art. 38) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Dark-pattern avoidance** — online-interface design must not deceive or manipulate recipients (Art. 25); this constrains consent flows, default settings and friction in complaint/notice paths [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Researcher data access** — VLOPs/VLOSEs must build vetted-researcher access interfaces (Art. 40); the TikTok/Meta/X actions show this is scrutinised closely [1][6][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: EU Digital Services Act: Foundations & Platform Obligations

text:
- **Safe harbour is conditional** — a hosting provider avoids liability only if it lacks actual knowledge of illegal content and acts **expeditiously** to remove/disable it upon obtaining knowledge (Art. 6); notice-and-action is the mechanism by which knowledge is acquired (Art. 16) [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **No general monitoring** — providers cannot be required to generally monitor or actively seek facts indicating illegality (Art. 8), but this does not bar specific orders (Arts. 9–10) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Logging and statements of reasons** — hosting operators must generate and retain **statements of reasons** for restrictions and support transparency reporting; retention must respect GDPR limits (see `gdpr-foundations`) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Establishment and legal representative** — non-EU intermediaries serving EU users must designate a **legal representative** (Art. 13) and are supervised by the DSC of that representative's Member State [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: EU Digital Services Act: Foundations & Platform Obligations

text:
- **UGC and chat can make a game an "online platform"** — if a game **stores and disseminates user content to the public** (public forums, mod hubs, shared creations, unmoderated public chat), the operator may be an online platform owing notice-and-action, complaint-handling and transparency duties; purely private/session chat is more likely a minor/ancillary feature outside Art. 3(i) [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess feature by feature.)*
- **Minor protection is acute** — games with large under-18 audiences engage **Art. 28** (no profiling-based advertising to minors; high privacy/safety by default) and heighten dark-pattern scrutiny of monetisation flows (Art. 25) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Marketplaces for items/skins** — player-to-player trading or third-party trader storefronts can trigger **Section 4** trader-traceability (KYBC) duties (Arts. 30–32) [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess.)*
- **Scale awareness** — a very large game platform could approach the **45m EU-user** VLOP threshold, bringing systemic-risk assessment into scope; monitor active-user metrics [1][4]. *(Best practice.)*
title: EU Digital Services Act: Foundations & Platform Obligations

text:
- **Recommender and moderation AI** — algorithmic feeds and automated content moderation are squarely within **Arts. 25–27** (dark patterns, recommender transparency) and, for VLOPs, are a named **systemic-risk** vector under Art. 34; automated moderation decisions still require Art. 17 statements of reasons [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Overlap with the AI Act** — where an intermediary deploys AI (e.g., recommender or generative features), the **AI Act (Reg (EU) 2024/1689)** may apply in parallel, including Art. 50 transparency for AI-generated/synthetic content; see `ai-act-foundations` [1]. *(Cross-reference.)*
- **GDPR overlap** — recommender profiling and ad targeting process personal data, so the **GDPR applies in full** (lawful basis, DPbDD, Art. 22 automated-decision safeguards); Art. 26/28 DSA rules on profiling-based ads reinforce this [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Classify each service by tier** (intermediary / hosting / online platform / marketplace / VLOP-candidate) and by role. *(OBLIGATION — foundational.)* [1][3]
2. **Confirm safe-harbour posture** — ensure conduct fits the Art. 4–6 exemptions and that no general-monitoring is imposed. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
3. **Build notice-and-action (Art. 16) and statements of reasons (Art. 17)**, including submission to the DSA Transparency Database where required. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Publish transparent terms and transparency reports** (Arts. 14–15; 24 for platforms). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **For online platforms:** stand up complaint handling, out-of-court dispute settlement, trusted-flagger priority, ad transparency, recommender transparency, dark-pattern review and minor protection (Arts. 20–28). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **For marketplaces:** implement trader traceability / KYBC (Arts. 30–32). *(OBLIGATION where applicable.)* [1]
7. **If approaching 45m EU users:** prepare systemic-risk assessment, mitigation, independent audit, ad repository and researcher-access interfaces (Arts. 33–43). *(OBLIGATION once designated; BEST PRACTICE to pre-build.)* [1][4]
8. **Map your DSC / establishment** and prepare for Commission oversight if a VLOP. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
9. **Run DSA and GDPR compliance together** for ad targeting, profiling and moderation data. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [1][2]
10. **Track live enforcement** (X, TikTok, Meta) for the Commission's evolving expectations on researcher access, ad repositories and notice design. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [6][7]

text:
The **EU Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925**, "DMA") is an *ex ante* competition-style regulation for large digital platforms. Its aim is to make digital markets more **contestable** (new entrants and rivals can compete) and **fair** (business users are not exploited by dominant platforms) [1][2]. Unlike traditional competition law, which acts *after* harm, the DMA imposes a fixed list of **do's and don'ts** on a small set of designated **gatekeepers** before harm occurs, and is enforced **solely by the European Commission** [1][2].

A firm becomes a **gatekeeper** when the Commission designates it under Article 3: it has a **significant impact on the internal market**, provides a **core platform service (CPS)** that is an **important gateway** for business users to reach end users, and enjoys an **entrenched and durable position**. Article 3 sets **rebuttable quantitative presumptions** for each limb (turnover/market-cap thresholds, and 45 million monthly active end users plus 10,000 yearly active business users in the EU) [1]. Designation attaches to specified CPS — the ten categories in Article 2 include app stores, search engines, social networks, messaging, operating systems, browsers, virtual assistants, cloud and online advertising [1].

Once designated, gatekeepers must comply with the obligations in **Articles 5, 6 and 7** — including no **self-preferencing**, no combining personal data across services without consent, allowing **sideloading** and third-party app stores, permitting **steering** to offers outside the platform, no forced bundling, data-access/portability duties, and **messaging interoperability** [1]. They must file **compliance reports** (Art. 11) and an **independently audited** consumer-profiling description (Art. 15). Breaches carry fines of up to **10% of total worldwide annual turnover**, rising to **20% for repeat infringement** (Art. 30) [1].

**Live-verified status (2026-07-11):** gatekeeper obligations became fully applicable on **7 March 2024** [4]; **seven** gatekeepers (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Booking, ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft) and **23** core platform services are currently designated [3]; and the Commission's **first non-compliance decisions (23 April 2025)** fined **Apple €500 million** (anti-steering, Art. 5(4)) and **Meta €200 million** (consent-or-pay, Art. 5(2)) [5][6]. On **8 July 2026** the General Court **upheld** Apple's gatekeeper designation for the App Store and iOS [7].
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
- The **DMA (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925)** entered into force on **1 November 2022**, applied from **2 May 2023**, and gatekeeper **obligations became fully applicable on 7 March 2024** [1][4]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Its twin goals are **contestability** and **fairness** in digital markets; it is enforced **exclusively by the European Commission**, not national competition authorities (Art. 1) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Gatekeeper designation (Art. 3)** rests on three limbs with **rebuttable quantitative presumptions**: significant internal-market impact (≥ €7.5bn EU turnover in each of the last 3 FYs **or** ≥ €75bn market cap), an important-gateway CPS (**≥45m monthly EU end users** and **≥10,000 yearly EU business users**), and an entrenched, durable position [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The DMA applies only to designated **core platform services** — ten categories in Art. 2 (app stores/intermediation, search, social networking, video-sharing, messaging, operating systems, browsers, virtual assistants, cloud, online advertising) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Articles 5–7** set self-executing and specifiable obligations: no **self-preferencing** (Art. 6(5)), **data-use limits** (Arts. 5(2), 6(2)), **sideloading** and third-party app stores (Art. 6(4)), **steering / anti-anti-steering** (Art. 5(4)), no **forced bundling/tying** (Arts. 5(7)–(8)), data access/portability (Arts. 6(9)–(10)), and **messaging interoperability** (Art. 7) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Gatekeepers must submit a **compliance report** within six months of designation and update it annually (Art. 11), plus an **independently audited** consumer-profiling description (Art. 15) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Penalties** reach **10% of total worldwide annual turnover**, or **20% for repeat infringement**; periodic penalty payments up to **5% of average daily worldwide turnover** (Art. 30); systematic non-compliance can trigger a **market investigation** and behavioural/structural remedies (Art. 18) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Live-verified enforcement:** the Commission's first non-compliance decisions (**23 April 2025**) fined **Apple €500m** and **Meta €200m** [5][6]; the General Court **upheld Apple's designation** on **8 July 2026** [7]. *(Legal fact — verified.)*

*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md`. DMA-specific terms are defined here; deeper per-obligation terms are deferred to `dma-obligations`.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Gatekeeper | An undertaking providing one or more core platform services that the Commission has **designated** under Art. 3 as having a significant internal-market impact, an important gateway CPS, and an entrenched, durable position. | [1] |
| Core platform service (CPS) | One of the ten service categories listed in Art. 2(2) (e.g. online intermediation/app stores, search engines, social networks, video-sharing, number-independent messaging, operating systems, browsers, virtual assistants, cloud, online advertising). Obligations attach to **designated** CPS. | [1] |
| Business user | A natural or legal person that, in a commercial or professional capacity, uses a core platform service to supply goods or services to end users (Art. 2(21)). | [1] |
| End user | A natural or legal person using a core platform service other than as a business user (Art. 2(20)). | [1] |
| Contestability | The degree to which firms can effectively enter, expand within, or challenge incumbents in a digital market — a core DMA objective (Recital 32 area). | [1][2] |
| Self-preferencing | A gatekeeper ranking or treating its own products/services more favourably than comparable third-party offers; prohibited in ranking, indexing and crawling by Art. 6(5). | [1] |
| Number-independent interpersonal communications service (NIICS) | An interpersonal communications service that does not connect with the public switched telephone network (e.g. many messaging apps); subject to interoperability duties under Art. 7. | [1] |

text:
Large online platforms increasingly act as private gatekeepers between businesses and consumers. Their scale, data advantages, network effects and control of app-distribution and ranking give them entrenched positions that traditional, case-by-case competition enforcement (Articles 101–102 TFEU) addresses only slowly and after harm has occurred [1][2]. The EU's response was a **regulatory** instrument setting **clear, pre-defined rules** for the largest platforms, applied uniformly and enforced centrally, so that markets stay open to challengers and business users are treated fairly [2].

The DMA was adopted on **14 September 2022** as Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, **entered into force on 1 November 2022**, and **started to apply on 2 May 2023** [1]. Potential gatekeepers then had to notify their qualifying CPS; the Commission made its **first designations on 6 September 2023**, and the designated gatekeepers had until **7 March 2024** to bring their CPS into compliance [3][4]. The DMA is one pillar of the EU's digital-rulebook alongside the **Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065)**, which addresses illegal content and systemic risks rather than market contestability [8].
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
The DMA regulates **designated gatekeepers** in respect of their **designated core platform services**. Its architecture:

- **Chapter I (Arts. 1–2)** — subject matter, scope, and definitions (incl. the ten CPS categories in Art. 2(2)). The Commission is the **sole enforcer**; Member States may not impose diverging obligations on gatekeepers for the same objective (Art. 1) [1].
- **Chapter II (Arts. 3–4)** — **designation** of gatekeepers (quantitative thresholds and rebuttable presumptions; market-investigation route) and review of designations.
- **Chapter III (Arts. 5–15)** — the **obligations**: self-executing duties (Art. 5), duties susceptible of further specification (Art. 6), messaging interoperability (Art. 7), plus anti-circumvention (Art. 13), concentration notifications (Art. 14), **compliance reporting** (Art. 11) and **audited profiling** disclosure (Art. 15).
- **Chapter IV (Arts. 16–19)** — **market investigations** (designation, systematic non-compliance, new services/practices).
- **Chapter V (Arts. 20–34)** — **investigatory and enforcement powers**, non-compliance decisions (Art. 29), **fines** (Art. 30), periodic penalty payments (Art. 31), and the **compliance function** (Art. 28).
- **Chapter VI (Arts. 35–54)** — final provisions, cooperation, and reviews.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 1 | Subject matter and scope; Commission is the **exclusive enforcer** of gatekeeper obligations. | [1] |
| Art. 2(2) | Definition of the **ten core platform service** categories. | [1] |
| Art. 3 | **Gatekeeper designation** — three limbs with rebuttable quantitative presumptions (turnover/market cap; 45m monthly end users + 10k yearly business users; entrenched/durable position). | [1] |
| Art. 5 | **Self-executing obligations** — e.g. no cross-service personal-data combination without consent (5(2)); allow steering/promotion of off-platform offers (5(4)); allow use of content acquired off-platform (5(5)); no forced use of the gatekeeper's identification/browser/payment services (5(7)); no tying/bundling of other CPS (5(8)). | [1] |
| Art. 6 | **Specifiable obligations** — no use of non-public business-user data to compete (6(2)); uninstall pre-installed apps and choice screens (6(3)); allow third-party app stores / **sideloading** (6(4)); no **self-preferencing** in ranking (6(5)); interoperability with OS/hardware features (6(7)); data portability and business-user data access (6(9)–(10)); FRAND access to app stores/search/social (6(12)). | [1] |
| Art. 7 | **Interoperability** of number-independent interpersonal communications services (messaging). | [1] |
| Art. 11 | **Compliance report** — file within six months of designation and update at least annually, describing how each obligation is met. | [1] |
| Art. 13 | **Anti-circumvention** — no behaviour that undermines effective compliance. | [1] |
| Art. 14 | Obligation to **inform the Commission of concentrations** in the digital sector. | [1] |
| Art. 15 | **Independently audited** description of consumer-profiling techniques; publish an overview. | [1] |
| Art. 18 | **Market investigation into systematic non-compliance** — behavioural or structural remedies. | [1] |
| Art. 28 | **Compliance function** — independent, adequately resourced, with compliance officers. | [1] |
| Art. 29 | **Non-compliance decisions** finding a breach and ordering compliance. | [1] |
| Art. 30 | **Fines** up to **10% of total worldwide annual turnover**; up to **20% for repeat infringement**. | [1] |
| Art. 31 | **Periodic penalty payments** up to **5% of average daily worldwide turnover**. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting terms [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 7–8 | The DMA complements, and does not replace, EU/national competition law; it pursues distinct objectives (contestability and fairness) through *ex ante* rules. | [1] |
| Recital 23 | Rationale for the **quantitative thresholds** as proxies for gateway power and entrenched position, subject to rebuttal. | [1] |
| Recital 32 area | **Contestability** — lowering barriers to entry and expansion so rivals can challenge gatekeepers. | [1] |
| Recital 62 area | **Self-preferencing** in ranking distorts contestability and fairness, hence the Art. 6(5) prohibition. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

The DMA is recent and its case law is emerging. The most significant judgment to date concerns **designation**, not the substantive obligations:

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Apple v Commission | General Court, Joined Cases **T-1079/23, T-1080/23 and T-214/24**, judgment **8 July 2026** (Press release CP 96/26) | The General Court **dismissed** Apple's challenge and **confirmed** its gatekeeper designation for the **App Store and iOS**, holding that the different App Store variants form a **single CPS**; challenges concerning **iMessage** were held inadmissible. | Confirms the Commission's Art. 3 designation methodology and the treatment of a service's variants as one CPS. [7] |

*Further non-compliance decisions (e.g. against Apple and Meta) are under appeal; those proceedings are tracked in `dma-enforcement-cases` (planned).* [5][6][7]

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (European Commission — not statutory text unless a specific obligation is cited).**

- The Commission frames the DMA around **two objectives — contestability and fairness** — and stresses that it applies a **closed, predictable list of obligations** to a small number of gatekeepers, enforced **centrally by the Commission** rather than by 27 national regimes [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Designation is service-specific.** The Commission designates named CPS, and it has both **added** services (e.g. Apple **iPadOS**, 29 April 2024) and, following review, **undesignated** others (e.g. Meta **Facebook Marketplace**, 23 April 2025), showing that designation is dynamic and evidence-based [3]. *(Regulatory interpretation / legal fact.)*
- **Compliance is outcome-tested, not box-ticking.** The Commission assesses whether measures are **effective**; its first non-compliance decisions found that Apple's steering restrictions and Meta's binary "consent or pay" model did **not** deliver the outcomes Articles 5(4) and 5(2) require [5][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation of Arts. 5(2), 5(4).)*
- The Commission has reported that, after its **first review**, the DMA "remains fit for purpose" and has opened opportunities for businesses and developers — signalling continuity rather than reopening the substantive obligations [2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Verification note:** the designation list and enforcement outcomes above were confirmed against the Commission's **gatekeepers portal** and news releases and the **Court of Justice** press service on **2026-07-11**; these are the items most likely to change and must be re-checked at each review [3][5][6][7]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
- **Sideloading and alternative app stores (Art. 6(4))** — gatekeeper operating systems must technically permit installation of third-party apps and app stores, which reshapes platform security models (notarisation, permissions, malware screening) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Steering and off-platform transactions (Arts. 5(4)–(5))** — apps and business users must be able to link out to, and complete, purchases outside the gatekeeper's channel without punitive restrictions [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Anti-self-preferencing in ranking (Art. 6(5))** — ranking, indexing and crawling must apply **transparent, fair and non-discriminatory** conditions to third parties versus the gatekeeper's own services [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Interoperability (Arts. 6(7), 7)** — third parties must get effective interoperability with OS/hardware features, and messaging gatekeepers must offer **interoperable** basic functionality (1:1 messaging, then groups and calls per the Art. 7 phasing) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Data access and portability (Arts. 6(9)–(10))** — real-time, continuous data portability for end users and access to business-user-generated data are architectural requirements (APIs, export tooling) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **For non-gatekeeper business users**, the technical impact is an **opportunity**: they can build on new interoperability, sideloading and data-access surfaces — but should design to the gatekeeper's published reference offers and monitor changes. *(Best practice.)*
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
- **Cloud computing is a CPS category (Art. 2(2)).** A hyperscale cloud provider could, on meeting the Art. 3 thresholds, be designated for its cloud service — bringing data-portability, interoperability and no-self-preferencing duties into infrastructure [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess designation status.)* No cloud service is designated as a CPS at this document's date [3]. *(Legal fact — verified.)*
- **Most hosting providers are not gatekeepers** and fall outside the DMA; their relevance is as **business users** of gatekeeper CPS (e.g. marketplaces, app stores, ad services) who now benefit from fairer terms and data access [1]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Multi-homing enablement** — DMA-driven data portability and interoperability make it easier for customers to move between hosts; providers should treat portability tooling as a competitive expectation. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
- **App-distribution changes matter most.** Game and game-service developers distributing through gatekeeper **app stores** gain rights to **steer** users to external offers, use **alternative app stores / sideloading**, and avoid **forced use** of the gatekeeper's in-app payment system (Arts. 5(4), 5(7), 6(4)) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers — opportunity for developers.)*
- **Cross-service data limits.** Where a game platform is itself a gatekeeper CPS (e.g. a social network or messaging service), combining player personal data across services requires **consent** (Art. 5(2)), reinforcing GDPR consent practice [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Real-time / player-data specifics are largely out of scope** — the DMA targets platform contestability, not game-server latency or matchmaking; those remain governed by GDPR and, where relevant, the AI Act. *(Interpretation.)*
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
- **Virtual assistants and AI-driven ranking are in scope.** "Virtual assistants" are an explicit CPS category (Art. 2(2)), and AI-based **ranking/recommendation** engines within designated CPS are subject to the **anti-self-preferencing** and transparency duties (Art. 6(5)) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Parallel regimes, not substitutes.** The DMA governs **market power**; the **AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)** governs AI **risk**, and the **GDPR** governs **personal data**. An AI recommender inside a gatekeeper CPS can engage all three simultaneously [1][9][10]. *(Interpretation — read together with `ai-act-foundations` and `gdpr-foundations`.)*
- **Emerging question:** whether **generative-AI / foundation-model** services will be designated as CPS is an open policy debate; the DMA's CPS list is fixed by Art. 2, so extension would require the market-investigation route or legislative change. Track, do not assume. *(Editorial recommendation.)* [1]
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Foundations & Gatekeeper Obligations

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** (gatekeeper must) / **BEST PRACTICE** (should) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (we suggest).

1. **Determine whether you are a gatekeeper.** Map turnover/market-cap and CPS user metrics against the Art. 3 thresholds; if presumptions are met, you must **notify** qualifying CPS. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
2. **If designated, stand up a compliance function** (Art. 28) and file the **Art. 11 compliance report** within six months, updated annually. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
3. **Implement Articles 5–7 by service:** enable sideloading/third-party stores, permit steering, remove self-preferencing in ranking, honour data-access/portability, deliver messaging interoperability, and stop cross-service data combination without consent. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Prepare the Art. 15 audited profiling description** and keep it current. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **Avoid circumvention (Art. 13).** Ensure remedies are **effective in practice** — the Commission tests outcomes, as the Apple/Meta decisions show. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][5][6]
6. **If you are a business user of a gatekeeper**, exercise your new rights (steering, portability, interoperability, FRAND access) and document any refusals for complaint to the Commission. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [1][2]
7. **Run DMA, GDPR and AI Act workstreams together** — consent (Art. 5(2)) overlaps GDPR; AI ranking overlaps the AI Act. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [1][9][10]
8. **Maintain a designation/enforcement watch-list** — re-verify the gatekeeper register and open proceedings at each review; they change. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [3]

text:
The **EU Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925**, "DMA") imposes a closed list of **do's and don'ts** on designated **gatekeepers** in respect of their designated **core platform services (CPS)**. This document goes beneath the foundational overview in `dma-foundations` and works through those obligations one by one: the **self-executing** duties in **Article 5**, the duties **susceptible of further specification** in **Article 6**, the **messaging interoperability** regime in **Article 7**, the **anti-circumvention** rule (Article 13), the **compliance-reporting** duty (Article 11) and **compliance function** (Article 28), the Commission's **specification proceedings** (Article 8), and the **enforcement and penalty** architecture (Articles 18, 29–31) [1].

The distinction between Articles 5 and 6 is structural and matters for compliance. **Article 5** obligations apply directly from the compliance date and are not, in principle, open to a "regulatory dialogue" — the gatekeeper must simply comply (e.g. no combining personal data across services without consent; no anti-steering or wide parity clauses; no forced use of the gatekeeper's browser engine, identification or payment service; no tying of further CPS) [1]. **Article 6** obligations are equally binding but the Commission may, under **Article 8(2)**, adopt a decision **specifying the measures** a gatekeeper must implement (e.g. sideloading, no self-preferencing in ranking, data portability and business-user data access, uninstall/defaults, and the Article 6(7) interoperability duty) [1]. **Article 7** governs interoperability of **number-independent interpersonal communications services (NIICS)** on a phased timeline [1].

**Live-verified status (2026-07-11):** **seven** gatekeepers (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Booking, ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft) and **23** core platform services are currently designated [2]. The Commission's **first non-compliance decisions (23 April 2025)** fined **Apple €500 million** for breaching the anti-steering obligation (Art. 5(4)) and **Meta €200 million** for its "consent or pay" model breaching the data-combination consent rule (Art. 5(2)) [3][4]. Separately, on **19 March 2025** the Commission adopted its **first Article 6(7) specification decisions**, setting out the interoperability measures Apple must deliver [5]. On **5 February 2026** the Commission decided that **Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated** [6], and on **8 July 2026** the General Court **upheld** Apple's existing gatekeeper designation [7].
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Gatekeeper Obligations in Depth

text:
- **Article 5** sets **self-executing** obligations that bind from the compliance date without a specification step: no cross-service personal-data combination without consent (5(2)); no wide price-parity / MFN clauses (5(3)); **anti-steering** — business users may promote and conclude off-platform offers free of charge (5(4)); use of off-platform-acquired content (5(5)); no forced use of the gatekeeper's identification, browser engine or payment service (5(7)); no tying of further CPS (5(8)); advertising-pricing transparency (5(9)–(10)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 6** obligations are binding but **susceptible of further specification** under Art. 8(2): no use of non-public business-user data to compete (6(2)); uninstall and choice screens (6(3)); third-party app stores / **sideloading** (6(4)); no **self-preferencing** in ranking, indexing, crawling (6(5)); switching freedom (6(6)); **interoperability** with OS/hardware features (6(7)); ad-measurement access (6(8)); end-user **data portability** (6(9)) and business-user **data access** (6(10)); search-data access on FRAND terms (6(11)); **FRAND** app-store/search/social access (6(12)); FRAND termination (6(13)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 7** requires designated **NIICS** (messaging) gatekeepers to make basic functionalities interoperable on request, on a **phased** timeline — 1:1 text and file-sharing at designation, group messaging within two years, and 1:1 then group voice/video calls within four years — while preserving security, including end-to-end encryption (7(3)), via a published **reference offer** (7(8)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Anti-circumvention (Art. 13)** prohibits any behaviour — contractual, commercial, technical or otherwise — that undermines effective compliance, including degrading conditions and making rights unreasonably difficult to exercise; consent refused under Art. 5(2) may be re-requested **no more than once per year** (13(6)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Gatekeepers must file an **Art. 11 compliance report** within six months of designation and update it annually, and maintain an **independent compliance function** with compliance officers reporting to management (Art. 28) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The Commission can **specify** Article 6 and 7 measures through **Art. 8 proceedings**; it exercised this for the first time in the **19 March 2025** Apple interoperability decisions (Art. 6(7)) [5]. *(Legal fact — verified.)*
- **Penalties** reach **10% of total worldwide annual turnover**, rising to **20% for repeat infringement** (Art. 30), with **periodic penalty payments** up to **5% of average daily worldwide turnover** (Art. 31); **systematic** non-compliance can trigger a market investigation and behavioural/structural remedies (Art. 18) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Worked enforcement:** the first non-compliance decisions (**23 April 2025**) fined **Apple €500m** (Art. 5(4)) and **Meta €200m** (Art. 5(2)) [3][4]; Alphabet's Google Play and Google Search compliance remain under investigation following **March 2025 preliminary findings** [8]; the General Court **upheld Apple's designation** on **8 July 2026** [7]. *(Legal fact — verified.)*

text:
*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md` (Gatekeeper, Core platform service, NIICS, Self-preferencing). Obligation-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Self-executing obligation | An Article 5 obligation that applies directly on the compliance date and, unlike Article 6 duties, is not subject to a Commission specification decision — the gatekeeper must comply as drafted. | [1] |
| Specifiable obligation | An Article 6 (or 7) obligation that is binding but which the Commission may render operational by adopting, under Art. 8(2), a decision **specifying** the measures the gatekeeper must implement. | [1] |
| Anti-steering | The Art. 5(4) prohibition on preventing business users, free of charge, from communicating and promoting offers (including at different prices) to end users acquired via the CPS, and concluding contracts with them, whether or not through the CPS. | [1] |
| Wide parity / MFN clause | A contractual term stopping a business user from offering the same goods/services on better terms through other channels; prohibited by Art. 5(3). | [1] |
| Sideloading | Installation and effective use of third-party software applications or third-party app stores on the gatekeeper's operating system, which Art. 6(4) requires be technically permitted (subject to proportionate security measures). | [1] |
| Self-preferencing | More favourable ranking, indexing or crawling of the gatekeeper's own services/products versus comparable third-party offers; prohibited by Art. 6(5), which requires transparent, fair and non-discriminatory conditions. | [1] |
| Reference offer | The published statement of technical details and general terms and conditions under which a NIICS gatekeeper provides interoperability (Art. 7(8)). | [1] |
| Specification proceeding (regulatory dialogue) | The Art. 8(2) process by which the Commission may adopt a decision specifying the measures a gatekeeper must implement to comply with Arts. 6 or 7. | [1][5] |
| Anti-circumvention | The Art. 13 duty not to undermine effective compliance by any behaviour — contractual, commercial, technical or of any other nature. | [1] |

text:
The DMA (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925) entered into force on 1 November 2022 and applied from 2 May 2023; the Commission made its first gatekeeper designations on 6 September 2023, and designated gatekeepers had until **7 March 2024** to bring their CPS into compliance with Articles 5, 6 and 7 [1][11]. The obligations were drafted as a **closed list** precisely so that they would be predictable and could be applied without the lengthy effects-analysis of traditional competition law [1][12].

The design choice that most shapes day-to-day compliance is the split between **Article 5 and Article 6**. Article 5 duties are "self-executing": Recital 65-area reasoning treats them as clear enough to apply without further specification. Article 6 duties are equally mandatory but the legislator recognised they might need operationalising for a given service; **Article 8** therefore lets the Commission engage in a "regulatory dialogue" and, where needed, adopt a **specification decision** setting out exactly what the gatekeeper must do [1]. Article 7 sits apart as a self-standing interoperability regime for messaging. This document is organised around that architecture, then turns to circumvention, reporting, the compliance function, specification and enforcement.
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Gatekeeper Obligations in Depth

text:
The obligations live in **Chapter III (Arts. 5–15)** of the DMA, with enforcement in **Chapter V (Arts. 20–34)** and market investigations in **Chapter IV (Arts. 16–19)** [1]. The obligation architecture:

- **Article 5 — obligations for gatekeepers** (self-executing do's and don'ts), sub-paragraphs 5(2)–5(10).
- **Article 6 — obligations susceptible of being further specified** under Article 8, sub-paragraphs 6(2)–6(13).
- **Article 7 — interoperability of number-independent interpersonal communications services** (messaging), with a phased functionality timeline and a reference-offer duty.
- **Article 8 — compliance and the specification mechanism**: the gatekeeper must ensure and demonstrate compliance; the Commission may specify Article 6/7 measures.
- **Article 11 — compliance report**; **Article 13 — anti-circumvention**; **Article 14 — concentration notifications**; **Article 15 — audited profiling description**.
- **Article 28 — compliance function** (independent, resourced, with compliance officers).
- **Enforcement**: **Article 18** (systematic non-compliance market investigation), **Articles 20–27** (investigatory powers, commitments, monitoring), **Article 29** (non-compliance decisions), **Article 30** (fines), **Article 31** (periodic penalty payments).

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 5(2) | No processing/combining of end-user personal data across the CPS and other services, no cross-use, and no sign-in to other services to combine data — **without consent**. | [1] |
| Art. 5(3) | No **wide parity / MFN** clauses: business users may offer the same products/services on different prices/conditions through third-party channels or their own. | [1] |
| Art. 5(4) | **Anti-steering**: allow business users, free of charge, to communicate and promote offers (incl. at different conditions) to end users acquired via the CPS, and to conclude contracts. | [1] |
| Art. 5(5) | Allow end users to access and use, via the CPS, content/subscriptions/features acquired from a business user off-platform. | [1] |
| Art. 5(6) | No restriction on business/end users raising non-compliance issues with public authorities (no anti-complaint clauses). | [1] |
| Art. 5(7) | No forced use of the gatekeeper's **identification service, web-browser engine, or payment service** (and supporting technical services). | [1] |
| Art. 5(8) | No **tying**: cannot require business/end users to subscribe to or register with any further CPS as a condition of use. | [1] |
| Art. 5(9)–(10) | Advertising **transparency**: give advertisers and publishers, on request, free daily information on prices and remuneration/fees. | [1] |
| Art. 6(2) | No use of **non-public data** generated by business users (and their end users) on the CPS to compete with them. | [1] |
| Art. 6(3) | Allow easy **uninstalling** of apps and changing of defaults; provide **choice screens** for default search/browser/virtual assistant. | [1] |
| Art. 6(4) | Allow third-party **app stores and sideloading**, with proportionate security measures permitted. | [1] |
| Art. 6(5) | No **self-preferencing** in ranking, indexing and crawling; transparent, fair, non-discriminatory conditions. | [1] |
| Art. 6(6) | No technical restrictions on end users **switching** between and subscribing to apps/services accessed via the CPS. | [1] |
| Art. 6(7) | **Interoperability**: free, effective interoperability with, and access to, the same OS/hardware/software features available to the gatekeeper's own services. | [1][5] |
| Art. 6(8) | Give advertisers/publishers, on request, free access to **performance-measuring tools** and verification data. | [1] |
| Art. 6(9) | **Data portability** for end users: free, effective, continuous and real-time access/portability of provided and generated data. | [1] |
| Art. 6(10) | **Business-user data access**: free, effective, continuous, real-time access to aggregated and non-aggregated data generated on the CPS. | [1] |
| Art. 6(11) | Give third-party search engines **FRAND** access to ranking, query, click and view data (personal data anonymised). | [1] |
| Art. 6(12) | **FRAND** general access conditions for business users to app stores, search engines and social-networking services. | [1] |
| Art. 6(13) | No disproportionate contract-**termination** conditions; termination on FRAND terms. | [1] |
| Art. 7 | **Interoperability of NIICS** (messaging): phased functionalities; security preserved; published reference offer. | [1] |
| Art. 8 | Gatekeeper must ensure/demonstrate compliance; Commission may **specify** Art. 6/7 measures (regulatory dialogue). | [1][5] |
| Art. 11 | **Compliance report** within six months of designation, updated at least annually. | [1] |
| Art. 13 | **Anti-circumvention** — no behaviour undermining effective compliance. | [1] |
| Art. 15 | **Independently audited** description of consumer-profiling techniques. | [1] |
| Art. 18 | **Market investigation** into systematic non-compliance → behavioural/structural remedies. | [1] |
| Art. 28 | **Compliance function** — independent, resourced, with compliance officers. | [1] |
| Art. 29 | **Non-compliance decision** finding a breach and ordering compliance. | [1] |
| Art. 30 | **Fines** up to **10%** of worldwide annual turnover; up to **20%** for repeat infringement. | [1] |
| Art. 31 | **Periodic penalty payments** up to **5%** of average daily worldwide turnover. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting terms (Art. 296 TFEU); cited here from the primary text [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 36–37 area | Rationale for the **Art. 5(2) consent** rule — combining personal data across services entrenches data advantages; consent must meet the GDPR standard. | [1] |
| Recital 50 area | **Anti-steering (Art. 5(4))** — business users must be able to steer customers to and complete transactions on more favourable terms outside the CPS. | [1] |
| Recital 52 area | No forced use of the gatekeeper's **identification, browser engine or payment** services (Art. 5(7)); leveraging is prevented. | [1] |
| Recital 62 area | **Self-preferencing (Art. 6(5))** in ranking distorts contestability and fairness. | [1] |
| Recital 64–65 area | **Sideloading (Art. 6(4))** and the proportionality of any security measures the gatekeeper may take. | [1] |
| Recital 8 area | Article 6 duties may require **further specification** by the Commission; Article 5 duties are directly applicable. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

The DMA's substantive obligations are recent and there is **no settled CJEU case law interpreting Articles 5–7** on the merits. The most significant judgment to date concerns **designation**, not the obligations:

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Apple v Commission | General Court, Joined Cases **T-1079/23, T-1080/23 and T-214/24**, judgment **8 July 2026** (Press release CP 96/26) | The General Court **dismissed** Apple's challenge and **confirmed** its gatekeeper designation for the **App Store and iOS**, treating App Store variants as a **single CPS**; **iMessage** challenges were held inadmissible. | Confirms who is bound by the Chapter III obligations; substantive-obligation challenges (e.g. appeals of the 23 April 2025 fines) are pending and tracked in `dma-enforcement-cases`. [7] |

*Appeals of the Article 5 non-compliance fines and challenges to the Article 6(7) specification decisions are emerging; they are tracked in `dma-enforcement-cases` (planned) rather than asserted here.* [3][4][5][7]
