text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (European Commission — not statutory text unless a specific obligation is cited).**

- **Compliance is outcome-tested, not formal.** The Commission's first non-compliance decisions found that Apple's steering restrictions did not deliver the outcome **Art. 5(4)** requires and that Meta's binary "consent or pay" model did not satisfy **Art. 5(2)**, because users had no equivalent, less-personal-data alternative [3][4]. *(Regulatory interpretation of Arts. 5(2), 5(4).)*
- **Article 6(7) is operationalised through specification.** On **19 March 2025** the Commission adopted two decisions specifying Apple's interoperability measures — one on **nine iOS connectivity features** for connected devices (smartwatches, headphones, TVs), the other on the **process** for handling developers' interoperability requests — with staged implementation deadlines running into 2026; this is the DMA's "regulatory dialogue" in action [5]. *(Regulatory interpretation of Arts. 6(7), 8.)*
- **Designation is service-specific and dynamic.** The Commission **added** services (Apple iPadOS, 29 April 2024), **undesignated** others (Meta Facebook Marketplace, 23 April 2025), and on **5 February 2026** decided that **Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated**, as neither is an important gateway for business users [2][4][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation / legal fact.)*
- **Open proceedings signal the Commission's reading of Article 6.** Following **March 2025 preliminary findings**, Alphabet remains under investigation for **anti-steering in Google Play (Art. 5(4))** and **self-preferencing on Google Search (Art. 6(5))**; the Commission's concern is that third-party services are not treated in a fair, non-discriminatory way against Alphabet's own [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation — preliminary, not a final finding.)*
- **Verification note:** the designation register, the status of the Article 6(7) specification decisions, and the open Alphabet proceedings above were confirmed against the Commission's DMA portal and news service on **2026-07-11**; these are the items most likely to change and must be re-checked at each review [2][5][6][8]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Gatekeeper Obligations in Depth

text:
- **Article 5(2) — data separation by architecture.** Combining end-user personal data across a designated CPS and other services (or across CPS) requires **GDPR-grade consent**; the engineering consequence is service-level data segregation, consent capture and enforcement, and a genuinely equivalent **less-personal-data** variant where consent is refused [1][10]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Article 5(4)/(7) — steering and payments.** Apps and business users must be able to link out to and complete purchases off-platform and must not be forced onto the gatekeeper's in-app payment, browser engine or identity service; this reshapes app-review rules, entitlement APIs and payment SDKs [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 6(4) — sideloading and alternative stores.** Operating systems must technically permit third-party apps and app stores, subject only to **proportionate** security measures (notarisation, malware screening, permissioning) — proportionality is the litigated edge [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 6(5) — ranking neutrality.** Ranking, indexing and crawling must apply transparent, fair, non-discriminatory conditions; this constrains recommender and search-ranking design and requires auditable ranking parameters [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 6(7) — interoperability surfaces.** Third parties must get effective, free interoperability with the same OS/hardware features the gatekeeper's own services use; the Apple specification decisions concretise this as **published APIs, staged betas and dispute resolution** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Articles 6(9)–(10) — real-time data pipes.** End-user **portability** and business-user **data access** must be continuous and real-time — i.e. export/streaming APIs, not batch dumps — with authorisation flows for third parties acting on the user's behalf [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 7 — messaging interoperability.** NIICS gatekeepers must expose interoperable messaging while **preserving end-to-end encryption and security** (Art. 7(3)); the technical detail is deferred to `dma-interoperability` [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*

- **Cloud computing is a CPS category (Art. 2(2)), but no cloud service is currently designated** [2]. A hyperscale cloud provider that met the Art. 3 thresholds would inherit Chapter III duties most relevant to infrastructure: **data portability** (6(9)), **business-user data access** (6(10)), **FRAND** access (6(12)) and **no self-preferencing** (6(5)) [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess designation status.)*
- **Most hosting providers are not gatekeepers.** Their practical interest is as **business users** of gatekeeper CPS (app stores, marketplaces, ad services) who can now assert the Article 5–6 rights — steering, FRAND terms, data access, no forced ancillary services [1]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Portability as a competitive baseline.** DMA-driven Art. 6(9)–(10) real-time portability raises customer expectations across hosting generally; providers should treat continuous export tooling as table stakes even when not themselves in scope. *(Editorial recommendation.)*

text:
- **App-distribution rights are the headline change for game developers.** Developers distributing through a gatekeeper **app store** can steer users to external offers (Art. 5(4)), avoid **forced in-app payment** (Art. 5(7)), and use **alternative app stores / sideloading** (Art. 6(4)) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers — opportunity for developers.)*
- **Cross-service player data needs consent.** Where a game platform is itself a gatekeeper CPS (e.g. a social network or messaging service), combining player personal data across services requires **Art. 5(2) consent**, reinforcing GDPR practice [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **FRAND store terms and switching.** Game storefront and subscription terms imposed by a gatekeeper must be **FRAND** (Art. 6(12)), and technical barriers to players switching services must be removed (Art. 6(6)) [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Real-time/matchmaking mechanics are out of scope** — the DMA targets platform contestability, not game-server latency; those remain governed by GDPR and, where relevant, the AI Act. *(Interpretation.)*
title: EU Digital Markets Act: Gatekeeper Obligations in Depth

text:
- **AI ranking sits inside Art. 6(5).** AI-based ranking/recommendation within a designated CPS must meet the **no-self-preferencing** and transparency conditions; the "fair and non-discriminatory" test applies to the model's treatment of third parties [1]. *(Legal obligation for gatekeepers.)*
- **Virtual assistants are a CPS category and an Art. 6(7) surface.** Interoperability and default/choice-screen duties (6(3), 6(7)) reach AI virtual assistants where designated [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Parallel regimes.** The DMA governs **market power**; the **AI Act (Reg (EU) 2024/1689)** governs AI **risk**; the **GDPR** governs **personal data**. An AI recommender inside a gatekeeper CPS can engage all three at once [1][10]. *(Interpretation — read with `ai-act-foundations` and `gdpr-foundations`.)*
- **Generative-AI as a future CPS is unresolved.** The CPS list is fixed by Art. 2; extending it to foundation-model services would require the market-investigation route or legislative change. Track, do not assume. *(Editorial recommendation.)* [1]

1. **Build a per-CPS obligation matrix.** For each designated CPS, map every applicable Art. 5 and Art. 6 sub-paragraph (and Art. 7 for NIICS) to a concrete measure and an owner. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
2. **Treat Article 5 as immediately binding.** Do not wait for a specification decision — 5(2) consent, 5(3) parity, 5(4) steering, 5(7) forced-service and 5(8) tying duties apply as drafted. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]

7. **Design against circumvention (Art. 13).** Ensure remedies are effective in practice; avoid degrading conditions or making rights hard to exercise, and do not re-request refused consent more than once a year. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]

9. **Maintain a designation/enforcement watch-list.** Re-verify the register, specification decisions and open proceedings at each review — they change. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [2][5][6][8]

title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
The **NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555**, "NIS2") is the EU's second-generation, horizontal cybersecurity law for network and information systems. It **repealed and replaced the original NIS Directive ((EU) 2016/1148) with effect from 18 October 2024** and pursues a **high common level of cybersecurity across the Union** by widening the range of covered sectors, harmonising **risk-management** and **incident-reporting** duties, and sharpening **supervision, governance accountability and enforcement** [1][5]. Because it is a **Directive**, it binds Member States as to the result but must be **transposed** into national law to take effect against organisations [1].

NIS2 sorts in-scope organisations into **essential entities** and **important entities** drawn from **18 sectors** listed in **Annex I (high criticality)** and **Annex II (other critical sectors)**, generally using a **size-cap rule** (medium-sized and large entities), with a number of entity types in scope **regardless of size** [1][5]. Covered entities must implement **cybersecurity risk-management measures** on an all-hazards basis — a minimum list of ten measure categories in **Article 21** — and report **significant incidents** through the **Article 23 cascade**: an **early warning within 24 hours**, an **incident notification within 72 hours**, and a **final report within one month** [1]. **Article 20** makes **management bodies** approve and oversee those measures and requires them to undergo **training**. Supervision and penalties are **differentiated**: essential entities face proactive (ex ante and ex post) supervision, important entities face reactive (ex post) supervision, and administrative fines run to **at least €10m or 2% of worldwide annual turnover** for essential entities and **at least €7m or 1.4%** for important entities [1].

The single most important — and most volatile — point is **transposition status**. The deadline was **17 October 2024**; most Member States missed it. The Commission opened infringement proceedings (letters of formal notice, November 2024; reasoned opinions to 19 Member States, 7 May 2025) and, on **8–9 July 2026, referred Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice**, asking for **lump-sum and daily financial penalties** until each notifies full transposition [6][7][8]. NIS2 also sits alongside sibling instruments: **DORA** is **lex specialis** for the financial sector, and the **Cyber Resilience Act** covers the security of products with digital elements [2][3].
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
- **NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555)** repealed the original NIS Directive **with effect from 18 October 2024** and aims for a **high common level of cybersecurity** across the EU; being a Directive, it applies through **national transposition** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- In-scope organisations are classified as **essential** or **important** entities across **18 sectors** in **Annex I** and **Annex II**, generally caught by a **medium/large size-cap**, with some entity types in scope **regardless of size** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 21** requires **all-hazards cybersecurity risk-management measures** — a minimum of **ten categories** (incident handling, business continuity, **supply-chain security**, vulnerability handling, cyber hygiene and training, cryptography, access control, MFA, etc.) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 23** imposes a staged reporting duty for **significant incidents**: **early warning within 24 hours**, **notification within 72 hours**, and a **final report within one month** [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 20** makes **management bodies accountable** — they must **approve and oversee** the risk-management measures and undergo **training** [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Supervision and penalties are **differentiated**: essential entities get **ex ante + ex post** supervision, important entities **ex post only**; fines reach **≥ €10m or 2%** of worldwide turnover (essential) and **≥ €7m or 1.4%** (important) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Live-verified transposition status:** the deadline (**17 October 2024**) was widely missed; on **8–9 July 2026** the Commission **referred Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice** (with a request for financial penalties), following reasoned opinions to 19 Member States on 7 May 2025 [6][7][8]. *(Confirmed today, not asserted — status is dynamic.)*
- NIS2 interacts with sibling law: **DORA is lex specialis** for finance (Art. 4 equivalence), and the **Cyber Resilience Act** governs security of **products with digital elements** [1][2][3]. *(Legal obligation / cross-reference.)*

text:
**In scope:** NIS2's purpose and legal character (Directive vs Regulation); the essential/important entity distinction; the Annex I/II sectors and the size-cap thresholds; the Article 21 cybersecurity risk-management measures; the Article 23 incident-reporting cascade and timelines; Article 20 governance and management-body accountability and training; registration duties; the differentiated supervision and enforcement/penalty regime; the current state of national transposition (**live-verified**); and the relationship to DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act at a foundational level.

**Out of scope (spun off to the research backlog):** The full **incident-reporting mechanics** and the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 detail (significant-incident thresholds, technical/methodological requirements for digital sectors) → `nis2-incident-reporting`; **sector-specific duties** and the Annex I/II sector-by-sector analysis → `nis2-sectors`; a **national transposition comparison** across Member States → `nis2-transposition-tracker`; the **Article 21 measures mapped to ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF** control-by-control → `nis2-controls-mapping`; the **DORA/NIS2 boundary** in depth → `dora-foundations`; the **Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Directive** companion regime → `cer-foundations`.

**Assumptions:** The reader understands the EU **Directive vs Regulation** distinction (a Directive requires national transposition; a Regulation is directly applicable). Where an entity processes personal data, the **GDPR applies in parallel** (see `gdpr-foundations`); a personal-data breach may trigger both NIS2 incident reporting and GDPR Art. 33 notification.

*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md`. NIS2-specific terms are defined here; deeper terms (significant incident thresholds, sector sub-definitions) are deferred to the backlog documents above.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Essential entity | An entity classified as "essential" under Art. 3(1) — broadly, large entities in the Annex I high-criticality sectors plus specified types in scope regardless of size (e.g., qualified trust service providers, TLD name registries, DNS providers, certain public-administration and critical entities). Subject to the fullest supervision. | [1] |
| Important entity | An entity within scope that is not an essential entity (Art. 3(2)) — typically medium-sized entities in Annex I sectors and entities in the Annex II "other critical" sectors. Subject to ex-post supervision. | [1] |
| Network and information system | An electronic communications network, any device or group of interconnected devices processing digital data, or the digital data such systems process/store/transmit for their operation, use, protection and maintenance (Art. 6(1)). | [1] |
| Significant incident | An incident that has caused or is capable of causing severe operational disruption of services or financial loss, or that has affected or is capable of affecting other persons by causing considerable material or non-material damage (Art. 23(3)). | [1] |
| Cybersecurity risk-management measures | The all-hazards technical, operational and organisational measures required by Art. 21 to manage risks to network and information systems and prevent/minimise incident impact. | [1] |
| Management body | The body (e.g., board/senior management) that under Art. 20 must approve the entity's risk-management measures, oversee their implementation, and follow training; members may be held liable. | [1] |
| CSIRT | A Computer Security Incident Response Team designated by each Member State (Art. 10) to which entities submit incident reports and which provides response support. | [1] |

text: The original **NIS Directive ((EU) 2016/1148)** was the EU's first horizontal cybersecurity law, but it left significant gaps: inconsistent national scoping of "operators of essential services", divergent security and reporting requirements, and weak supervision and enforcement. As dependence on digital infrastructure and the frequency of cross-border cyber incidents grew, the EU replaced it with **NIS2** to raise and harmonise the baseline [1][5]. NIS2 **broadens the sectoral scope**, replaces the old operator-identification approach with a **size-cap rule** plus **essential/important** tiers, **standardises** risk-management and incident-reporting duties, introduces **management-body accountability**, and materially **strengthens supervision and penalties** [1][5]. It was adopted on **14 December 2022**, entered into force on **16 January 2023**, and **repealed the NIS Directive with effect from 18 October 2024**, with a **transposition deadline of 17 October 2024** [1]. It forms part of a wider EU cyber and resilience package alongside **DORA** (finance), the **Cyber Resilience Act** (products), and the **Critical Entities Resilience (CER) Directive** (physical resilience) [1][2][3].
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
NIS2 is a **Directive**: it sets out the obligations Member States must achieve, but the **legally binding rules for organisations are the national transposition measures** [1]. Its structure:

- **Chapter I (Arts. 1–6)** — subject matter, scope, definitions, and the relationship with sector-specific EU acts (**Art. 4** equivalence / lex specialis).
- **Chapter II (Arts. 7–13)** — national cybersecurity frameworks: strategies, competent authorities, single points of contact, **CSIRTs**, and cooperation.
- **Chapter III (Arts. 14–19)** — EU-level cooperation: the **Cooperation Group**, the **CSIRTs network**, **EU-CyCLONe** (crisis coordination), peer reviews.
- **Chapter IV (Arts. 20–25)** — the **core obligations on entities**: **governance (Art. 20)**, **cybersecurity risk-management measures (Art. 21)**, coordinated risk assessments of critical supply chains (Art. 22), **reporting obligations (Art. 23)**, use of European cybersecurity **certification** schemes (Art. 24), and **standardisation** (Art. 25).
- **Chapter V (Arts. 26–27)** — **jurisdiction and territoriality** (Art. 26) and the **registry of entities** maintained by ENISA for certain digital service types (Art. 27).
- **Chapter VII (Arts. 31–37)** — **supervision and enforcement**: supervisory measures for **essential entities (Art. 32)** and **important entities (Art. 33)**, and **administrative fines (Art. 34)**.
- Scope is fixed by **Art. 2** together with **Annex I** (high-criticality sectors) and **Annex II** (other critical sectors); entity classification is in **Art. 3**.

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 2 + Annexes I, II | Scope: sectors covered and the size-cap rule (medium/large), with entities in scope regardless of size in defined cases. | [1] |
| Art. 3 | Classification of entities as **essential** or **important**. | [1] |
| Art. 3(4) | Member States establish and maintain a **list of essential and important entities** (deadline 17 April 2025). | [1] |
| Art. 4 | Relationship with sector-specific EU acts — where equivalent, those apply as **lex specialis** (e.g., DORA for finance). | [1][2] |
| Art. 20 | **Governance** — management bodies approve and oversee risk-management measures and must undergo **training**; liability for infringements. | [1] |
| Art. 21 | **Cybersecurity risk-management measures** — all-hazards approach; minimum list of ten measure categories, incl. supply-chain security. | [1] |
| Art. 22 | Union-level coordinated security risk assessments of critical ICT supply chains. | [1] |
| Art. 23 | **Reporting obligations** for significant incidents — **24h early warning, 72h notification, 1-month final report**; recipient notification. | [1] |
| Art. 24 | Use of European cybersecurity **certification** schemes (may be mandated by implementing act). | [1] |
| Art. 26 | Jurisdiction and territoriality (main-establishment rule for certain digital providers). | [1] |
| Art. 27 | **Registration** — ENISA registry for DNS, TLD, cloud, data-centre, CDN, managed (security) service providers and online marketplaces/search/social. | [1] |
| Art. 32 | Supervisory and enforcement measures for **essential entities** (ex ante + ex post). | [1] |
| Art. 33 | Supervisory and enforcement measures for **important entities** (ex post only). | [1] |
| Art. 34 | **Administrative fines** — essential: max ≥ €10m or 2% worldwide turnover; important: max ≥ €7m or 1.4%. | [1] |
| Art. 41 | **Transposition** — Member States adopt and publish measures by **17 October 2024**, applying them from **18 October 2024**. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting terms (Art. 296 TFEU); cited here from the primary text [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 4 | Purpose — remove divergences by setting minimum rules for a coordinated regulatory framework and improving the functioning of the internal market. | [1] |
| Recital 8 | The original NIS Directive's shortcomings (fragmented scope and supervision) motivating the reform. | [1] |
| Recital 28 area | Relationship with sector-specific Union acts and the equivalence/lex specialis mechanism (e.g., DORA). | [1] |
| Recital 79 area | Incident-reporting design — the multi-stage approach balancing rapid warning against complete information. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable at the foundational level.** NIS2 is recent and, as a Directive whose substantive obligations bite through national law, there is no settled CJEU case law interpreting its risk-management or reporting provisions. The only NIS2 litigation to date concerns **enforcement of the transposition duty against Member States** — the Commission's referrals of Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice (July 2026) are **infringement actions under Art. 258/260 TFEU**, not interpretations of the substantive obligations, and are tracked as **emerging** rather than asserted here [8]. [1]

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames NIS2 as a **unified legal framework to uphold cybersecurity in 18 critical sectors**, requiring medium-sized and large entities in those sectors to take risk-management measures and notify significant incidents [5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ENISA** supports implementation with **technical guidance** — notably its *Technical Implementation Guidance on cybersecurity risk-management measures*, which maps the Art. 21 measures (as specified for certain digital sectors by the Implementing Regulation) to actionable evidence and controls [9][10]. *(Regulatory guidance — supports, does not replace, national law.)*
- **Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 (17 October 2024)** lays down **technical and methodological requirements** for the Art. 21(2) measures and specifies when an incident is **"significant"** for defined digital-infrastructure, ICT-service-management and digital-provider entities (DNS, TLD, cloud, data centres, CDNs, managed and managed-security service providers, online marketplaces/search engines/social platforms, trust service providers) [4]. *(Legal obligation for those entity types; regulatory specification of Art. 21/23.)*
- **Transposition is incomplete and enforced:** the Commission's own **transposition state-of-play** page records which Member States have and have not notified full transposition (a **dynamic list**), and its infringement track — **formal notices (Nov 2024) → reasoned opinions to 19 Member States (7 May 2025) → CJEU referrals of four Member States (8–9 July 2026)** — shows active enforcement [6][7][8]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verify the live list per Member State.)*
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
- **Scope triage first** — determine whether the organisation meets the **size-cap** (or is in scope regardless of size), which **Annex I/II sector(s)** it falls in, and whether it is **essential or important**; this drives every downstream duty and the supervision tier [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **All-hazards control set (Art. 21)** — implement the ten measure categories: risk-analysis and information-system security policies; **incident handling**; **business continuity, backup and disaster recovery, crisis management**; **supply-chain security**; security in acquisition/development/maintenance incl. **vulnerability handling and disclosure**; policies to assess measure effectiveness; **basic cyber hygiene and security training**; **cryptography/encryption** policies; **HR security, access control and asset management**; and **multi-factor authentication**, secured voice/video/text and secured emergency communications [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Standards alignment** — the Art. 21 measures map naturally onto **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** (ISMS) and **NIST CSF 2.0**; using a recognised framework provides evidence of the "appropriate and proportionate" standard and eases audits, though it does not by itself satisfy national law [11][12]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Incident-reporting pipeline** — build the capability to detect a **significant incident** and emit a **24h early warning**, a **72h notification** (with initial severity/impact assessment and indicators of compromise) and a **1-month final report** to the CSIRT/competent authority, plus **recipient notification** where required (Art. 23) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Digital-sector specifics** — entities within the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 scope should engineer to its **detailed technical requirements** and **significant-incident thresholds** rather than the Directive's general wording [4]. *(Legal obligation for those entities.)*
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
- **Cloud, data-centre, CDN and hosting providers are squarely in scope** — "digital infrastructure" and "ICT service management (B2B)" are **Annex I high-criticality sectors**; cloud computing service providers, data-centre service providers, content-delivery-network providers and managed/managed-security service providers are named entity types, and several must **register with ENISA under Art. 27** [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Registration and jurisdiction** — for certain digital providers, **Art. 26** fixes jurisdiction by **main establishment** (broadly, where cybersecurity decisions are taken) and **Art. 27** requires submission of registration details to ENISA; multi-country hosting operators should identify their **main establishment** and the **competent authority/CSIRT** accordingly [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Supply-chain security flows downstream** — because Art. 21(2)(d)/(e) require **supply-chain and product/service security**, in-scope customers will impose NIS2-driven contractual and assurance requirements on their hosting and managed-service providers; providers should expect **security clauses, evidence requests and incident-cooperation duties** [1]. *(Legal obligation for the customer; best practice for providers to anticipate.)*
- **Logging and evidence** — incident-reporting and supervisory-audit duties require robust **logging, detection and retention**; align retention with **GDPR** limits where personal data is involved (see `gdpr-foundations`). *(Best practice.)*
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
- **Most pure game-hosting is not directly in NIS2 scope** — online gaming and entertainment are **not** among the Annex I/II sectors, so a studio or game-server operator is generally **not** an essential/important entity *by virtue of gaming alone* [1][5]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **But underlying infrastructure roles can pull an operator in** — if the operator also provides **cloud computing, data-centre, CDN or managed-security services**, or is a **DNS/domain-registration** provider, those **digital-infrastructure/ICT** activities are in scope regardless of the gaming context [1]. *(Legal obligation — assess by activity, not by industry label.)*
- **Third-party dependency risk** — even when out of direct scope, game hosts rely on cloud/CDN/managed providers that **are** in scope; their NIS2 **supply-chain security** duties will propagate as contractual security and incident-cooperation requirements [1]. *(Best practice — expect and prepare for these.)*
- **Watch adjacent regimes** — player-facing platforms may separately engage the **DSA** (if they store and disseminate user content to the public) and the **GDPR**; NIS2 does not displace those. *(Cross-reference.)*
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
- **AI/ML systems are network and information systems** — where an in-scope entity operates AI systems, those systems fall within the **all-hazards Art. 21** risk-management duty (data security, access control, vulnerability handling, robustness), so AI security is part of NIS2 compliance, not separate from it [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Overlap with the AI Act** — for **high-risk AI systems**, the AI Act's **accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity** requirements run in parallel with NIS2's entity-level duties; an organisation may owe both. See `ai-act-foundations`. *(Cross-reference.)*
- **AI in incident detection** — AI-driven detection and response can help meet the tight **Art. 23** timelines, but automated triage must not delay the **24h/72h** clock or degrade the accuracy of reports [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **GDPR overlap** — where AI processes personal data, the **GDPR applies in full**; a security incident may trigger **both** NIS2 Art. 23 reporting and GDPR Art. 33 breach notification, on **different clocks and to different authorities** [1]. *(Legal obligation — run both.)*
title: NIS2 Directive: Foundations, Scope & Cybersecurity Obligations

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Determine scope and tier** — assess size-cap, Annex I/II sector and essential/important classification for **each Member State of operation**, and identify the competent authority/CSIRT. *(OBLIGATION — foundational.)* [1][5]
2. **Confirm the applicable national law** — because NIS2 binds through transposition, identify the **transposing statute** in each relevant Member State; where none is in force yet, track its progress (transposition is incomplete). *(OBLIGATION where transposed; EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION to track where not.)* [1][6][8]
3. **Register where required** — submit Art. 27 registration details (and comply with any Art. 3(4) national listing) for in-scope digital service types. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Implement the Art. 21 measures** — stand up the ten measure categories on an all-hazards basis, ideally mapped to ISO/IEC 27001 / NIST CSF. *(OBLIGATION; BEST PRACTICE for the mapping.)* [1][11][12]
5. **Build the Art. 23 reporting capability** — detection, severity assessment, and the **24h / 72h / 1-month** report flow to the CSIRT, plus recipient notification. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Engage the management body** — secure board approval and oversight of the measures and complete Art. 20 **training**; document accountability. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
7. **Address supply-chain security** — impose and evidence security requirements on ICT suppliers and service providers (Art. 21(2)(d)/(e)). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
8. **Apply the digital-sector implementing rules** — where in scope, engineer to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690's technical requirements and significant-incident thresholds. *(OBLIGATION for those entities.)* [4]
9. **Map overlaps** — where DORA applies, treat it as **lex specialis** (Art. 4); coordinate NIS2 and GDPR breach processes; watch CRA product duties. *(OBLIGATION + cross-reference.)* [1][2][3]
10. **Track transposition and enforcement** — monitor the Commission's state-of-play page and infringement actions; adjust to each national law as it lands. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [6][8]

- **Phase 0 — Scope & tier assessment:** Determine in-scope status, sector, essential/important tier, and competent authority/CSIRT per Member State. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Legal baseline:** Identify the transposing national law (or its status) for each relevant Member State; complete Art. 3(4)/Art. 27 registration. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 2 — Risk-management measures:** Implement the Art. 21 ten-category control set, mapped to ISO/IEC 27001 / NIST CSF; close gaps. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 3 — Incident reporting:** Build detection, severity assessment and the 24h/72h/1-month reporting workflow; run tabletop drills. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 4 — Governance:** Board approval and oversight of measures; management-body training; documented accountability. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 5 — Supply chain & overlaps:** Supplier security programme; coordinate DORA (finance), GDPR breach and CRA product duties. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 6 — Monitor & adapt:** Track transposition/enforcement and the Implementing Regulation guidance; adjust to national law. *Effort:* Ongoing.

title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
This document is the deep dive on the **NIS2 significant-incident reporting regime**. It explains **what counts as a "significant incident"**, **who must report what, to whom and by when**, and how the NIS2 duty interacts with the **GDPR** personal-data-breach regime and the **DORA** financial-sector incident regime. It supports incident-response, legal and engineering teams building a reporting capability that survives contact with a live incident and a regulator's audit [1][5].

A **significant incident** is defined at two levels. **Article 23(3)** of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 sets the qualitative test: an incident is significant if it *has caused or is capable of causing severe operational disruption of the services or financial loss* for the entity, **or** *has affected or is capable of affecting other persons by causing considerable material or non-material damage* [1]. For eleven named digital-infrastructure, ICT-service-management and digital-provider entity types, **Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690** converts that test into **quantitative thresholds** — for example, a **direct financial loss above EUR 500 000 or 5% of annual turnover (whichever is lower)**, exfiltration of trade secrets, death or serious harm to a person, or availability, integrity and confidentiality thresholds specific to each service (e.g., a cloud service *completely unavailable for more than 30 minutes*) [2].

The heart of the regime is the **Article 23(4) reporting cascade**: an **early warning within 24 hours** of becoming aware of a significant incident, a fuller **incident notification within 72 hours**, an **intermediate report on request**, and a **final report within one month** of the notification (with a **progress report** if the incident is still ongoing) [1]. Reports go to the **CSIRT or the competent authority**; the CSIRT should respond **within 24 hours** of the early warning [1]. NIS2 runs **in parallel** with the GDPR (a personal-data breach still triggers **Art. 33/34**) and **defers to DORA as lex specialis** for financial entities, who report under DORA Art. 19 instead of NIS2 Art. 23 [1][3][4].
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
- A **significant incident** is defined by the two-limb qualitative test in **Art. 23(3)** — severe operational disruption/financial loss to the entity, or considerable material/non-material damage to others [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- For **eleven digital entity types**, **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690** specifies **quantitative and qualitative thresholds**; the cross-sector triggers include **direct financial loss > EUR 500 000 or 5% of turnover (whichever is lower)**, trade-secret exfiltration, **death or serious harm to a person**, and suspected malicious unauthorised access capable of severe disruption [2]. *(Legal obligation for those entities — live-verified 2026-07-11.)*
- The **Art. 23(4) cascade** is fixed: **early warning ≤ 24 h**, **incident notification ≤ 72 h**, **intermediate report on request**, **final report ≤ 1 month**, plus a **progress report** for still-ongoing incidents [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Reports are made to the **CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority**; the CSIRT should give a **response within 24 h** of the early warning, including mitigation guidance and, on request, technical support [1]. *(Legal obligation / recipient duty.)*
- **Trust service providers** have a **derogation**: significant incidents affecting their trust services are notified **within 24 hours** [1]. *(Legal obligation — sector-specific.)*
- Entities must, **where appropriate, notify recipients of their services** of significant incidents and of significant cyber threats and the remedies available (**Art. 23(1)–(2)**) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Cross-border** incidents are shared by the CSIRT/competent authority/single point of contact with **other affected Member States and ENISA** (**Art. 23(6)**); regulators may **inform the public** (**Art. 23(7)**) [1]. *(Legal obligation on recipients.)*
- **Voluntary notification** of non-significant incidents, near misses and cyber threats is expressly permitted under **Art. 30**, without creating additional liability [1]. *(Best practice — enabled.)*
- **Parallel regimes:** a personal-data breach still triggers **GDPR Art. 33 (72 h) / Art. 34**; **financial entities report under DORA Art. 19**, not NIS2 Art. 23 (NIS2 Art. 4 lex specialis) — the three regimes have **different clocks, recipients and thresholds** [1][3][4]. *(Legal obligation — run each on its own terms.)*
- **Failure to report** is enforced through Arts. 32–34: supervisory measures and administrative fines to **≥ €10m or 2%** of worldwide turnover (essential) and **≥ €7m or 1.4%** (important) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*

It supports: (a) **legal research** — pinning the exact triggers, deadlines, recipients and report contents to primary text; (b) **incident-response readiness** — a runbook, timeline and checklist teams can execute against the 24 h / 72 h / 1-month clock; and (c) **cross-regime coordination** — deciding, in the first hour of an incident, which of NIS2, GDPR and DORA apply and on which clocks. text:
**In scope:** The meaning of "significant incident" under Art. 23(3) and the quantitative/qualitative thresholds in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 for the covered digital entity types; the Art. 23(4) reporting cascade (early warning, incident notification, intermediate report, final report, progress report) and the special trust-service-provider timing; who reports to whom (CSIRT / competent authority) and recipient duties (Art. 23(5)–(7)); notification of recipients of services and of cyber threats (Art. 23(1)–(2)); cross-border and voluntary notification (Arts. 23(6), 30); the interplay with GDPR Art. 33/34 and DORA Art. 17–19; and supervision/penalties for reporting failures (Arts. 32–34). A reporting **runbook, timeline and checklist**, and a **NIS2 vs GDPR vs DORA comparison table**, are included.

**Out of scope (covered elsewhere):** The full **Art. 21 risk-management measures** and the technical/methodological requirements in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 (control-by-control) → `nis2-foundations` and a planned `nis2-controls-mapping`; **scope, entity classification and registration** → `nis2-foundations` / planned `nis2-sectors`; the **national transposition comparison** → planned `nis2-transposition-tracker`; the **DORA incident-classification and reporting mechanics** in depth (RTS/ITS templates, exact DORA hour deadlines) → `dora-foundations` and planned DORA sub-topics; the **GDPR breach process** in depth → `gdpr-foundations`; **CRA product-vulnerability reporting** → `cyber-resilience-act`.

**Assumptions:** The reader has read `nis2-foundations` and understands the essential/important entity distinction and the Directive-vs-Regulation point (NIS2 binds through national transposition). Where personal data is involved the **GDPR applies in parallel**; where the entity is a financial entity, **DORA applies as lex specialis**.

text:
*Shared terms (essential entity, important entity, significant incident, CSIRT) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Reporting-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Significant incident | An incident that has caused or is capable of causing severe operational disruption of the services or financial loss for the entity, or that has affected or is capable of affecting other natural or legal persons by causing considerable material or non-material damage (Art. 23(3)). | [1] |
| Early warning | The first-stage notification under Art. 23(4)(a), due within **24 hours** of becoming aware of a significant incident, indicating (where applicable) whether the incident is suspected to be unlawful/malicious or could have cross-border impact. | [1] |
| Incident notification | The second-stage report under Art. 23(4)(b), due within **72 hours**, updating the early warning with an initial assessment including severity, impact and (where available) indicators of compromise. | [1] |
| Intermediate report | A status update the entity must provide **on request** of the CSIRT or competent authority (Art. 23(4)(c)). | [1] |
| Final report | The Art. 23(4)(d) report due **within one month** of the incident notification, containing a detailed description, severity/impact, root cause/threat type, applied mitigations and any cross-border impact. | [1] |
| Progress report | Where the incident is still ongoing when the final report is due, a report submitted at that time, with a final report following within one month of handling the incident (Art. 23(4)(e)). | [1] |
| Competent authority | The national authority designated under NIS2 Art. 8 to supervise and enforce; a permitted recipient of incident reports alongside the CSIRT. | [1] |
| Single point of contact (SPOC) | The national liaison designated under Art. 8(3) exercising a cross-border coordination function for incident information (Art. 23(6)). | [1] |
| Recipient of services | A user of the entity's service which the entity must, where appropriate, notify of a significant incident likely to adversely affect it, or of a significant cyber threat (Art. 23(1)–(2)). | [1] |
| Voluntary notification | Notification, under Art. 30, of incidents, cyber threats and near misses that are not significant (or by entities outside scope), without imposing additional obligations or liability. | [1] |
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text: The original NIS Directive ((EU) 2016/1148) required incident notification but left the trigger ("substantial"/"significant" impact) and the timing to divergent national implementation, producing inconsistent, hard-to-aggregate reporting across the Union [1][5]. NIS2 responds by **harmonising the reporting duty into a single multi-stage cascade** with fixed outer deadlines and by empowering the Commission to fix **quantitative thresholds** for the most cross-border digital sectors, so that "significant" means the same thing for a cloud or DNS provider regardless of Member State [1][2][5]. Recital-level design (see `nis2-foundations`) makes the cascade deliberately staged: a **fast early warning** to enable rapid situational awareness and assistance, followed by **progressively complete information** as the entity's own understanding matures, so that speed does not come at the cost of accuracy [1]. The Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 — adopted **17 October 2024** and applicable from **18 October 2024** — is the first exercise of the Art. 23(11) power and specifies both the Art. 21 technical measures and the significant-incident thresholds for eleven digital entity types [2].
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
The reporting duty sits in **Chapter IV** of NIS2. **Article 23** is the operative provision; it is supported by **Article 30** (voluntary notification), **Article 35** (incidents entailing a personal-data breach), **Article 4** (relationship with sector-specific acts such as DORA), and the supervision/enforcement machinery in **Articles 32–34**. For eleven digital entity types the thresholds are specified by **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690**, adopted under **Art. 23(11)** [1][2].

The Article 23 structure:

- **Art. 23(1)** — the core duty: notify **the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority**, without undue delay, of any **significant incident**; and, where appropriate, **notify recipients** of services of a significant incident likely to adversely affect the service.
- **Art. 23(2)** — where appropriate, notify recipients of a **significant cyber threat** and of any measures or remedies they can take.
- **Art. 23(3)** — the **definition** of a significant incident (two limbs).
- **Art. 23(4)** — the **cascade**: (a) early warning ≤ 24 h; (b) incident notification ≤ 72 h; (c) intermediate report on request; (d) final report ≤ 1 month; (e) progress report for ongoing incidents — with a **24-hour derogation for trust service providers**.
- **Art. 23(5)** — the **CSIRT/competent-authority response** within 24 h of the early warning (feedback, mitigation guidance, technical support, law-enforcement guidance where relevant).
- **Art. 23(6)** — **cross-border**: the SPOC/CSIRT/competent authority informs other affected Member States and **ENISA**.
- **Art. 23(7)** — the authority/CSIRT **may inform the public** (after consulting the entity) where public awareness is needed.
- **Art. 23(11)** — the Commission adopts **implementing acts** further specifying when an incident is significant (delivered as Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690) [1][2].

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 23(1) | Notify CSIRT/competent authority of significant incidents without undue delay; notify affected recipients where appropriate. | [1] |
| Art. 23(2) | Where appropriate, notify recipients of significant cyber threats and available remedies. | [1] |
| Art. 23(3) | Definition of a **significant incident** (two limbs). | [1] |
| Art. 23(4)(a) | **Early warning** within **24 hours** of awareness. | [1] |
| Art. 23(4)(b) | **Incident notification** within **72 hours** of awareness (initial assessment, severity, impact, IoCs). | [1] |
| Art. 23(4)(c) | **Intermediate report** on request of the CSIRT/competent authority. | [1] |
| Art. 23(4)(d) | **Final report** within **one month** of the incident notification (detailed description, root cause, mitigations, cross-border impact). | [1] |
| Art. 23(4)(e) | **Progress report** where the incident is still ongoing, plus a final report within one month of handling it. | [1] |
| Art. 23(4) (TSP derogation) | **Trust service providers** notify significant incidents affecting their trust services within **24 hours**. | [1] |
| Art. 23(5) | CSIRT/competent authority response within **24 hours** of the early warning (feedback, guidance, technical support). | [1] |
| Art. 23(6) | Cross-border information-sharing with other affected Member States and **ENISA** via the SPOC. | [1] |
| Art. 23(7) | Authority may **inform the public**, after consulting the entity. | [1] |
| Art. 23(11) | Commission implementing acts specifying significant-incident cases (→ Reg (EU) 2024/2690). | [1][2] |
| Art. 30 | **Voluntary notification** of non-significant incidents, near misses and cyber threats. | [1] |
| Art. 35 | Incidents **entailing a personal-data breach**: cooperation with, and information to, the GDPR supervisory authority. | [1][3] |
| Art. 4 | Relationship with sector-specific acts (**DORA** as lex specialis for financial entities). | [1][4] |
| Arts. 32–34 | Supervision and **administrative fines** for infringements, including reporting failures. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting terms (Art. 296 TFEU); cited from the primary text [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 101 area | The **multi-stage** reporting approach — early warning then progressively complete information — balances rapid response against report accuracy. | [1] |
| Recital 102 area | The 24 h early warning is to enable the CSIRT to offer **assistance/mitigation**, not to impose a heavy initial burden. | [1] |
| Recital 104 area | **Voluntary reporting** and information-sharing should be encouraged without additional liability (Art. 30). | [1] |
| Recital 6 / Art. 4 area | Where a sector-specific Union act (e.g., **DORA**) imposes at least equivalent reporting, it applies as **lex specialis**. | [1][4] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** NIS2's reporting provisions are recent and bite through national transposition; there is no CJEU case law interpreting Art. 23 or Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 to date. The only NIS2 litigation so far concerns **enforcement of the transposition duty against Member States** (infringement actions under Art. 258/260 TFEU — see `nis2-foundations`), not the substance of the reporting cascade. Interpretive weight currently rests on the primary text and Commission/ENISA guidance [1][5][6].

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames NIS2 reporting as a harmonised duty to notify **significant incidents** through a staged process, with the Implementing Regulation providing the sector detail for digital infrastructure and providers [5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ENISA's NIS2 Technical Implementation Guidance** maps the Art. 21 measures and, for the covered entities, aligns them with the **significant-incident parameters** of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 — a practical reference for building detection and classification logic that feeds the reporting clock [6][7]. *(Regulatory guidance — supports, does not replace, national law.)*
- **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690** is the authoritative specification of "significant" for the eleven digital entity types. Its **Article 3** sets cross-cutting triggers (financial loss, trade-secret exfiltration, death/serious harm, suspected malicious unauthorised access), its **Article 4** aggregates **recurring incidents** (same root cause, at least twice in six months, collectively meeting the financial-loss threshold) into one significant incident, and its **entity-specific articles (5–14)** set availability/integrity thresholds per service [2]. *(Legal obligation for those entities; regulatory specification of Art. 23(3).)*
- **National transposition adds detail:** the CSIRT/competent authority split, the reporting **portal and format**, and any permitted stricter timing are set by each Member State's transposing law; the Art. 23 cascade and the Implementing Regulation thresholds are the **harmonised floor**, not the whole picture [1][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verify the national law.)*
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
- **Detection-to-classification pipeline** — the reporting clock starts when the entity **becomes aware** of a significant incident, so detection must feed a **classification decision** quickly. Engineer automated signals (availability monitors, integrity/authenticity checks, unauthorised-access alerts) that map directly onto the Art. 23(3) limbs and the Implementing Regulation thresholds [1][2]. *(Best practice; obligation to report once significant.)*
- **Threshold instrumentation for digital entities** — covered entity types should instrument the **specific metrics** that make an incident significant: complete-unavailability timers (e.g., 30 minutes for cloud/CDN/DNS/managed services; 20 minutes for trust services), **limited-availability** user-percentage/absolute thresholds (>5% or >1 million EU users, whichever is smaller), and **integrity/confidentiality** compromise detection [2]. *(Legal obligation for those entities.)*
- **Report content readiness** — pre-build templates that capture what each stage needs: early warning (unlawful/malicious suspicion, cross-border flag); 72 h notification (severity, impact, indicators of compromise); final report (detailed description, **root cause/threat type**, mitigations, cross-border impact) [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Recurring-incident aggregation** — implement logic to detect **repeat incidents with a common root cause** (Art. 4 of the Implementing Regulation) that collectively cross the financial-loss threshold, since these become a single reportable significant incident [2]. *(Legal obligation for covered entities.)*
- **Clock and evidence discipline** — timestamp "awareness", preserve forensic evidence and log the decision trail; supervisory audit (Arts. 32–33) will test whether the 24 h / 72 h / 1-month deadlines were met and whether classification was reasonable [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Standards alignment** — align the process with **ISO/IEC 27035** (incident management) and **NIST SP 800-61** (incident handling) so the NIS2 stages sit inside a recognised lifecycle (detect → triage → respond → report → learn) [9][10]. *(Best practice.)*
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
- **Cloud, data-centre, CDN, DNS and managed/managed-security providers are exactly the entities the Implementing Regulation targets** — they must instrument the service-specific thresholds in Arts. 5–10 of Reg (EU) 2024/2690 and be able to fire an Art. 23 early warning within 24 hours of a qualifying outage or compromise [1][2]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Availability arithmetic is the operational crux** — "completely unavailable for more than 30 minutes" and "limited availability affecting >5% or >1 million EU users, whichever is smaller, for more than one hour" are **measurable SLIs**; hosting platforms should map these onto existing SLO monitoring so classification is automatic, not manual [2]. *(Best practice; obligation to report once crossed.)*
- **Multi-tenant blast radius and recipient notification** — where an incident is likely to adversely affect customers, the Art. 23(1) duty to **notify recipients** overlaps with contractual incident-notification SLAs; align the two so a single event does not produce inconsistent customer and regulator messaging [1]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **Supply-chain propagation** — an in-scope customer's NIS2 duties flow down as contractual incident-cooperation and evidence obligations; hosts should expect to feed customers the data they need for their own Art. 23 reports [1]. *(Best practice — anticipate.)*
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
- **Pure game hosting is generally out of NIS2 scope** — online gaming is not an Annex I/II sector, so a studio or game-server operator is usually **not** obliged to report under Art. 23 by virtue of gaming alone (see `nis2-foundations`) [1][5]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Infrastructure roles pull an operator in** — if the operator also runs **cloud, data-centre, CDN, DNS or managed-security** services, those activities are in scope and the Implementing Regulation thresholds apply to them regardless of the gaming context; a qualifying outage of that infrastructure is reportable [1][2]. *(Legal obligation — assess by activity.)*
- **Upstream dependency reporting** — even when out of direct scope, game hosts depend on in-scope cloud/CDN/DNS providers whose incidents will be reported (and whose recipient-notifications the host will receive); build intake for these so downstream player-facing decisions are informed [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Parallel player-data duties** — a security incident affecting player personal data still triggers **GDPR Art. 33/34** independently of NIS2, on the GDPR clock; do not treat "out of NIS2 scope" as "no reporting duty" [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
- **AI systems are in the reporting perimeter** — where an in-scope entity operates AI/ML as part of its network and information systems, an incident affecting those systems (availability, integrity, unauthorised access, data compromise) can be a **significant incident** and is reported through the same Art. 23 cascade [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **AI-assisted detection helps meet the clock** — anomaly detection and automated triage can shorten time-to-awareness and support the 24 h / 72 h deadlines, but automation must not **delay** the awareness timestamp or degrade report accuracy (the cascade rewards timely, then complete, information) [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Distinguish AI Act serious-incident reporting** — high-risk AI providers/deployers have a **separate** serious-incident reporting duty under the AI Act (a different regime, recipient and threshold); NIS2 reporting does not discharge it, and vice versa (see `ai-act-high-risk`). *(Cross-reference — parallel duties.)*
- **GDPR overlap for AI on personal data** — an AI-related security incident touching personal data triggers **GDPR Art. 33/34** in parallel with NIS2 [3]. *(Legal obligation — run both.)*
title: NIS2: Significant-Incident Reporting

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

## Reporting runbook (per significant incident)

1. **Detect and record "awareness"** — the moment a reasonable assessment concludes an incident may be significant, timestamp it; this starts the 24 h / 72 h clocks. *(OBLIGATION — foundational.)* [1]
2. **Classify against the thresholds** — apply Art. 23(3) and, for covered entities, the Implementing Regulation Arts. 3–14 thresholds (financial loss, malicious access, availability/integrity limits, recurring-incident aggregation). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2]
3. **Send the early warning ≤ 24 h** — to the CSIRT or competent authority; flag suspected unlawful/malicious cause and potential cross-border impact. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Notify recipients where appropriate** — tell affected service recipients (and, for cyber threats, the remedies) under Art. 23(1)–(2), coordinated with contractual SLAs. *(OBLIGATION where appropriate.)* [1]
5. **Send the incident notification ≤ 72 h** — update the early warning with severity, impact and indicators of compromise. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Engage the CSIRT response** — use the ≤ 24 h feedback, request mitigation guidance and technical support, and act on law-enforcement guidance if criminality is suspected. *(BEST PRACTICE — use the entitlement.)* [1]
7. **Provide intermediate reports on request** — supply status updates whenever the CSIRT/competent authority asks. *(OBLIGATION when requested.)* [1]
8. **Submit the final report ≤ 1 month** — detailed description, severity/impact, root cause/threat type, applied and ongoing mitigations, cross-border impact; if still ongoing, submit a **progress report** now and a final report within one month of handling. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
9. **Run parallel regimes** — if personal data is affected, run **GDPR Art. 33/34** on its own clock (following EDPB breach-notification guidance); if the entity is a financial entity, report under **DORA Art. 19**, not NIS2 (Art. 4 lex specialis). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][3][4][8]
10. **Post-incident learning** — feed root cause into Art. 21 measures and update the runbook; consider **voluntary notification** (Art. 30) of near misses. *(BEST PRACTICE / EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [1]

## Indicative timeline

```
T0        Awareness of a (potentially) significant incident  → start clocks, classify
≤ T0+24h  EARLY WARNING to CSIRT/competent authority (Art. 23(4)(a))
          [Trust service providers: 24h notification for TSP-affecting incidents]
≤ 24h     CSIRT/competent-authority RESPONSE (feedback + mitigation guidance) (Art. 23(5))
≤ T0+72h  INCIDENT NOTIFICATION (severity, impact, IoCs) (Art. 23(4)(b))
on request INTERMEDIATE REPORT (status updates) (Art. 23(4)(c))
≤ +1 month FINAL REPORT after the notification (root cause, mitigations, cross-border) (Art. 23(4)(d))
if ongoing PROGRESS REPORT now + FINAL REPORT within 1 month of handling (Art. 23(4)(e))
parallel   GDPR Art. 33 (≤72h) / Art. 34 where personal data breached; DORA Art. 19 for financial entities
```

## NIS2 vs GDPR vs DORA reporting — comparison

*Distinct regimes with different triggers, clocks and recipients; an incident can engage more than one.*

| Dimension | NIS2 (Art. 23) | GDPR (Arts. 33–34) | DORA (Arts. 17–19) |
|-----------|----------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Trigger | **Significant incident** (Art. 23(3) + Reg 2024/2690 thresholds) [1][2] | **Personal-data breach** (Art. 4(12)) [3] | **Major ICT-related incident** (Art. 18 classification) [4] |
| Who reports | Essential/important entities [1] | Controller (processor → controller) [3] | Financial entities [4] |
| Recipient | **CSIRT or competent authority**; recipients of services [1] | **Supervisory authority**; data subjects (high risk) [3] | **Competent authority** (via ESA templates) [4] |
| Initial clock | **Early warning ≤ 24 h** of awareness [1] | Notify SA **≤ 72 h** of awareness (unless no risk) [3] | **Initial notification** on a short RTS/ITS clock [4] |
| Second stage | **Incident notification ≤ 72 h** [1] | Phased/supplementary info allowed (Art. 33(4)) [3] | **Intermediate report** [4] |
| Final stage | **Final report ≤ 1 month** (+ progress report) [1] | No fixed final-report deadline [3] | **Final report** (RTS/ITS timing) [4] |
| Notify affected people | Recipients of services where appropriate [1] | Data subjects where **high risk** (Art. 34) [3] | Clients where appropriate [4] |
| Relationship | Parallel to GDPR; **defers to DORA** (Art. 4) [1][4] | Parallel to NIS2/DORA [3] | **Lex specialis** for financial entities [4] |
| Max fines | ≥ €10m/2% (essential); ≥ €7m/1.4% (important) [1] | €20m/4% (Art. 83) [3] | Penalties/remedies by competent authority (Art. 50) [4] |

**Practical rule (EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION):** in the first hour, ask three questions in parallel — *Is it a significant incident (NIS2)? Does it involve a personal-data breach (GDPR)? Are we a financial entity or serving one (DORA)?* — and start each applicable clock independently. Do not assume one report satisfies another; the recipients and deadlines differ [1][3][4].

text:
1. How does the entity determine the moment of **"awareness"** that starts the 24 h / 72 h clocks, and is it timestamped and evidenced? *(Art. 23(4) [1].)*
2. How are incidents classified as **significant**, and (for covered entities) how are the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 thresholds instrumented, including recurring-incident aggregation? *(Art. 23(3); Reg 2024/2690 [1][2].)*
3. Can the entity demonstrate delivery of the **early warning (≤ 24 h)**, **incident notification (≤ 72 h)**, **intermediate reports on request**, and **final report (≤ 1 month)**? *(Art. 23(4) [1].)*
4. If a **trust service provider**, is the **24 h** derogation applied to TSP-affecting incidents? *(Art. 23(4) [1].)*
5. How are **recipients of services** notified of significant incidents and cyber threats, and is this coordinated with contractual SLAs? *(Art. 23(1)–(2) [1].)*
6. How are **cross-border** incidents flagged for onward sharing with other Member States and ENISA? *(Art. 23(6) [1].)*
7. How are **parallel GDPR (Art. 33/34)** and **DORA (Art. 19)** duties triggered and run alongside NIS2, and how is Art. 35 cooperation handled for personal-data-breach incidents? *(Arts. 4, 35 [1]; [3]; [4].)*
8. What evidence would withstand **supervisory audit** of a reporting decision, including a decision not to report? *(Arts. 32–34 [1].)*

title: DORA: Foundations & Digital Operational Resilience for Finance

text:
The **Digital Operational Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554**, "DORA") is the EU's single, directly applicable rulebook for the **information and communication technology (ICT) risk** of the financial sector. Its purpose is to make the EU financial system able to **withstand, respond to and recover from** all types of ICT-related disruption and threat — from cyber-attacks to third-party outages — by replacing a patchwork of national and sectoral operational-resilience rules with **uniform requirements** across banking, securities, insurance and pensions [1][5]. DORA **entered into force on 16 January 2023 and applies from 17 January 2025** (Art. 64), a date **live-verified** for this document against the European Commission, EIOPA and ESMA [1][5][6][7].

DORA has a broad **scope**: it binds around twenty categories of "financial entities" — credit institutions, payment and e-money institutions, investment firms, **crypto-asset service providers**, insurance and reinsurance undertakings and intermediaries, central securities depositories, central counterparties, trading venues, fund managers, credit-rating agencies and more — and, critically, reaches the **ICT third-party service providers** that serve them (Art. 2) [1]. Obligations are organised into **five pillars**: (1) **ICT risk management** (governance and a documented framework, Arts. 5–16); (2) **ICT-related incident** management, classification and reporting (Arts. 17–23); (3) **digital operational resilience testing**, including **threat-led penetration testing (TLPT)** for the most significant entities (Arts. 24–27); (4) **ICT third-party risk management** plus a **Union Oversight Framework** for **critical ICT third-party providers (CTPPs)** (Arts. 28–44); and (5) **information sharing** on cyber threats (Art. 45) [1]. A **proportionality** principle (Art. 4) scales duties to size and risk, with a simplified framework for smaller entities (Art. 16) [1].

The regime is operationalised by the three **European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs — EBA, EIOPA, ESMA)** through **RTS and ITS** (e.g. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 specifying the ICT risk-management framework [4]): a first batch has applied since 17 January 2025 and further standards apply in tranches [8]. The Union Oversight Framework became concrete on **18 November 2025**, when the ESAs designated the **first list of critical ICT third-party providers (reported as 19)** — hyperscale cloud, core-banking, payments and market-infrastructure providers — placing them under **direct ESA oversight** for the first time [9]. DORA is **lex specialis** to NIS2 for financial entities and operates **alongside the GDPR** where personal data is involved [1][2][3].
title: DORA: Foundations & Digital Operational Resilience for Finance

text:
- **DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554)** entered into force **16 January 2023** and **applies from 17 January 2025** (Art. 64) — live-verified against Commission and ESA sources [1][5][6]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- DORA delivers **uniform ICT-risk requirements** for the EU financial sector, replacing fragmented national/sectoral operational-resilience rules with a single directly applicable regulation [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Scope is broad:** ~20 categories of **financial entities** (banks, payment/e-money institutions, investment firms, **crypto-asset service providers**, insurers and intermediaries, CSDs, CCPs, trading venues, fund managers, credit-rating agencies, etc.) plus their **ICT third-party providers** (Art. 2) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pillar 1 — ICT risk management:** the management body is **ultimately accountable** and must maintain a documented ICT risk-management **framework** with protection, detection, response and recovery controls (Arts. 5–6) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pillar 2 — Incidents:** entities must **manage, classify** major ICT-related incidents and **report** them to competent authorities on a harmonised timeline, with an option to report significant cyber threats (Arts. 17–19) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pillar 3 — Testing:** a **digital operational resilience testing** programme is mandatory, and the most significant entities must undergo **threat-led penetration testing (TLPT)** at least every three years (Arts. 24–26) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pillar 4 — Third-party risk & Oversight:** entities must manage **ICT third-party risk** and meet mandatory **contractual** requirements (Arts. 28–30); designated **critical ICT third-party providers (CTPPs)** fall under a **Union Oversight Framework** with a **Lead Overseer** (Arts. 31–44) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pillar 5 — Information sharing:** DORA **enables** voluntary cyber-threat intelligence sharing within trusted communities (Art. 45) [1]. *(Legal obligation to permit; participation is voluntary.)*
- **Oversight is live:** on **18 November 2025** the ESAs designated the **first CTPPs (reported as 19)** — hyperscale cloud, core-banking, payments and market-infrastructure providers — now under direct ESA oversight [9]. *(Confirmed, not asserted.)*
- **RTS/ITS in tranches:** a first batch of technical standards has applied since **17 January 2025**, with further RTS/ITS applying progressively — always check the current status [8]. *(Regulatory — verify.)*
- DORA is **lex specialis to NIS2** for financial entities and runs **in parallel with the GDPR** for personal data [1][2][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*

**In scope:** DORA's purpose and the case for uniform ICT-risk rules; the definition of "financial entity" and the reach to ICT third-party providers (Art. 2); the **proportionality** principle (Art. 4); the **five pillars** at a foundational level — ICT risk management and governance (Arts. 5–16), ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Arts. 17–23), digital operational resilience testing including TLPT (Arts. 24–27), ICT third-party risk management and the **Union Oversight Framework** for **CTPPs** (Arts. 28–44), and information sharing (Art. 45); the role of the **ESAs** and the **RTS/ITS**; enforcement and penalties (Art. 50); and the relationship to **NIS2** and the **GDPR**. The **17 January 2025 application date**, the **RTS/ITS tranche status** and the **first CTPP designation** are **live-verified**.

**Out of scope (spun off to the research backlog):**

- The **TLPT** regime in depth — scoping, phases, the TIBER-EU alignment, threat intelligence and red-teaming mechanics (Arts. 26–27 and RTS) → `dora-tlpt`.
- The **CTPP Oversight Framework** mechanics — designation criteria, Lead Overseer powers, recommendations, penalties and the joint examination teams (Arts. 31–44) → `dora-oversight-framework`.
- **RTS/ITS-by-RTS** analysis — ICT risk-management framework, incident classification/reporting, register of information, subcontracting, threat-led testing standards → `dora-technical-standards`.
- The **register of information** and **ICT third-party contractual** duties in operational detail (Arts. 28–30) → `dora-third-party-contracts`.
- **Sub-sector specifics** (e.g., crypto-asset service providers under MiCA, insurance under Solvency II) → respective sub-topic documents.

**Assumptions:** The reader understands the EU regulation/directive distinction and the role of the three ESAs. Where a financial entity processes personal data, the **GDPR applies in parallel** (see `gdpr-foundations`). DORA does not displace prudential or conduct requirements; it sits alongside them.

text:
*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md`. DORA-specific terms are defined here; deeper terms (TLPT, Lead Overseer mechanics) are deferred to the backlog documents above.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Digital operational resilience | The ability of a financial entity to build, assure and review its operational integrity and reliability by ensuring — directly or via ICT third-party providers — the full range of ICT-related capabilities needed to keep providing services and preserve their quality through disruptions (Art. 3(1)). | [1] |
| ICT risk | Any reasonably identifiable circumstance in relation to the use of network and information systems which, if materialised, may compromise the security of the network and information systems, of any technology-dependent tool or process, of operations and processes, or of the provision of services (Art. 3(5)). | [1] |
| Financial entity | Any of the categories of undertaking listed in Art. 2(1) to which DORA applies (e.g. credit institutions, payment/e-money institutions, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers, insurers, CSDs, CCPs, trading venues, fund managers). | [1] |
| ICT third-party service provider | An undertaking providing ICT services to financial entities (Art. 3(19)); DORA reaches these providers directly through the third-party-risk and oversight regime. | [1] |
| Critical ICT third-party provider (CTPP) | An ICT third-party service provider designated as critical by the ESAs under Art. 31, thereby brought within the Union Oversight Framework. | [1][9] |
| ICT-related incident | A single event or a series of linked events unplanned by the financial entity that compromises the security of network and information systems and has an adverse impact on the availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of data or services (Art. 3(8)). | [1] |
| Major ICT-related incident | An ICT-related incident with a high adverse impact on the network and information systems that support critical or important functions, classified under Art. 18 and reportable under Art. 19. | [1] |
| Threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) | A controlled attempt to test the resilience of live production systems by mimicking the tactics, techniques and procedures of real-life threat actors, based on targeted threat intelligence (Art. 3(17); Art. 26). | [1] |
| Lead Overseer | The ESA (EBA, EIOPA or ESMA) appointed under Art. 31/33 to conduct oversight of a given designated CTPP. | [1][9] |
title: DORA: Foundations & Digital Operational Resilience for Finance

text: Before DORA, ICT and operational-resilience requirements for EU financial firms were spread across sectoral prudential rules (e.g. banking, insurance, markets) and non-binding supervisory guidelines (such as the EBA guidelines on ICT and security risk management), supplemented by uneven national regimes. This left **gaps and inconsistencies**: obligations differed by sub-sector and Member State, third-party (especially cloud) concentration risk was addressed only indirectly, and incident reporting was fragmented. As financial services digitised and came to depend on a small number of large ICT and cloud providers, the systemic exposure grew [1][5]. DORA is part of the Commission's 2020 **Digital Finance Package**; it consolidates ICT-risk rules into one **directly applicable regulation**, adds a **direct oversight regime** for the most systemically important ICT providers, and gives the ESAs a mandate to fill in the detail through **RTS/ITS**. It was adopted on **14 December 2022**, entered into force on **16 January 2023**, and applies from **17 January 2025**, giving the sector a two-year run-up [1][5][6]. An accompanying **DORA amending Directive (EU) 2022/2556** aligned existing sectoral directives; that alignment directive is noted here but is out of scope for detailed treatment.
title: DORA: Foundations & Digital Operational Resilience for Finance

text:
DORA applies to the financial entities listed in **Art. 2** and, through the third-party regime, reaches their **ICT third-party service providers**. Its structure follows the **five pillars** [1]:

- **Chapter I (Arts. 1–4)** — subject matter, scope, definitions, and the **proportionality principle** (Art. 4).
- **Chapter II (Arts. 5–16) — ICT risk management (Pillar 1):** governance and organisation with the **management body ultimately accountable** (Art. 5); the **ICT risk-management framework** and its components — identification, protection and prevention, detection, response and recovery, backup, learning and communication (Arts. 6–14); and a **simplified framework** for certain smaller entities (Art. 16).
- **Chapter III (Arts. 17–23) — ICT-related incident management, classification and reporting (Pillar 2):** an incident-management process (Art. 17), **classification** of incidents and cyber threats (Art. 18), **reporting** of major incidents (and optional reporting of significant cyber threats) to competent authorities (Art. 19), harmonised content/templates (Arts. 20–21), and operational or security payment-related incidents (Art. 23).
- **Chapter IV (Arts. 24–27) — Digital operational resilience testing (Pillar 3):** a testing programme (Art. 24), testing of tools and systems (Art. 25), **advanced testing via TLPT** at least every three years for entities identified by competent authorities (Art. 26), and requirements for testers (Art. 27).
- **Chapter V (Arts. 28–44) — ICT third-party risk (Pillar 4):** *Section I* — key principles for sound management of third-party risk, a mandatory **register of information**, pre-contract due diligence and **key contractual provisions** (Arts. 28–30); *Section II* — the **Union Oversight Framework**: **designation of CTPPs** (Art. 31), oversight structure (Art. 32), **tasks and powers of the Lead Overseer** (Arts. 33, 35), and competent-authority follow-up (Art. 42).
- **Chapter VI (Art. 45) — Information-sharing arrangements (Pillar 5):** financial entities may exchange cyber-threat information and intelligence within trusted communities.
- **Chapters VII–VIII (Arts. 46–56)** — competent authorities, cooperation across the ESAs, and **administrative penalties and remedial measures** (Art. 50).
- **Art. 64** — entry into force (**16 January 2023**) and application (**17 January 2025**).

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable at the foundational level.** DORA is recent and only became applicable on 17 January 2025, so there is no settled CJEU case law interpreting its substantive obligations.
