text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames DORA as ensuring the financial sector "can stay resilient through a severe operational disruption," delivered through one directly applicable regulation plus delegated/implementing acts that specify how entities and authorities comply [5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **ESAs (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA)** jointly develop and publish the **RTS/ITS** that make DORA operational. A **first set** — covering the ICT risk-management framework, incident classification, the ICT third-party policy and the register-of-information template — has applied since **17 January 2025**, with a **second set** (subcontracting, threat-led testing, oversight and CTPP designation criteria, reporting details) applying progressively [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verify current tranche.)*
- **Register of information:** entities must maintain a structured register of all contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers and report it to competent authorities using the ESAs' template (annually), a key input to the criticality assessment [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **CTPP designation is dynamic:** on **18 November 2025** the ESAs designated the **first CTPPs (reported as 19)** — spanning hyperscale cloud, core-banking/fintech, payments and market-infrastructure providers — following a prescriptive Art. 31 methodology based on systemic impact, systemic importance of reliant entities, concentration and substitutability. Each CTPP is placed under a **Lead Overseer**, must nominate an EU coordination point and pays oversight fees; the list is re-assessed over time [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verify the live list.)*
- **Oversight powers with an indirect enforcement lever:** the Lead Overseer can request information, conduct investigations and inspections, and issue **recommendations**; if a CTPP does not comply, the ESAs may make the non-compliance public and, as a last resort, competent authorities may require financial entities to **suspend or terminate** use of the provider's services [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: DORA: Foundations & Digital Operational Resilience for Finance

text:
- **Stand up the ICT risk-management framework first** — a documented framework (Art. 6) with mapped **critical or important functions**, asset/dependency inventories, and protection, detection, response and recovery controls is the backbone every other pillar builds on [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Incident classification and reporting pipeline** — implement Art. 18 classification logic (materiality thresholds for impact, clients affected, downtime, data losses, geographical spread, economic impact) and Art. 19 reporting workflows (initial, intermediate and final notifications) on the ESAs' templates [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Resilience testing programme** — a risk-based programme (Art. 24) combining vulnerability assessments, scans and penetration tests (Art. 25); the most significant entities must additionally run **TLPT** on live systems at least every three years (Art. 26), which requires threat-intelligence sourcing and controlled red-teaming [1]. *(Legal obligation for identified entities.)*
- **Third-party register and contracts** — maintain the **register of information** and ensure ICT contracts contain the Art. 30 key provisions (access/audit rights, sub-contracting conditions, exit strategies, service levels, incident cooperation) before signing or renewing [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Concentration and exit planning** — assess ICT concentration risk, especially on providers likely to be CTPPs, and build tested **exit/substitution** strategies so a suspension/termination direction is executable [1][9]. *(Best practice; obligation elements under Arts. 28–30.)*

- **Cloud and hosting providers are directly in view** — a hosting or cloud provider serving financial entities is an **ICT third-party service provider** (Art. 3(19)); if systemically important it may be designated a **CTPP** and brought under **direct ESA oversight** (the first designations on 18 Nov 2025 included hyperscale cloud and data-centre providers) [1][9]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*

- **AI in ICT risk and operations** — where a financial entity uses AI/ML in ICT operations (e.g. anomaly detection, fraud/security tooling, resilience automation), those systems are part of its **ICT estate** and fall within the Art. 6 framework, incident management and testing pillars [1]. *(Legal obligation — as ICT.)*
- **AI Act overlap** — certain AI uses in financial services (e.g. **creditworthiness/credit-scoring** and risk pricing in life/health insurance) are **high-risk** under the AI Act (Reg (EU) 2024/1689); DORA's operational-resilience duties apply **in parallel** with, not instead of, AI Act conformity duties — see `ai-act-foundations` [1]. *(Cross-reference; parallel application.)*

- **GDPR overlap** — AI processing personal data (customers, transactions) remains fully governed by the **GDPR** alongside DORA [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*

title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
**Threat-led penetration testing (TLPT)** is the most demanding element of DORA's third pillar — digital operational resilience testing (Arts. 24–27 of **Regulation (EU) 2022/2554**) [1]. Where the baseline testing programme (Art. 24) and the toolbox of vulnerability assessments, scans and ordinary penetration tests (Art. 25) apply to **all** financial entities on a risk-based, at-least-annual basis, **TLPT is reserved for the most significant entities** and is a fundamentally different exercise: an intelligence-led, adversarial red-team test conducted on **live production systems** that support **critical or important functions**, mimicking the tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) of real-world threat actors, at least **once every three years** (Art. 26) [1].

This document goes deep on the TLPT regime. It explains the testing pillar and how it fits the wider ICT risk-management framework; **which entities must perform TLPT and how competent authorities identify them** (Art. 26(8)); how **scope** is set around critical or important functions — including functions **outsourced to ICT third-party providers**; the end-to-end **TLPT lifecycle** (preparation/scoping → threat-intelligence-led targeting → red-team testing → closure and purple-teaming → remediation); and the requirements for **testers and threat-intelligence providers**, including the internal-versus-external rules (Art. 27) [1]. It gives a practical scoping methodology and maps TLPT against ordinary penetration testing and ISO/IEC 27001.

The single most important status point — **live-verified** for this document — is that the enabling RTS is **no longer a draft**. The European Commission adopted **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1190** on **13 February 2025**; it was published in the **Official Journal on 18 June 2025** and **entered into force on 8 July 2025** (the twentieth day after publication), specifying the criteria for identifying in-scope entities, the scope/methodology/results requirements, the standards for internal testers, and the **mutual-recognition** and cooperation arrangements under Art. 26(11) [2][4]. In parallel, the **Eurosystem's TIBER-EU framework** was updated on **11 February 2025** to align with DORA — renaming the "White Team" to **"Control Team"**, making **purple-teaming mandatory**, and synchronising deliverables with the RTS — so that a TIBER-EU test can serve as the recognised means of conducting a DORA TLPT [5][6][7].
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
- **TLPT sits at the top of DORA's testing pillar (Arts. 24–27):** all entities run a risk-based testing programme (Art. 24) and a testing toolbox (Art. 25); only identified significant entities run **TLPT** on live systems at least **every three years** (Art. 26) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **TLPT is defined narrowly:** a controlled test of **live production ICT systems** mimicking real threat-actor **TTPs**, driven by **targeted threat intelligence**, covering **critical or important functions** (Art. 3(17); Art. 26(1)–(2)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The enabling RTS is finalised and in force — verified:** **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1190** under **Art. 26(11)** was adopted **13 Feb 2025**, published in the OJ **18 Jun 2025**, and applies from **8 Jul 2025** [2][4]. *(Confirmed, not asserted.)*
- **Competent authorities identify who is in scope** using criteria set in the RTS (impact-related factors, systemic importance and ICT risk profile), not simple size thresholds (Art. 26(8); Reg (EU) 2025/1190) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Scope must reach ICT third parties:** where a critical or important function is provided by an **ICT third-party provider**, that provider's systems fall within the TLPT scope, with pooled-testing options and safeguards (Art. 26(2)–(4)) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **The lifecycle is prescribed:** preparation/scoping, threat-intelligence-led red-teaming on production, **closure with mandatory purple-teaming**, and a remediation plan, ending in an **attestation** enabling EU-wide **mutual recognition** (Art. 26(4)–(7); TIBER-EU) [1][5][7]. *(Legal obligation + framework guidance.)*
- **Testers are tightly regulated (Art. 27):** they must have proven suitability, capability and independence; **internal testers** are allowed only with competent-authority approval and safeguards, external testers must be used for **one in every three tests**, and the **threat-intelligence provider must always be external** (Arts. 26(8), 27) [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **TIBER-EU is the recognised implementation path — verified:** the Eurosystem updated **TIBER-EU on 11 Feb 2025** to align with DORA (Control Team, mandatory purple-teaming, RTS-synchronised deliverables); the **ECB** issued an SSM implementation guide in **November 2025** [5][6][7]. *(Regulatory framework — verified.)*
- **TLPT ≠ ordinary pentesting:** it is broader in scope (whole functions, live systems, real TTPs), longer (months), intelligence-led and scenario-based; it complements but does not replace Art. 25 penetration testing or ISO/IEC 27001/27002 controls testing [1][11][12][13]. *(Best practice / interpretation.)*

text:
*Shared terms (digital operational resilience, TLPT, CTPP) are in `GLOSSARY.md`. TLPT-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) | A framework that mimics the tactics, techniques and procedures of real-life threat actors perceived as a genuine cyber threat, delivering a controlled, bespoke, intelligence-led (red-team) test of the financial entity's critical live production systems (Art. 3(17)). | [1] |
| Critical or important function | A function whose disruption would materially impair the financial entity's financial performance or the soundness/continuity of its services and activities, or whose discontinued/defective performance would materially impair continued compliance with authorisation conditions or other DORA obligations (Art. 3(22)). | [1] |
| Red team | The team of testers that emulates a real adversary, seeking to compromise in-scope targets through intelligence-led attack scenarios without prior knowledge shared with defenders. | [1][5] |
| Blue team | The financial entity's defenders (security operations, incident response) who, during the active test, are unaware they are being tested (except the Control Team). | [5] |
| Control Team (formerly "White Team") | The small, trusted group inside the financial entity that commissions, controls and keeps the TLPT secret, managing risk and liaising with testers and the authority; renamed from "White Team" in the DORA-aligned TIBER-EU update. | [5][7] |
| Purple teaming | A collaborative replay/closure phase in which red and blue teams work together to walk through the attack scenarios, transfer knowledge and validate detections; **mandatory** under the DORA-aligned TIBER-EU framework. | [5][7] |
| Threat-intelligence (TI) provider | The external provider that produces the **Targeted Threat Intelligence Report** — the threat landscape, threat-actor profiles and attack scenarios that drive the red-team test; under DORA the TI provider must always be external (Art. 26(8)). | [1][5] |
| Attestation | The document confirming a TLPT was performed in accordance with the requirements, provided by the authorities solely for the purpose of **mutual recognition** across the EU (Art. 26(7)). | [1] |
| TIBER-EU | The Eurosystem's *Threat Intelligence-Based Ethical Red Teaming* framework — the common EU methodology for intelligence-led red-team testing, updated in 2025 to serve as the recognised way to conduct a DORA TLPT. | [5][6] |
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
Before DORA, intelligence-led red-teaming of financial firms was **voluntary and fragmented**. The **Bank of England's CBEST** scheme (2014) pioneered regulator-driven, threat-intelligence-led testing; the **ECB launched TIBER-EU in 2018** as a common Eurosystem framework, adopted by a growing set of national central banks and authorities on an opt-in basis. These schemes proved the model — realistic, scenario-based tests on live systems reveal resilience gaps that checklist audits and scoped penetration tests miss — but participation and methodology varied by jurisdiction, and there was no single legal obligation, no consistent identification of who should be tested, and only informal cross-border recognition [5][6].

DORA converts this good practice into **hard law** for the EU financial sector. Art. 26 makes intelligence-led testing on live production systems **mandatory** for identified significant entities, on a common methodology, with a **legal basis for mutual recognition** so that a single test can satisfy authorities across the EU [1]. Critically, DORA **did not discard TIBER-EU** — instead the Eurosystem **re-based TIBER-EU onto DORA** in February 2025, so the established framework becomes the operational vehicle for the legal duty, and financial entities and TI/red-team providers can continue to use familiar processes and roles (now DORA-conformed) [5][7]. The regime is completed by the **Art. 26(11) RTS**, finalised as **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1190**, which fills in the identification criteria, scope, methodology, tester standards and cooperation/mutual-recognition mechanics [2][4].
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
DORA's **Chapter IV (Arts. 24–27)** establishes the "digital operational resilience testing" pillar. It has two tiers [1]:

- **Baseline testing (all financial entities, except microenterprises on a risk-based frequency):**
  - **Art. 24 — General requirements.** Every financial entity (other than those on the simplified regime) must establish, maintain and review a **sound and comprehensive digital operational resilience testing programme** as an integral part of its ICT risk-management framework, applying a **risk-based approach** and covering ICT systems and applications supporting critical or important functions. Tests are carried out by **independent parties** (internal or external) and adverse findings are fully addressed [1].
  - **Art. 25 — Testing of ICT tools and systems.** The programme must include a **range of assessments and tests** — vulnerability assessments and scans, open-source analyses, network security assessments, gap analyses, physical security reviews, questionnaires and scanning software, source-code reviews where feasible, scenario-based tests, compatibility/penetration testing and end-to-end testing — with critical ICT systems tested **at least yearly** [1].

- **Advanced testing (identified significant entities only):**
  - **Art. 26 — Advanced testing of ICT tools, systems and processes based on TLPT.** Identified entities must carry out **TLPT at least every three years** (competent authorities may adjust the frequency to the entity's risk profile and operational circumstances), covering **several or all critical or important functions** and performed on **live production systems**; the test must include those functions even where they are **outsourced to ICT third-party providers** [1].
  - **Art. 27 — Requirements for testers.** Sets the suitability, capability, independence and (for external testers) insurance requirements, and governs the use of **internal testers** [1].

**Interpretation (distinct from the statutory text):** The two tiers are cumulative — TLPT does not displace the Art. 24/25 programme; an in-scope entity runs both. TLPT is deliberately **outcome-focused and adversarial**: it tests **protection, detection, response and recovery** capabilities of people, processes and technology under realistic attack, rather than confirming the presence of controls. The **Art. 26(11) RTS** (Reg (EU) 2025/1190) is the binding detail; the **TIBER-EU framework** is the recognised *how-to* the ECB/Eurosystem and national authorities expect entities to follow [1][2][5][7].

## Relevant Articles

| Art. 24 | General requirement — a **risk-based digital operational resilience testing programme** for all non-simplified entities. | [1] |
| Art. 25 | The **testing toolbox** (vulnerability assessments, scans, penetration tests, etc.); critical systems tested at least yearly. | [1] |
| Art. 26(1) | **TLPT at least once every three years** for identified entities (frequency adjustable to risk). | [1] |

| Art. 26(4) | **Pooled testing** where multiple entities/ICT third parties share systems; safeguards and a lead entity. | [1] |
| Art. 26(5)–(7) | Test conduct, and the **attestation** issued **solely for mutual recognition** across the EU. | [1] |
| Art. 26(8) | Competent authorities **identify** the entities required to perform TLPT; rules on testers and the always-external **threat-intelligence provider**. | [1] |

## Relevant Recitals

| Recital 47 area | Advanced testing through TLPT is warranted for entities that are significant and ICT-mature, to raise the sector's overall resilience. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** TLPT is a recent, technical supervisory obligation that became operative with DORA's application on 17 January 2025 and its RTS on 8 July 2025; there is no CJEU or domestic case law interpreting Arts. 26–27 or Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1190. Interpretive weight rests on the Regulation, the RTS, and the ECB/ESA and national TIBER guidance [1][2][5]. Any future disputes (e.g. over identification decisions or attestations) would be tracked in the backlog rather than asserted here.

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **The Art. 26(11) RTS is final and in force.** The European Commission adopted **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1190** on **13 February 2025**; it was published in the **Official Journal on 18 June 2025** and **entered into force on 8 July 2025**. It specifies: the **criteria** competent authorities use to identify entities required to perform TLPT; requirements on **scope, testing methodology and results**; the **requirements and standards governing the use of internal testers**; and the forms of **supervisory and other cooperation** needed for TLPT implementation and **mutual recognition** [2][4]. The European Commission catalogues this RTS among DORA's delegated acts [8], and EIOPA's overview confirms that the testing pillar operates from DORA's 17 January 2025 application date [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verified.)*
- **The ESAs developed the RTS "in agreement with the ECB".** DORA Art. 26(11) uniquely requires ECB agreement, reflecting the ECB/Eurosystem's ownership of TIBER-EU; the EBA hosts the joint RTS on behalf of the three ESAs [1][4]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **TIBER-EU is the recognised delivery framework — and it was re-based on DORA.** On **11 February 2025** the Eurosystem published an updated **TIBER-EU framework** aligned with DORA and its RTS: the **"White Team" was renamed "Control Team"**, **purple-teaming was made mandatory**, process steps were synchronised with the **RTS deliverables and timelines**, and guidance documents were added so authorities can reference TIBER-EU directly [5][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verified.)*
- **The ECB issued SSM implementation guidance.** In **November 2025** the ECB (Banking Supervision) published a **TIBER-EU implementation guide** explaining how to implement TIBER-EU for a DORA TLPT within the Single Supervisory Mechanism [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verified.)*
- **Compliance and attestation.** Where an entity follows the TIBER-EU process and the DORA/RTS requirements, the process concludes with an **attestation** confirming the test was performed as required — the instrument that enables **EU-wide mutual recognition** so the test need not be repeated for each Member State's authority (Art. 26(7)) [1][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Identification is supervisory and risk-based, not a bright-line size test.** Competent authorities identify in-scope entities using the RTS criteria — grounded in impact-related factors, the systemic character of the entity, and its ICT risk profile/maturity — so being large does not automatically mean in-scope, and being identified reflects supervisory judgement (Art. 26(8); Reg (EU) 2025/1190) [1][2]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
- **Treat TLPT as an intelligence-led, full-scope engagement, not a scoped pentest.** The red team works from a **Targeted Threat Intelligence (TTI) Report** to build realistic **attack scenarios** against whole critical/important functions on **live production**, exercising the full kill chain (reconnaissance, initial access, persistence, lateral movement, actions on objectives) while defenders remain unaware [1][5]. *(Best practice grounded in the Art. 26 obligation.)*
- **Protect the production estate.** Because testing is on live systems, the **Control Team** must run rigorous **risk management** — legal sign-off, a tested rollback/"leg-up" and abort process, out-of-band communications, and safeguards so the test cannot cause the very disruption it simulates (Art. 26 requires controlled testing) [1][5]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Map critical or important functions to underlying assets first.** A defensible scope requires a current inventory linking each critical/important function (Art. 3(22)) to applications, infrastructure, identities and **ICT third-party dependencies**; this is drawn from the Art. 6 framework — specified in detail by the ICT risk-management RTS (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774) — and the register of information [1][3]. *(Best practice; obligation to maintain the framework/register under DORA.)*
- **Include third-party-run functions and plan pooled testing.** Where a critical/important function runs on an ICT third-party provider (e.g. cloud, core-banking, payments), the provider's in-scope systems must be tested; **pooled TLPT** with a designated lead entity is available where several entities rely on shared systems, subject to Art. 26(4) safeguards and provider cooperation [1][10]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*
- **Instrument detection and response for the purple-teaming replay.** Value is realised in **closure**: the mandatory purple-teaming replay compares red-team actions against blue-team telemetry and detections, producing concrete SOC/EDR/logging improvements — build for this by preserving detailed test logs [5][7]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Feed findings into remediation and re-testing.** Adverse findings must be addressed under Art. 24's "fully address" duty; track remediation to closure and re-validate high-severity gaps [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
- **Cloud/hosting providers are frequently in TLPT scope.** If a critical or important function of a financial-entity customer runs on your platform, your relevant systems fall within that customer's TLPT; expect **contractual cooperation** obligations (access, coordination, safe testing windows) flowing from Art. 30 and the third-party-risk regime [1]. *(Legal obligation for the financial entity; commercial reality for the host.)*
- **CTPPs and concentration.** A hosting/cloud provider designated a **critical ICT third-party provider** already sits under direct ESA oversight; TLPT of dependent entities adds resilience assurance over the same estate, and **pooled testing** is likely where many entities share the platform [1][10]. *(Regulatory context.)*
- **Live-system safety.** Testing on production shared infrastructure demands provider-side safeguards (blast-radius limits, tenant isolation assurances, coordinated abort procedures) so a red-team scenario cannot degrade other tenants — a key subject of pooled-testing safeguards under Art. 26(4) [1][5]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Evidence and logging.** Hosts should be able to supply the telemetry needed for the purple-teaming replay and remediation validation without breaching other customers' confidentiality [5]. *(Best practice.)*
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text: **Not Applicable — with the same narrow caveat as `dora-foundations`.** TLPT is an obligation of **identified significant financial entities**; ordinary game hosting and studios are outside DORA entirely. It becomes relevant only where a games business is itself a financial entity (e.g. a scaled in-game **crypto-asset service provider** under MiCA, or an embedded payments/e-money arm) that a competent authority **identifies** for TLPT, or where a studio supplies ICT services underpinning a critical or important function of such an entity — in which case its systems could be pulled into that entity's TLPT scope on the third-party terms above [1]. Standard player-facing game security testing is governed by general good practice (see `cybersecurity-foundations`), not DORA TLPT.
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
- **AI systems on in-scope functions are legitimate TLPT targets.** Where AI/ML supports a critical or important function (fraud detection, credit decisioning, trading surveillance, security automation), those models, data pipelines and inference endpoints are part of the ICT estate and can be included in the red-team scope and scenarios [1]. *(Legal obligation — as ICT.)*
- **AI-specific attack scenarios.** Threat intelligence should reflect AI-relevant TTPs (data/model poisoning, prompt injection against LLM-backed services, model theft, evasion of ML-based detection); purple-teaming should validate whether such attacks are detected [1][5]. *(Best practice.)*
- **AI at ICT third parties.** AI services bought from providers underpinning in-scope functions are captured just like any other third-party dependency, with cooperation and pooled-testing considerations [1][10]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **AI Act and GDPR run in parallel.** High-risk AI in financial services carries AI Act robustness/cybersecurity duties (see `ai-act-foundations`), and any personal data on tested systems remains governed by the GDPR; TLPT does not displace either [1]. *(Cross-reference; parallel application.)*
title: DORA: Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

**A practical TLPT scoping methodology (recommended):**

1. **Confirm identification status.** Establish whether your competent authority has identified the entity for TLPT under Art. 26(8) and the RTS criteria; if not yet identified but plausibly in scope (systemic role, ICT maturity), prepare proactively. *(OBLIGATION once identified; EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION to prepare early.)* [1][2]
2. **Enumerate critical or important functions.** Use the Art. 3(22) definition and the Art. 6 framework to list functions whose disruption would materially impair the business or compliance. *(OBLIGATION — framework; foundational to scope.)* [1]
3. **Map functions to assets and third parties.** For each function, trace supporting applications, infrastructure, identities, data flows and **ICT third-party dependencies** (from the register of information). *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [1]
4. **Select the TLPT scope with the authority.** Choose several or all critical/important functions to cover, including third-party-run ones; validate the scope specification with the competent authority/TIBER team. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2]
5. **Stand up the Control Team and risk controls.** Appoint the small trusted Control Team, secure legal sign-off, and define the abort/rollback and out-of-band comms before any active testing on production. *(BEST PRACTICE — required for controlled testing.)* [1][5]
6. **Procure compliant TI and red-team providers.** Engage an **external threat-intelligence provider** and testers meeting Art. 27 requirements; if using internal red-teamers, obtain authority approval and manage conflicts, and remember external testers are required for **one in every three tests**. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2]
7. **Run the intelligence-led red-team test on live systems.** Deliver the Targeted Threat Intelligence Report, then execute scenario-based attacks against in-scope functions with the blue team unaware. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][5]
8. **Close with mandatory purple-teaming.** Replay scenarios collaboratively, capture detection/response gaps and transfer knowledge. *(OBLIGATION under the DORA-aligned framework.)* [5][7]
9. **Remediate and obtain the attestation.** Produce a remediation plan, address adverse findings, and secure the **attestation** for EU-wide mutual recognition. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
10. **Schedule the next cycle.** Plan the next TLPT within the **three-year** cadence (or the authority-adjusted frequency), and integrate lessons into the Art. 24/25 programme. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]

6. How were adverse findings **remediated**, and were high-severity gaps re-validated? *(Art. 24 [1].)*
7. Was an **attestation** obtained, and is **mutual recognition** relied on across Member States? *(Art. 26(5)–(7) [1].)*
8. Is the next TLPT scheduled within the **three-year** cadence (or the authority-adjusted frequency), and are lessons fed into the Art. 24/25 programme? *(Art. 26(1) [1].)*

text:
The **EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847**, "CRA") is the first horizontal EU law to impose **mandatory cybersecurity requirements on products** — hardware and software — placed on the Union market. Where NIS2 secures **entities** and DORA secures **financial-sector operations**, the CRA secures the **product** itself, across its whole lifecycle, from design through the end of its support period [1][2][5]. It applies to **"products with digital elements" (PDE)** — any software or hardware product whose intended or reasonably foreseeable use includes a direct or indirect data connection to a device or network (Art. 3(1)) — subject to carve-outs for products already governed by equivalent sectoral law (e.g. medical devices, motor vehicles, civil aviation) [1][5].

This document details the CRA's mechanics: the **scope** and the PDE concept; the **essential cybersecurity requirements** in **Annex I** (secure-by-design and secure-by-default product properties, plus a vulnerability-handling regime including an SBOM and a coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure policy) [1]; the **risk-based product classes** — *default*, *important* (Class I and Class II, Annex III) and *critical* (Annex IV) — and the **conformity-assessment routes** each triggers, culminating in **CE marking** [1][5]; the **reporting duties** to ENISA and CSIRTs for **actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents** through the ENISA **single reporting platform** (24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification, 14-day final report) [1][7]; and the differentiated obligations of **manufacturers, importers, distributors** and **open-source software stewards** [1].

Three points dominate. First, the **phased timeline** (Art. 71): entry into force **10 December 2024**; conformity-assessment-body (notified-body) provisions from **11 June 2026**; **reporting obligations from 11 September 2026**; **full application from 11 December 2027** [1][5]. Second, **CE marking becomes a cybersecurity gate** — non-compliant PDE cannot lawfully be placed on the EU market, with fines up to **€15m or 2.5% of worldwide turnover** for breaching the essential requirements [1]. Third, the CRA **complements rather than duplicates** NIS2 and the AI Act: a secure product (CRA) is an input to a secure entity (NIS2) and to a robust high-risk AI system (AI Act) [1][2][3].
title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Product Cybersecurity Foundations

text:
- The **CRA (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)** imposes **binding, horizontal cybersecurity requirements on products with digital elements** placed on the EU market; as a Regulation it is **directly applicable** in all Member States without transposition [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Scope** turns on the **"product with digital elements" (PDE)** definition (Art. 3(1)) — hardware or software with a direct/indirect data connection — with **exclusions** for products covered by equivalent sectoral law (medical devices, motor vehicles, civil aviation, marine equipment) and for genuinely **non-commercial open source** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation / scope.)*
- **Annex I** sets the **essential requirements**: Part I = **secure-by-design / secure-by-default product properties** (no known exploitable vulnerabilities at release, secure default configuration, protection of confidentiality/integrity, data minimisation, resilience to DoS, minimised attack surface, security logging, secure updates); Part II = **vulnerability handling** (SBOM, timely remediation, free security updates, a coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure policy) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Products are risk-classified as **default** (self-assessment), **important Class I** (Annex III — self-assessment only if harmonised standards/schemes are applied, else third-party), **important Class II** (Annex III — third-party), and **critical** (Annex IV — may require **European cybersecurity certification**); compliant products bear the **CE marking** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Manufacturers must provide **security updates for a support period of at least five years** (or the expected use time, if shorter) (Art. 13) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Reporting (Art. 14, via the ENISA single reporting platform, Art. 16):** for an **actively exploited vulnerability** or a **severe incident**, a **24-hour early warning**, a **72-hour notification**, and a **14-day / final report** to the designated CSIRT and ENISA — **applies from 11 September 2026** [1][5][7]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- Obligations cascade across the supply chain: **manufacturers (Art. 13)**, **importers (Art. 19)**, **distributors (Art. 20)** and, in a lighter-touch regime, **open-source software stewards (Art. 24)** [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Phased timeline (Art. 71):** entry into force **10 Dec 2024**; notified-body provisions **11 Jun 2026**; reporting duties **11 Sep 2026**; **full application 11 Dec 2027** — **live-verified against EUR-Lex and the Commission** [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — confirm before relying.)*
- **Penalties (Art. 64):** up to **€15m or 2.5% of worldwide annual turnover** for breaching the essential requirements or Arts. 13/14; €10m/2% and €5m/1% for lesser breaches [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The CRA **complements NIS2 (entities) and the AI Act (AI systems)** — product security is an input to entity security and to AI robustness/cybersecurity, not a substitute [1][2][3]. *(Cross-reference.)*

text:
*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md` (incl. "product with digital elements", "CIA triad"). Only CRA-specific terms are narrowed here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Product with digital elements (PDE) | Any software or hardware product and its remote data-processing solutions, whose intended or reasonably foreseeable use includes a direct or indirect logical or physical data connection to a device or network (Art. 3(1)). | [1] |
| Important product with digital elements | A PDE listed in **Annex III**, whose core functionality carries a heightened cybersecurity risk (Class I and Class II); triggers stricter conformity-assessment routes (Art. 7). | [1] |
| Critical product with digital elements | A PDE listed in **Annex IV** whose compromise could cause the most significant disruption; may be required to hold a **European cybersecurity certificate** (Art. 8). | [1] |
| Manufacturer | A natural/legal person who develops or manufactures PDE, or has them designed/developed/manufactured, and markets them under its own name or trademark (Art. 3(13)); bears the primary CRA obligations (Art. 13). | [1] |
| Open-source software steward | A legal person, other than a manufacturer, that systematically and sustainedly supports the development of specific free and open-source PDE intended for commercial activities (Art. 3(14)); subject to a lighter-touch regime (Art. 24). | [1] |
| Actively exploited vulnerability | A vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without the owner's permission (Art. 3(42)); triggers Art. 14 reporting. | [1] |
| Support period | The period during which a manufacturer must handle vulnerabilities and supply security updates — **at least five years**, or the product's expected use time if shorter (Art. 13(8)). | [1] |
| CE marking | The marking by which a manufacturer indicates a PDE conforms with the CRA (and other applicable Union harmonisation law), affixed before market placement (Arts. 29–30). | [1] |

text:
Products with digital elements — from routers and IoT sensors to operating systems and mobile apps — have become a routine vector for cyberattacks, yet before the CRA there was **no horizontal EU rule requiring them to be secure**. Security was addressed piecemeal (sectoral product law, voluntary standards such as ETSI EN 303 645 for consumer IoT, or entity-level duties under NIS2), leaving two structural gaps the Commission identified: a **low level of cybersecurity** in many products, and **insufficient information** for users to choose and configure products securely [5][6][9]. The CRA closes those gaps by making cybersecurity a **CE-marking condition** for placing PDE on the market — the same "New Legislative Framework" mechanism used for product safety and electromagnetic compatibility, now extended to cyber [1][5].

The CRA was adopted as **Regulation (EU) 2024/2847** on 23 October 2024, published in the Official Journal on 20 November 2024, and **entered into force on 10 December 2024** [1][5]. Because it is a **Regulation**, it is **directly applicable** in every Member State — a deliberate contrast with NIS2, a Directive whose fragmented national transposition the EU found unsatisfactory. The CRA sits within a coherent EU cyber package: **NIS2** (entity risk management and incident reporting), **DORA** (financial-sector operational resilience), the **Cybersecurity Act (Regulation (EU) 2019/881)** (ENISA's mandate and the European cybersecurity certification framework), and the **AI Act** (trustworthy AI, including cybersecurity of high-risk systems) [1][2][3][4].

text:
The CRA is a **directly applicable Regulation** structured around the New Legislative Framework for products. Its architecture:

- **Chapter I (Arts. 1–6)** — subject matter, **scope**, **definitions** (incl. Art. 3(1) PDE), and the relationship with other Union law (sectoral carve-outs).
- **Chapter II (Arts. 13–26)** — **obligations of economic operators**: manufacturers (Art. 13), their reporting duties (Art. 14), the ENISA **single reporting platform** (Art. 16), importers (Art. 19), distributors (Art. 20), and **open-source software stewards** (Art. 24); classification of **important** (Art. 7) and **critical** (Art. 8) products sits at the start of the scope/obligation machinery.
- **Chapter III (Arts. 27–28)** — **conformity**: presumption of conformity via harmonised standards, and the **EU declaration of conformity**.
- **Chapter IV (Arts. 29–34)** — **CE marking** (Arts. 29–30) and **conformity-assessment procedures** (Art. 32), performed by **notified bodies** where third-party assessment is required.
- **Chapters V–VII** — notification of conformity-assessment bodies, **market surveillance and enforcement**, and **delegated/implementing powers** (to update Annexes III/IV, specify the SBOM format, and detail reporting).
- **Penalties** — **Art. 64** (administrative fines).
- Substance lives in the **Annexes**: **Annex I** (essential requirements — product properties + vulnerability handling), **Annex II** (information to users), **Annex III** (important products, Class I/II), **Annex IV** (critical products), **Annex V** (EU declaration of conformity), **Annex VI** (conformity-assessment procedures).

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Art. 3(1) | Definition of "product with digital elements" — anchors the entire scope. | [1] |
| Art. 6 + Annex I | Products may be made available only if they meet the **essential cybersecurity requirements** in Annex I. | [1] |
| Art. 7 + Annex III | **Important** products with digital elements (Class I and Class II) — stricter conformity routes. | [1] |
| Art. 8 + Annex IV | **Critical** products with digital elements — may require a European cybersecurity certificate. | [1][4] |
| Art. 13 | **Manufacturers' obligations** — risk assessment; meet Annex I; security updates for a **support period of ≥5 years**; documentation; conformity assessment; CE marking. | [1] |
| Art. 14 | **Reporting** of **actively exploited vulnerabilities** and **severe incidents** — 24h early warning, 72h notification, 14-day/final report (applies **11 Sep 2026**). | [1][5] |
| Art. 16 | Establishment of the **single reporting platform** operated by ENISA. | [1][7] |
| Art. 19 | **Importers' obligations** — place on the market only compliant, CE-marked PDE; verify manufacturer conformity. | [1] |
| Art. 20 | **Distributors' obligations** — act with due care that PDE bear CE marking and required documentation. | [1] |
| Art. 24 | **Open-source software stewards** — lighter-touch duties (cybersecurity policy, cooperation, vulnerability reporting). | [1] |
| Arts. 29–30 | **CE marking** — general principles and rules for affixing. | [1] |
| Art. 32 + Annex VI | **Conformity-assessment procedures** — internal control (Module A), EU-type examination (B+C), or full quality assurance (H). | [1] |
| Art. 64 | **Administrative fines** — up to €15m / 2.5% (essential requirements, Arts. 13/14); €10m / 2%; €5m / 1%. | [1] |
| Art. 71 | **Entry into force and application** — 10 Dec 2024; Ch. IV bodies 11 Jun 2026; reporting 11 Sep 2026; full application 11 Dec 2027. | [1][5] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting articles (Art. 296 TFEU); cited from the primary text [1].*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| Recital 1 area | Rationale — PDE are a frequent, successful attack vector; low product cybersecurity and inadequate updates cause cross-border harm, justifying horizontal rules. | [1] |
| Recital on scope/exclusions | Products already subject to equivalent Union cybersecurity requirements (e.g. medical devices, motor vehicles, civil aviation) are excluded to avoid double regulation. | [1] |
| Recital on open source | Free and open-source software developed or supplied outside a commercial activity is not covered; stewards of commercially-relied-upon OSS get a proportionate, lighter regime. | [1] |
| Recital on support period | Manufacturers should determine the support period by expected product use; it should normally be at least five years. | [1] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** The CRA is a new instrument whose substantive obligations do not begin to apply until 11 September 2026 (reporting) and 11 December 2027 (full application), so there is no CJEU or national case law interpreting it. Interpretive weight currently rests on the Regulation's text, Commission guidance, ENISA materials and — once adopted — harmonised standards and delegated/implementing acts [1][5][8]. This will be revisited at the next review.

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** frames the CRA as introducing **mandatory cybersecurity requirements across the whole product lifecycle**, built on **security-by-design and by-default**, transparency to users, and vulnerability handling, evidenced by **CE-marked conformity** — deliberately phased so manufacturers can prepare (full application 11 Dec 2027) [5][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
- The Commission's **summary of the legislative text** confirms the operational split: **self-assessment** for the majority of products (default class); **third-party assessment** for important Class II and critical products; and, for important Class I, self-assessment **only if harmonised standards or a certification scheme are applied**, otherwise third-party [5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ENISA** operates the **single reporting platform** (SRP) that is the CRA's single entry point for manufacturers and stewards to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents "only once" rather than to multiple national authorities; ENISA states the SRP is to be operational by **11 September 2026**, aligning with the Art. 14 reporting start date [7]. *(Regulatory interpretation / operational.)*
- **ENISA and the Commission's Joint Research Centre** have published a **CRA Requirements–Standards Mapping**, identifying which existing and forthcoming European/international standards can support the Annex I requirements and where **gaps** remain to be filled by new harmonised standards — signalling that the standards landscape is **not yet complete** [8]. *(Regulatory interpretation — plan around evolving standards.)*
- Regulators treat **harmonised standards as the practical route to conformity**: products conforming to a harmonised standard (once cited in the Official Journal) enjoy a **presumption of conformity** with the corresponding Annex I requirements, but the essential requirements — not the standard — remain the legal test [1][5]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Product Cybersecurity Foundations

text:
- **Scope triage first** — determine whether a product is a **PDE** (Art. 3(1)) and whether an **exclusion** applies (products under equivalent sectoral law; non-commercial open source; pure SaaS that is not a remote data-processing solution integral to the product). This determines everything downstream [1][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Engineer to Annex I Part I (product properties)** — secure-by-default configuration; **no known exploitable vulnerabilities** at placing on the market; protection of confidentiality and integrity (encryption of stored/transmitted data as appropriate); **data minimisation**; access control; resilience to and mitigation of **denial-of-service**; **minimised attack surface**; security-relevant **logging**; and **secure, ideally automatic, updates** with the ability to roll back [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Stand up Annex I Part II (vulnerability handling)** — maintain an **SBOM** covering top-level dependencies; identify and remediate vulnerabilities **without delay**; provide **free security updates** for the support period; run a **coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy** and a contact address; and, after fixing, share information about resolved vulnerabilities [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Map the product to a class and route** — *default* → **Module A internal control** (self-assessment); *important Class I* → self-assessment **only** if harmonised standards/scheme applied, else **notified-body** third-party (Module B+C or H); *important Class II* → **third-party**; *critical (Annex IV)* → third-party and potentially **European cybersecurity certification** (Cybersecurity Act) [1][4][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Standards alignment** — align the SDLC to **ISO/IEC 27001** (ISMS) and **NIST CSF 2.0** for process assurance, and to product baselines such as **ETSI EN 303 645** (consumer IoT) pending citation of CRA-specific harmonised standards; track the **ENISA/JRC standards mapping** for gap areas [8][9][10][11]. *(Best practice; presumption of conformity attaches only to harmonised standards once cited.)*
- **Build the reporting pipeline** — instrument the product and the PSIRT so an **actively exploited vulnerability** or **severe incident** can be detected and pushed to the **ENISA SRP** within the **24h / 72h / 14-day** windows from 11 Sep 2026 [1][7]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Product Cybersecurity Foundations

text:
- **"Remote data-processing solutions" can pull hosting into product scope** — where a hosted/cloud component is **integral to a PDE** (its absence would prevent the product performing its functions), that remote solution falls within the product's CRA conformity, even though standalone SaaS is generally outside scope [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — assess integration.)*
- **Update and reporting infrastructure** — meeting the Annex I secure-update duty and the Art. 14 reporting timelines requires reliable hosted **update-distribution** and **vulnerability-intake/PSIRT** infrastructure; provision for signed updates, rollback and secure telemetry [1][7]. *(Best practice grounded in a legal outcome.)*
- **Shared-responsibility clarity** — where a manufacturer relies on an IaaS/PaaS provider for the product's back end, the **manufacturer remains the CRA obligated party**; contractually secure the provider's cooperation on vulnerability handling and incident evidence (see the shared-responsibility model in `cybersecurity-foundations`) [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Overlap with NIS2 for the operator** — a cloud/hosting operator may itself be a NIS2 **essential/important entity**; NIS2 duties on the operator run **in parallel** with the CRA duties on the product manufacturer — different obligated parties, different instruments [1][2]. *(Legal obligation — distinguish the roles.)*
title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Product Cybersecurity Foundations

text:
- **Game hardware and companion software are PDE** — consoles, controllers with connectivity, VR headsets, and downloadable game clients or launchers with a data connection are **products with digital elements** and fall within the CRA; their manufacturers owe the Annex I and vulnerability-handling duties [1][5]. *(Legal obligation — assess product scope.)*
- **Online game services vs products** — a purely server-side, subscription **game service** is closer to SaaS and generally outside direct CRA product scope, but any **distributed client** or **connected device** it ships is in scope; the boundary is the product, not the service [1][5]. *(Interpretation.)*
- **Update duty meets live-ops** — the Annex I **secure-update** obligation and the **≥5-year support period** interact with games' live-ops patch cadence: security updates must remain **free** and available for the support period even after feature updates cease [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Vulnerability disclosure for game clients** — anti-cheat drivers, DRM and networking stacks in game clients are security-sensitive; a **CVD policy** and SBOM (Annex I Part II) are required, and an actively exploited client vulnerability triggers Art. 14 reporting [1][7]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Product Cybersecurity Foundations

text:
- **AI-enabled products are PDE too** — a hardware or software product embedding an AI/ML component is a **product with digital elements**; the CRA's Annex I requirements apply to it as to any other PDE, adding secure-by-design and vulnerability-handling duties on top of any AI Act obligations [1][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **CRA ↔ AI Act interface** — for **high-risk AI systems**, the AI Act (Arts. 8–15) requires accuracy, robustness and **cybersecurity by design**; the CRA is designed to **dovetail** so that a high-risk AI system which is also a PDE and **conforms to the CRA** is presumed to meet the AI Act's cybersecurity requirement to the extent covered — reducing double conformity work while both instruments still apply [1][3]. *(Cross-reference; legal obligation under both.)*
- **AI-specific attack surface** — model/data poisoning, adversarial inputs and prompt injection are cybersecurity risks to be addressed in the Annex I **risk assessment** and vulnerability handling for AI-embedding products; SBOMs should extend to model and dependency provenance [1]. *(Best practice, grounded in the Annex I risk-assessment duty.)*
- **Reporting overlap** — an actively exploited vulnerability in an AI-embedding PDE triggers **CRA Art. 14** reporting; if the same event affects a NIS2 entity or a personal-data breach, **NIS2 Art. 23** and **GDPR Art. 33** clocks may run in parallel to different authorities [1][2]. *(Legal obligation — run the relevant clocks.)*
title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Product Cybersecurity Foundations

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** (where the CRA requires the outcome) / **BEST PRACTICE** (standards consensus) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (this pipeline's suggestion).

1. **Inventory products and triage scope** — list every hardware/software product placed (or to be placed) on the EU market, decide PDE status (Art. 3(1)) and whether an exclusion applies. *(OBLIGATION — foundational.)* [1][5]
2. **Classify each PDE** — default, important Class I/II (Annex III) or critical (Annex IV); this fixes the conformity route. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][5]
3. **Run the Art. 13 cybersecurity risk assessment** — and let it drive design, development, production and maintenance decisions; document it. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Implement Annex I** — Part I product properties (secure-by-default, no known exploitable vulnerabilities, encryption, DoS resilience, logging, secure updates) and Part II vulnerability handling (SBOM, remediation, free updates, CVD policy). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
5. **Set and publish the support period** — at least five years unless expected use is shorter; commit to free security updates for that period. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
6. **Select and execute the conformity route** — internal control (Module A) or, where required, a **notified body** (B+C or H); draw up the **EU declaration of conformity** and affix the **CE marking**. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
7. **Stand up Art. 14 reporting** — PSIRT, detection and the **24h/72h/14-day** flow to the **ENISA single reporting platform** and the coordinating CSIRT; ready **before 11 Sep 2026**. *(OBLIGATION — phased.)* [1][7]
8. **Align importers/distributors** — verify CE marking, documentation and manufacturer conformity before making PDE available (Arts. 19–20). *(OBLIGATION for those operators.)* [1]
9. **Handle open-source stewardship** — where you steward commercially-relied-upon OSS, adopt a cybersecurity policy and cooperate on vulnerability handling (Art. 24). *(OBLIGATION for stewards — lighter-touch.)* [1]
10. **Track evolving standards and acts** — monitor CEN/CENELEC/ETSI harmonised standards, the ENISA/JRC mapping, and delegated/implementing acts (Annex III/IV, SBOM format); adopt harmonised standards to gain the presumption of conformity. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [8]

text:
- **Phase 0 — Product inventory & scope:** Catalogue products; determine PDE status and exclusions; identify the obligated role (manufacturer/importer/distributor/steward). *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 1 — Classification & route:** Classify each PDE (default/important I-II/critical); select the conformity-assessment route and identify a notified body where needed. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 2 — Annex I engineering:** Implement product properties (Part I) and vulnerability handling (Part II) in the SDLC; produce SBOMs; establish the CVD policy and support period. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 3 — Reporting readiness:** Stand up the PSIRT and the 24h/72h/14-day reporting flow to the ENISA SRP; run drills — **target before 11 Sep 2026**. *Effort:* Medium.
- **Phase 4 — Conformity & CE marking:** Complete conformity assessment; draw up the EU declaration of conformity; affix CE marking; assemble technical documentation — **before 11 Dec 2027**. *Effort:* High.
- **Phase 5 — Sustain & adapt:** Operate vulnerability handling across the support period; track harmonised standards, the ENISA/JRC mapping and delegated/implementing acts; adopt standards for presumption of conformity. *Effort:* Ongoing.

text:
**Cybersecurity** is the cross-cutting technical and organisational discipline of protecting information systems, networks and data against threats to their **confidentiality, integrity and availability** (the "CIA triad"). This document establishes the foundations of that discipline as it underpins the EU/UK legal regimes — it is the "how" of security that laws such as **NIS2 Art. 21** [2], **DORA** [3] and **GDPR Art. 32** [1] require but do not fully specify. It deliberately stays **distinct** from the law-specific documents (`nis2-foundations`, `dora-foundations`) and from `privacy-engineering-foundations` (which covers data-protection-by-design); this document covers the security **frameworks, standards and controls** those laws lean on.

It sets out: core concepts (CIA triad, defence-in-depth, least privilege, zero trust); the two dominant management frameworks — **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** (an auditable **Information Security Management System**, ISMS) with its companion control set **ISO/IEC 27002:2022** (93 controls in four themes) [10][11], and the **NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0** (February 2024), whose **six Functions are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover** — **Govern being the function newly elevated in the 2.0 release** [12][13][14]; UK **NCSC** guidance including **Cyber Essentials** (five technical controls) [7][8]; **ENISA**'s EU-level role [9]; **OWASP Top 10:2025** for application security [15]; and operational disciplines (vulnerability/patch management, incident response, supply-chain security).

Three conclusions dominate. First, **frameworks are best practice, not law** — but they are the recognised means of **discharging** the legal security duties in NIS2, DORA and the GDPR [1][2][3]. Second, the **product-security frontier is now regulated**: the **EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)** imposes binding security requirements on products with digital elements, phased to **full application on 11 December 2027** [4][5]. Third, security is **risk-based and continuous**: controls must be selected, tested and improved against a live threat picture, not certified once and forgotten.

- The **CIA triad** — confidentiality, integrity, availability — is the organising model of information security and the outcome that legal duties like **GDPR Art. 32** demand [1]. *(Best practice; the outcome is a legal obligation under Art. 32.)*
- **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** specifies an auditable **ISMS**; **ISO/IEC 27002:2022** provides the companion set of **93 controls** across **four themes** (organisational, people, physical, technological) [10][11]. *(Best practice / standard.)*
- **NIST CSF 2.0** (Feb 2024) organises cybersecurity into **six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover**; **Govern** was **added as a core Function in 2.0** to place risk governance at the centre [12][13][14]. *(Best practice / standard — verified.)*
- **NCSC Cyber Essentials** defines a baseline of **five technical controls** (firewalls, secure configuration, security update management, user access control, malware protection); **Cyber Essentials Plus** adds independent technical audit [7]. *(Best practice / government scheme.)*
- **OWASP Top 10:2025** is the current consensus list of the most critical web-application security risks, led by **Broken Access Control (A01)** [15]. *(Best practice / standard.)*
- **Defence-in-depth, least privilege, fail-safe defaults and zero trust** are foundational architectural principles — the first three trace to Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); zero trust is codified in **NIST SP 800-207** [16][17]. *(Best practice / academic.)*
- Frameworks **operationalise legal duties**: NIS2 **Art. 21(2)** lists ten minimum risk-management measures, DORA imposes an ICT risk-management framework, and GDPR **Art. 32** requires security appropriate to the risk — all satisfiable through ISO 27001 / NIST CSF controls [1][2][3]. *(Legal obligation, met via best practice.)*
- The **Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)** makes product cybersecurity a **legal obligation** for manufacturers of products with digital elements; it entered into force **10 Dec 2024** and applies fully from **11 Dec 2027** (reporting duties from 11 Sep 2026) [4][5]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*

*Shared terms are in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only cybersecurity-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| CIA triad | The three core security objectives: **confidentiality** (only authorised access), **integrity** (accuracy and non-tampering) and **availability** (accessible when needed). GDPR Art. 32 names confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience as required security properties. | [1] |
| Information Security Management System (ISMS) | A systematic, risk-based management framework of policies, processes and controls for protecting information, specified by ISO/IEC 27001. | [10] |
| Defence-in-depth | Layering independent controls so that the failure of one does not compromise the system; rooted in the security design principles of Saltzer & Schroeder. | [8][17] |
| Least privilege | The principle that every user, process and component should have only the minimum access rights needed for its function (Saltzer & Schroeder). | [17] |
| Zero trust | A security model that removes implicit trust based on network location and continuously verifies every access request per-resource; defined for architecture by NIST SP 800-207. | [16] |
| Vulnerability management | The continuous process of identifying, assessing, prioritising and remediating (e.g. patching) security weaknesses in systems and software. | [8] |
| Cyber Essentials | A UK government-backed baseline certification (NCSC) built on five technical controls; **Cyber Essentials Plus** adds independent technical verification. | [7] |
| Product with digital elements | A software or hardware product (and its remote data-processing solutions) whose intended/foreseeable use includes a data connection, regulated for cybersecurity by the Cyber Resilience Act. | [4][5] |

text:
Information security as a discipline predates the internet, but its modern framing crystallised around the **CIA triad** and a body of **design principles** articulated in Saltzer & Schroeder's 1975 paper *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems* — economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, least privilege, complete mediation, and defence-in-depth thinking that still underpins practice today [17]. As systems networked and threats professionalised, organisations needed **repeatable, auditable** ways to manage security, giving rise to **management-system standards** (the ISO/IEC 27000 family) and **outcome frameworks** (the NIST Cybersecurity Framework) [10][12].

In parallel, the EU and UK moved security from voluntary good practice toward **legal duty**. The GDPR (2016) made "security of processing" a statutory obligation for personal data (Art. 32) [1]; **NIS2** (2022) imposed risk-management and incident-reporting duties on essential and important entities (Art. 21) [2]; **DORA** (2022) did the same for the financial sector's ICT risk [3]; and the **Cyber Resilience Act** (2024) extended binding cybersecurity requirements to **products** placed on the EU market [4][5]. None of these laws prescribes a complete control set — they demand *appropriate*, *risk-based* measures — which is precisely why the **frameworks and standards** in this document matter: they are the recognised means of meeting the legal outcome.

text:
This document describes a **discipline**, not a single instrument. It nonetheless sits directly beneath several binding instruments, which it helps implement. The legal duties are stated in their dedicated documents; summarised here for mapping:

- **GDPR Art. 32 (security of processing)** — controllers/processors must implement TOMs appropriate to the risk, expressly including pseudonymisation, encryption, and confidentiality/integrity/availability/resilience, plus regular testing of effectiveness [1]. *(Legal obligation — personal data.)*
- **NIS2 Art. 21 (cybersecurity risk-management measures)** — essential and important entities must take appropriate, proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures; **Art. 21(2)** enumerates **ten minimum measures** (risk analysis and information-system security policies; incident handling; business continuity/backup/crisis management; supply-chain security; security in acquisition/development/maintenance incl. vulnerability handling; policies to assess effectiveness; cyber hygiene and training; cryptography/encryption; HR security, access control and asset management; multi-factor authentication and secured communications) [2]. *(Legal obligation — see `nis2-foundations`.)*
- **DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554)** — financial entities must maintain an **ICT risk-management framework**, plus incident reporting, resilience testing and third-party risk management [3]. *(Legal obligation — see `dora-foundations`.)*
- **Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)** — manufacturers of **products with digital elements** must meet essential cybersecurity requirements, handle vulnerabilities, and report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents [4][5]. *(Legal obligation — phased; see `cyber-resilience-act`.)*

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| GDPR Art. 32 | Security of processing — risk-appropriate TOMs; CIA + resilience; encryption/pseudonymisation; effectiveness testing. | [1] |
| NIS2 Art. 21(1) | Appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational risk-management measures (all-hazards, proportionality). | [2] |
| NIS2 Art. 21(2) | Ten minimum measures (incl. incident handling, business continuity, supply-chain security, cryptography, MFA, vulnerability handling). | [2] |
| NIS2 Art. 23 | Incident-reporting obligations (early warning, notification, final report). | [2] |
| DORA Arts. 5–16 | ICT risk-management framework (governance, protection, detection, response, recovery, learning). | [3] |
| CRA Art. 13 + Annex I | Essential cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements and vulnerability handling. | [4] |
| CRA Art. 14 | Reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents (applies from 11 Sep 2026). | [4][5] |

## Relevant Recitals

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| GDPR Recital 83 | Security measures should be risk-based, guarding against accidental/unlawful destruction, loss, alteration or disclosure. | [1] |
| NIS2 Recital 79 area | Risk-management measures should follow an all-hazards approach and reflect the state of the art and relevant standards. | [2] |
| CRA Recital 1 area | Rationale — products with digital elements are a frequent vector of successful cyberattacks; horizontal product-security rules are needed. | [4] |

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting articles.*

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable.** Cybersecurity is a cross-cutting technical discipline rather than a single legal instrument, so there is no distinct body of case law interpreting "cybersecurity" as such. Enforcement turning on inadequate security measures arises under specific instruments — e.g. GDPR Art. 32 fines, and (in future) NIS2/CRA enforcement — and is addressed in the law-specific documents (`nis2-foundations`, `dora-foundations`) and in `privacy-engineering-foundations`. **REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **ENISA** (the EU Agency for Cybersecurity) supports NIS2 implementation, publishes the annual **Threat Landscape**, maintains the CRA single reporting platform, and promotes the use of European/international standards to meet the legal risk-management duties [9]. *(Regulatory / technical guidance.)*
- The **UK NCSC** frames good security around accessible baselines: **Cyber Essentials** (five technical controls) for a common-threat baseline, and the **10 Steps to Cyber Security** for board-level programme structure — both explicitly best-practice guidance, not law, though widely referenced in procurement [7][8]. *(Regulatory / government guidance.)*
- The **European Commission** presents the CRA as introducing **mandatory** cybersecurity requirements across a product's lifecycle, with **security-by-design and by-default**, vulnerability handling and CE-marked conformity — phased so manufacturers can prepare (full application 11 Dec 2027) [5][6]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
- Regulators consistently treat **standards as the means, not the end**: certifying to ISO/IEC 27001 or aligning to NIST CSF is strong evidence of appropriate measures, but does not by itself prove compliance with a specific legal duty on specific facts [2][10]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

text:
**Core principles (BEST PRACTICE, with academic roots):**

- **Defence-in-depth** — layer independent controls (network, host, application, data, identity) so no single failure is catastrophic [8][17].
- **Least privilege & fail-safe defaults** — grant minimum access; deny by default (Saltzer & Schroeder) [17].
- **Zero trust** — remove implicit network-location trust; authenticate and authorise every request per-resource with continuous verification (NIST SP 800-207) [16].
- **Complete mediation & secure defaults** — check every access; ship secure-by-default configurations (a CRA requirement for products) [4][17].

**Management frameworks:**

- **ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (ISMS)** — a certifiable management system: context, leadership, risk assessment/treatment, an applicability statement over Annex A controls, operation, and continual improvement (Plan-Do-Check-Act) [10].
- **ISO/IEC 27002:2022** — the companion guidance detailing **93 controls** grouped into **four themes**: **organisational (37), people (8), physical (14), technological (34)** — a consolidation of the 2013 edition's 114 controls/14 clauses, with new controls such as threat intelligence, secure coding and data leakage prevention [11].
- **NIST CSF 2.0** — a technology-neutral outcome framework of **six Functions** — **Govern** (risk governance, roles, policy, supply-chain risk — **the Function elevated to core status in the 2.0 release**), **Identify**, **Protect**, **Detect**, **Respond**, **Recover** — with Categories, Subcategories and Implementation Tiers/Profiles for tailoring [12][13][14].

**Application security:** map development against the **OWASP Top 10:2025**, whose current leading risks include **A01 Broken Access Control**, **A02 Security Misconfiguration**, **A03 Software Supply Chain Failures**, **A04 Cryptographic Failures** and **A05 Injection** [15]. Supply-chain failures rising into the top three reflects the growing weight of dependency and build-pipeline risk.

**Operational disciplines (foundational):** continuous **vulnerability and patch management** (inventory, scanning, risk-based prioritisation, timely remediation); **incident response** (prepare-detect-analyse-contain-eradicate-recover-learn), aligned to NIS2/CRA reporting timelines; and **supply-chain security** (SBOMs, supplier assurance, secure build pipelines) — each an explicit NIS2 Art. 21(2) measure [2][8].

- **Shared-responsibility model** — in IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, the provider secures the underlying platform while the customer remains responsible for configuration, identity, data and application security; **security misconfiguration (OWASP A02)** is a leading cloud failure mode [15]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Framework-aligned cloud controls** — map hosting controls to **ISO/IEC 27002:2022** technological controls (access control, cryptography, logging, network security) and to CSF **Protect/Detect** outcomes; cloud-specific extensions to the ISMS exist where PII is processed (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`) [11][12]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Zero trust for cloud** — identity-centric, per-request authorisation is well suited to distributed cloud estates; adopt NIST SP 800-207 tenets rather than perimeter assumptions [16]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Logging, resilience and backup** — availability and recoverability are explicit legal outcomes (GDPR Art. 32; NIS2 Art. 21(2) business continuity/backup); ensure immutable, tested backups and centralised logging [1][2]. *(Legal obligation, met via controls.)*

- **Availability and abuse resistance** — real-time game services are high-value **DDoS** targets; availability (the "A" of the triad) requires upstream mitigation, rate-limiting and capacity planning [1]. *(Best practice grounded in the Art. 32 availability outcome.)*
- **Application security for game backends** — account, entitlement and matchmaking services face the same **OWASP Top 10** risks (broken access control, injection, misconfiguration); apply secure-SDLC and dependency scanning [15]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Anti-cheat and telemetry as security-sensitive data** — protect anti-cheat and moderation pipelines with least privilege and strong access control; where they process personal data, GDPR Art. 32 applies in parallel [1]. *(Best practice / legal overlap.)*
- **Connected devices and the CRA** — game hardware, consoles and companion apps with digital elements may fall within the **Cyber Resilience Act**, engaging product-security and vulnerability-handling duties [4][5]. *(Legal obligation — assess product scope.)*

text:
- **Securing AI systems** — AI/ML systems inherit all conventional security duties (access control, encryption, logging) and add attack surfaces: adversarial inputs, model/data poisoning, prompt injection and model theft. Treat the model, training data and pipeline as assets under the ISMS [10]. *(Best practice.)*
- **AI Act cybersecurity overlap** — high-risk AI systems must be accurate, robust and **cybersecure by design** (AI Act Arts. 8–15); the controls in this document are the means of meeting that duty — see `ai-act-foundations` and `ai-governance-foundations`. *(Cross-reference; legal obligation under the AI Act.)*
- **Supply-chain and provenance** — model and dependency provenance (SBOMs, signed artefacts) address OWASP A03 (software supply-chain failures) and the CRA's vulnerability-handling expectations for products embedding AI [4][15]. *(Best practice.)*
- **AI as a security tool** — AI assists detection (anomaly detection, triage) but introduces false-positive/adversarial risks; keep human oversight in Detect/Respond functions [12]. *(Editorial recommendation.)*

Labels: **OBLIGATION** (where a cited law requires the outcome) / **BEST PRACTICE** (standards consensus) / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION** (this pipeline's suggestion).

1. **Adopt a management framework** — implement **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** (ISMS) and/or align to **NIST CSF 2.0**; use ISO/IEC 27002:2022 as the control catalogue. *(BEST PRACTICE — and the recognised way to evidence NIS2/DORA/GDPR duties.)* [10][11][12]
2. **Start with a baseline** — achieve **Cyber Essentials** (five controls) as a minimum bar, then mature toward the fuller framework. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [7]
3. **Run a risk-based control-selection** — assess risks, then select and justify controls in a Statement of Applicability; do not deploy controls blindly. *(BEST PRACTICE; proportionality is a legal requirement under NIS2 Art. 21(1).)* [2][10]
4. **Govern first (CSF 2.0)** — establish roles, policy, risk appetite and supply-chain governance under the **Govern** Function before optimising technical controls. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [12][13]
5. **Operate vulnerability & patch management** — maintain asset inventory, scan continuously, prioritise by risk, patch to defined SLAs. *(OBLIGATION where NIS2/CRA apply — vulnerability handling.)* [2][4]
6. **Prepare incident response** — maintain a tested IR plan mapped to statutory reporting timelines (NIS2 Art. 23; CRA Art. 14 from 11 Sep 2026). *(OBLIGATION where those laws apply.)* [2][4][5]
7. **Secure the software supply chain** — require SBOMs, verify dependencies, secure build pipelines (OWASP A03). *(OBLIGATION under NIS2 Art. 21(2); BEST PRACTICE otherwise.)* [2][15]
8. **Embed application security** — test against the **OWASP Top 10:2025** across the SDLC. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [15]
9. **Move toward zero trust** — adopt identity-centric, per-request authorisation per NIST SP 800-207. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [16]
10. **Assess CRA product scope** — if you make products with digital elements, plan for essential requirements and reporting ahead of the phased dates. *(OBLIGATION — phased to 11 Dec 2027.)* [4][5]
