title: Consumer Rights: Foundations (EU & UK)
legal_basis: Directive 2011/83/EU; Directive 2005/29/EC; Directive 93/13/EEC; Directive (EU) 2019/770; Directive (EU) 2019/771; Directive (EU) 2019/2161; Consumer Rights Act 2015; Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013; Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024

text:
Consumer-protection law sets the baseline rules for how businesses may market, contract with and treat consumers — natural persons acting outside their trade. For digital businesses (e-commerce, apps, SaaS, games, streaming and subscriptions) it governs pre-contract disclosure, the right to cancel distance purchases, quality rights in goods, services and **digital content**, the fairness of standard contract terms, and the honesty of commercial practices including pricing and reviews.

In the **EU**, the framework is a set of harmonising Directives: the **Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU (CRD)** (pre-contract information; 14-day right of withdrawal) [1]; the **Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC (UCPD)** (the general prohibition on misleading and aggressive practices, plus a blacklist) [2]; the **Unfair Contract Terms Directive 93/13/EEC (UCTD)** (non-negotiated terms causing significant imbalance are not binding) [3]; and the 2019 "digital content" pair — **Directive (EU) 2019/770** on the supply of digital content and services and **Directive (EU) 2019/771** on the sale of goods [4][5]. The **"Omnibus" / Modernisation Directive (EU) 2019/2161** (applicable since **28 May 2022**) added transparency duties on **price reductions**, **fake reviews** and **online marketplaces**, and put stronger penalties behind the UCPD [6].

In the **UK**, the **Consumer Rights Act 2015 (CRA)** consolidated goods, services and — importantly — **digital content** quality rights [7], and the **Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013** carry the CRD's distance-selling information and cancellation rules [8]. The decisive recent change is the **Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (DMCCA)** [9]: it received Royal Assent on **24 May 2024**, and its consumer provisions began to commence on **6 April 2025**, replacing the 2008 unfair-trading regime, banning **fake reviews** and **drip pricing**, and — critically — giving the **Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) direct enforcement powers** with fines up to **£300,000 or 10% of global annual turnover** [9][10][11][12]. The DMCCA **subscription-contracts** regime was **delayed to Spring 2027** by the government's consultation response of 2 April 2026 [12][13]. Consumer law operates alongside — not instead of — the GDPR and the Digital Services Act (see `gdpr-foundations`, `dsa-foundations`).

text:
- **Consumer law is a distinct layer** from data-protection and platform law: it governs pre-contract disclosure, cancellation, quality/conformity and fair dealing for **consumers** (natural persons acting outside a trade) [1][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **EU CRD (2011/83/EU)** requires extensive **pre-contract information** and a **14-day right of withdrawal** for distance/off-premises contracts, with defined exceptions (e.g. supply of digital content where the consumer consents to immediate performance and waives withdrawal) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **UCPD (2005/29/EC)** prohibits misleading and aggressive practices via a general clause plus an Annex I **blacklist** of always-unfair practices; the **Omnibus Directive** added fake-review and price-reduction rules [2][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **UCTD (93/13/EEC)** makes **unfair non-negotiated terms non-binding** and requires plain, intelligible language; core-price and subject-matter terms escape assessment only if transparent [3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Directives (EU) 2019/770 and 2019/771** created harmonised **conformity (quality) rights** for **digital content/services** and for goods (including goods with digital elements), applicable in Member States since **1 January 2022** [4][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **UK CRA 2015** gives statutory quality rights in **goods, services and digital content** (satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, as described) with a tiered remedy structure [7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **DMCCA 2024** (Royal Assent **24 May 2024**) commenced its core consumer-protection provisions on **6 April 2025**, replacing the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008 and banning **fake reviews** and **drip pricing** [9][10][11]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- The DMCCA gives the **CMA direct enforcement** (no court finding required) with penalties up to **£300,000 or 10% of global annual turnover** for consumer-law breaches; in its first year the CMA opened investigations into 14 businesses and issued penalties (e.g. an AA driving-school drip-pricing case) [11][12]. *(Legal obligation — in force.)*
- The DMCCA **subscription-contracts** regime (pre-contract info, renewal reminders, cooling-off, easy exit) was **postponed to Spring 2027** by the DBT consultation response of **2 April 2026** — plan to that date, but treat it as movable [12][13]. *(Legal obligation — not yet in force.)*

**In scope:** The EU consumer-protection instruments relevant to digital businesses (CRD, UCPD, UCTD, Directives 2019/770 and 2019/771, and the Omnibus Directive); the UK CRA 2015, Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, and the DMCCA 2024 consumer-protection provisions at a foundational level; live-verified DMCCA commencement status; and how the regime interacts with the GDPR and DSA.

**Assumptions:** The reader understands the difference between a **consumer** (natural person acting outside trade) and a **trader/business**. Personal-data processing in any consumer transaction remains governed by the GDPR in parallel (see `gdpr-foundations`).

*Shared cross-cutting terms (personal data, controller, online platform) are defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only consumer-law terms of art used in this document are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Consumer | A natural person acting for purposes wholly or mainly outside that person's trade, business, craft or profession (CRD Art. 2(1); CRA 2015 s.2(3)). | [1][7] |
| Trader | Any natural or legal person acting for purposes relating to their trade, business, craft or profession in consumer transactions (CRD Art. 2(2)). | [1] |
| Distance contract | A contract concluded without simultaneous physical presence of trader and consumer, using exclusively means of distance communication (CRD Art. 2(7)). | [1] |
| Right of withdrawal | The consumer's right to withdraw from a distance/off-premises contract within 14 days without reason and without cost (CRD Arts. 9–16). | [1] |
| Digital content | Data produced and supplied in digital form (CRD Art. 2(11); Directive (EU) 2019/770 Art. 2(1)); under the CRA 2015 it carries statutory quality rights. | [1][4][7] |
| Conformity | The requirement that goods/digital content/services meet subjective and objective quality criteria (Directive (EU) 2019/770 Arts. 6–8; 2019/771 Arts. 5–7). | [4][5] |
| Unfair commercial practice | A business-to-consumer practice contrary to professional diligence that materially distorts consumers' economic behaviour, or a misleading/aggressive practice, or one on the Annex I blacklist (UCPD Arts. 5–9, Annex I). | [2] |
| Unfair contract term | A non-individually-negotiated term that, contrary to good faith, causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights to the consumer's detriment (UCTD Art. 3). | [3] |
| Drip pricing | Advertising an initial ("headline") price and then adding mandatory or effectively unavoidable charges later in the purchase journey; banned as an unfair practice under the DMCCA. | [9][11] |
| Subscription contract | A contract under which a consumer is periodically supplied goods/services/digital content for payment, typically with automatic renewal; subject to the DMCCA's (not-yet-in-force) subscription regime. | [9][13] |
title: Consumer Rights: Foundations (EU & UK)
legal_basis: Directive 2011/83/EU; Directive 2005/29/EC; Directive 93/13/EEC; Directive (EU) 2019/770; Directive (EU) 2019/771; Directive (EU) 2019/2161; Consumer Rights Act 2015; Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013; Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024

text:
EU consumer law developed as a series of minimum- and later **maximum-harmonisation** Directives to build the internal market while protecting consumers. The **UCTD (1993)** and **UCPD (2005)** set fairness baselines for terms and practices; the **CRD (2011)** harmonised pre-contract information and the withdrawal right for distance and off-premises contracts, replacing the older Distance Selling Directive [1][2][3]. As commerce moved to paid apps, streaming and cloud services, the EU adopted the 2019 "digital content" pair — **Directive (EU) 2019/770** (supply of digital content/services) and **Directive (EU) 2019/771** (sale of goods, including goods with digital elements) — applicable in Member States from **1 January 2022** [4][5]. The **Omnibus / Modernisation Directive (EU) 2019/2161**, applicable since **28 May 2022**, modernised the older Directives for the digital economy: transparency of **price reductions**, disclosure of **paid ranking** and whether reviews are verified, a ban on **fake/incentivised reviews**, information duties for **online marketplaces**, and GDPR-style **penalties** (up to at least 4% of turnover for widespread cross-border infringements) [6].

The UK implemented the EU baseline while a Member State. The **Consumer Rights Act 2015** consolidated and modernised goods/services rights and, for the first time in UK statute, created a dedicated **digital content** category [7]. The **Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013** transposed the CRD [8]. After Brexit these instruments were retained. The UK then diverged and modernised through the **Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024**, which — alongside a new digital-markets competition regime — overhauled consumer enforcement: it replaced the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008, codified banned practices (including fake reviews and drip pricing), and gave the **CMA** the power to decide breaches and levy fines **directly**, rather than only through the courts [9][10][11].

text:
Consumer protection for a digital business is best understood as **four functional layers**, each with an EU and a UK instrument:

1. **Pre-contract information & cancellation** — EU: **CRD 2011/83/EU** [1]; UK: **Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013** [8].
2. **Fair commercial practices** (marketing, pricing, reviews) — EU: **UCPD 2005/29/EC** as amended by the **Omnibus Directive** [2][6]; UK: **DMCCA 2024 Part 4 Ch. 1** (replacing the 2008 Regulations) [9][11].
3. **Fair contract terms** — EU: **UCTD 93/13/EEC** [3]; UK: **CRA 2015 Part 2** [7].
4. **Quality / conformity rights & remedies** — EU: **Directives (EU) 2019/770 and 2019/771** [4][5]; UK: **CRA 2015 Part 1** (goods, services, digital content) [7].

The **DMCCA** adds a fifth, cross-cutting layer for the UK: **enforcement** (Part 3) and **subscription contracts** (Part 4 Ch. 2, not yet in force) [9]. Consumer law is generally **fully harmonised** in the EU for the CRD and the 2019 Directives (Member States may not add or subtract), whereas the UCTD sets a minimum floor.

## Relevant Articles

*Selected foundational provisions. EU Directive articles bind via national transposition; UK statutory sections apply directly.*

| Provision | Obligation | Source |
|-----------|------------|--------|
| CRD Arts. 5–6 | Mandatory pre-contract information (identity, price incl. taxes, delivery, withdrawal rights, duration/termination of contracts). | [1] |
| CRD Arts. 9–16 | 14-day right of withdrawal for distance/off-premises contracts; model withdrawal form; exceptions (incl. digital content with prior consent and waiver, Art. 16(m)). | [1] |
| UCPD Arts. 5–9 + Annex I | Prohibition of unfair (misleading/aggressive) practices; Annex I "blacklist" of always-unfair practices. | [2] |
| UCPD Art. 6a (via Omnibus) / Art. 7(6) | Fake-review prohibition; disclosure of whether reviews are from actual purchasers; disclosure of paid ranking. | [2][6] |
| Price Indication Dir. Art. 6a (via Omnibus) | Price-reduction announcements must state the prior lowest price in the preceding 30 days. | [6] |
| UCTD Arts. 3–6 + Annex | Unfair non-negotiated terms not binding; plain-language requirement; indicative "grey list" of suspect terms. | [3] |
| Dir. (EU) 2019/770 Arts. 6–14 | Conformity criteria, trader liability and remedies for digital content and digital services. | [4] |
| Dir. (EU) 2019/771 Arts. 5–14 | Conformity, liability and remedies for goods, including goods with digital elements. | [5] |
| CRA 2015 ss.9–11, 34–36 | Goods and digital content to be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, and as described. | [7] |
| CRA 2015 ss.19–24, 42–45 | Consumer remedies: repair/replacement, price reduction, right to reject / refund tiers. | [7] |
| CRA 2015 ss.49–50, 62 | Services with reasonable care and skill; fairness test for consumer contract terms. | [7] |
| DMCCA 2024 Part 3 | CMA direct enforcement of consumer protection law; penalties (fines and enhanced consumer measures). | [9] |
| DMCCA 2024 Part 4 Ch. 1 + Sch. 20 | Protection from unfair trading; 32 always-unfair practices (incl. fake reviews, drip pricing). | [9][11] |
| DMCCA 2024 Part 4 Ch. 2 | Subscription contracts regime (pre-contract info, reminders, cooling-off, exit) — **not yet commenced**. | [9][13] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals are non-binding but aid construction of the Directives.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| CRD Recital 4–5 | Full harmonisation of information and withdrawal rules to remove internal-market barriers and boost consumer confidence. | [1] |
| UCPD Recital 6–8 | The Directive protects consumers' economic interests via a general prohibition plus specific misleading/aggressive categories. | [2] |
| Dir. (EU) 2019/770 Recital 19–20 | Digital content/services covered irrespective of medium; addresses "data as counter-performance" (paying with personal data). | [4] |
| Omnibus Dir. Recital 47–49 | Rationale for review-transparency and fake-review measures as consumers increasingly rely on reviews. | [6] |

## Relevant Case Law

| Case | Court / Citation | Holding | Relevance |
|------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| *Content Services v Bundesarbeitskammer* | CJEU, C-49/11, ECLI:EU:C:2012:419 | Making information available only via a hyperlink does not satisfy "durable medium" pre-contract disclosure requirements. | Digital pre-contract disclosure must be provided durably, not merely linked [1]. |
| *Verein für Konsumenteninformation v Amazon* | CJEU, C-191/15, ECLI:EU:C:2016:612 | A term in online T&Cs choosing the trader's home-country law can be unfair if it misleads the consumer about applicable mandatory rules. | Illustrates UCTD fairness control over standard online terms [3]. |
| *(UK DMCCA case law)* | — | To be added as CMA direct-enforcement decisions and any appeals develop from 2025 onward. | Not Applicable at foundational level (regime new) [9][12]. |

*Case citations above are illustrative of established EU consumer-law principles; full case-law treatment is deferred to sub-topic documents. Neutral citations were not independently re-verified against a court database at `sources_verified` and are labelled REGULATORY INTERPRETATION / EDITORIAL context rather than load-bearing primary authority.*

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- The **European Commission** treats the CRD, UCPD, UCTD and the 2019 Directives as an integrated consumer *acquis*, and has issued guidance notices on each (e.g. UCPD guidance, price-indication guidance) explaining how the Omnibus changes on reviews, ranking and price reductions apply to online traders [14][15]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The **CMA** interprets the DMCCA unfair-trading provisions in its guidance **"Unfair commercial practices" (CMA207)**: the provisions **replace and update the 2008 CPUT Regulations** and apply to commercial practices occurring **from 6 April 2025**; **Schedule 20** lists **32 practices that are unfair in all circumstances**, including fake reviews and hidden/drip fees [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation of a legal obligation.)*
- On **enforcement approach**, the CMA said it would focus its first 12 months on the most **egregious** conduct — objectively false information, aggressive practices targeting the vulnerable, banned practices (fake reviews), hidden fees, and clearly imbalanced terms — and applied a **grace period** of roughly six months before actively enforcing the **fake-review** rules [11][12]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- The CMA's **one-year review (April 2026)** reports real enforcement: investigations into **14 businesses**, settlements, 157 advisory letters, and concrete outcomes such as a **drip-pricing** case (AA / BSM driving schools) with consumer refunds and a multi-million-pound penalty [12]. *(Regulatory interpretation / factual.)*
- On **subscriptions**, the **DBT** confirmed in its **2 April 2026** consultation response that the new regime is **delayed to Spring 2027**; the CMA's own communications now say "new rules are expected to come into force in Spring 2027" [12][13]. *(Regulatory statement — not yet law; track for change.)*

text:
- **Checkout price transparency** — display the **total price inclusive of taxes and all mandatory charges** up front; do not reveal unavoidable fees only late in the flow (drip pricing is a banned practice in the UK and misleading under the UCPD) [9][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Pre-contract information capture** — surface CRD/CCR-mandated information (identity, price, delivery, duration, withdrawal rights, cancellation form) and record that it was provided on a **durable medium**, not just a hyperlink [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Cancellation / withdrawal journeys** — implement a working **14-day** withdrawal mechanism for distance sales, with the model form; for digital content delivered immediately, capture the consumer's **express consent and acknowledgement of loss of withdrawal** before performance [1][8]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Reviews systems** — do not publish or commission **fake or incentivised reviews**; disclose whether and how reviews are verified as coming from actual purchasers; disclose **paid ranking/placement** [2][6][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Reference-price / discount logic** — where advertising a price reduction to EU consumers, compute the "was" price as the **lowest price in the prior 30 days** [6]. *(Legal obligation, EU.)*
- **Digital-content conformity & updates** — build **update delivery** and conformity guarantees into digital products; the 2019/770 regime and CRA extend quality liability across the supply period, including required updates [4][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Terms drafting** — standard terms must be in **plain, intelligible language**; avoid terms on the UCTD "grey list" / CRA fairness blacklist (e.g. disproportionate exit charges, unilateral variation) [3][7]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
- Consumer-law duties fall on the **trader** (the business contracting with the consumer), not the hosting/infrastructure provider as such; a pure IaaS/PaaS host is not usually the "trader" toward the end consumer. *(Interpretation.)*
- However, **billing, checkout, paywall and subscription-management components** that a host or platform provides on the trader's behalf must support compliant flows (total-price display, cancellation, withdrawal, renewal reminders once the DMCCA subscription rules commence) [1][9][13]. *(Best practice / obligation flows through to the trader.)*
- **Marketplaces/platforms** have their own information duties under the Omnibus Directive (e.g. disclosing whether a third-party seller is a trader) and under the **DSA** (see `dsa-foundations`); a hosting business that operates a marketplace should not assume it is out of scope [6]. *(Legal obligation for marketplace operators.)*

text:
- **In-game purchases, loot boxes, virtual currency and DLC** are digital-content/services supplies: pre-contract price transparency, honest presentation, and conformity rights apply; presenting the true total cost (avoiding drip/obscured pricing of virtual-currency bundles) is directly relevant [1][4][7][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Subscriptions and auto-renewing battle passes / memberships** will fall within the DMCCA subscription regime (reminders, cooling-off, easy exit) once it commences in **Spring 2027**; design renewal and cancellation journeys now [9][13]. *(Obligation once in force — prepare early.)*
- **Fake or incentivised reviews / ratings** of games or in-game items are banned; review-manipulation and shill ratings are Schedule 20 practices [9][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Children as consumers** — much game spend involves minors; combine consumer-law fairness with the data-protection children's rules (see `uk-gdpr-foundations`, ICO Children's Code) and avoid aggressive/manipulative practices targeting the vulnerable [2][11]. *(Legal obligation + best practice.)*

legal_basis: Directive 2011/83/EU; Directive 2005/29/EC; Directive 93/13/EEC; Directive (EU) 2019/770; Directive (EU) 2019/771; Directive (EU) 2019/2161; Consumer Rights Act 2015; Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013; Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024

text:
- **AI-generated or AI-amplified fake reviews** are squarely within the fake-review bans (UCPD Art. 6a as amended; DMCCA Sch. 20) regardless of whether a human or a model authored them [2][6][11]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Dark patterns / manipulative UX**, including AI-personalised persuasion and choice architecture that distorts a consumer's decision, can be an **unfair (aggressive or misleading) commercial practice**; the UCPD/DMCCA fairness tests apply to algorithmic interfaces, and the DSA separately restricts dark patterns on platforms (see `dsa-foundations`) [2][11]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **Automated/dynamic and personalised pricing** must still meet transparency duties (total price, and — EU — the 30-day reference-price rule for advertised reductions); personalised pricing based on automated decision-making must be disclosed under the CRD as amended and engages the GDPR (see `gdpr-foundations`) [1][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **AI chatbots/agents that contract with consumers** do not displace the trader's pre-contract information and withdrawal duties; the trader remains responsible for what its automated agent tells the consumer [1]. *(Interpretation.)*

Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Display total, inclusive prices** (taxes + mandatory fees) before the consumer commits; eliminate drip pricing. *(OBLIGATION.)* [9][11]
2. **Provide full pre-contract information on a durable medium** and confirm the contract afterwards (identity, price, delivery, duration, withdrawal). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][8]
3. **Offer a working 14-day withdrawal** for distance sales; for immediate digital content, capture express consent + waiver of withdrawal before performance. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][8]
4. **Ban fake/incentivised reviews and disclose verification and paid ranking**; audit any review or ratings feature. *(OBLIGATION.)* [2][6][11]
5. **Apply the EU 30-day reference-price rule** to advertised reductions for EU consumers. *(OBLIGATION, EU.)* [6]
6. **Honour statutory quality/conformity rights and remedies** for goods, services and digital content, including required updates. *(OBLIGATION.)* [4][5][7]
7. **Review standard terms for fairness** — plain language; remove imbalanced terms (unfair exit charges, unilateral variation). *(OBLIGATION.)* [3][7]
8. **Prepare subscription journeys now** for the DMCCA regime (pre-contract info, renewal reminders, cooling-off, easy/online exit), targeting the **Spring 2027** date but tracking DBT/CMA updates. *(BEST PRACTICE — obligation once in force.)* [9][13]
9. **Maintain a DMCCA commencement watch-list** and a CMA-enforcement risk view given direct fines up to 10% of global turnover. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [11][12]
10. **Run consumer-law and GDPR/DSA compliance together** — one checkout touches all three. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [1]

text:
**Cloud hosting** — the provision of on-demand compute, storage and platform/software services (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) — sits at the intersection of nearly every EU/UK digital-compliance regime. This document is a **cross-cutting synthesis** of how cloud and infrastructure hosting must comply, pulling together obligations that the topic-specific foundations documents establish in depth. It does **not** restate those regimes in full; it maps them onto the hosting provider and the cloud customer and sets out a concrete **responsibility matrix**.

Five threads dominate. First, the **shared-responsibility model**: providers secure the platform "of" the cloud, customers secure what they put "in" it — but responsibility for a control is not the same as **accountability**, which the cloud customer (typically the data **controller**) cannot outsource [1]. Second, **data-protection roles**: a hosting provider is usually a **processor**, requiring a GDPR **Article 28** data-processing agreement (DPA) and **Article 32** security of processing; where hosting entails storage or access from outside the EEA, **Chapter V / Schrems II** transfer rules apply [1][6][12]. Third, **sector security law**: cloud, data-centre, CDN and managed-service providers are named **"digital infrastructure" entities** under **NIS2** [2], and a cloud provider serving financial entities is an **ICT third-party provider** under **DORA** that may be designated a **critical ICT third-party provider (CTPP)** under direct ESA oversight — the first such designations were made on 18 November 2025 [3][11]. Fourth, the **Data Act** makes cloud "data processing services" directly subject to **switching, portability and interoperability** duties, with switching charges prohibited from **12 January 2027** [4][10]. Fifth, **security standards and certification**: ISO/IEC 27001 with the cloud extensions **27017** (cloud security) and **27018** (cloud PII), plus **CSA STAR**, are the recognised assurance vehicles, while the **EUCS** remains **not yet adopted** [13][14][15][16][18][7][8].

The single most important operational message: **map every control to an owner** (provider vs. customer), keep GDPR **accountability** with the customer, and treat certifications as **evidence, not a compliance guarantee**.

text:
- The **shared-responsibility model** allocates security controls between provider and customer, but **GDPR accountability stays with the controller** — usually the cloud customer — and cannot be contracted away [1]. *(Best practice; accountability is a legal obligation under GDPR Art. 5(2).)*
- A hosting provider is typically a **processor**; the customer must put an **Article 28 DPA** in place with the mandatory terms (sub-processor controls, security, assistance, deletion/return) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Article 32** requires security of processing appropriate to the risk (encryption, pseudonymisation, CIA + resilience, effectiveness testing) — met in cloud through the provider's platform controls **and** the customer's configuration [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Where hosting stores or exposes personal data outside the EEA, **Chapter V** transfer mechanisms and the **Schrems II** requirement to assess third-country government-access risk and add supplementary measures apply [1][6][12]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **NIS2** names **cloud computing, data-centre, CDN and managed/managed-security service providers** as "digital infrastructure" / "ICT service management" entities — squarely in scope as essential or important entities, with several required to register with ENISA [2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **DORA** treats a cloud provider serving financial entities as an **ICT third-party provider**; if systemically important it may be designated a **CTPP** under direct ESA oversight (first designations 18 Nov 2025), and financial-entity contracts must carry the **Art. 30** key provisions [3][11]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- The **Data Act** subjects cloud "data processing services" to **switching, export and interoperability** duties; **switching charges are prohibited from 12 January 2027** [4][10]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- **ISO/IEC 27017** (cloud security controls) and **ISO/IEC 27018** (PII in public cloud) extend ISO/IEC 27001/27002 for cloud; **CSA STAR** provides a cloud-specific assurance registry [13][14][15][16][18]. *(Best practice / standards.)*
- The **EUCS** cloud certification scheme is, at this document's date, **still a candidate/draft** under the Cybersecurity Act (only the **EUCC** products scheme has been adopted); do not assume EUCS certification is available [5][7][8][9]. *(Verified status — not asserted.)*

It supports: (a) allocating obligations across the provider/customer boundary (the responsibility matrix); (b) triaging which regimes apply to a given hosting arrangement (GDPR processor/transfer duties, NIS2, DORA, Data Act); and (c) choosing assurance vehicles (ISO/IEC 27001/27017/27018, CSA STAR, and — when adopted — EUCS). **In scope:** The shared-responsibility model and a provider/customer **responsibility matrix**; GDPR **controller/processor** roles for hosting, **Article 28** DPAs and **Article 32** security at a foundational, cross-referencing level; **international transfers** for cloud (**Chapter V / Schrems II**) at a foundational level; **NIS2** obligations for cloud/infrastructure providers; **DORA** for cloud serving financial entities including **CTPP** oversight; the **Data Act** cloud-switching, portability and interoperability rules including the phase-out of switching charges; security standards (**ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018, 27701**, **CSA STAR**); and the status of the **EUCS** under the Cybersecurity Act.

**Out of scope (spun off to the research backlog):**

- **Transfer-mechanism mechanics** — SCC module selection, Transfer Impact Assessments, supplementary measures, the UK IDTA/Addendum → `international-transfers` (planned).
- **EUCS in detail** — assurance levels (Basic/Substantial/High), sovereignty requirements and the adoption debate → `eucs-deep-dive` (planned).
- **Provider-specific shared-responsibility models** — AWS/Azure/GCP control matrices and service-by-service splits → `cloud-provider-responsibility-matrices` (planned).
- **Data Act cloud-switching mechanics** → `data-act-cloud-switching` (planned).
- **DORA CTPP oversight mechanics and Art. 30 contract detail** → `dora-oversight-framework`, `dora-third-party-contracts` (planned).

**Assumptions:** The reader has read `gdpr-foundations` (controller/processor, Chapter V), and can consult `nis2-foundations`, `dora-foundations`, `data-act-foundations`, `privacy-engineering-foundations` and `cybersecurity-foundations`. *Shared terms — controller, processor, ISMS, CIA triad, essential/important entity, CTPP, data processing service — are defined in `GLOSSARY.md`. Only cloud-hosting-specific terms are defined here.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Shared-responsibility model | The division of security and compliance controls between the cloud provider (responsible for security "of" the cloud — hardware, virtualisation, physical facilities) and the customer (responsible for security "in" the cloud — data, identity, configuration, application). The split shifts across IaaS/PaaS/SaaS. | [1][13] |
| IaaS / PaaS / SaaS | Cloud service models: Infrastructure- (compute/storage/network), Platform- (managed runtime/middleware) and Software-as-a-Service (managed application). More is provider-managed moving from IaaS to SaaS, shifting the responsibility boundary. | [15] |
| Data processing service | An on-demand, scalable cloud or edge computing service (Data Act Art. 2(8)); the Data Act term that brings cloud providers within its switching/interoperability regime. | [4] |
| ICT third-party service provider | An undertaking providing ICT services (including cloud/hosting) to financial entities (DORA Art. 3(19)); reached directly by DORA's third-party-risk and oversight regime. | [3] |
| EUCS | The candidate **European Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services**, developed by ENISA under the Cybersecurity Act (Reg (EU) 2019/881); **not yet adopted** as an implementing act at this document's date. | [5][7][8] |
| CSA STAR | The Cloud Security Alliance's Security, Trust, Assurance & Risk programme — a public registry and multi-level (self-assessment / third-party certification / continuous) cloud-assurance scheme built on the Cloud Controls Matrix. | [18] |

text:
Cloud hosting reorganised IT from owned, on-premises assets into **shared, multi-tenant, on-demand services** operated by third parties — often across borders and at hyperscale. That shift concentrated both **capability** and **risk**: a handful of providers now underpin large parts of the economy, so their security, resilience, portability and jurisdictional exposure became matters of public regulation rather than private contract alone.

EU/UK law responded on several fronts, each addressed in its own foundations document. The **GDPR** (2016) made the **controller/processor** split and **security of processing** binding, and — after **Schrems II** (2020) invalidated Privacy Shield — turned international transfers into a case-by-case risk assessment [1][6]. **NIS2** (2022) brought cloud, data-centre and CDN providers into a horizontal cybersecurity regime as **digital-infrastructure** entities [2]. **DORA** (2022) added a financial-sector regime with, for the first time, **direct EU oversight** of the most critical ICT (including cloud) providers [3]. The **Data Act** (2023) attacked **vendor lock-in**, making switching and interoperability legal duties for cloud "data processing services" [4]. And the **Cybersecurity Act** (2019) created the EU certification framework under which a cloud-specific scheme (**EUCS**) has been drafted but — unlike the products scheme (**EUCC**) — **not yet adopted** [5][8]. This document synthesises those threads for the hosting context.

text:
This document describes a **cross-cutting application**, not a single instrument. The binding duties live in the instruments below (and in their dedicated documents); they are summarised here as they bear on cloud hosting.

- **GDPR (Reg (EU) 2016/679)** — **Art. 28** (processor obligations and mandatory DPA terms), **Art. 32** (security of processing), and **Chapter V, Arts. 44–50** (transfers to third countries). The hosting provider is normally a **processor**; the customer is normally the **controller** and retains accountability (Art. 5(2)) [1]. *(Legal obligation — see `gdpr-foundations`, `privacy-engineering-foundations`.)*
- **NIS2 (Dir (EU) 2022/2555)** — cloud computing, data-centre, CDN and managed/managed-security service providers are **Annex I "digital infrastructure" / "ICT service management" (B2B)** entity types; in-scope providers are **essential or important entities** subject to Art. 21 risk-management measures and Art. 23 incident reporting, and several must **register with ENISA (Art. 27)** [2]. *(Legal obligation — see `nis2-foundations`.)*
- **DORA (Reg (EU) 2022/2554)** — a cloud provider serving financial entities is an **ICT third-party service provider** (Art. 3(19)); customers must embed the **Art. 30 key contractual provisions**, and systemically important providers may be designated **CTPPs (Art. 31)** under the **Union Oversight Framework** with a **Lead Overseer** (Arts. 31–44) [3]. *(Legal obligation — see `dora-foundations`.)*
- **Data Act (Reg (EU) 2023/2854)** — "data processing services" must remove **switching** obstacles, support **export/portability** and **interoperability** (Chapter VI, Arts. 23–31; Chapter VIII, Arts. 33–36), and **stop charging switching fees from 12 January 2027** (Art. 29); Art. 32 adds safeguards against unlawful third-country governmental access to non-personal data [4]. *(Legal obligation — phased; see `data-act-foundations`.)*
- **Cybersecurity Act (Reg (EU) 2019/881)** — establishes the EU cybersecurity **certification framework**; ENISA prepared the **EUCS** candidate cloud scheme, which **has not been adopted** as an implementing act at this document's date [5][7][8]. *(Framework in force; the cloud scheme is not yet adopted.)*

## Relevant Articles

| Article | Obligation | Source |
|---------|------------|--------|
| GDPR Art. 28 | Processor obligations; mandatory DPA terms (documented instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processor authorisation, assistance, deletion/return, audit). | [1] |
| GDPR Art. 32 | Security of processing — risk-appropriate TOMs; encryption/pseudonymisation; CIA + resilience; effectiveness testing. | [1] |
| GDPR Arts. 44–50 | Transfers to third countries — adequacy, appropriate safeguards (SCCs, BCRs), derogations; Schrems II risk assessment. | [1][6] |
| NIS2 Art. 21 | Cybersecurity risk-management measures for essential/important entities (incl. supply-chain security). | [2] |
| NIS2 Art. 23 | Significant-incident reporting (early warning, notification, final report). | [2] |
| NIS2 Art. 27 | ENISA registration for cloud, data-centre, CDN, DNS, managed/managed-security providers and certain digital services. | [2] |
| DORA Art. 30 | Key contractual provisions required in ICT service arrangements (audit/access, security, incident cooperation, sub-outsourcing, exit). | [3] |
| DORA Arts. 31–44 | Designation of CTPPs and the Union Oversight Framework (Lead Overseer powers). | [3][11] |
| Data Act Arts. 23–31 | Switching between data-processing services; removal of obstacles; **Art. 29** gradual withdrawal of switching charges (prohibited from 12 Jan 2027). | [4][10] |
| Data Act Arts. 33–36 | Interoperability of data, data-sharing mechanisms and data-processing services. | [4] |
| Data Act Art. 32 | Safeguards against unlawful third-country governmental access to non-personal data held in the EU. | [4] |
| Cybersecurity Act Arts. 46–54 | EU cybersecurity certification framework; European schemes (assurance levels basic/substantial/high). | [5] |

## Relevant Recitals

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| GDPR Recital 81 | Controllers should use only processors providing sufficient guarantees; the relationship is governed by a contract (Art. 28). | [1] |
| GDPR Recital 83 | Security measures should be risk-based, guarding against accidental/unlawful destruction, loss, alteration or disclosure. | [1] |
| Data Act Recital 80 area | Rationale for removing switching obstacles and lock-in in data-processing services. | [4] |
| Cybersecurity Act Recital 65 area | Certification schemes should raise trust and assurance in ICT products, services and processes across the internal market. | [5] |

*Recitals are not binding but aid interpretation of the enacting articles.*

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable at the foundational level, with one cross-referenced exception.** Cloud hosting is a cross-cutting application rather than a single instrument, so there is no distinct body of "cloud hosting" case law. The one directly load-bearing judgment is **Schrems II** (C-311/18, ECLI:EU:C:2020:559), which invalidated the EU–US Privacy Shield and conditioned reliance on Standard Contractual Clauses on a case-by-case assessment of third-country access risk and supplementary measures — foundational for cloud transfers and treated in `gdpr-foundations` [6]. NIS2, DORA and the Data Act are too recent for settled case law on their cloud-facing provisions [2][3][4].

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **EDPB** — on transfers, **Recommendations 01/2020** set out the six-step methodology (know your transfers, identify the mechanism, assess third-country law, adopt supplementary measures, procedural steps, re-evaluate) that operationalises Schrems II for cloud data flows; SCCs alone do not suffice where third-country law compromises them [12]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ENISA** — prepared the **EUCS** candidate scheme under the Cybersecurity Act and maintains the certification portal; ENISA's own page presents EUCS as a **draft candidate** scheme, not an adopted regulation [7]. ENISA also supports NIS2 implementation for digital-infrastructure providers. *(Regulatory / technical guidance.)*
- **European Commission** — confirms that under the certification framework the **only adopted scheme is EUCC** (Common Criteria, for ICT products, available from 27 February 2025); a cloud services scheme is **not among the adopted schemes**, and the Commission proposed a **revision of the Cybersecurity Act on 20 January 2026** partly to unblock scheme development [8][9]. On the Data Act, the Commission frames the switching rules as targeting **vendor lock-in**, requiring removal of commercial, technical and contractual obstacles and withdrawal of switching charges over a transition period [10]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **ESAs (EBA/EIOPA/ESMA)** — designated the **first CTPPs on 18 November 2025** (reported as 19 providers, including hyperscale cloud), placing them under direct oversight with a Lead Overseer; the list is re-assessed over time, so cloud customers in finance should track it [11]. *(Regulatory interpretation — verify the live list.)*
- Regulators consistently treat **certification as evidence, not proof**: ISO/IEC 27001/27017/27018 or CSA STAR are strong evidence of appropriate measures but do not by themselves discharge a specific legal duty on specific facts [8][13]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
title: Cloud Hosting: Compliance Foundations
legal_basis: Cross-cutting — Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) Arts. 28, 32 & Chapter V; Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2); Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA); Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act); Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (Cybersecurity Act)

text:
- **The responsibility boundary shifts by service model** — in **IaaS** the customer owns the OS, runtime, data, identity and configuration; in **PaaS** the provider absorbs the runtime/middleware; in **SaaS** the provider manages nearly everything except data, identity/access and tenant configuration. Misconfiguration on the customer side of the line is the dominant cloud failure mode [1][13][15]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Encryption and key management** — encryption at rest/in transit and, where feasible, **customer-managed keys (BYOK/HYOK)** support Art. 32 and reduce exposure to provider or third-country access; key custody is a decisive control for transfer-risk mitigation [1][12]. *(Legal obligation, met via controls.)*
- **Tenant isolation and identity** — strong multi-tenant isolation, least-privilege IAM, and per-request authorisation (zero-trust) are core cloud controls; identity is the primary perimeter (see `cybersecurity-foundations`) [1]. *(Best practice.)*
- **Logging, resilience and backup** — availability and recoverability are explicit legal outcomes (GDPR Art. 32; NIS2 Art. 21 business continuity/backup; DORA response/recovery); ensure immutable, tested backups, centralised logging and a tested exit/portability path [1][2][3]. *(Legal obligation, met via controls.)*
- **Portability and interoperability by design** — the Data Act makes **export in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format** and **functional equivalence (where feasible)** engineering requirements, not just contract clauses; build open interfaces and avoid proprietary lock-in ahead of the 12 Jan 2027 charge phase-out [4][10]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- **Sub-processor / sub-outsourcing transparency** — maintain a current sub-processor register and flow-down controls; this serves GDPR Art. 28, DORA Art. 30 sub-outsourcing conditions and NIS2 supply-chain security simultaneously [1][2][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*

## Cloud responsibility matrix

**BEST PRACTICE / EDITORIAL** — an indicative allocation; the exact split is defined by the specific service and contract (provider-specific matrices are deferred to `cloud-provider-responsibility-matrices`). "P" = provider-led, "C" = customer-led, "S" = shared.

| Control domain | IaaS | PaaS | SaaS | Anchoring obligation |
|----------------|------|------|------|----------------------|
| Physical / data-centre security | P | P | P | NIS2 Art. 21; ISO 27017 [2][15] |
| Host / hypervisor / virtualisation | P | P | P | NIS2 Art. 21; ISO 27017 [2][15] |
| Network controls (segmentation, firewalling) | S | S | P | GDPR Art. 32; ISO 27017 [1][15] |
| Operating system / patching | C | P | P | GDPR Art. 32; NIS2 Art. 21 [1][2] |
| Application security / secure SDLC | C | S | P | GDPR Art. 32; OWASP (see `cybersecurity-foundations`) [1] |
| Identity & access management | C | C | S | GDPR Art. 32 [1] |
| Data classification & encryption (incl. keys) | C | C | S | GDPR Art. 32; ISO 27018 [1][16] |
| Configuration / tenant hardening | C | C | C | GDPR Art. 32; ISO 27017 [1][15] |
| Logging, monitoring & incident detection | S | S | S | NIS2 Art. 23; DORA Arts. 17–19 [2][3] |
| Backup, resilience & tested recovery | S | S | S | GDPR Art. 32; NIS2 Art. 21; DORA [1][2][3] |
| International-transfer safeguards | S | S | S | GDPR Chapter V; Schrems II [1][6] |
| DPA / Art. 28 terms & sub-processor control | S | S | S | GDPR Art. 28 [1] |
| Exit, portability & switching support | S | S | S | Data Act Arts. 23–31 [4] |
| **GDPR accountability** | **C** | **C** | **C** | GDPR Art. 5(2) [1] |

**Key point:** accountability (bottom row) is **always the customer/controller's** and never shifts with the service model, even where the provider performs the underlying control [1].

text:
*This document is itself the hosting synthesis; this section states the provider- and customer-facing obligations directly.*

- **Provider as processor** — a hosting provider processing personal data on a customer's instructions is a **processor** and must accept **Art. 28** terms; acting outside instructions, or determining purposes/means, risks re-characterisation as a **controller** with direct liability [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **NIS2 direct scope** — cloud, data-centre, CDN and managed/managed-security providers are **digital-infrastructure/ICT-service-management** entities; in-scope providers must implement Art. 21 measures, report significant incidents (Art. 23) and register with ENISA (Art. 27) where required [2]. *(Legal obligation — assess role, per Member State.)*
- **DORA for financial-sector hosting** — providers serving financial entities must support **Art. 30** contract rights (audit/access, security, incident cooperation, sub-outsourcing controls, exit assistance); a **CTPP** designation adds direct ESA oversight duties (EU coordination point, cooperation with the Lead Overseer, oversight fees) [3][11]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Data Act switching duties** — providers must remove switching obstacles, give pre-contractual switching information, support export/interoperability, and **stop charging switching fees from 12 January 2027**; hosting contracts must carry the mandated switching clauses, and Art. 13 unfair-term protections constrain terms imposed on SME customers [4][10]. *(Legal obligation — phased.)*
- **Transfers and government-access exposure** — where the estate spans non-EEA regions or a provider is subject to third-country access laws, apply **Chapter V** mechanisms with a transfer-risk assessment and supplementary measures (encryption/key custody, split processing), and address the Data Act Art. 32 non-personal-data safeguard in parallel [1][4][6][12]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Assurance posture** — evidence controls via **ISO/IEC 27001** plus **27017/27018** (and **27701** where the estate processes PII at scale) and/or **CSA STAR**; treat these as accountability evidence, and monitor **EUCS** for eventual adoption before relying on it [13][15][16][17][18][7]. *(Best practice.)*

text:
- **Most pure game hosting is not a NIS2 digital-infrastructure entity** — online gaming is not among the NIS2 Annex I/II sectors, so a studio or game-server operator is generally not an essential/important entity *by virtue of gaming alone*; but if it *also* provides cloud, data-centre, CDN or managed-security services, those activities pull it into scope regardless of the gaming context (see `nis2-foundations`) [2]. *(Interpretation — assess by activity.)*
- **Cloud switching applies to game backends** — studios hosting on cloud/edge "data processing services" benefit from the Data Act switching rules as **customers**, and (if they resell managed hosting) may owe them as **providers** [4][10]. *(Legal obligation — assess role.)*
- **Player personal data stays under the GDPR** — telemetry, accounts and matchmaking data that are personal remain governed by GDPR Art. 28/32 and Chapter V; children's-data defaults heighten the duty (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`) [1][6]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **DORA only via a financial nexus** — game hosting engages DORA only where the operator is itself a financial entity (e.g. a MiCA crypto-asset service provider or embedded payments arm) or supplies ICT services to one [3]. *(Interpretation — narrow.)*

text:
- **Cloud-hosted AI inherits every hosting duty** — training/inference workloads on cloud infrastructure carry the same Art. 28/32, transfer, NIS2 and (in finance) DORA obligations as any other workload; the model, training data and pipeline are assets in the responsibility matrix [1][2][3]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Managed AI / model-as-a-service is a processor relationship** — using a provider's hosted model to process personal data typically makes the provider a **processor** requiring an Art. 28 DPA, with special attention to whether prompts/outputs are reused for provider model training (which can breach instructions/purpose limitation) [1]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Transfers bite hard for AI** — hosted-model APIs often route to non-EEA regions; apply Chapter V assessment and prefer EEA/in-region inference or customer-managed keys [1][6][12]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **AI Act overlap** — high-risk AI systems' security, robustness and data-governance duties run in parallel with hosting controls; see `ai-act-foundations` / `ai-governance-foundations`. *(Cross-reference.)*

1. **Map roles and the responsibility boundary** — for each service, document controller/processor status and the provider/customer control split (use the matrix above). *(OBLIGATION to allocate — GDPR Arts. 28/32; BEST PRACTICE for the matrix.)* [1]
2. **Put Article 28 DPAs in place** — with every provider and sub-processor, including sub-processor authorisation, security, assistance and deletion/return terms. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
3. **Implement Article 32 controls** — encryption (prefer customer-managed keys), IAM/least privilege, isolation, logging, tested backups, and regular effectiveness testing. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1]
4. **Assess and safeguard transfers** — inventory non-EEA data flows, apply Chapter V mechanisms and the EDPB six-step method, add supplementary measures. *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][6][12]
5. **Confirm NIS2 status** — determine whether the provider (or the customer's own infrastructure role) is an essential/important digital-infrastructure entity; implement Art. 21 measures, Art. 23 reporting and Art. 27 registration where applicable. *(OBLIGATION where in scope.)* [2]
6. **Finance: embed DORA third-party controls** — include Art. 30 key provisions, maintain the register of information, assess CTPP exposure and build tested exit strategies. *(OBLIGATION where DORA applies.)* [3][11]
7. **Prepare for Data Act switching** — remove switching obstacles, expose export/interoperability, and eliminate switching charges by **12 January 2027**. *(OBLIGATION — phased.)* [4][10]
8. **Adopt cloud assurance standards** — ISO/IEC 27001 with 27017/27018, and/or CSA STAR; obtain provider certifications and audit reports (e.g. SOC 2) as accountability evidence. *(BEST PRACTICE.)* [13][15][16][18]
9. **Track EUCS and the Cybersecurity Act revision** — do not assume EUCS certification exists; monitor adoption and the 2026 CSA revision. *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)* [7][8][9]
10. **Design a tested exit** — maintain and rehearse a portability/exit plan so switching, DORA substitutability and resilience expectations are executable. *(BEST PRACTICE; obligation elements under Data Act and DORA.)* [3][4]

title: Game Hosting: Compliance Foundations
legal_basis: UK GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679; DPA 2018 (esp. ss.9, 123); ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC & PECR 2003; Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA); Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act); consumer-protection law (UCPD 2005/29/EC as amended by 2019/2161; DMCCA 2024); Gambling Act 2005; Online Safety Act 2023

text:
Online and multiplayer **game hosting** is not governed by a single "games law". It sits at the intersection of the compliance regimes already documented in this knowledge base, and its distinctive risk profile comes from three facts: games are **very likely to be accessed by children**, they are **data-rich real-time services** (player identifiers, telemetry, voice/chat), and they are **monetised** through in-game purchases, subscriptions and randomised items. This document maps those overlapping obligations for operators hosting games for EU and UK audiences and points to the foundational documents where each regime is treated in depth.

Five themes dominate. First, **children's data**: the age of valid consent for information-society services is **13 in the UK** (DPA 2018 s.9) against a GDPR default of 16 (Member States may set any age down to 13) [1][2], and the **ICO Age-Appropriate Design Code ("Children's Code")** imposes 15 design standards on services likely to be accessed by children — squarely including games [3][14][15]. Second, **player identifiers and telemetry** are personal data, so data minimisation and purpose limitation apply to accounts, device IDs, matchmaking and anti-cheat (cross-ref `privacy-engineering-foundations`). Third, **ePrivacy/PECR** governs the analytics and advertising **SDKs** typical of games: non-essential storage/access needs consent before it fires [4][5]. Fourth, where a game **hosts user-generated content, chat or a marketplace** it can be an "intermediary"/"online platform" under the **DSA**, and in the UK a user-to-user service under the **Online Safety Act 2023** [6][10][21]. Fifth, **monetisation** engages consumer-protection law (dark-pattern and pricing rules under the UCPD/Omnibus and the UK **DMCCA 2024**) and the **loot-box** debate [8][9][11][12][16][17].

On the two items that most often go stale: the UK **has not** brought loot boxes within the Gambling Act 2005, relying instead on **industry-led Ukie guidance (July 2023)** and monitoring [16][17]; and **PEGI overhauled its criteria from June 2026** so that games with paid random items now carry a **PEGI 16** rating (PEGI 18 for social-casino mechanics) rather than only an informational notice [18][19]. Both positions were live-verified for this document.

text:
- Game hosting has **no bespoke statute**; compliance is the *union* of GDPR/UK GDPR, ePrivacy/PECR, the DSA (and UK Online Safety Act), consumer law, the AI Act and cybersecurity duties, with children's protection as the through-line. *(Editorial synthesis.)*
- The **consent age** for online services is **13 in the UK** (DPA 2018 s.9) and **16 by GDPR default**, adjustable by Member States down to 13 — multi-territory games must gate per jurisdiction [1][2]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- The **ICO Children's Code** applies to any online service (games included) **"likely to be accessed by children"** in the UK and requires high-privacy defaults, data minimisation, geolocation off by default, and no manipulative nudges; it is issued under **DPA 2018 s.123** and enforceable since 2 September 2021 [3][14][15]. *(Legal obligation / regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Player identifiers, device IDs, IP addresses, telemetry, matchmaking and anti-cheat data are personal data**; minimisation, purpose limitation and retention limits apply (cross-ref `gdpr-foundations`, `privacy-engineering-foundations`). *(Legal obligation.)*
- **In-game analytics/ads SDKs** store or read information on the device and require **consent before firing** under Art. 5(3) ePrivacy / PECR — "strictly necessary" is read narrowly and excludes analytics and advertising [4][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- Games that **host user-generated content, chat or a marketplace** may be **intermediary/hosting services or "online platforms" under the DSA** (notice-and-action, minors' protection in Art. 28, no dark patterns in Art. 25), and **user-to-user/search services under the UK Online Safety Act 2023** [6][10][21]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **In-game purchases, subscriptions and dark patterns** engage consumer law: the EU **UCPD (as amended by the Omnibus Directive)** and **Consumer Rights Directive**, and in the UK the **DMCCA 2024** (drip-pricing ban in force 6 April 2025; subscription rules expected 2026) [9][11][12][13]. *(Legal obligation; cross-ref `consumer-rights-foundations` (planned).)*
- **Loot boxes** are **not** regulated under the UK **Gambling Act 2005**; the government (July 2022) found an *association* but no established *causal* link with harm and adopted **industry-led Ukie guidance (18 July 2023)** — children should not buy loot boxes without parental consent, with spending controls and probability disclosure [8][16][17]. *(Legal / regulatory fact — live-verified.)*
- **PEGI changed its rating criteria from June 2026**: paid random items now attract **PEGI 16** (PEGI 18 for social-casino mechanics) and blockchain/NFT mechanics **PEGI 18**, replacing the 2020 "Includes Paid Random Items" notice-only approach [18][19]. *(Regulatory/industry fact — live-verified.)*
- **AI Act transparency (Art. 50)** applies to in-game **AI chatbots** (disclose the user is interacting with AI) and **generative/synthetic content** (machine-readable marking); most game AI (NPC behaviour, matchmaking) is **minimal-risk** with no mandatory obligations [7] (cross-ref `ai-act-foundations`). *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*

*Shared terms (personal data, consent, controller, processor, online platform, intermediary service) are defined in `GLOSSARY.md` and carry over. Only game-specific terms are defined here; deeper areas are deferred to the backlog documents named in Scope.*

| Term | Definition | Source |
|------|------------|--------|
| Information-society service (ISS) | A service normally provided for remuneration, at a distance, by electronic means and at the individual request of a recipient — the category to which the child-consent age rules attach. Online games are ISS. | [1][2] |
| Children's Code (Age-Appropriate Design Code) | The ICO statutory code of practice under DPA 2018 s.123 setting 15 design standards for online services likely to be accessed by children. | [3][14][15] |
| Likely to be accessed by children | The ICO threshold triggering the Children's Code: the possibility that the service is accessed by under-18s is more probable than not, judged on the nature and appeal of the service. Games are typically caught. | [14][15] |
| Telemetry | Behavioural and technical event data emitted by a game client/server (inputs, sessions, performance, crash, matchmaking, anti-cheat signals); where linkable to a player it is personal data. | [1] |
| Loot box / paid random item | An optional in-game purchase where the player does not know exactly what they receive before buying (loot boxes, card packs, gacha, prize wheels), bought with real money and/or in-game currency. | [17][18] |
| Dark pattern (online choice architecture) | An interface design that materially distorts or impairs a user's ability to make free, informed choices (e.g. drip pricing, forced action, nagging, obstructed cancellation). | [6][9][11] |
| PEGI | Pan-European Game Information — the self-regulatory age-rating system used across most of Europe (statutory in some states); applies content descriptors and, from June 2026, interactive-risk age categories. | [18][19] |

text: Games moved from boxed, single-player products to **always-online services** monetised by microtransactions, subscriptions and randomised content, hosting large volumes of **user-generated content** (chat, voice, mods, user-built levels, item marketplaces). That shift pulled games into regimes designed for other sectors. Data-protection law applies because games process rich behavioural data about a population **disproportionately made up of children**; the EU/UK responded with a lowered but explicit child-consent age and, in the UK, a design code specifically for children's online services [1][2][3]. The **ePrivacy** cookie/SDK rule reaches the analytics and ad tooling that games embed [4]. The **DSA** and the UK **Online Safety Act 2023** reach games that host public UGC or a marketplace [6][10]. Consumer-protection law and the **loot-box** controversy reach monetisation design [8][9][16][17]. And the **AI Act** now reaches AI-driven characters, chatbots and generative content [7]. This document exists because no single foundational document captures that intersection for a games operator.

text:
Game hosting is governed by the *cumulative* application of several instruments. The table states the obligation source plainly; interpretation is separated into the Regulatory Interpretation section.

## Relevant Articles

| Provision | Obligation (as relevant to game hosting) | Source |
|-----------|------------------------------------------|--------|
| GDPR Art. 8 | Child's consent to ISS valid from **16**; Member States may lower to **not below 13**; controller must make reasonable efforts to verify parental authorisation for younger children. | [1] |
| DPA 2018 s.9 | Sets the UK ISS child-consent age at **13** (modifying Art. 8(1)). | [2] |
| DPA 2018 s.123 | Requires the ICO to prepare the **Age-Appropriate Design Code**; the Code is the statutory basis of the Children's Code. | [3] |
| GDPR Arts. 5, 6, 25, 32 | Principles (minimisation, purpose/storage limitation), lawful basis, data-protection by design/default, and security — apply to accounts, telemetry, anti-cheat (see `gdpr-foundations`, `privacy-engineering-foundations`). | [1] |
| ePrivacy Art. 5(3) / PECR reg. 6 | Consent required before storing/accessing information on the device (analytics/ad **SDKs**, local storage), unless strictly necessary for a requested service. | [4][5] |
| DSA Arts. 6, 16, 25, 28, 33 | Hosting-service liability conditions; notice-and-action; **prohibition on dark patterns**; **protection of minors** (no profiling-based ads to minors; safety/privacy by design); VLOP threshold (45m avg. monthly EU users). | [6] |
| Online Safety Act 2023 (UK) | Duties on user-to-user and search services (illegal-content and children's-safety duties), regulated by Ofcom — applies to many games with chat/UGC. | [10][21] |
| AI Act Art. 50 | Transparency: disclose to users they are interacting with an **AI system** (e.g. chatbots) and mark **AI-generated/synthetic content** in machine-readable form. | [7] |
| UCPD 2005/29/EC (as amended by Omnibus 2019/2161) | Prohibits unfair/misleading/aggressive commercial practices, including certain dark patterns, and adds transparency duties (rankings, reviews). | [11][12] |
| Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU | Pre-contractual information, digital-content rules and cancellation rights relevant to purchases/subscriptions. | [13] |
| DMCCA 2024 (UK) | Unfair-commercial-practices regime (incl. **drip pricing** banned from 6 Apr 2025), subscription-contract rules (expected 2026), CMA direct-enforcement powers. | [9] |
| Gambling Act 2005 (UK) | Licensing regime for gambling; the government has decided **not** to extend it to loot boxes at this time. | [8][16][17] |

## Relevant Recitals

*Recitals aid interpretation and are not binding operative provisions.*

| Recital | Interpretive point | Source |
|---------|--------------------|--------|
| GDPR Recital 38 | Children merit **specific protection** as they may be less aware of risks and their rights — the interpretive anchor for children's-data measures in games. | [1] |
| GDPR Recital 58 | Information addressed to children should be in **clear, plain language** a child can easily understand. | [1] |
| DSA Recital 71 | Minors' protection online justifies design measures and the ban on profiling-based advertising to minors. | [6] |
| AI Act Recital 132 | Transparency obligations for AI that interacts with people and for synthetic/generated content, so users know what they are dealing with. | [7] |

## Relevant Case Law

**Not Applicable at this level.** This is a sector synthesis; the load-bearing judgments live in the foundational documents and are not re-litigated here — e.g. *Planet49* (C-673/17) on cookie/SDK consent (`eprivacy-foundations`), and *Breyer*/*Nowak* on the breadth of "personal data" (`gdpr-foundations`). Game-specific domestic case law (e.g. on loot boxes as gambling) is emerging unevenly across Member States and is deferred to `loot-box-regulation` (planned). [4][6]

text:
**REGULATORY INTERPRETATION (not statutory text).**

- **ICO — Children's Code.** The ICO treats the Code as applying to services **"likely to be accessed by children"**, a lower bar than "directed at" children; most games meet it. The 15 standards require the **best interests of the child** as a primary consideration, **high-privacy defaults**, **data minimisation**, **geolocation off by default**, transparency in child-friendly terms, and **no nudge techniques** that push children to weaken privacy or over-share. Enforceable since 2 September 2021 [14][15]. *(Regulatory interpretation of GDPR/DPA duties.)*
- **UK loot boxes.** DCMS's July 2022 response found a **consistent association** between loot-box use and problem gambling but concluded a **causal link is not established**, and decided **not** to amend or extend the Gambling Act 2005; it set the objective that **children should not buy loot boxes without parental consent** and pursued **industry-led** protections [16][17]. The trade body **Ukie published industry guidance on 18 July 2023** (default restrictions for under-18s, spending controls, probability disclosure), with government monitoring over a 12-month implementation period and independent research via the Video Games Research Framework [16]. *(Regulatory position — live-verified; policy, not statute.)*
- **PEGI.** Since April 2020 PEGI applied an informational **"Includes Paid Random Items"** notice. From **June 2026** PEGI introduced **interactive-risk categories**: games submitted with **paid random items are rated PEGI 16** (PEGI 18 for social-casino mechanics), **blockchain/NFT** mechanics **PEGI 18**, time-/quantity-limited offers PEGI 12, "play-by-appointment" mechanics PEGI 7–12, and entirely unrestricted communication features PEGI 18 [18][19]. *(Industry self-regulation — live-verified; statutory in some Member States.)*
- **CMA (UK) / DMCCA.** The CMA now has **direct enforcement** of consumer law under the DMCCA; the ban on **drip pricing** and the updated unfair-commercial-practices list took effect **6 April 2025**, and dedicated **subscription-contract** rules are expected in 2026 [9]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **EDPB / DSA supervision.** For games that are online platforms, the Commission and national Digital Services Coordinators enforce the DSA, including the **dark-patterns ban (Art. 25)** and **minors' protection (Art. 28)** (see `dsa-foundations`) [6]. *(Regulatory interpretation.)*

text:
- **Data mapping first.** Inventory every player-data flow: account/identity, device IDs, IP, session/telemetry, voice/chat, purchase history, matchmaking, and **anti-cheat** signals. Most are personal data; classify by lawful basis and retention (see `privacy-engineering-foundations`). *(Best practice grounded in obligation.)* [1]
- **Data minimisation in telemetry.** Collect the minimum event data needed for the stated purpose; pseudonymise where possible; separate analytics identifiers from account identity; set retention limits and delete/aggregate on schedule. *(Legal obligation — Art. 5.)* [1]
- **Consent-before-set for SDKs.** Gate analytics/ad SDKs and any non-essential device storage/access behind consent; only strictly-necessary functions (save state, security, load balancing, anti-fraud session) may fire pre-consent [4][5]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Child-aware defaults.** Where the service is likely to be accessed by children, ship **high-privacy defaults**, geolocation and social discovery **off by default**, and profiling/behavioural-ad features off, per the Children's Code [14][15]. *(Regulatory interpretation of obligation.)*
- **Age assurance.** Implement proportionate age-assurance/parental-consent flows for the 13/16 thresholds and for age-rated content; avoid collecting more identity data than the assurance purpose needs. *(Best practice; age-assurance detail → backlog.)* [2][14]
- **No manipulative UX.** Avoid dark patterns in purchase, consent and cancellation flows — relevant simultaneously under the Children's Code (nudges), DSA Art. 25, and consumer law [6][11][14]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*

*Cloud/infrastructure mechanics are treated in `cloud-hosting-foundations` (planned sibling); only game-relevant points are noted here.*

- **Controller/processor split.** A studio/publisher is typically the **controller**; the cloud/game-hosting provider and managed live-ops vendors are **processors** needing Art. 28 contracts (see `gdpr-foundations`). *(Legal obligation.)*
- **International transfers.** Global player bases mean cross-border flows; apply the EU/UK transfer mechanisms (adequacy, SCCs, UK IDTA/Addendum) — see `uk-gdpr-foundations` and the transfers backlog. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Server/network logs as personal & traffic data.** Game-server and network logs may be personal data and, for communications features, traffic data — apply minimisation and retention limits (see `eprivacy-foundations`). *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Resilience & availability.** Availability is both a security objective (GDPR Art. 32 names resilience) and a player-trust issue; design for **DDoS** mitigation, capacity and failover (see Security below and `cybersecurity-foundations`). *(Legal obligation / best practice.)* [1][20]

text:
This is the core section — the game-specific overlay on the regimes above.

- **Children everywhere.** Treat games as **likely to be accessed by children** unless robust, evidenced age assurance shows otherwise; apply the Children's Code, the 13/16 consent thresholds, and DSA Art. 28 minors' protections together [1][2][14]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **UGC, chat and marketplaces → platform duties.** If players can post content others see (chat, voice, mods, user levels) or trade items, assess **DSA** intermediary/online-platform status (notice-and-action, T&Cs, minors' protection, transparency; VLOP if ≥45m EU users) and, in the UK, **Online Safety Act 2023** user-to-user duties enforced by Ofcom [6][10][21]. *(Legal obligation; operations → `ugc-moderation` (planned).)*
- **Monetisation design.** In-game purchases, currencies, battle passes and subscriptions must present **clear pricing** (no drip pricing), honest scarcity/urgency claims, and easy cancellation; dark patterns are prohibited under the DSA, UCPD/Omnibus and DMCCA [6][9][11][12][13]. *(Legal obligation; detail → `consumer-rights-foundations` (planned).)*
- **Loot boxes / paid random items.** UK: **not** within the Gambling Act 2005; comply with **Ukie industry guidance** (no under-18 purchase without parental consent, spending controls, **probability disclosure**) and monitor for any policy change [8][16][17]. EU: treatment **diverges by Member State** (some apply gambling or consumer law to certain mechanics) — flagged for `loot-box-regulation` (planned). Rating: from **June 2026 PEGI rates paid random items PEGI 16+** [18][19]. *(Legal/regulatory — live-verified; assert nothing beyond the sourced positions.)*
- **Age ratings (PEGI).** Ensure submissions reflect the **June 2026 interactive-risk criteria**; games with paid random items, blockchain/NFT items, or unrestricted communications now face higher age bands, which in turn affects marketing, store placement and the Children's-Code "likely to be accessed" analysis [18][19]. *(Industry obligation where PEGI applies; statutory in some states.)*
- **Anti-cheat & account security.** Anti-cheat clients process personal (sometimes device/system) data and must be minimised, disclosed and secured; account-takeover is a leading player-harm vector — enforce strong authentication and abuse monitoring (see Security) [1][23]. *(Legal obligation / best practice.)*
- **In-game AI.** Chatbots and generative content trigger AI Act Art. 50 transparency; most NPC/matchmaking AI is minimal-risk (see AI Considerations) [7]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*

text:
- **Transparency for interactive AI (AI Act Art. 50).** In-game **AI chatbots / conversational NPCs** must disclose to the player that they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from context [7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Synthetic/generative content marking.** Where a game **generates** images, audio, video or text with AI, providers must mark outputs as artificially generated in **machine-readable** form (Art. 50) — relevant to generative asset pipelines and AI-authored content [7]. *(Legal obligation.)*
- **Most game AI is minimal-risk.** NPC behaviour, pathfinding, difficulty scaling, matchmaking and cheat-detection heuristics are generally **minimal-risk** under the AI Act, attracting no mandatory obligations beyond voluntary codes — but confirm none crosses into prohibited practices (e.g. manipulative techniques exploiting children's vulnerabilities) or high-risk use [7] (see `ai-act-foundations`). *(Regulatory interpretation.)*
- **Profiling of children.** AI-driven personalisation/recommendation that profiles children collides with the Children's Code and DSA Art. 28 minors' protections; keep such profiling **off by default** for children [6][14]. *(Legal obligation / interpretation.)*
- **Training-data governance.** Behavioural/telemetry data reused to train models needs a lawful basis and, for device-level collection, valid ePrivacy consent (see `eprivacy-foundations`, `ai-governance-foundations`) [1][4]. *(Legal obligation.)*

text:
Labels: **OBLIGATION** / **BEST PRACTICE** / **EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION**.

1. **Run a "likely to be accessed by children" assessment** for each title and, if positive, implement the Children's Code standards and jurisdiction-aware consent gating (13 UK / 16 EU default). *(OBLIGATION.)* [1][2][14]
2. **Gate all non-essential SDKs behind consent** (analytics, attribution, ads); document strictly-necessary classifications. *(OBLIGATION.)* [4][5]
3. **Map and minimise telemetry/anti-cheat data**, set retention limits, and pseudonymise analytics identifiers. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [1]
4. **Assess DSA / Online Safety Act status** for any UGC, chat or marketplace features; stand up notice-and-action, T&Cs and minors' protections accordingly. *(OBLIGATION.)* [6][10]
5. **Audit monetisation for dark patterns and pricing compliance** (no drip pricing; honest urgency; easy cancellation); align with UCPD/Omnibus and DMCCA. *(OBLIGATION.)* [9][11][12]
6. **For loot boxes/paid random items:** disclose probabilities, block under-18 purchases without parental consent, provide spending controls, and follow Ukie guidance; track any regulatory change. *(OBLIGATION per policy + BEST PRACTICE.)* [16][17]
7. **Refresh PEGI submissions** against the June 2026 interactive-risk criteria and reconcile ratings with marketing and the children's-access analysis. *(OBLIGATION where PEGI applies.)* [18][19]
8. **Add AI transparency** to chatbots and mark AI-generated content; confirm no game AI is prohibited/high-risk. *(OBLIGATION.)* [7]
9. **Harden accounts and infrastructure** (strong auth, anti-cheat data governance, DDoS mitigation, incident response) per `cybersecurity-foundations`. *(OBLIGATION + BEST PRACTICE.)* [20][22][23][24]
10. **Maintain a games-compliance watch-list** for the fast-moving items (loot boxes, PEGI, DMCCA subscriptions, Children's-Code updates). *(EDITORIAL RECOMMENDATION.)*

text:
**Compliance operations** is the discipline of running a compliance programme as a managed system rather than a series of one-off legal responses. Its anchor duty in EU/UK law is **accountability**: GDPR **Article 5(2)** requires a controller not merely to comply with the data-protection principles but to be able to **demonstrate** compliance [1]. The same accountability logic — documented governance, assigned senior responsibility and evidence on demand — now recurs across the digital rulebook: **NIS2 Article 20** makes management bodies approve and oversee cybersecurity risk measures (and undergo training) [2], and **DORA Article 5** makes the management body of a financial entity *ultimately accountable* for ICT risk [3]. A compliance programme is how an organisation satisfies all of these at once.

This document assembles the operating model. Governance and accountability are structured through the **Three Lines Model** (operational management; risk and compliance oversight; independent internal audit) [15], underpinned by a **Compliance Management System (CMS)** — the certifiable **ISO 37301:2021** standard — and a **risk-management framework** built on **ISO 31000:2018** [11][12]. On that spine sit the **core operational artefacts** every regime reuses: records of processing (GDPR **Art. 30**), data protection impact assessments (**Art. 35**), risk registers, policies and procedures, training and awareness, third-party/vendor management (**Art. 28**; DORA Art. 28), and — most time-critical — **incident and breach management** [1][3].

Three conclusions dominate. First, **accountability is a legal obligation, not an option**: the programme itself is the evidence [1][2][3]. Second, **build once, report many**: a single incident can trigger GDPR 72-hour breach notification (Art. 33), NIS2 reporting (Art. 23, 24h/72h/1-month) and DORA major-incident reporting (Art. 19) on *different clocks to different authorities* — so the operating model, not the individual law, is what makes this survivable [1][2][3]. Third, **standards operationalise the duties**: ISO 37301, ISO 31000 and the Three Lines Model are voluntary but load-bearing — the recognised route to systematic, auditable accountability [11][12][15].
